questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A resident had a needle stick injury while dealing with a Hepatitis B positive patient. Serology was done and HBsAg was negative and the Anti-HBs was >105 mIU/ml. What is the next step of management?
options: No treatment required as he already has Hep B antibody titres from vaccination
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. No treatment required as he already has Hep B antibody titres from vaccination

The given clinical scenario of needle-stick injury shows that HBsAg is negative and the anti-HBs is >105 mIU/ml. This suggests that the resident has had routine vaccination for Hep B infection. Since the antibody titers are more than 10 mIU/ml, no treatment is required.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A stool sample is collected. The specimen is processed for examination and is labeled at different levels as A, B, C, and D. Identify the level at which parasitic ova will be seen when viewed under a microscope.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. D

The parasitic ova will be seen in a specimen taken from level D.

The image shows a formol-ether sedimentation technique to concentrate the ova in the bottom (D) part of the tube. It is used for samples in which the concentration of parasitic ova is scanty. It is useful for all helminth ova/eggs and parasitic cysts. The ether adsorbs the fecal debris and floats. Formalin fixes and preserves the specimen.

This method is useful for all helminth eggs and protozoan cysts.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A young male presents to the STD clinic with painful lesions as shown in the image. What is the most likely microscopic finding of the lesion?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Tzank cells

Clusters of vesicles are seen on an erythematous base in the image, suggesting a diagnosis of genital herpes. Tzanck cells or multinucleated giant cells are present on microscopy.

The Tzanck smear is a rapid, sensitive, and inexpensive diagnostic method for herpes simplex infections. Smears are prepared from the lesions, from the base of vesicles and stained with a 1% aqueous solution of O-toluidine blue for 15 seconds. Multinucleated giant cells with faceted nuclei and homogeneously stained ground glass chromatin (Tzanck cells) are seen.

Mucocutaneous herpetic lesions are thin-walled, umbilicated vesicles, the roof of which breaks down, leaving tiny superficial ulcers which heal without scarring.  Painful and pruritic lymphadenopathy may be seen. The most common site of cutaneous lesions is the face - on the cheeks, chin, around the mouth, or on the forehead - and is caused by herpes simplex virus-1. Genital infections are more commonly caused by herpes simplex virus-2.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Affinity maturation is due to:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Somatic hypermutation

Affinity maturation is due to somatic hypermutation.

Affinity maturation is the process by which antibodies gain increased affinity, avidity, and anti-pathogen activity. It is a result of somatic hypermutation (SHM) of immunoglobulin genes in B cells, coupled to selection for antigen binding.

This process occurs in the germinal centers and proceeds for weeks after acute infection or vaccination, or for many cycles during chronic infection. The resulting antibodies can be highly mutated from their germline-encoded counterparts, with increases of several orders of magnitude in affinity for antigen compared to the corresponding naïve B cell receptors (BCRs).

Other options:

Option A: Isotype switching, also known as class switch recombination, is a process where the constant region of the antibody heavy chain is changed, leading to a switch in the antibody isotype (e.g., from IgM to IgG). This process is crucial for the functional properties of antibodies but is not directly involved in affinity maturation.

Option C: mRNA splicing is a cellular process that involves the removal of introns and the joining of exons to generate mature mRNA. While this process is essential for the production of functional antibodies, it is not specifically associated with affinity maturation. Affinity maturation primarily occurs through somatic hypermutation.

Option D: VDJ rearrangement is the process by which the variable regions of immunoglobulin genes are assembled from gene segments (V, D, and J segments). This process contributes to the diversity of antibodies but is distinct from affinity maturation. Affinity maturation occurs after VDJ rearrangement and is driven by somatic hypermutation in the variable regions.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: All of the following is true regarding scrub typhus except:
options: Produces NLF producing colonies in MacConkey agar
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Produces NLF producing colonies in MacConkey agar

The organism causing scrub typhus i.e Orientia tsutsugamushi is non-cultivable on cell-free media like MacConkey agar.

Scrub Typhus is also known as chigger borne typhus. The vector is trombiculid mite. Humans are infected when they are bitten by the mite larvae known as chiggers.

The incubation period is 1- 3 weeks. The patient typically develops a characteristic eschar at the site of the mite bite, with regional lymphadenopathy and maculopapular rash.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: False about the Ebola virus is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Transmitted by mosquito

Ebola virus is not transmitted by mosquito.

Ebola virus is the cause of an emerging disease called Ebola virus disease and is widespread in Africa. It belongs to the Filoviridae family.

Fruit bats act as reservoir hosts of the virus and it is transmitted to humans only accidentally. Human to human transmission is through direct contact with blood or body fluids of an infected symptomatic person.

The incubation period of the disease is 2 to 21 days. Symptoms include fever, intense weakness, vomiting, diarrhea, rashes, and, in extreme cases, internal and external bleeding. The current treatment is mainly supportive. Nosocomial transmission seen.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text:
Galactomannan in serum is seen in:

1. Invasive aspergillosis
2. Systemic candidiasis
3. Mucormycosis
4. Cryptococcosis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1 only

The galactomannan assay is used for the diagnosis of invasive (deep-seated) mycoses caused by Aspergillus species.

Galactomannan is a component of the cell wall of Aspergillus. It can be detected in serum or bronchoalveolar lavage by ELISA for the diagnosis of invasive aspergillosis in adults and children. This test is especially useful in hematopoietic stem cell transplant recipients or patients with hematologic malignancies. Invasive aspergillosis affects the lungs and presents with fever, cough, dyspnea, and hemoptysis. The organism may spread to the eye, gastrointestinal tract, kidney, liver or brain, leading to abscesses and necrotic lesions.

Other diagnostic features of invasive aspergillosis are:

• Positive culture from the affected organ
• Microscopy showing narrow, septate hyphae with branching at 45o and conidiophores
• Halo sign on CT scan

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: GeneXpert detects mutations in which of the following genes?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. rpoB

Gene Xpert identifies mutations in the rpoB gene to detect rifampicin resistance (RR).

Other options:

inhA and KatG- involved in resistance against isoniazid

pncA- involved in resistance against pyrazinamide

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Identify the condenser _____
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. B

Condensor lens of microscope is marked as B in the image. The purpose of the condenser lens is to focus the light onto the specimen.

A is coarse focusing knob.

C is objective lens. There are usually 3 or 4 objective lenses on a microscope. They almost always consist of 4X, 10X, 40X and 100X powers.

D is Illuminator. It is a steady light source used in place of a mirror.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Identify the organism shown in this image.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Ascaris lumbricoides

The given image shows large cylindrical worms with tapering ends, and thus represents Ascaris lumbricoides (roundworm).

Ascaris lumbricoides is the most common of human helminths and is distributed worldwide. It is the largest nematode parasite in the human intestine. The adult worms are large cylindrical worms, with tapering ends. The anterior end is more pointed than the posterior. It appears white outside the body.

Its natural host is humans. There is no intermediate host. Adult worms live in the small intestine - jejunum and ileum. Humans acquire infectionby consuming food or water contaminated with nightsoil or human feces containing eggs. The eggs contain the infective rhabditiform larva.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text:
In which of the following situations will you use a sanitizer?

A. Before examining the patient
B. After examining the patient
C. After touching the patient's surroundings
D. Hands are visibly soiled
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. A, B & C only

You should use a sanitiser before and after examining the patient and after touching the patients' surroundings. The hands should be washed with soap and water thoroughly in case they are visibly soiled.

Sanitization is the process through which pathogenic organisms are reduced to safe levels on inanimate objects to reduce the likelihood of cross-infections. It is a component of hand-hygiene, which is demonstrated by the image below.

Note: Disinfectants like chlorhexidine and alexidine have a biguanide functional group. They are mostly used as oral disinfectants and hand products. They are bactericidal but not sporicidal. Mycobacteria are also resistant to these compounds.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text:
Match the following E.coli with their respective pathogenesis.

E. coli
Mechanism of action

1. ETEC
A. Produces a heat-stable toxin and causes activation of guanylyl cyclase

2. EIEC
B. Invades intestinal mucosal cells

3. EHEC
C. Produces a toxin against vascular endothelium cells

4. EPEC
D. Adheres to the mucosal surface and causes effacement of microvilli
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. A-1,B-2,C-3,D-4

The correctly matched pairs are as follows:

E. coli
Mechanism of action

1. ETEC
A. Produce a heat-stable toxin and cause activation of guanylyl cyclase

2. EIEC
B. Invades intestinal mucosal cells

3. EHEC
C. Produces a toxin against vascular endothelium cells

4. EPEC
D. Adhere to the mucosal surface and cause effacement of microvilli

The various strains of Escherichia coli are:

• Enterotoxigenic E. coli (ETEC) is the most common organism that causes diarrhea in travelers. It produces the following toxins:

• LT (heat-labile toxin)- acts by ↑cAMP
• ST (heat-stable toxin)- two types of ST are known, ST-A (ST-I) and ST-B (ST-II)

• ST-A is soluble in methanol and acts by ↑cGMP in the intestine.
• ST-B is insoluble in methanol, and the mode of action is not known.

• Enteroinvasive E. coli (EIEC) invade interstitial epithelial cells in the intestine and cause a condition resembling shigellosis. This ability is determined by a plasmid, detection of which can also be a diagnostic test. Sereny's test was employed to diagnose EIEC but it is not in use anymore.
• Enterohemorrhagic E. coli (EHEC) produces verocytotoxin, which targets vascular endothelium. It causes hemorrhagic colitis and hemolytic uremic syndrome.
• Enteropathogenic E. coli (EPEC) causes infantile diarrhea in developing countries. It adheres to the mucosal surface of small intestine using EAF and LEE and causes effacement of microvilli. This leads to attachment and effacement lesions of intestinal cells.
• Enteroaggregative E. coli (EAEC) produces the stacked brick pattern of adherence on hep-2 cells. EAEC has been associated with persistent diarrhea. Intestinal colonization of EAEC is mediated by AAF (aggregative adherence fimbriae). EAEC produces EAST-1 toxin (enteroaggregative heat-stable toxin) which is considered to be a major virulence factor.

Match the following:

Parasite

1. Flagella

Correct answer: B. A-3, B-2, C-1, D-4

Parasite

Pseudopod

Balantidium coli
Cilia

Flagella

No Particular organ

Identification features of Trichomonas vaginalis:

• Pear-shaped or ovoid
• Short undulating membrane reaching upto the middle of the body
• It has four anterior flagella and fifth running along the outer margin of the undulating membrane, which is supported at its base by a flexible rod, costa
• A prominent axostyle runs throughout the length of the body and projects posteriorly like a tail
• The cytoplasm shows prominent siderophillic granules, which are most numerous alongside the axostyle and costa
• Jerky or twitching type of mobility

The above image shows Trichomonas vaginalis : 1-anterior flagella, 2-kinetosomes, 3-parabasal body, 4-costa, 5-parabasal fibers, 6-undulating membrane, 7-posterior flagellum, 8-hydrogenosomes, 9-axostyle, 10-nucleus, 11-pelta.

Obligate parasite - Organism cannot survive outside host

• No cystic stage. Trophozoites are infective forms
• Sexual transmission is the main route of infection. Other modes are fomites, babies during passage through infected birth canal
• Affects squamous epithelium - Intracellular edema and so called chicken-like epithelium, is the most characteristic feature of trichomoniasis
• Habitat: Vagina and cervix in female and urethra in males
• Clinical features: Often asymptomatic in males. In females, it leads to pruritic vaginitis with greenish yellow discharge, strawberry mucosa and dysuria
• Diagnosis: By wet mount microscopy of vaginal or urethral discharge, Culture (gold standard - Cysteine-peptone-liver-maltose (CPLM) medium and plastic envelope medium (PEM)), PCR, and by demonstration of antigen in vaginal smear by ELISA
• Treatment: Metronidazole is the drug of choice and simultaneous treatment of both partners is recommended

The given image is the trophozoite form of the Balantidium coli.

Balantidium coli occurs in two stages

• Trophozoites are oval in shape and contain two nuclei. There is the presence of cilia over the entire surface and are larger around the mouth. Its anterior end is narrow and the posterior end is broad.  At the anterior end, there is a groove leading to the mouth (cytostome). Posteriorly, there is a small anal pore (cytopyge).
• Cysts are smaller, round with a micronucleus, a macronucleus and many contractile vacuoles.

Living trophozoites/cysts are yellowish or greenish in color on wet mount.

The image given above shows Toxoplasma gondii which has two types of life cycles:

• Enteric cycle
• Exoenteric cycle

The enteric cycle occurs in definitive hosts such as cats. Exoenteric cycle occurs in intermediate hosts such as humans, mice, rats, etc.

Both sexual reproduction (gametogony) and asexual reproduction (schizogony) occur within the mucosal epithelial cells of the small intestine of the cat.

Sporozoites from the oocysts and bradyzoites from the tissue cysts enter the intestinal mucosa and multiply asexually. Tachyzoites are formed within the intermediate host.

Tachyzoites continue to multiply and spread locally by lymphatic system and blood, while the bradyzoites multiply slowly inside the tissue cyst.

The dormant bradyzoites inside the cyst may be reactivated in immune suppression causing renewed infection in the host.

Images b-1 and b-3 showing the Trophozoite and Cystic form of Balamuthia mandrillaris in Salmonella Shigella (SS) Agar respectively.

Balamuthia Mandrillaris

B. mandrillaris is a free-living ameba, which is a newly identified species reported to cause granulomatous amebic encephalitis (GAE).

Morphology
It exists in ameboid trophozoite stage. The flagellate stage is absent

• It is relatively large (12-60 μm), irregular in shape and actively motile by broad pseudopodia.
• Cyst of B. mandrillaris are usually spherical (6-20 μm), surrounded by a three-layered cyst wall: (1) outer irregular ectocyst, (2) a middle mesocyst and (3) an inner endocyst round wall. Under light microscopy, it appears to have two walls: (1) an outer irregular wall and (2) an inner smooth wall.
• Infection is transmitled through respiratory tract, skin lesions, or eyes.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Pneumonia due to a gram-negative pleomorphic bacillus growing on chocolate agar which is catalase and oxidase-positive is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Haemophilus influenzae

Pneumonia due to a gram-negative pleomorphic bacillus growing on chocolate agar which is catalase and oxidase-positive is most likely Haemophilus influenza.

Haemophilus pneumonia typically occurs in infants and is accompanied by empyema and sometimes meningitis as well. In older children and adults, the picture is of lobar pneumonia. Sputum is collected for the detection and isolation of Hemophilus. As the bacillus is very sensitive to low temperatures, specimens should never be refrigerated before inoculation. H.infiuenzae is a Gram-negative, non-motile, non-sporing bacillus, exhibiting considerable pleomorphism. In sputum, it usually occurs as clusters of coccobacillary forms.

The bacillus has fastidious growth requirements. The accessory growth factors, named X and V, present in the blood are essential for growth. Catalase and
oxidase reactions are positive. Nitrates are reduced to nitrites. Biotyping has been done on the basis of indole production.

Cultures may be preserved for about a month on chocolate agar slopes. Chocolate agar is made by heating blood agar to 80-90°C for 15-20 minutes. This causes the release of V factor from within the erythrocytes.

Treatment- Amoxycillin-clavulanate or clarithromycin is more effective in treating respiratory infections by Haemophilus influenzae.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Specimen handling for molecular testing of SARS CoV 2 would require
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. BSL2

Specimen handling for molecular testing of SARS CoV 2 would require BSL-2 or equivalent facilities. Attempts to culture the virus requires minimum BSL-3 facilities.

SARS CoV 2 virus can cause coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19)

Microbiology and pathology laboratories performing diagnostic tests on a stool or respiratory specimen should handle potential SARS-CoV specimens using standard biosafety level (BSL)-2.

Note: Biosafety levels include a specific combination of work practices, safety equipment, and facilities that are designed to minimize the exposure of workers and the environment to infectious agents. There are four biosafety levels.

BSL-1: Work can be done on an open bench or table and PPE needed. Eg: Non-pathogenic E.coli.

BSL-2: Work to be done in the biosafety cabinet with PPE. Eg: Staphylococcus aureus.

BSL-3 laboratory has appropriate PPE and respirators might be required. All work performed within BSC(biosafety cabinet). Entrance is through 2 sets of self-closing and locking doors. Eg: when dealing with Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

BSL-4: This is the highest level of biological safety, where containment of microbes is done, which are fatal without treatment and vaccines. Eg: Ebola and Marburg viruses.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: The disruption of which of the following is responsible for watery diarrhea in cholera caused by Vibrio?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Zonula occludens

The disruption of zonula occludens is responsible for watery diarrhea in cholera caused by Vibrio cholerae.

Zonula occludens toxin (Zot) is an enterotoxin elaborated by Vibrio cholerae that increases intestinal permeability by interacting with a mammalian cell receptor with subsequent activation of intracellular signaling leading to the disassembly of the intercellular tight junctions.

Mechanism of action of cholera toxin:

• The cholera toxin molecule consists of 1 A and 5 B subunits. The B (binding) units attach to the GM1 ganglioside receptors on the surface of jejunal epithelial cells. The A (active) subunit, on being transported into the enterocyte, dissociates into A1 and A2. A2 fragment only links biologically active A1 to the B subunit.
• A1 causes prolonged activation of cellular adenylate cyclase and accumulation of cAMP, leading to outpouring into the small intestinal lumen, of large quantities of water and electrolytes. This leads to watery diarrhea which is isotonic with plasma but contains much more potassium and bicarbonate.
• The toxin also inhibits the intestinal absorption of sodium and chloride.
• All clinical manifestations and complications in cholera result from the massive water and electrolyte depletion thus caused.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text:
The following are true about chancroid:

A. School of fish appearance
B. Bleeds on touch
C. Painful
D. Groove sign
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. A B & C

Chancroid is a painful genital ulcer caused by Haemophilus ducreyi, which is a gram-negative coccobacillus. Microscopic appearance of H. ducreyi is called the school of fish appearance or railroad appearance. Chancroid ulcers have a soft base that bleeds easily to touch. They also cause painful lymphadenopathy.

The image below shows the 'school-of-fish' appearance characteristic of H. ducreyi.

Note: Groove sign is a characteristic sign seen in lymphogranuloma venereum. It refers to the depression created by the inguinal ligament as it passes between the groups of inflamed inguinal lymph nodes.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: The given life cycle belongs to which of the following organisms?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Leptospira

The life cycle shown in the above image is suggestive of leptospirosis.

It is caused by contact with the urine or blood of an infected organism. It is a zoonotic disease, with rats being the most well-known reservoirs.

Illness is classically biphasic after an incubation period of up to 1 month. The stages are:

• Acute leptospiremic phase- organism can be cultured from blood.
• Resolving immune phase- organism can be cultured from urine.

The stages may not be clinically distinguishable.

Most cases are asymptomatic but a few may present with severe manifestations. Clinical features include:

• High-grade fever
• Hepatic dysfunction
• Renal impairment
• Hemorrhages- gastrointestinal, pulmonary (most common), petechiae and purpura

The severe form is known as Weil's disease, with a triad of hemorrhage, jaundice, and acute kidney injury.

Treatment of choice is IV penicillin or IV ceftriaxone.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: The life cycle of an organism is given below. Identify the vector involved.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Trombiculid mite

The given life cycle is of trombiculid mite which acts as a vector for scrub typhus. Humans are seen to be infected when they are bitten by the mite larvae (chiggers).

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: The presence of antibodies against SARS CoV 2 in the blood likely indicates
options: Previous infection even if patient has been asymptomatic
That the patient is in window period
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Previous infection even if patient has been asymptomatic

The presence of antibodies against SARS CoV 2 in the blood likely indicates a previous infection even if the patient has been asymptomatic.

Antibodies most commonly become detectable 1–3 weeks after symptom onset, at which time evidence suggests that infectiousness likely is greatly decreased and that some degree of immunity from future infection has developed. But it is imperative to note that the information on SARS CoV 2 is still emerging.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: The transplacental transmission of the organism given in the image which causes microcephaly is-
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Zika virus

The image shows transplacental transmission of a virus, leading to microcephaly, with the Aedes mosquito as its vector. Among the given options, Zika virus has the above features.

Zika virus is a mosquito-borne Flavivirus mainly transmitted through Aedes aegypti. Zika virus infection presents with mild symptoms of fever, rash, conjunctivitis, malaise, headache and muscle and joint pain. These symptoms usually last for 2-7 days. Maternal infection during pregnancy leads to congenital Zika syndrome or microcephaly.

The complications of Zika virus infection include Guillain-Barré syndrome, neuropathy, and myelitis.

Note: NCDC Delhi and the National Institute of Virology Pune are the only institutes that have the capacity to provide the diagnosis in an acute febrile stage. RT-PCR is the standard test available for the diagnosis of Zika virus infection.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Type IV hypersensitivity is due to?
options: Cell mediated and antibody mediated response
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Cell mediated response

Type IV hypersensitivity is due to the cell-mediated response.

Type IV or cell-mediated hypersensitivity reaction: These reactions are induced by sensitized T cells which on contact with the specific antigen releases cytokines that produce biological effects on leucocytes, macrophages, and tissue cells.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: What is the causative organism for the condition shown in the image below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Echinococcus granulosus

The given image shows a hydatid cyst in the liver. It is caused by Echinococcus granulosus.

Echinococcus granulosus is the most common causative agent in hydatid cysts, while Echinococcus multilocularis and Echinococcus ligartus account for a small number of cases.

Dogs are the definitive hosts of E. granulosus. Sheep are the usual intermediate hosts, but humans are accidental intermediate hosts. Humans are end-stage hosts of the parasite since there is no human to human transmission.

Approximately 75% of hydatid cysts are located in the right lobe of the liver and are solitary. The clinical presentation of a hydatid cyst is largely asymptomatic until complications occur. The most common presenting symptoms are abdominal pain, dyspepsia, and vomiting. The most frequent sign is hepatomegaly.

The life cycle of Echinococcus is depicted in the image below:

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following disease has the highest mortality once clinically manifested?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Rabies

Rabies has the highest mortality once clinically presented.

Rabies is a vaccine-preventable, zoonotic, viral disease of the central nervous system. Rabies virus is a bullet-shaped rhabdovirus containing ssRNA. It spreads to humans by bites or contact with the saliva of rabid animals (bats, dogs, cats). Once clinical symptoms appear, rabies is virtually 100% fatal. The disease can be divided into 3 phases:

1. Prodromal phase: It lasts 2-10 days. Patients present with malaise, headache, photophobia, vomiting, and fever.  They may also have parasthesias, pain or pruritus near the site of exposure.
2. Acute neurologic phase: It lasts 2-7 days. In the more common encephalitic rabies, Hydrophobia (fear of water) or aerophobia (fear of breeze) can be seen. Swallowing liquids precipitates painful spasms of the throat muscles. Patients may also have nervousness, hallucinations, excessive lacrimation, salivation, perspiration and pupillary dilation. Convulsive seizures may occur
3. Coma and death (due to cardiorespiratory arrest)

In about 20% of patients, paralytic rabies is seen. Flaccid muscle weakness is seen, which progresses to quadriparesis and facial palsy.

Note: In rabid animals, the virus depicts two modes of spread:

• Centripetal spread: The virus enters the peripheral neurons. It moves via retrograde fast axonal transport towards the spinal cord or brainstem a.k.a the central nervous system (CNS) at a speed of up to 250 mm/day. Once within the CNS, it spreads quickly to other regions in the CNS through fast axonal transport. It infects neurons primarily, but may rarely infect astrocytes.
• Centrifugal spread: After CNS infection is established, it spreads along the sensory and autonomic nerves to salivary glands, adrenal glands, skin

Rabies virus replicates in acinar cells of the salivary glands and is secreted in the saliva of rabid animals that serve as vectors.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following is the enzyme conjugate in the given ELISA technique?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. B

The enzyme conjugate in the given ELISA technique is 'B'.

Other options:

A- Substrate - it will be cleaved by the enzyme present on the conjugate antibody.

B - Conjugate - it is an antibody that binds to the detection antibody. It is labeled with an enzyme that cleaves the substrate to form a color product/dye.

C - Detection antibody-binds the antigen. We direct our conjugate against this.

D - Capture Antibody-forms the base, on which antigen (say rotavirus from feces) from the patient sample binds.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following method is employed to measure the viral load?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Real time PCR

Viral load can be measured by the real time-PCR technique.

Real time-PCR assays are commonly used for viral load quantification of HIV, hepatitis C virus, hepatitis B virus, and CMV.

Other options:

• Western blotting is used for the detection of protein.
• ELISA is an immunosorbent assay used to detect antigens of infectious agents present in clinical specimens.
• Immuno electrophoresis includes electrophoretic separation of antigens followed by an antigen-antibody reaction.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which protein is present in the HPV vaccine?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. L1

The HPV vaccines use virus-like particles (VLPs) that consist of the HPV L1 major capsid protein. The L1 protein self-assembles into VLPs when expressed in eukaryotic cells.

These VLPs contain the same epitopes as the HPV virion. But they do not contain genetic material and cannot transmit infection. The immunogenicity of the HPV vaccines relies on the development of conformational neutralizing antibodies to epitopes displayed on viral capsids.

The nonavalent HPV vaccine works against strains 6,11,16,18,31,33,45,52 and 58. It is usually commercialized in the name of Gardasil 9.

HPV VACCINE
HPV TYPES COVERED

Quadrivalent

6, 11,

16, 18

Bivalent
16, 18

Nonavalent
6, 11, 16, 18, 31, 33, 45, 52, 58

Recent update: Gardasil 9 has received expanded indication which now includes the prevention of oropharyngeal and other head and neck cancers caused by HPV types 16,18,31,33,45,52,58.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: 22-year-old student comes to the physician complaining of 4 days of fever, double vision, and painful swelling around his eyes. He also has significant muscle pain in his neck and jaw muscles. Two weeks ago the patient returned from a trip to Goa. One week after his return, he developed abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea . These symptoms resolved spontaneously. He has a history of intravenous drug abuse but recently completed a drug rehabilitation program. His temperature is 38.3°C (101°F), blood pressure is 110/70 mmHg, pulse is 92/min, and respirations are 14/min. Physical examination shows subungual splinter hemorrhages, periorbital edema, and chemosis. Lungs are clear to auscultation. Cardiac examination shows no murmurs. The abdomen is soft and nontender without organomegaly. Laboratory results are as follows: Mean corpuscular volume: 13.0 g/dL Platelets: 228,000/mm³ Leukocytes: 10,500/mm³ Neutrophils: 56% Eosinophils: 22% Lymphocytes: 23% Creatine kinase: 220 U/L Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Trichinellosis

Trichinellosis is a parasitic infection caused by ingestion of undercooked pork or wild game containing Trichinella larvae. The disease typically occurs in two phases:

1.

Intestinal phase (≈1 week after ingestion)

2.

Abdominal pain

3. Nausea, vomiting
4.

Diarrhea

5.

Muscle invasion phase (1–3 weeks later)

Larvae migrate to skeletal muscle, producing:

6.

Fever

7. Severe myalgia (especially jaw, neck, and extraocular muscles)
8. Periorbital edema and chemosis (very characteristic finding)
9. Eosinophilia
10. Elevated creatine kinase (CK) due to muscle inflammation
11. Possible splinter hemorrhages

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: 26-year-old woman comes to the office due to a flulike illness with low-grade fever, malaise, nausea, and anorexia. The patient has no significant medical history and takes no medications. She occasionally smokes marijuana and has used injection drugs in the past. She has had several sexual partners. Temperature is 37.9°C (100.2°F), blood pressure is 121/78 mmHg, and pulse is 86/min. The patient has scleral icterus. Cardiopulmonary examination is unremarkable. Laboratory results are as follows: • Total bilirubin - 44.8 mg/dL • Aspartate aminotransferase - 11,222 U/L • Alanine aminotransferase - 21,184 U/L • Hepatitis B surface antibody - positive • Hepatitis B core antibody - positive • Hepatitis B surface antigen - negative • Hepatitis A IgM antibody - positive • Hepatitis A lgG antibody - negative • Hepatitis C antibody - negative After discussing the findings, the patient says she is worried that she may transmit the disease to her boyfriend. Which of the following interventions for the boyfriend is most likely to decrease his risk of disease acquisition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hepatitis A vaccination

Acute hepatitis A infection is indicated by positive anti-HAV IgM and negative IgG. Hepatitis A is transmitted via the fecal–oral route, including close household or sexual contact.

Post-exposure prophylaxis for close contacts is Hepatitis A vaccination, which stimulates active immunity and reduces the risk of disease acquisition.

Why not other options:

A. Barrier contraceptive use: Hepatitis A spreads mainly by the fecal–oral route, not primarily through sexual fluids; condoms alone do not adequately prevent transmission.

C. Hepatitis B immune globulin: Used for post-exposure prophylaxis of Hepatitis B, not Hepatitis A.

D. Hepatitis B vaccination: Prevents Hepatitis B infection, but this patient has acute Hepatitis A.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: 40-year-old man with chronic cough and weight loss is diagnosed with pulmonary tuberculosis. Histopathology of lung biopsy shows granulomas with central caseous necrosis. The organism survives within macrophages by inhibiting phagolysosome fusion. Which of the following components of Mycobacterium tuberculosis is primarily responsible for this property?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Sulfatides

Mycobacterium tuberculosis is an intracellular pathogen that survives and replicates within macrophages by evading host killing mechanisms.

Key virulence–function correlations:

• Sulfatides → inhibit phagosome–lysosome fusion → allow intracellular survival
• Cord factor (trehalose dimycolate) → induces granuloma formation and TNF-α release
• Mycolic acids → confer acid-fastness and resistance to desiccation/chemicals
• Lipoarabinomannan (LAM) → modulates macrophage response

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 10-year-old boy is brought to the physician with ataxia, myoclonus, and visual problems. His parents say that he began acting strangely and having difficulty with school work several months ago. After the appropriate workup, a brain biopsy is obtained and an RNA virus containing hemagglutinin is cultured from the tissue sample. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis

Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE) is a progressive neurodegenerative disease of childhood caused by persistent infection with a mutant measles virus (an RNA virus with hemagglutinin).

It typically presents years after measles infection with:

• Behavioral and cognitive decline
• Myoclonus
• Ataxia
• Visual disturbances
• Progressive neurological deterioration

Why not other options:

A. Guillain-Barré syndrome: Acute peripheral neuropathy causing ascending weakness and areflexia; no chronic cognitive decline or myoclonus.

B. Multiple sclerosis: Autoimmune demyelinating disease of CNS in young adults; not caused by an RNA virus.

C. Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy: Caused by JC virus (DNA virus) in immunocompromised patients; no hemagglutinin-containing RNA virus.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 12-year-old child in an endemic region is scheduled to receive the Dengvaxia vaccine. The pediatrician explains that this vaccine is a live recombinant chimeric vaccine in which the structural genes of dengue virus are inserted into the backbone of another attenuated virus strain. Which viral strain is used as the backbone for the Dengvaxia vaccine?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Yellow fever 17D strain

Dengvaxia (CYD-TDV) is a live attenuated recombinant chimeric dengue vaccine.

Vaccine design:

•

The structural genes (prM and E proteins) of the four dengue virus serotypes (DENV 1–4) are inserted into the genetic backbone of the attenuated Yellow fever 17D virus.

•

This creates a chimeric virus that stimulates immunity against dengue.

Key features:

• Provides immunity against all four dengue serotypes.
• Recommended mainly for individuals with prior dengue infection in endemic areas

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 13-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his mother because of a 6-hour history of severe eye pain and blurry vision. He wears soft contact lenses and has not removed them for 2 days. Ophthalmologic examination shows a deep corneal ulcer, severe conjunctival injection, and purulent discharge on the right. Treatment with topical ciprofloxacin is initiated. A culture of the ocular discharge is most likely to show which of the following?
options: Gram-negative spiral bacteria visible on dark-field microscopy
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Gram-negative, oxidase-positive bacilli

Contact lens–associated keratitis is most commonly caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa, especially when lenses are worn for prolonged periods. Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a gram-negative, oxidase-positive bacillus that can rapidly cause corneal ulcers, severe pain, purulent discharge, and vision impairment.

Why not other options:

B. Gram-positive, coagulase-positive cocci: Staphylococcus aureus; causes skin infections and some keratitis but not classically linked to contact lens–associated ulcers.

C. Gram-negative spiral bacteria on dark-field microscopy: Treponema pallidum; causes syphilis, not acute purulent corneal ulcer.

D. Gram-positive, bacitracin-sensitive cocci: Streptococcus pyogenes; causes pharyngitis and skin infections, not typical contact lens keratitis.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 19-year-old man comes to the OPD due to a week of persistent dry cough that disturbs his sleep. He has also had a sore throat, headaches, and fatigue. Yesterday, he noticed a rash on his arms and legs. Temperature is 37.8⁰C (100⁰F), blood pressure is 115/78 mmHg, pulse is 86/min, and respirations are 16/min. Mild pharyngeal erythema is present. There is no cervical lymphadenopathy. A faint macular rash is present on the extremities. Chest x-ray reveals increased interstitial markings and a small right-sided pleural effusion. Which of the following organisms is most likely causing this patient's condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Mycoplasma pneumoniae

Mycoplasma pneumoniae causes atypical pneumonia in adolescents and young adults, characterized by persistent dry cough, mild fever, interstitial infiltrates on chest X-ray, and extrapulmonary manifestations such as maculopapular rash or hemolytic anemia. It lacks a cell wall and commonly causes “walking pneumonia.”

Why not other options:

A. Epstein-Barr virus: Infectious mononucleosis → lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly.

B. S. pneumoniae: Typical pneumonia → productive cough, lobar consolidation.

C. Legionella: Severe pneumonia with diarrhea, hyponatremia.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 19-year-old woman with cystic fibrosis presents with fever, productive cough, and worsening dyspnea. Sputum culture grows an oxidase-positive, gram-negative bacillus producing a blue-green pigment. Which of the following statements is correct regarding the exotoxin produced by this organism?
options: The exotoxin activates adenylate cyclase via ADP-ribosylation of a Gs protein, similar to cholera toxin, producing the diarrheal symptoms seen in this condition
The exotoxin inhibits elongation factor-2 (EF-2) via ADP-ribosylation, halting host protein synthesis
The exotoxin inhibits Rho-GTPase, disrupting the actin cytoskeleton and causing colonic epithelial cell death, similar to C. difficile toxins A and B
The exotoxin blocks release of the inhibitory neurotransmitters GABA and glycine at spinal inhibitory synapses, producing the muscular rigidity seen in this infection
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. The exotoxin inhibits elongation factor-2 (EF-2) via ADP-ribosylation, halting host protein synthesis

| Feature | Description |

| ------- | ----------- | ---

| Organism | Pseudomonas aeruginosa (oxidase-positive, gram-negative bacillus, blue-green pyocyanin pigment; classic cause of pneumonia in cystic fibrosis)

| Toxin | Exotoxin A

| Mechanism | ADP-ribosylation of EF-2 → inhibition of protein synthesis — mechanistically identical to diphtheria toxin (C. diphtheriae), despite arising from an entirely different organism and causing a different disease (CF pneumonia/contact lens keratitis vs. pharyngeal diphtheria)

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 21-year-old man, known case of HIV AIDS, comes to the OPD due to fever, malaise, myalgia, and nonproductive cough. Temperature is 38.3°C (100.9°F), blood pressure is 120/70 mmHg, pulse is 96/min, and respirations are 16/min. Physical examination reveals lung crackles. Chest x-ray shows patchy parenchymal infiltrates with enlarged mediastinal and hilar lymph nodes. Which of the following is most likely to be present in this patient's pulmonary lesions?
options: Budding yeasts with a thick capsule
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Macrophages with intracellular small yeasts

Histoplasma capsulatum infection is common in immunocompromised patients (e.g., AIDS) and causes pulmonary infection with fever, cough, and mediastinal/hilar lymphadenopathy.

The organism is a dimorphic fungus that appears in tissue as small intracellular yeasts within macrophages.

Why not other options:

A. Budding yeasts with a thick capsule: Seen in Cryptococcus neoformans, which causes meningitis in AIDS.

C. Round spherules with multiple endospores: Seen in Coccidioides immitis.

D. Septate hyphae with dichotomous branching: Seen in Aspergillus species.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 22-year-old man comes with complaints of intermittent bloody diarrhea for 3 weeks after consuming street food during his travel. He is febrile and has RUQ tenderness. Which of the following is the infective form of the likely protozoan causing this disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Mature quadrinucleate cyst

Entamoeba histolytica is transmitted through the fecal–oral route by ingestion of mature cysts in contaminated food or water, commonly from street food or poor sanitation.

Key life-cycle forms:

•

Mature quadrinucleate cyst

o    Infective stage

o    Resistant to gastric acid

o    Transmitted via contaminated food or water

•

Trophozoite

o    Invasive and pathogenic form

o    Causes amoebic dysentery and may spread via the portal circulation to produce liver abscess (explaining RUQ tenderness)

•

Precyst

o    Transitional stage during encystation

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 22-year-old man with 2 days of fever, cough, sore throat, and runny nose comes to the OPD. Lung sounds are clear to auscultation. A nasopharyngeal swab is obtained. Naked viral particles are seen, and purified RNA molecules are extracted from these particles. Once introduced into human cells, the purified RNA molecules induce viral protein synthesis and viral genome replication. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Rhinovirus

Rhinovirus is the most common cause of the common cold, presenting with fever, sore throat, cough, and rhinorrhea with usually normal lung examination.

Rhinovirus is a non-enveloped (naked), positive-sense single-stranded RNA virus. Its RNA acts directly as mRNA, so when introduced into host cells it can immediately initiate viral protein synthesis and genome replication.

Why not other options:

A. HIV: Enveloped retrovirus with two copies of +ssRNA that requires reverse transcriptase to form DNA before protein synthesis.

B. Influenza virus type A: Enveloped, negative-sense RNA virus; its RNA cannot directly act as mRNA and requires viral RNA polymerase.

C. Respiratory syncytial virus: Enveloped, negative-sense RNA virus; RNA must first be transcribed to mRNA.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 22-year-old woman presents with fever, rash, lymphadenopathy 2 weeks after high-risk sexual exposure. HIV ELISA antibody test is non-reactive. Which test is most likely to detect infection at this stage?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. p24 antigen

During acute HIV infection (2–4 weeks after exposure), patients may develop fever, rash, lymphadenopathy, and flu-like symptoms, but HIV antibodies may not yet be detectable due to the window period.

• p24 antigen appears earlier than antibodies in the blood and can detect infection during this early phase.
• ELISA antibody and Western blot become positive later (after seroconversion).
• CD4 count is not used for early diagnosis.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 24-year-old male from Bihar presents with prolonged low-grade fever, significant weight loss, and progressive abdominal distension over 3 months. Examination reveals splenomegaly, pallor, and skin hyperpigmentation around the mouth. Laboratory work-up shows pancytopenia. For confirmation of diagnosis, which of the following is the most appropriate test?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Bone marrow aspirate microscopy

This question tests identification and confirmatory diagnosis of visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar).

• Endemic area: Bihar
• Prolonged fever + weight loss
• Massive splenomegaly
• Pancytopenia
• Skin hyperpigmentation (“kala-azar”)

Core concept: Definitive diagnosis = demonstration of amastigotes (LD bodies) in tissue

Best confirmatory test: Bone marrow aspirate microscopy which Shows intracellular Leishmania donovani bodies

Other options (why incorrect):

• rK39 test → screening test (not confirmatory)
• Aldehyde test (Napier) → outdated, nonspecific
• Montenegro test → negative in active visceral disease (used in cutaneous form)

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 24-year-old male presents to the outpatient clinic with fever, sore throat, rash, and generalized lymphadenopathy 10 days after unprotected sexual exposure. Acute retroviral syndrome is suspected. The clinician wants to make an early diagnosis before seroconversion occurs. Which test should be ordered first to identify HIV infection at this stage?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. HIV RNA PCR (NAT)

During acute HIV infection (acute retroviral syndrome), symptoms such as fever, sore throat, rash, and lymphadenopathy occur before seroconversion, when HIV antibodies are not yet detectable.

Earliest detectable marker:

• HIV RNA by PCR (Nucleic Acid Test – NAT) detects viral RNA within \~7–10 days after infection, making it the most sensitive test during the window period.

Sequence of HIV markers after infection:

1.  HIV RNA (PCR/NAT) – earliest detection

2.  p24 antigen

3.  HIV antibodies (ELISA/Western blot)

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 25-year-old male went for trekking, came with a history of rash. Weil Felix test revealed elevated Ox 2 and Ox 19 titers. What is the most likely organism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Rickettsia Rickettsiae

The Weil–Felix test is a heterophile agglutination test that detects antibodies produced against Rickettsial infections by their cross-reaction with Proteus O antigens.

Key interpretation pattern:

| Weil–Felix antigen | Associated disease

| ------------------ | ------------------

| OX-2 and OX-19 positive | Spotted fever group rickettsiae

| OX-19 positive only | Typhus group rickettsiae

| OX-K positive | Scrub typhus

OX-2 and OX-19 titers elevated → indicates spotted fever group. The most common organism in this group is Rickettsia rickettsii, which causes Rocky Mountain spotted fever.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 25-year-old man presents with tingling of lips and mouth, nausea, and flushing. He gives a history of eating a Mahi-Mahi fish about an hour back and that it had an unusual taste. He responds well to treatment with intravenous antihistamines. Which of the following is not true?
options: Epinephrine may be used in refractory cases
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Due to sea food allergy

•

Scombroid fish poisoning occurs after ingestion of improperly stored fish such as tuna or mahi-mahi that contain high levels of histamine produced by bacterial decarboxylation of histidine.

•

It presents with flushing, oral tingling, headache, nausea, and a peppery or unusual taste shortly after ingestion.

•

Symptoms mimic an allergic reaction but are due to histamine toxicity rather than a true seafood allergy.

•

Treatment is with antihistamines.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 25-year-old woman from a tropical region presents with a brown, macular lesion on the palm of her hand. There is no itching or scaling. Microscopic examination of skin scrapings reveals brownish, branched, septate hyphae along with budding cells. What is the most likely causative agent?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Exophiala werneckii

Tinea nigra is a superficial fungal infection characterized by brown-to-black macular patches, usually on the palms or soles, without itching or scaling.

Causative organism: Exophiala (Hortaea) werneckii, a dematiaceous (pigmented) fungus.

• Brown, septate, branched hyphae
• Budding yeast-like cells
• Pigmentation due to melanin in the fungal cell wall
• Infection is superficial and benign.
• Treated effectively with topical antifungals or keratolytic agents.

Why not other options:

A. Malassezia furfur: Causes pityriasis versicolor → hypopigmented/hyperpigmented scaly patches on trunk, not palm macules.

C. Trichophyton rubrum: Dermatophyte causing tinea corporis/pedis, with itching and scaling, not pigmented macules.

D. Candida albicans: Causes moist intertrigo or oral thrush with erythema and satellite lesions, not brown palm lesions.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 26-year-old man comes to the OPD due to a 3-day-history of dysuria and urethral discharge. Gram stain of the discharge reveals numerous neutrophils with intracellular diplococci. A sample of the discharge is placed on an antibiotic-containing medium, and bacterial colonies are cultured. Which of the following terms best describes the medium?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Selective

Selective media contain antibiotics or inhibitory substances that suppress the growth of unwanted organisms while allowing the desired pathogen to grow.

For Neisseria gonorrhoeae, specimens are commonly cultured on Thayer–Martin medium, a selective medium containing antibiotic that inhibit normal flora but permit growth of N. gonorrhoeae.

Why not other options:

A. Differential medium: Distinguishes organisms based on biochemical reactions (e.g., lactose fermentation on MacConkey agar) but does not inhibit other bacteria.

B. Enrichment medium: Enhances growth of a particular organism from a mixed sample without necessarily suppressing others (e.g., tetrathionate broth for Salmonella).

C. Reducing medium: Used for anaerobic bacteria by removing oxygen (e.g., thioglycollate broth).

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 26-year-old man develops dysuria and purulent urethral discharge following unprotected sex with a new partner. Nucleic acid amplification testing is positive for Neisseria gonorrhea infection. The patient develops antibody against the bacterial pili that enhance attachment to host cells. His symptoms resolve with adequate treatment. His partner does not receive treatment. Several weeks later, the patient develops N gonorrhoeae reinfection after repeat exposure to the same partner. Which of the following is the most likely reason for the lack of long-lasting immunity against the bacteria despite antibody formation in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Antigenic variation

Neisseria gonorrhoeae frequently causes reinfection despite prior antibody formation because it undergoes antigenic variation of its surface pili and outer membrane proteins.

These genetic changes alter antigenic structures, allowing the bacteria to evade previously formed antibodies and preventing the development of long-lasting protective immunity.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 26-year-old pregnant woman in her second trimester presents with eye pain, photophobia, and headache. Fundoscopy reveals a fluffy white lesion and optic disc swelling. To rule out toxoplasmosis, her physician orders a serological test. Which of the following tests is the gold standard for diagnosis of toxoplasmosis?
options: ELISA using maternal serum to detect IgG and IgM
PCR of amniotic fluid for toxoplasma DNA
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Sabin-Feldman dye test

The Sabin–Feldman dye test is the gold standard serological test for toxoplasmosis.

• Detects Toxoplasma gondii–specific IgG antibodies.
• Patient serum is mixed with live tachyzoites, complement, and methylene blue dye.
• If antibodies are present, tachyzoites are lysed and do not take up the dye (dye exclusion).
• Extremely sensitive and specific for detecting Toxoplasma antibodies.
• Used as the reference test in many laboratories

Why not other options:

A. Animal inoculation of amniotic fluid: Historical research method; not used routinely for diagnosis.

B. ELISA using maternal serum to detect IgG and IgM: Common screening test, but not the gold standard.

D. PCR of amniotic fluid for toxoplasma DNA: Useful for detecting fetal infection, especially in pregnancy, but not the reference serological test.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 26-year-old pregnant woman is diagnosed with HIV during antenatal screening. She has never received treatment previously. According to the National AIDS Control Organisation guidelines, the most appropriate management is:
options: Start ART only if CD4 count is below 350 cells/mm³
Start lifelong ART immediately, irrespective of CD4 count
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Start lifelong ART immediately, irrespective of CD4 count

India follows the Treat All policy:

• Every HIV-positive person should receive lifelong ART, irrespective of CD4 count or clinical stage.
• This reduces maternal disease progression and prevents mother-to-child transmission.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 27-year-old woman comes to the OPD due to joint pain. Her symptoms began 10 days ago and consist of bilateral pain in the metacarpophalangeal joints, proximal interphalangeal joints, wrists, knees, and ankles. She describes joint stiffness lasting 10-15 minutes on awakening in the morning. The patient has also had associated fatigue and a few episodes of loose bowel movements associated with mild skin itching and patchy redness. She has no fever, weight loss, or lymphadenopathy. She works as an elementary school teacher. On examination, there is tenderness of the involved joints without swelling or redness. Which of the following is most likely elevated in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Anti-parvovirus B19 IgM antibodies

Parvovirus B19 infection in adults commonly presents with acute symmetric polyarthralgia involving small joints (MCP, PIP, wrists), often mimicking rheumatoid arthritis. Symptoms are usually mild, transient, and associated with viral prodrome or rash.

The infection is common in school settings, and recent infection is indicated by elevated anti–Parvovirus B19 IgM antibodies.

Why not other options:

A. Anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies: Seen in rheumatoid arthritis (chronic, >1 hr morning stiffness).

B. Anti-double-stranded DNA antibodies: Seen in SLE.

C. Anti-parvovirus B19 IgM antibodies: Nonspecific marker of autoimmune diseases.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 28-year-old healthcare worker undergoes screening after needle-stick injury. An ELISA test is performed to detect antibodies against a viral antigen. The test yields a positive result, but confirmatory testing later shows no infection. Which of the following best explains this false-positive result?
options: ELISA has high specificity but low sensitivity
Cross-reactivity of antibodies with similar antigens
Inability of ELISA to detect low antibody levels
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cross-reactivity of antibodies with similar antigens

ELISA (Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay) is primarily used as a screening test due to its high sensitivity.

• High sensitivity → detects even small amounts of antigen/antibody
• Lower specificity → prone to false positives, most commonly due to cross-reactivity
• Types of ELISA:

• Direct / Indirect ELISA → detects antibodies
• Sandwich ELISA → detects antigens (most specific format)

• Clinical implication: A positive ELISA must be confirmed with a more specific test (e.g., Western blot, PCR)

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 28-year-old man presents with fever, agitation, hydrophobia, and a history of a stray dog bite 6 weeks earlier. Rabies is clinically suspected. The clinician wants to perform the most sensitive test for confirming the diagnosis of rabies in the ante-mortem period. Which of the following investigations should be performed?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. RT-PCR for rabies viral RNA

• Rabies diagnosis in the ante-mortem period relies on detection of rabies viral RNA using RT-PCR, which is the most sensitive and specific test.
• Specimens used for RT-PCR: Saliva, CSF and Nuchal skin biopsy (hair follicle nerves)
• RT-PCR allows early detection of viral RNA before death, making it the preferred confirmatory test when rabies is clinically suspected.

Why not other options:

A. Direct fluorescent antibody test: Gold standard for post-mortem brain tissue, not most sensitive ante-mortem test.

B. Negri body detection on histopathology: Seen on brain histopathology after death; low sensitivity.

D. Viral culture in mice: Slow and rarely used for clinical diagnosis.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 28-year-old pregnant woman with HIV infection is being evaluated for factors associated with an increased risk of vertical (mother-to-child) transmission of HIV. All of the following are recognized risk factors for vertical transmission of HIV except:
options: Preterm delivery before 34 weeks of gestation
Prolonged rupture of membranes for more than 4 hours
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. High maternal CD4 count (>500 cells/mm³)

Risk factors for vertical transmission of HIV include:

• High maternal viremia (most important risk factor)
• Low maternal CD4 count
• Preterm delivery (<34 weeks)
• Prolonged rupture of membranes (>4 hours)
• Low birth weight
• Maternal vitamin A deficiency

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 28-year-old woman presents with fever, right upper quadrant pain, and marked eosinophilia. She gives a history of consuming raw aquatic plants during travel. Ultrasound shows multiple hypoechoic lesions in the liver. Stool examination is negative for ova. Serology is positive for a trematode infection. Which of the following is the most likely causative parasite?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Fasciola hepatica

Fasciola hepatica (liver fluke) infection has two distinct phases:

• Acute (hepatic/migratory phase):

• Ingestion of metacercariae on aquatic plants
• Larvae migrate through liver parenchyma
• Causes fever, RUQ pain, eosinophilia
• Stool exam negative (no egg production yet)

•

Chronic phase:

• Adult worms reside in bile ducts
• Leads to biliary obstruction

Eggs appear in stool

Other Options:

Option A. Clonorchis sinensis

• Acquired from raw fish, not aquatic plants
• Primarily biliary disease, no hepatic migration phase

Option C. Entamoeba histolytica

• Causes liver abscess, but no eosinophilia
• Transmitted via fecal-oral route, not plants

Option D. Echinococcus granulosus

• Causes hydatid cysts (large, well-defined)
• No acute migratory phase with eosinophilia

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 29-year-old male presents to the emergency department with a 3-day history of high-grade fever, altered mental status, and severe respiratory distress. His family reports that he recently attended a wedding in a rural area of Kozhikode district of Kerala, where he consumed freshly tapped toddy (tapped from the sap of palm trees), a local drink. Over the next day, three more individuals from the same wedding presented with similar symptoms. On examination, the patient appears lethargic, disoriented, with reduced chest sounds on the right side. His CSF analysis reveals an elevated protein count with normal glucose and an increase in lymphocytes. Given the clinical presentation and his recent history, which of the following infectious agents is most likely responsible for this outbreak?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Nipah virus

Nipah virus is a zoonotic paramyxovirus transmitted from fruit bats (Pteropus species) to humans, often through contaminated food such as raw palm sap (toddy).

• Acute febrile illness
• Rapidly progressive encephalitis (altered mental status)
• Severe respiratory distress
• High case fatality rate

Epidemiological clues:

• Consumption of fresh palm sap contaminated by bat secretions
• Clusters of cases/outbreaks
• Reported outbreaks in Kerala (especially Kozhikode district)

CSF findings:

• Lymphocytic pleocytosis
• Elevated protein
• Normal glucose (suggestive of viral encephalitis)

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 3-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department due to high fever, vomiting, and lethargy. His symptoms started 1 day ago but rapidly worsened over the last few hours. Physical examination shows hypotension, tachycardia, neck stiffness, and a petechial rash over the trunk and lower extremities. While being evaluated, the patient develops apnea and systole. Despite aggressive resuscitation efforts, the patient dies. Autopsy would most likely reveal which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Adrenal hemorrhage

• Neisseria meningitidis infection can cause meningococcemia, characterized by high fever, petechial rash, hypotension, and rapid progression to septic shock in children.
• Severe endotoxemia may lead to Waterhouse–Friderichsen syndrome, which involves bilateral adrenal hemorrhage, resulting in acute adrenal insufficiency and cardiovascular collapse.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 3-year-old child presents with acute abdominal pain and bloody diarrhea. Stool culture on egg yolk agar shows opaque, opalescent colonies which display loss of opacity when grown on a medium containing anti-alpha toxin. This phenomenon is known as Nagler’s reaction. What type of reaction is it?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Neutralisation

Nagler’s reaction is a neutralization test used to identify Clostridium perfringens based on the activity of its alpha toxin (lecithinase).

• C. perfringens produces alpha toxin, which hydrolyzes lecithin in egg yolk agar, producing opaque, opalescent colonies.
• When anti–alpha toxin antibodies are added to one half of the medium, the toxin is neutralized, resulting in loss of opacity on that side.

Interpretation:

• Opacity present on the control side
• Opacity inhibited on the antitoxin side → positive Nagler reaction

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 31-year-old man comes to the office due to a week of low-grade fever, dry cough, and right-sided chest pain. The pain is intermittent, sharp, and worse with deep inhalation or cough. The patient also notes mild "achiness" in his knees and ankles that started around the same time. He does not use tobacco, alcohol, or illicit drugs. The patient is an Army officer, and he returned after completing desert training exercises in Rajasthan. He does not know if other participants developed similar symptoms. Temperature is 37.8°C (100°F). Blood pressure is 120/80 mmHg, pulse is 78/min, and respirations are 16/min. Lung auscultation shows right-sided crackles. No joint swelling or tenderness is present, but there are erythematous, tender nodules on the bilateral shins. Chest x-ray reveals a right lower lobe infiltrate with a prominent right hilum. Which of the following is most likely causing this patient's condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Coccidioides immitis

Coccidioides immitis causes coccidioidomycosis (Valley fever), acquired by inhalation of arthroconidia from soil in desert regions.

• Fever, dry cough, pleuritic chest pain
• Pulmonary infiltrates with hilar lymphadenopathy
• Erythema nodosum on the shins
• Arthralgia (“desert rheumatism”)

Why not other options:

A. Blastomyces dermatitidis: Seen in North America near rivers/lakes; often causes pulmonary infection with verrucous skin lesions, not erythema nodosum.

C. Histoplasma capsulatum: Associated with bird/bat droppings (caves); may cause pulmonary disease with hilar lymphadenopathy but erythema nodosum and desert exposure are more typical of Coccidioides.

D. Legionella pneumophila: Causes atypical pneumonia with GI symptoms (diarrhea), confusion, and hyponatremia, not erythema nodosum.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 32-year-old laboratory worker develops sudden onset high-grade fever, chills, severe headache, and pneumonia after accidental exposure to infected animal tissue while working in a research facility. The organism involved is a highly infectious Gram-negative coccobacillus that can be transmitted via aerosols and is considered a potential biological weapon by the CDC. Which of the following organisms is classified as a Category A bioterrorism agent according to the CDC?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Francisella tularensis

This question tests recognition of Category A bioterrorism agents and their clinical presentation, especially Francisella tularensis.

• Laboratory exposure → high infectivity
• Aerosol transmission
• Acute illness:

• High-grade fever, chills
• Severe headache
• Pneumonia (inhalational form)

Core concept: Category A bioterrorism agents (CDC):

• Easily disseminated / transmitted
• High mortality
• Cause public panic
• Require special preparedness

Examples (high-yield list):

• Francisella tularensis (tularemia)
• Bacillus anthracis
• Yersinia pestis
• Variola virus
• Botulinum toxin

High-yield differentiation:

• Brucella → undulating fever, not Category A
• Coxiella → Q fever (Category B)
• Burkholderia pseudomallei → melioidosis (not Category A)

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 32-year-old male from coastal Tamil Nadu presents with scrotal swelling, fever, and lymphangitis. Peripheral blood film is done at 11 PM showing microfilariae. His wife has similar symptoms but her blood film is equivocal. What is the most sensitive concentration method and the DOC with its dose schedule?
options: Knott's technique; DEC 6mg/kg × 12 doses with 2-day gap
Membrane filtration; DEC 6mg/kg × 12 doses with 2-day gap
DEC provocation test; Albendazole 400mg single dose
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Membrane filtration; DEC 6mg/kg × 12 doses with 2-day gap

Diagnosis methods:

| Method | Detail | Sensitivity

| ------ | ------ | -----------

| Peripheral blood film | IOC | Standard

| Membrane filtration | Most sensitive | Highest

| Knott's technique | Centrifuge blood in 2% formalin | Less sensitive than membrane filtration

| DEC provocation test | 100mg DEC oral → blood test after 1hr | For equivocal/night blood not possible

• DEC provocation test timing: 10 PM – 2 AM (peak microfilaraemia). Wife = equivocal → DEC provocation test indicated (but NOT the most sensitive concentration method).

Treatment:

| Drug | Dose | Schedule

| ---- | ---- | --------

| DEC (DOC) | 6mg/kg/day | 12 doses: 6 doses → 2-day gap → 6 doses

| MDA: DEC | 6mg/kg/day | Bi-annual

| MDA: Albendazole | 400mg | Bi-annual

| MDA: Ivermectin | 150–200 mcg/kg | Bi-annual

MDA now bi-annual, 3-drug regimen, synchronised with national deworming day: 10 February and 10 August.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 32-year-old male presents to the clinic with fatigue, jaundice, and elevated liver enzymes. He reports recent unprotected sexual encounters and has a history of intravenous drug use. During further investigation of his blood sample, a specific particle associated with this viral infection is identified under the electron microscope. Which of the following structures, when transmitted, is capable of leading to infection in another person?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Dane particles

| Particle Type | Size (nm) | Genome Present | Composition

| ------------- | --------- | -------------- | -----------

| Dane Particle | 42 | Yes | Complete virions (Genome + HBsAg)

| Spherical Particles | 22 | No | Surface proteins (Small HBsAg)

| Tubular Particle | 22 | No | Surface proteins (Medium HBsAg)

| Filamentous Particle | 22 | No | Surface proteins (HBsAg)

| — | 22 | No | HBsAg

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 32-year-old man HIV positive male presents with cough, fever, and weight loss for 3 weeks. Which is recommended as the initial diagnostic test under the National Tuberculosis Elimination Programme?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. TruNAAT

In a PLHIV with presumptive TB (cough, fever, weight loss ×3 weeks — 3 of the 4-symptom screen positive), NTEP mandates an upfront molecular test (NAAT) as the initial diagnostic. Truenat and CBNAAT (Xpert MTB/RIF) are the two approved upfront NAATs, so C is the answer here.

Option-by-option distractor analysis

| Option | Verdict | Reasoning

| ------ | ------- | ---------

| A. Ziehl-Neelsen smear | ✗ | TB in HIV is often paucibacillary/smear-negative → low sensitivity. Not first-line in PLHIV. Also, ZN needs \~10⁴ bacilli/mL to turn positive.

| B. LJ culture | ✗ | Gold standard for viability/DST, but slow (6–8 weeks) — useless as an initial rapid diagnostic. It's a follow-on/confirmatory test.

| C. TruNAAT | ✓ | Upfront molecular NAAT — high sensitivity, detects paucibacillary TB, gives result in \~1 hour, and Truenat MTB-RIF Dx also flags rifampicin resistance.

| D. Line probe assay (LPA) | ✗ | A molecular test, but used for drug-resistance characterization (1st-line LPA → INH/RIF; 2nd-line LPA → FQ/injectables) on smear-positive samples or culture isolates — not the initial screening diagnostic.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 32-year-old man presents with high-grade fever, hypotension, tachycardia, and altered mental status after a traumatic wound infection. Blood cultures grow gram-negative bacilli, and endotoxin-mediated septic shock is suspected. Which innate immune receptor is primarily responsible for recognizing the endotoxin component of these organisms?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Toll-like receptor 4

Endotoxin (lipopolysaccharide, LPS) from Gram-negative bacteria is recognized by Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4) on innate immune cells such as macrophages and dendritic cells.

• LPS binds to LPS-binding protein (LBP) in plasma.
• The complex interacts with CD14 and TLR4–MD2 receptor complex on immune cells.
• This activates NF-κB signaling, leading to release of pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6).
• Excessive cytokine release results in systemic inflammation, vasodilation, hypotension, and septic shock.

Why not other options:

A. RIG-I–like receptors: Detect viral RNA in the cytoplasm, mainly involved in antiviral immunity.

C. C-type lectin receptors: Recognize fungal cell wall carbohydrates (e.g., β-glucans, mannans).

D. NOD-like receptor 1: Detects bacterial peptidoglycan fragments inside the cytoplasm, not LPS.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 32-year-old man working as a restaurant cook was diagnosed with typhoid fever 8 months ago. He recovered completely and has remained asymptomatic since. Over the past few weeks, multiple patrons who consumed food prepared by him developed culture-confirmed Salmonella Typhi infection. Stool cultures from the cook repeatedly test positive despite the absence of symptoms. This individual is best classified as which type of carrier?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Temporary carrier

• Temporary carriers are individuals who carry and transmit the pathogen for a period of more than 3 months but less than a year.

• Convalescent carrier refers to a person who has recovered from a disease but continues to shed the infectious agent for a period of 3 weeks to 3 months after recovery.

• Chronic carriers are individuals who continue to carry and shed the pathogen for a period of more than a year.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 32-year-old sexually active woman presents with vaginal itching and frothy discharge for one week. On speculum examination, the cervix appears erythematous with punctate hemorrhagic spots. A motile, flagellated protozoan is suspected. Which of the following culture media cannot be used for identification of the causative organism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Novy–Nicolle–McNeal medium

Trichomonas vaginalis is a motile, flagellated protozoan causing trichomoniasis, a common sexually transmitted infection.

• Frothy, yellow-green vaginal discharge
• Vaginal itching
• “Strawberry cervix” (punctate hemorrhages)

Laboratory diagnosis:

• Wet mount microscopy → motile flagellated trophozoites
• Culture media used for T. vaginalis:

o    Diamond medium

o    Trussell & Johnson medium

o    Feinberg–Whittington medium

Not used: Novy–Nicolle–McNeal (NNN) medium, which is used for Leishmania culture, not Trichomonas.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 32-year-old shepherd presents with slowly enlarging cervical lymph nodes that are firm and occasionally discharge thick, caseous material. Histopathology shows granulomas with central necrosis. Culture yields a Gram-positive, non–spore-forming, pleomorphic bacillus arranged in palisades. The organism is non–toxin producing. Which of the following laboratory findings would best help differentiate this organism from Corynebacterium diphtheriae?
options: Presence of metachromatic granules on Albert stain
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Urease positivity

Corynebacterium pseudotuberculosis is a zoonotic, Gram-positive pleomorphic bacillus that causes chronic granulomatous (caseous) lymphadenitis, especially in individuals with animal exposure.

Key differentiating features:

• Urease positive → important lab differentiator
• Non–toxin producing (unlike C. diphtheriae)
• Produces phospholipase D → facilitates tissue invasion and lymphatic spread
• Causes caseating granulomas with sinus formation

Comparison with C. diphtheriae:

• C. diphtheriae → toxin-mediated disease, Elek test positive, urease negative
• C. pseudotuberculosis → urease positive, zoonotic granulomatous disease

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 34-year-old cattle handler presents with fever for the past 3 weeks. The fever shows a characteristic pattern of rising for a few days, then subsiding for a few days, and then recurring again. He also has night sweats, malaise, arthralgia, and hepatosplenomegaly. He gives a history of consuming unpasteurized milk. The described pattern of fever is classically associated with infection by:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Brucella melitensis

This question tests recognition of brucellosis based on its characteristic fever pattern and exposure history.

• Occupation: cattle handler (zoonotic exposure)
• Consumption of unpasteurized milk
• Symptoms:

• Undulating (wave-like) fever → hallmark
• Night sweats (often with “mousy” odor)
• Arthralgia, malaise
• Hepatosplenomegaly

Core concept: Brucella melitensis causes undulant fever

• Fever rises for days → subsides → recurs

High-yield differentiation:

• Salmonella typhi → step-ladder fever
• Plasmodium vivax → tertian fever (every 48 hrs)
• Leptospira → biphasic fever

| Fever Pattern | Description | Classic Diseases

| ------------- | ----------- | ----------------

| Continuous fever | Temperature remains above normal with minimal fluctuation (<1°C) | Typhoid fever

| Remittent fever | Daily fluctuation >1°C but never returns to normal | Infective endocarditis

| Intermittent fever | Fever spikes but returns to normal between spikes | Malaria

| Tertian fever | Fever every 48 hours | Plasmodium vivax malaria, Plasmodium ovale malaria

| Quartan fever | Fever every 72 hours | Plasmodium malariae malaria

| Step-ladder fever | Gradual daily rise in temperature | Typhoid fever

| Undulating fever | Fever rises and falls over days–weeks | Brucellosis

| Relapsing fever | Fever episodes separated by afebrile periods | Relapsing fever

| Pel–Ebstein fever | Cyclical fever (few days fever + few days normal) | Hodgkin lymphoma

| Saddleback fever | Fever subsides then recurs after few days | Dengue fever

| Biphasic fever | Two distinct fever phases | Leptospirosis

| Hectic (septic) fever | Wide swings with chills and sweating | Sepsis, Tuberculosis

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 34-year-old researcher accidentally exposes a viral sample to alcohol during a lab procedure. He recalls that alcohol can disrupt certain viral structures. Which of the following statements is true regarding the structure of viral envelopes and capsids?
options: Hemagglutinin is a protein subunit found exclusively in non-enveloped viruses
Non-enveloped viruses are more alcohol labile than enveloped viruses
Viral envelope is composed of lipids derived from the host cell membrane
Capsid in enveloped viruses gives the virus its pleomorphic shape
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Viral envelope is composed of lipids derived from the host cell membrane

Viral envelopes are lipid bilayers derived from the host cell membrane (usually plasma membrane, ER, or Golgi) during viral budding.

• Envelope contains host-derived lipids with viral glycoproteins (spikes) embedded in it.
• The lipid envelope makes viruses susceptible to alcohol, detergents, and drying.
