• These glycoproteins help in attachment and entry into host cells.

Capsid vs Envelope:

• Capsid: Protein coat that protects the viral genome.
• Envelope: Host-derived lipid layer surrounding the capsid in enveloped viruses.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 34-year-old woman comes to the OPD due to 3 days of discomfort and swelling in the right axilla. She is a veterinarian and volunteers as a swim coach at her children's school. Temperature is 36.9°C (98.4°F). On physical examination, there is an enlarged, tender axillary lymph node on the right, measuring about 3 cm and with slight surrounding erythema but no skin breakdown. There is no other area of lymphadenopathy. Several scratch marks are seen on the right arm. The organism responsible for the lymphadenopathy is also associated with which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Bacillary angiomatosis

The patient likely has cat-scratch disease, caused by Bartonella henselae. It presents with localized painful lymphadenopathy (often axillary) following a cat scratch or bite.

• Regional lymphadenopathy near the site of scratch
• Mild fever or malaise
• History of cat exposure or scratches

Associated condition:

• Bacillary angiomatosis, a vascular proliferative disease seen mainly in immunocompromised patients (especially HIV), also caused by Bartonella henselae.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 35-year-old farmer sustains a deep contaminated wound from a rusty nail, presenting 10 hours later. He received a complete tetanus immunization course 11 years ago. Correct management is:
options: Wound care + TT single dose + hTIg
Wound care + complete TT course + hTIg
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Wound care + TT single dose + hTIg

• Wound classification: >6 hours + contaminated = unclean wound.
• Full immunization >10 years ago (Category C) + unclean wound = wound care + TT single dose + hTIg.

| Category | Immunization status | Clean wound | Unclean wound

| -------- | ------------------- | ----------- | -------------

| A | Full immunization <5 years | Wound care only | Wound care only

| B | Full immunization 5–10 years | Wound care only | Wound care + TT

| C | Full immunization >10 years | Wound care + TT | Wound care + TT + hTIg

| D | Unknown/never immunized | Wound care + TT complete course | Wound care + TT complete course + hTIg

• Clean wound = presented within 6 hrs, sterile cut.
• Unclean wound = >6 hrs, unsterile/contaminated/open wound.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 35-year-old immunocompromised patient on long-term voriconazole therapy for invasive aspergillosis presents with complaints of seeing colored halos and flashes of light shortly after drug administration. These visual disturbances typically last less than 30 minutes. Which of the following best describes this characteristic side effect of voriconazole?
options: Papilledema due to raised intracranial pressure
Transient visual disturbances due to altered electroretinogram activity
Retinal detachment due to fungal chorioretinitis
Optic neuritis due to mitochondrial toxicity
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Transient visual disturbances due to altered electroretinogram activity

Voriconazole causes transient visual disturbances in \~30% of patients, including:

• Photophobia
• Blurred vision
• Color vision changes
• Flashes/halos

Mechanism: Altered electroretinogram (ERG) activity — affects retinal photoreceptors transiently.

Key features:

| Feature | Detail

| ------- | ------

| Onset | Within 30 min of dose

| Duration | < 30 min

| Reversibility | Fully reversible

| Action needed | Usually no discontinuation required

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 36-year-old HIV-positive man (CD4 count 110/µL) presents with recurrent oral thrush not responding to fluconazole. KOH mount shows budding yeast cells with pseudohyphae. Germ tube test is positive. On further testing, the isolate produces abundant clustered chlamydospores and fails to grow when incubated in hypertonic saline. The most likely organism is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Candida dubliniensis

Candida dubliniensis is an opportunistic yeast that commonly causes recurrent oral candidiasis in HIV-infected patients.

• Budding yeast with pseudohyphae
• Germ tube positive (similar to Candida albicans)
• Produces abundant clustered chlamydospores
• Fails to grow in hypertonic saline (6.5% NaCl) and grows poorly at higher temperatures, helping differentiate it from C. albicans.
• Often associated with fluconazole-resistant oral thrush in immunocompromised individuals.

Why not other options:

A. Candida albicans: Germ tube positive and forms chlamydospores but grows in hypertonic saline and at higher temperatures (unlike C. dubliniensis).

B. Candida tropicalis: Germ tube negative and usually does not form chlamydospores.

D. Candida glabrata: Does not form pseudohyphae or germ tubes; appears as small budding yeast only.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 38-year-old patient presents with dry nocturnal cough, dyspnea, and wheezing. Blood tests show marked eosinophilia and elevated IgE, with no microfilaria in the blood. A chest X-ray reveals mottled shadows. The patient has a history of travel to endemic areas. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Weingarten's Syndrome

Tropical pulmonary eosinophilia (Weingarten’s syndrome) is a hypersensitivity reaction to filarial parasites, mainly Wuchereria bancrofti and Brugia malayi.

• Paroxysmal nocturnal cough
• Dyspnea and wheezing
• Marked peripheral eosinophilia
• Elevated IgE levels
• Chest X-ray showing diffuse or mottled pulmonary infiltrates
• Microfilariae usually absent in peripheral blood
• Caused by immune hypersensitivity to trapped microfilariae in pulmonary tissues.

Why not other options:

A. Loeffler’s syndrome: Transient pulmonary eosinophilia due to helminth larval migration (e.g., Ascaris); mild, self-limiting, not marked IgE elevation with nocturnal cough.

B. Miliary tuberculosis: Causes diffuse millet-seed nodules on X-ray, no eosinophilia or high IgE.

D. Chronic eosinophilic pneumonia: Causes peripheral lung infiltrates (“photographic negative of pulmonary edema”), not linked to filarial exposure

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 4-year-old child is brought with complaints of persistent fever, and cough without sputum for 3 weeks. As per the National Tuberculosis Elimination Programme guidelines, what should be the next step in management?
questions.explanation: Correct answer: B. Chest X-ray

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 4-year-old child weighing 18 kg is newly diagnosed with HIV and needs ART. The paediatric ART plan discussed includes 2 NRTIs plus a third agent appropriate for young children. Which regimen is most appropriate for a child under 6 years or under 20 kg?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Abacavir + Lamivudine + LPV/r combination

For children under 6 years of age or weighing <20 kg with HIV infection, the preferred first-line ART regimen includes:

• Two NRTIs: Abacavir (ABC) + Lamivudine (3TC)
• Third agent: Lopinavir/ritonavir (LPV/r) (a boosted protease inhibitor)

Reason:

• LPV/r-based regimens are preferred in young children because they have better efficacy and resistance profiles compared with NNRTI-based regimens in this age group.

Regimen: Abacavir + Lamivudine + Lopinavir/ritonavir

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 40-year-old male presents to the emergency department with a high fever, chills, and dark-coloured urine. He recently returned from a trip to a malaria-endemic region in West Africa and self-treated with antimalarial medication. On examination, he is febrile (39.5°C), tachycardic, and has jaundice. Laboratory investigations show: ● Hemoglobin: 8 g/dL ● LDH: Elevated ● Urinalysis: Dark brown urine, positive for haemoglobin. ● Total Bilirubin: 4 mg/dL. Which of the following best explains the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Blackwater fever

Blackwater fever is a severe complication of Plasmodium falciparum malaria characterized by massive intravascular hemolysis.

• High fever and chills
• Severe hemolytic anemia (↓ hemoglobin)
• Hemoglobinuria → dark “blackwater” urine
• Jaundice and elevated bilirubin
• Often associated with antimalarial drug exposure (historically quinine) and repeated malaria infections.

Why not other options:

A. Benign malaria: Usually due to Plasmodium vivax/ovale → milder disease, no massive hemolysis or hemoglobinuria.

B. Septicemic malaria: Refers to secondary bacterial sepsis with malaria, not characterized by dark hemoglobinuria.

C. Algid malaria: Severe falciparum malaria with shock, hypotension, and cold clammy skin, mimicking septic shock.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 40-year-old man on intermittent anti-tuberculosis therapy develops acute shortness of breath, fever, and cough 2 hours after taking his medications. Chest radiograph shows bilateral pulmonary infiltrates with hypoxemia. Which of the following drugs in his regimen is most strongly associated with acute pulmonary hypersensitivity syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Rifampicin

This question tests recognition of drug-induced hypersensitivity reactions in anti-tubercular therapy, particularly rifampicin-associated flu-like and pulmonary syndromes.

• Rifampicin hypersensitivity syndrome:

• More common with intermittent therapy
• Onset: within hours of drug intake
• Features:

• Fever, chills
• Dyspnea, cough
• Acute pulmonary infiltrates + hypoxemia
• Can mimic ARDS

• Mechanism: Immune-mediated (type III hypersensitivity–like reaction)
• Why rifampicin is the answer:

• Classic drug causing flu-like syndrome + acute pulmonary reaction
• Strong association with intermittent dosing regimens

High-yield differentiation of ATT drugs:

• Isoniazid → peripheral neuropathy, hepatotoxicity
• Pyrazinamide → hyperuricemia
• Ethambutol → optic neuritis
• Rifampicin → flu-like syndrome, thrombocytopenia, hypersensitivity reactions

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 42-year-old male from central India presents with prolonged fever, weight loss, oral discomfort, and bleeding gums. Examination reveals painful palatal ulcers. Laboratory evaluation shows pancytopenia. On detailed history, he reports frequent spelunking with his friends. Which of the following is the most likely causative organism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Histoplasma capsulatum

Histoplasma capsulatum is a dimorphic fungus that causes histoplasmosis, often acquired by inhalation of spores from soil contaminated with bird or bat droppings, especially in environments such as caves (spelunking).

• Causes disseminated infection in immunocompromised individuals.

• Clinical findings may include:

o    Prolonged fever and weight loss

o    Pancytopenia due to bone marrow involvement

o    Painful oral or palatal ulcers

o    Hepatosplenomegaly

Why not other options:

A. Paracoccidioides brasiliensis: Causes paracoccidioidomycosis in Latin America, not typical in India; “pilot wheel” yeast.

B. Coccidioides immitis: Causes Valley fever, endemic to Southwestern USA and desert regions, not linked to caves/bat guano.

D. Blastomyces dermatitidis: Causes blastomycosis in North America, associated with soil/wood, not spelunking.

Parasitology

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 42-year-old man with HIV infection on a stable antiretroviral therapy (ART) regimen for the last 6 months presents with chronic, non-bloody watery diarrhea for 3 weeks. Stool examination is negative for ova, parasites, and bacterial pathogens. There is no history of fever or weight loss. His CD4 count is improving and viral load is suppressed. Despite dietary modification and loperamide, symptoms persist. Which of the following drugs is most appropriate for management of this patient’s diarrhea?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Crofelemer

Crofelemer is used for the treatment of noninfectious diarrhea in patients with HIV receiving antiretroviral therapy (ART). Indicated for chronic, noninfectious diarrhea associated with ART when stool studies are negative for infectious causes.

• Crofelemer inhibits CFTR chloride channels and calcium-activated chloride channels in the intestinal epithelium.
• This reduces chloride and water secretion into the intestinal lumen, thereby decreasing watery diarrhea.
• It does not affect intestinal motility, making it safer for long-term use compared with antimotility agents.

Why not other options:

A. Octreotide: Used for secretory diarrhea due to tumors (VIPoma, carcinoid) or severe refractory diarrhea, not routine ART-associated diarrhea.

B. Rifaximin: Antibiotic used for traveler’s diarrhea, SIBO, hepatic encephalopathy, not noninfectious ART-related diarrhea.

D. Cholestyramine: Used for bile acid malabsorption diarrhea (eg, post-ileal resection), not ART-induced diarrhea.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 45-year-old diabetic farmer from a tropical region presents with fever, weight loss, and multiple abscesses in liver and spleen. Blood culture grows a Gram-negative bacillus showing bipolar (“safety pin”) staining. The organism forms wrinkled colonies on culture and is intrinsically resistant to many antibiotics. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Melioidosis

Burkholderia pseudomallei causes melioidosis, an important infection in tropical regions with characteristic clinical and laboratory clues.

Key learning points:

• Risk factors:

o    Diabetes mellitus (most important)

o    Exposure to soil and contaminated water (farmers)
• Clinical features:

o    Multiple abscesses (liver, spleen, lungs)

o    Chronic or acute infection → known as a “great mimicker”
• Laboratory clues:

o    Gram-negative bacillus with bipolar (“safety pin”) staining

o    Wrinkled colonies on culture

o    Intrinsic resistance to many antibiotics

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 45-year-old man on dialysis undergoes Mantoux testing as part of the shown TPT pathway. Mantoux is negative and he has no evidence of active TB. What is the next step?
options: Follow up only and no TPT
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Follow up only and no TPT

Application of Tuberculosis Preventive Therapy (TPT) guidelines and identification of who qualifies for prophylaxis vs observation.

• TPT is indicated only in high-risk individuals, such as:

• HIV-positive patients
• Close household contacts of active TB cases
• Immunosuppressed patients (selected groups)

• Mantoux test (TST):

• Negative result → suggests no latent TB infection
• In absence of symptoms and no active TB → no treatment required

Clinical reasoning in this case:

• Patient is on dialysis (chronic illness but not automatic TPT indication)
• Mantoux negative + no active TB
• Therefore → no evidence of latent or active infection

Correct approach: No TPT needed → follow-up only

Why other options are wrong:

• Starting TPT regardless → overtreatment
• ATT → only for active TB
• Repeated CBNAAT → unnecessary without suspicion

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 45-year-old man undergoes an allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplant. He is CMV-seropositive and has no evidence of active CMV disease. To prevent post-transplant CMV reactivation, he is started on a newer antiviral agent that is not associated with myelosuppression or nephrotoxicity, unlike older anti-CMV drugs. Which of the following drugs was most likely prescribed?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Letermovir

Cytomegalovirus (CMV) reactivation is a common complication after allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT), particularly in CMV-seropositive patients. Prophylactic antiviral therapy is often used to prevent CMV disease.

Letermovir is a newer antiviral drug used specifically for CMV prophylaxis in HSCT recipients.

Mechanism of action:

• Inhibits the CMV terminase complex (UL56).
• Prevents cleavage and packaging of viral DNA into virions, blocking viral replication.

Not associated with myelosuppression or nephrotoxicity, unlike older anti-CMV drugs such as ganciclovir/valganciclovir.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 45-year-old man with pulmonary tuberculosis presents after 3 months of anti-tubercular therapy with complaints of tingling, numbness, and burning sensation in both feet, in a stocking distribution. His regimen includes isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Isoniazid

Isoniazid (INH) commonly causes peripheral neuropathy, presenting as tingling, numbness, and burning sensation in a stocking–glove distribution. INH interferes with vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) metabolism. Pyridoxine deficiency impairs neuronal function, leading to sensory neuropathy. Risk factors:

• Malnutrition
• Diabetes
• Alcoholism
• HIV infection
• Pregnancy
• Chronic kidney disease

Why not other options:

A. Ethambutol: Causes optic neuritis → decreased visual acuity and red-green color blindness, not peripheral neuropathy.

C. Pyrazinamide: Causes hyperuricemia → gout/arthralgia, not neuropathy.

D. Rifampicin: Causes hepatotoxicity, orange discoloration of body fluids, drug interactions, not neuropathy.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 45-year-old patient with a penicillin allergy presents with enterococcal endocarditis. Which of the following drugs can be used safely in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Vancomycin

Enterococcal endocarditis is commonly caused by Enterococcus faecalis or Enterococcus faecium. Standard therapy usually involves β-lactam antibiotics (e.g., penicillin or ampicillin) often combined with an aminoglycoside. However, in patients with a penicillin allergy, an alternative drug must be used.

Vancomycin is effective against gram-positive organisms including Enterococcus and is commonly used for:

• Enterococcal endocarditis
• MRSA infections
• Patients with severe β-lactam allergy

Why other options are incorrect

• A. Aztreonam – active mainly against gram-negative bacteria, not Enterococcus.

C. Ceftriaxone – a cephalosporin; may cross-react in penicillin allergy and has limited activity against Enterococcus.

D. Piperacillin – a β-lactam penicillin, contraindicated in penicillin-allergic patients.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 49-year-old man comes to the OPD due to a 3-week history of fever, weight loss, and anorexia. Both blood cultures grow Streptococcus gallolyticus. Echocardiogram reveals vegetations on the mitral valve. Other than antibiotic treatment, what additional step is recommended in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Colonoscopy

Streptococcus gallolyticus (formerly Streptococcus bovis) bacteremia or infective endocarditis is strongly associated with colorectal neoplasia, including colorectal cancer and adenomatous polyps. Therefore, all patients diagnosed with S. gallolyticus bacteremia or endocarditis should undergo colonoscopy to evaluate for an underlying colorectal malignancy or premalignant lesion, even if gastrointestinal symptoms are absent. Early detection allows identification and treatment of occult colorectal cancer.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 5-year-old child presents with profuse watery diarrhea after drinking contaminated water from a swimming pool. Stool examination with modified acid-fast staining shows small round oocysts. What is the diagnostic form of above given organism detected in stool?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Sporulated Oocyst

This question tests identification of coccidian parasites causing watery diarrhea and their diagnostic forms in stool microscopy.

• Child with profuse watery diarrhea
• Exposure: contaminated water (swimming pool)
• Modified acid-fast stain → small round oocysts

→ Suggests Cryptosporidiosis (most likely)

• The diagnostic stage detected in stool = sporulated oocyst
• These oocysts are:

• Immediately infective
• Contain sporozoites
• Acid-fast positive

In Cryptosporidium parvum:

• Oocysts are passed in already sporulated form
• This explains rapid transmission via water

High-yield differentiation:

• Cryptosporidium → sporulated oocyst (infective when passed)
• Cyclospora / Cystoisospora → unsporulated when passed → sporulate outside

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 52-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis presents with a 2-week history of fever, dry cough, progressive shortness of breath, and fatigue. She has been receiving adalimumab therapy for the past 6 months after negative tuberculosis screening before treatment initiation. Examination reveals bilateral crackles, generalized lymphadenopathy, and mild hepatosplenomegaly. Chest radiography demonstrates bilateral diffuse pulmonary nodules with hilar lymphadenopathy, and a urine fungal antigen test is positive. Which of the following pathogenic mechanisms is primarily responsible for the development of this infection?
options: Tissue invasion by overgrowth of endogenous flora
Production of an antiphagocytic polysaccharide capsule
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Intracellular multiplication within macrophages

This patient most likely has disseminated histoplasmosis caused by Histoplasma capsulatum, an opportunistic fungal infection associated with TNF-α inhibitor therapy (eg, adalimumab).

Key clues include:

• TNF-α inhibitor use
• Fever, cough, and dyspnea
• Bilateral pulmonary nodules with hilar lymphadenopathy
• Hepatosplenomegaly and generalized lymphadenopathy (dissemination)
• Positive Histoplasma urine antigen

Pathogenesis:

• Histoplasma spores are inhaled into the lungs.
• They convert to yeast forms at body temperature.
• The yeasts are phagocytosed by alveolar macrophages but survive and replicate intracellularly.
• TNF-α is essential for macrophage activation and granuloma maintenance; its inhibition impairs intracellular killing, allowing dissemination.

Why the other options are incorrect?

• B. Invasion of vascular endothelial cells: Characteristic of Aspergillus, which causes angioinvasive disease in severely immunocompromised patients.
• C. Tissue invasion by overgrowth of endogenous flora: Typical of Candida infections following disruption of normal flora or neutropenia.
• D. Production of an antiphagocytic polysaccharide capsule: Characteristic of Cryptococcus neoformans, whose capsule is a major virulence factor.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 54-year-old man comes to the clinic with fever, exertional dyspnoea, and non productive cough for one week. He was diagnosed with HIV infection 3 years ago but has been asymptomatic since. He has not been taking his medications consistently. His temperature is 38.9°C (102°F), blood pressure is 120/80 mmHg, pulse is 100/min, and respirations are 28/min. The patient's pulse oximetry shows 80% on room air. With use of a 100% nonrebreather mask, his oxygen saturation increases to 92%. Laboratory results are as follows: • Hemoglobin - 9.6 g/dL • Platelets - 120,000/mm³ • Leukocytes - 8,000/mm³ (no bands) Arterial blood gases on room air: • pH - 7.45 • PaO₂ - 54 mmHg • PaCO₂ - 44 mmHg Chest x-ray shows diffuse bilateral interstitial infiltrates. His CD4 count is 190/mm³ and lactate dehydrogenase level is 400 U/L. What is the most appropriate next step in management of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and corticosteroids

This patient with HIV (CD4 <200), fever, nonproductive cough, dyspnea, hypoxemia, and diffuse bilateral interstitial infiltrates is most consistent with Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP).

Treatment depends on severity:

• First-line therapy: Trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX)
• Add corticosteroids when PaO₂ <70 mmHg or A–a gradient ≥35 mmHg because inflammation during treatment can worsen hypoxemia.

This patient has PaO₂ = 54 mmHg, indicating moderate–severe PJP, so TMP-SMX + corticosteroids is indicated.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 58-year-old man on multiple antibiotics is suspected to have pseudomembranous colitis. The criteria for the diagnosis of the suspected condition include all, except:
options: Detection of toxin in stool by PCR
Stool wet mount microscopy to visualize the organism
≥3 unformed stools per 24 h for ≥2 days)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Stool wet mount microscopy to visualize the organism

Pseudomembranous colitis is an antibiotic-associated colitis caused by Clostridioides difficile, resulting from disruption of normal gut flora and production of toxins A and B that damage the colonic mucosa. Diagnosis is based on:

1.      Clinical criteria: ≥3 unformed stools in 24 hours without another identifiable cause.

2.      Laboratory confirmation: Detection of C. difficile toxin or toxin gene in stool (e.g., PCR or toxin immunoassay).

3.      Endoscopic findings (if required): Pseudomembranes seen on colonoscopy or sigmoidoscopy.

Why option B is incorrect:

• Stool wet mount microscopy is not used to diagnose C. difficile infection, because the organism cannot be reliably identified by routine stool microscopy and diagnosis depends on toxin detection rather than visualization.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 6-month-old infant is brought to the hospital with a 1-week history of high-grade fever, irritability, poor feeding, and progressive lethargy. Examination shows pallor, petechiae over the trunk and limbs, and moderate hepatomegaly. Complete blood counts reveal leukopenia and thrombocytopenia. A viral workup shows ELISA positivity for the pp65 antigen. Which viral agent is the most likely cause of this presentation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. HHV-5

Human Herpesvirus-5 (HHV-5), also called Cytomegalovirus (CMV), commonly causes systemic infection in infants, especially congenital or perinatal CMV infection.

• Fever, lethargy, poor feeding
• Hepatomegaly
• Petechiae (“blueberry muffin rash”)
• Cytopenias such as leukopenia and thrombocytopenia

Laboratory diagnosis:

• Detection of CMV pp65 antigen by ELISA or antigenemia assay.
• PCR for CMV DNA can also be used.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 6-year-old boy is brought to the OPD due to sore throat and fever. Examination shows mild tonsillar erythema with exudates. A sample from the exudates is obtained. On microscopic evaluation, there are clumped, gram-positive bacteria with polar granules that stain deeply with aniline dyes. Which of the following best explains the pathogenicity of the organism most likely responsible for this patient's condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Impairment of protein synthesis

Corynebacterium diphtheriae appears as gram-positive, club-shaped bacilli arranged in clusters (“Chinese letter” pattern) with metachromatic (Babes–Ernst) polar granules that stain deeply with aniline dyes.

Its pathogenicity is due to the diphtheria toxin, an A-B exotoxin that ADP-ribosylates elongation factor-2 (EF-2), leading to inhibition of protein synthesis and cell death.

Why not other options:

A. Increase cAMP: Seen with cholera toxin and pertussis toxin, which increase intracellular cAMP causing secretory diarrhea.

B. Blockade of neurotransmitter release: Seen with Clostridium botulinum (blocks acetylcholine release) and Clostridium tetani (blocks inhibitory neurotransmitters).

C. Widespread T-cell activation: Caused by superantigens such as Staphylococcus aureus TSST-1 or Streptococcus pyogenes exotoxins.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 62-year-old male presents with recurrent episodes of urinary tract infections caused by highly motile Gram-negative bacilli. The microbiology lab wants to visualize the flagella to assess motility pattern and number. A staining method is selected in which the flagella are thickened using a mordant before being impregnated with dye. Which combination most accurately represents this technique?
options: Basic fuchsin as stain with tannic acid as mordant
Methylene blue as stain with iodine as mordant
Safranin as stain with phenol as mordant
Carbol fuchsin as stain with gram’s iodine as mordant
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Basic fuchsin as stain with tannic acid as mordant

Special staining techniques used to demonstrate bacterial flagella, which are otherwise too thin to be visualized under light microscopy.

• Flagella are not visible with routine stains (Gram stain) because of their extremely thin diameter (\~20 nm)
• Specialized stains like Leifson stain are used

Principle of flagella staining:

• A mordant (e.g., tannic acid) coats and thickens the flagella
• This allows the dye (e.g., basic fuchsin) to bind and make them visible

Correct combination: Basic fuchsin (stain) + tannic acid (mordant) → Leifson stain

High-yield associations:

• Used for identifying motility patterns (monotrichous, lophotrichous, peritrichous)
• Common organisms tested:

• Proteus → highly motile (swarming)
• Vibrio → polar flagella
• E. coli → peritrichous flagella

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 70-year-old diabetic woman comes to the physician complaining of progressive, severe pain and discharge from her left ear for the past 2 days. On examination, moving or touching the pinna produces extreme pain. Otoscopic examination shows granulation tissue in the left ear canal with a scant amount of discharge. Which of the following microbiological characteristics best describes the infecting organism?
options: Comma-shaped and grows well in high pH
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Motile and oxidase positive

A severe, painful ear infection with granulation tissue in the external auditory canal in an elderly diabetic patient suggests malignant (necrotizing) otitis externa.

Causative organism: Pseudomonas aeruginosa

• Gram-negative bacillus
• Motile
• Oxidase positive
• Non–lactose fermenter
• Produces blue-green pigments (pyocyanin, pyoverdine)

Clinical significance:

• Occurs mainly in elderly diabetic or immunocompromised patients
• Infection can spread to skull base causing osteomyelitis

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 70-year-old man with a history of chronic smoking presented with fever, confusion, diarrhea and cough. Chest X-ray revealed bilateral infiltrates. Gram stain, immunofluorescence testing was done on sputum sample and came negative for organisms. Serology findings are given below. Which of the following organisms is responsible for this presentation? Serum Na+ – 120 meq/L AST – 62 IU/L ALT – 56 IU/L HIV – Positive
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Legionella

Legionella pneumophila causes atypical pneumonia characterized by high fever, confusion, diarrhea, and cough, often seen in elderly or immunocompromised patients (e.g., HIV).

Typical laboratory clues include:

• Hyponatremia (low serum sodium)
• Elevated liver enzymes (AST/ALT)
• Negative Gram stain and routine sputum cultures because the organism is intracellular and stains poorly

Why not other options:

A. Streptococcus: Gram-positive diplococci seen on Gram stain; typical lobar pneumonia.

C. Klebsiella: Currant-jelly sputum; Gram-negative bacilli visible on Gram stain.

D. Pneumocystis: Causes dry cough and dyspnea in HIV; no diarrhea or hyponatremia.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A blood bank technician needs to sterilize serum without exposing it to heat, as heat may denature proteins. A method is used in which fluid is passed through a thick asbestos pad placed in a metal holder for bacterial removal. Which sterilization method is being used?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Seitz filtration

Seitz filtration is a filtration sterilization method used for heat-sensitive liquids such as serum, vaccines, enzymes, and antibiotics.

• The liquid is passed through a Seitz filter, which consists of a thick asbestos pad mounted in a metal holder.
• The filter removes bacteria and particulate matter without exposing the fluid to heat, thereby preserving protein structure and biological activity.

Why not other options:

• A. Hot air oven: Dry heat sterilization (160–180 °C) used for glassware, powders, oils—would denature serum proteins.
• B. Autoclave: Moist heat (121°C under pressure) used for culture media and instruments—not suitable for heat-sensitive fluids like serum.
• D. Pasteurization: Uses moderate heat to reduce pathogens in milk; does not achieve complete sterilization.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A butcher develops a painful malignant pustule on his hand after handling a sick animal carcass. The lesion is suspected to be caused by Bacillus anthracis. Before surgical handling and further wound care, the exposed surface is disinfected using a method called duckering, which involves:
options: 0.5% sodium hypochlorite at room temperature for 10 minutes
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 2% formaldehyde at 30–40°C for 20 minutes

Duckering is a surface disinfection method used in suspected anthrax lesions before surgical handling or laboratory examination to prevent contamination by Bacillus anthracis spores.

Method:

• Application of 2% formaldehyde
• At 30–40°C
• For 20 minutes

Purpose:

• Inactivates Bacillus anthracis spores on the surface of the lesion.
• Prevents environmental contamination and laboratory-acquired infection.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A chronic smoker with persistent cough was found to have a lung mass on imaging. A bronchoscope was used to obtain a lung biopsy. Based on the Spaulding classification, what category does this medical device fall under, and what is the appropriate sterilisation or disinfection agent?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Semi-critical device and Glutaraldehyde

| Risk Category | Recommended Method | Medical Device / Equipment

| ------------- | ------------------ | --------------------------

| 1. Critical device (high risk): Items that enter a normally sterile site | Sterilisation • If heat resistant: Hot air oven or autoclave • If heat sensitive: Ionising radiation or ethylene oxide or plasma sterilisation | Surgical instruments, implants/prosthesis, rigid endoscopes, syringes, needles, CuT, urinary catheter

| 2. Semi-critical device (intermediate risk): Items in contact with mucous membranes or body fluids | High-level disinfection (HLD): Glutaraldehyde, ortho-phthalaldehyde, formaldehyde, hydrogen peroxide | Respiratory equipment, non-invasive flexible endoscopes, bedpans, urine bottles

| 3. Non-critical (low-risk): Items in contact with intact skin | Intermediate or Low-level disinfection (ILD / LLD): Phenols, chlorhexidine, isopropyl alcohol, povidone iodine, etc. | Patient items: Blood pressure cuffs, ECG electrodes, thermometers, stethoscopes Environmental surfaces: Computers, bed rails, food utensils, bedside tables, patient furniture, floor

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A farmer presenting with fever off and on for the past 4 years was diagnosed to be suffering from chronic brucellosis. All of the following serological tests would be helpful in the diagnosis at this state except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Standard Agglutination test

Chronic brucellosis often shows low or absent IgM antibodies, while IgG and incomplete (blocking) antibodies predominate. Therefore, some serological tests become more useful than others in chronic infection.

Serological tests in brucellosis:

•

Standard Agglutination Test (SAT)

o    Mainly detects IgM antibodies.

o    Useful in acute brucellosis, but may be negative in chronic disease.

•

2-Mercaptoethanol (2-ME) test

o    Destroys IgM antibodies and measures IgG levels.

o    Helpful for chronic or persistent infection.

•

Complement Fixation Test (CFT)

o    Detects IgG antibodies.

o    Useful in chronic brucellosis.

•

Coombs (antiglobulin) test

o    Detects incomplete or blocking antibodies that may not agglutinate normally.

o    Important for diagnosing chronic cases.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A freshly passed stool sample suspected of containing Shigella needs to be transported to the microbiology lab with minimal viability loss. Which transport medium is most appropriate?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Sach’s Buffered Glycerol Saline

Shigella is a fragile enteric pathogen that rapidly loses viability outside the body. Therefore, stool samples suspected of containing Shigella require a special transport medium to preserve the organism during transport.

Sach’s Buffered Glycerol Saline (SBGS) is the preferred transport medium for Shigella because:

• Buffered saline maintains a stable pH.
• Glycerol protects the bacteria and maintains viability.
• It prevents overgrowth of commensal organisms during transport.

Why not other options:

A. Carry–Blair: General stool transport medium; not ideal for fragile Shigella.

B. Stuart: Transport medium for swab specimens, not stool.

D. Wilson–Blair: Selective culture medium for Salmonella, not a transport medium.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A hospitalized patient develops bloodstream infection with Enterococcus faecium that is resistant to vancomycin. Genetic analysis reveals alteration in the terminal amino acids of peptidoglycan precursors. Which of the following best explains the mechanism of resistance?
options: Replacement of D-Ala-D-Ala with D-Ala-D-Ser in peptidoglycan precursors
Replacement of D-Ala-D-Ala with D-Ala-D-Lac in peptidoglycan precursors
Increased production of altered penicillin-binding proteins
Enzymatic inactivation of vancomycin by bacterial enzymes
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Replacement of D-Ala-D-Ala with D-Ala-D-Lac in peptidoglycan precursors

Vancomycin inhibits cell wall synthesis by binding to the D-Ala–D-Ala terminus of peptidoglycan precursors.

Mechanism of resistance (VRE):

• Target modification → replacement of D-Ala–D-Ala with D-Ala–D-Lac
• Leads to marked reduction in drug binding affinity
• Mediated by Van genes (e.g., VanA, VanB)

Important distinctions:

• Not due to β-lactamase or enzymatic drug destruction
• Not due to altered PBPs (seen in MRSA)
• Not due to efflux or porin changes

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A man who is fond of exotic cuisine develops perioral numbness after eating the pufferfish. The given poisoning is due to which of the folowing toxins?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Tetrodotoxin

This question tests identification of marine toxin poisoning based on clinical presentation and source.

• Tetrodotoxin (TTX):

• Found in pufferfish (fugu)
• Causes perioral numbness, paresthesia → paralysis
• Mechanism: blocks voltage-gated Na⁺ channels → prevents nerve conduction

• Clinical features:

• Early: perioral tingling, numbness
• Later: weakness, paralysis, respiratory failure
• Consciousness usually preserved

• Differentiation (high-yield):

• Saxitoxin: shellfish poisoning (similar mechanism but different source)
• Ciguatoxin: reef fish → causes reversal of hot/cold sensation
• Curare: NMJ blocker, not food poisoning

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A municipality health officer reviews malaria data. State API = 0.7, but one district has API = 1.3. The SPR in that district suddenly doubled over 2 weeks. Which NVBDCP classification category applies to this state and what does the SPR specifically indicate?
options: Category 0 (Prevention of re-establishment); SPR = operational efficiency
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Category 2 (Pre-elimination); SPR = outbreak indicator

NVBDCP state classification:

| Classification | State API | District API | Category

| -------------- | --------- | ------------ | --------

| Intensified Malaria Control | >1 | — | 3

| Pre-elimination | <1 | Few districts >1 | 2

| Elimination | <1 | <1 | 1

| Prevention of re-establishment | — | 0 | 0

State API = 0.7 (<1) BUT one district = 1.3 (>1) = Pre-elimination = Category 2.

Malaria indicators:

| Indicator | Formula | Measures

| --------- | ------- | --------

| API | Confirmed cases/Population × 1000 | Malaria prevalence

| ABER | Slides examined/Population × 100 | Fever prevalence (operational efficiency)

| SPR | Slides +ve/Slides examined × 100 | Outbreak indicator

Sudden doubling of SPR = outbreak signal, not prevalence trend.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A newborn is delivered to an HIV-positive mother. The infant has received perinatal HIV prophylaxis and is scheduled for early infant diagnosis. According to guidelines, when should cotrimoxazole prophylaxis be initiated in this child?
options: At 6 weeks of age, regardless of HIV status
Only if the infant tests HIV positive at 6 months
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. At 6 weeks of age, regardless of HIV status

Infants born to HIV-positive mothers are at increased risk of opportunistic infections, especially Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP).

Guideline recommendation:

• Cotrimoxazole prophylaxis should be started at 6 weeks of age in all HIV-exposed infants, regardless of their HIV test result, because infection status may not yet be definitively known.
• Continued until HIV infection is definitively ruled out or lifelong if the child is confirmed HIV-positive.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient develops prosthetic valve endocarditis 2 years after valve replacement surgery. Which of the following organisms is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Streptococcus viridans

Late prosthetic valve endocarditis (occurring >1 year after valve replacement) is most commonly caused by Streptococcus viridans, which originates from the oral cavity and enters the bloodstream after dental procedures or poor oral hygiene.

Key Point:

• Early prosthetic valve endocarditis (<1 year): usually Staphylococcus epidermidis (coagulase-negative staphylococci) from surgical contamination.
• Late prosthetic valve endocarditis (>1 year): resembles native valve endocarditis, most commonly due to Streptococcus viridans.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient on a multidrug regimen for XDR-tuberculosis presents after 6 weeks of treatment with bilateral, symmetric tingling and numbness starting below the knees, along with new-onset thrombocytopenia. Which drug in the regimen is most likely responsible, and via what mechanism does it act against M. tuberculosis?
options: Linezolid — binds 23S rRNA of the 50S ribosomal subunit, blocking initiation of protein synthesis
Cycloserine — inhibits D-alanine racemase and ligase
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Linezolid — binds 23S rRNA of the 50S ribosomal subunit, blocking initiation of protein synthesis

Linezolid toxicity should be suspected in patients receiving prolonged therapy for MDR/XDR-TB who develop peripheral neuropathy and thrombocytopenia. These adverse effects result from inhibition of mitochondrial protein synthesis, which is particularly evident after several weeks of treatment. The patient’s:

• Bilateral symmetric distal paresthesias (stocking distribution neuropathy)
• New-onset thrombocytopenia

are classic adverse effects of linezolid.

Mechanism of Action:

• Linezolid binds to the 23S rRNA component of the 50S ribosomal subunit.
• Prevents formation of the 70S initiation complex.
• Inhibits the initiation step of bacterial protein synthesis.

| Drug | Mechanism | Characteristic Toxicity

| ---- | --------- | -----------------------

| Linezolid | Binds 23S rRNA of 50S subunit | Neuropathy, thrombocytopenia

| Bedaquiline | Inhibits mycobacterial ATP synthase | QT prolongation

| Clofazimine | Generates reactive oxygen species | Skin discoloration

| Cycloserine | Inhibits D-alanine racemase and ligase | Psychosis, seizures

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient on ATT for MDR-TB is started on ART for newly diagnosed HIV. After initiating ART, he develops paradoxical worsening — fever, lymphadenopathy, new pulmonary infiltrates at 3 weeks. What is the most likely diagnosis, and at which ART organization level would this patient ideally be managed?
options: Treatment failure; ART Plus centre (Medical college)
Immune Reconstitution Inflammatory Syndrome (IRIS); ART Plus centre
New opportunistic infection; Link ART centre
Drug reaction to Rifabutin; ART centre (District hospital)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Immune Reconstitution Inflammatory Syndrome (IRIS); ART Plus centre

• Diagnosis: Paradoxical worsening AFTER starting ART = IRIS (Immune Reconstitution Inflammatory Syndrome).
• Mechanism: recovering immune system mounts inflammatory response against existing TB antigens → clinical deterioration despite microbiological improvement.
• Timing: typically, 2–12 weeks after ART initiation.
• Prevention: starting ATT FIRST → waiting 2 weeks → then ART (reduces IRIS risk).
• Organization level: NACO ART hierarchy:

| Level | Facility

| ----- | --------

| Centre of Excellence (CoE) | HIV research institutes

| ART Plus | Medical colleges

| ART Centre | District hospitals

| Link ART Centre | Block > CHC > PHC

• IRIS in HIV-TB coinfection = complex case → requires ART Plus centre (Medical college level).
• Link workers = from general community/population (bottom level).

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient presented with a prolonged fever of unknown origin (PUO), raising suspicion of brucellosis. To confirm the diagnosis, various dilutions of the patient's serum sample are prepared for a standard agglutination test. The outcome is as follows: Agglutination is observed at serum dilutions of 1:20 and 1:40, while no agglutination occurs at dilutions of 1:80 and 1:160. What factor is accountable for the lack of agglutination in the last two dilutions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Antigen excess

Agglutination tests depend on the formation of an optimal antigen–antibody lattice, which occurs only when antigen and antibody are present in equivalent proportions (zone of equivalence).

In this case

• Agglutination occurs at 1:20 and 1:40 → zone of equivalence
• No agglutination at higher dilutions (1:80, 1:160) because the antibody becomes diluted, resulting in relative antigen excess (postzone phenomenon).

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient presents with mental confusion, visual and auditory hallucinations, perceived changes of body shape, swelling of the tongue and a fear of impending death after he was treated for primary chancre of syphilis with an intramuscular injection. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Hoigne syndrome

Hoigne syndrome (pseudoanaphylactic reaction) is a rare neuropsychiatric reaction that occurs shortly after intramuscular injection of procaine penicillin, commonly used in the treatment of syphilis.

• Sudden mental confusion
• Visual and auditory hallucinations
• Feeling of impending death
• Perceptual disturbances (e.g., altered body shape)
• Anxiety, agitation
• Sometimes tongue swelling or dysarthria

| Feature | Hoigne syndrome | Jarisch–Herxheimer reaction

| ------- | --------------- | ---------------------------

| Cause | Procaine toxicity after IM penicillin | Cytokine release from rapid spirochete destruction

| Onset | Immediately after injection | 1–12 hours after treatment

| Symptoms | Hallucinations, anxiety, fear of death | Fever, chills, myalgia, worsening rash

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient undergoes RT-PCR testing for a viral infection. The report shows a Ct (cycle threshold) value of 15. Another patient tested on the same platform shows a Ct value of 32. Which of the following best explains this difference?
options: Higher Ct value indicates higher viral load
Lower Ct value indicates higher viral load
Ct value is independent of viral load
Both values indicate equal viral infectivity
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Lower Ct value indicates higher viral load

The Ct (cycle threshold) value in RT-PCR represents the number of amplification cycles required for the viral nucleic acid to become detectable.

• Ct value is inversely proportional to viral load

o    Low Ct (e.g., <20) → high viral load

o    High Ct (e.g., >30–35) → low viral load

Interpretation:

• Early detection (low Ct) → more viral RNA present initially
• Late detection (high Ct) → less viral RNA

Clinical relevance:

• Helps estimate infectivity and stage of infection
• Must be interpreted cautiously due to sampling technique and assay variability

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient with a deep soft-tissue abscess caused by S. aureus fails to clear infection despite adequate neutrophil response. The organism is known to express a virulence factor that binds the Fc portion of IgG, preventing opsonization and phagocytosis. Which virulence factor is responsible?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Protein A

Staphylococcus aureus evades immune clearance using Protein A, an important virulence factor present on its cell wall.

• Protein A binds the Fc portion of IgG antibodies.
• This prevents the Fc region from interacting with Fc receptors on phagocytes.
• As a result, opsonization and phagocytosis are inhibited, allowing the bacteria to persist despite neutrophil presence.
• Contributes to persistent infections and abscess formation caused by S. aureus.

Why not other options:

A. M protein: Virulence factor of Streptococcus pyogenes, prevents phagocytosis by inhibiting complement deposition.

C. Capsule antigen K: Seen in E. coli and some other bacteria; helps resist phagocytosis but does not bind Fc of IgG.

D. Streptolysin O: A hemolysin toxin of Streptococcus pyogenes that damages cell membranes, not involved in IgG binding.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A sandfly bite victim from Bihar develops fever, weight loss, and massive splenomegaly. The sandfly responsible has specific characteristics. A community health worker uses a field test for surveillance. Simultaneously a researcher wants the gold standard confirmation. Match the correct investigations and identify the unique characteristic of the sandfly vector that explains why indoor residual spraying (IRS) is effective against it:
options: Surveillance: RK39; Gold standard: Aldehyde test; sandfly cannot fly
Surveillance: Aldehyde test of Napier; Gold standard: LD bodies in culture; sandfly only hops
Surveillance: Peripheral blood film; Gold standard: RK39; sandfly is nocturnal
Surveillance: RK39; Gold standard: LD bodies; sandfly hops long distances
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Surveillance: Aldehyde test of Napier; Gold standard: LD bodies in culture; sandfly only hops

Investigations:

| Test | Purpose | Notes

| ---- | ------- | -----

| RK39 | IOC for individual diagnosis | Serological

| Aldehyde test of Napier | Community surveillance | Field applicable

| LD body identification from culture | Gold standard | Spleen/blood smear

Sandfly characteristics:

| Feature | Detail

| ------- | ------

| Wings | Lanceolate

| Flight range | None — only hops

| Body | Hairy (cannot sustain flight)

| Feeding | Nocturnal, painful bite

Because sandfly only hops and cannot fly, it stays close to walls and ground → IRS (Indoor Residual Spraying) is highly effective — sandfly rests on sprayed walls after feeding → dies. DDT = insecticide of choice for Kala Azar vector control.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A scientist studying mobile genetic elements finds DNA segments capable of changing their chromosomal position. Such elements were first discovered in maize, and the discovery was later awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. Which scientist received this award for demonstrating transposable elements?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Barbara McClintock

• Transposable elements (“jumping genes”) are mobile DNA sequences that can move from one location to another within the genome, altering gene expression and causing mutations.

• These elements were first discovered in maize (corn) by Barbara McClintock, who demonstrated that certain DNA segments could change their chromosomal position and influence neighboring genes. For this discovery, Barbara McClintock received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1983.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A soldier presents with fever, rash not involving the palms and soles and myalgia. There is also history of louse infestation in the soldier barracks. The probable causative organism is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. R. prowazekii

Epidemic typhus is caused by Rickettsia prowazekii and is transmitted by the human body louse. It commonly occurs in crowded conditions such as military barracks, prisons, or refugee camps. Clinical features include:

• High fever
• Severe headache and myalgia
• Maculopapular rash that begins on the trunk and spreads outward but typically spares the palms and soles

Why not other options:

• R. conorii: Causes Mediterranean spotted fever transmitted by ticks; rash usually involves palms and soles.
• R. typhi: Causes endemic (murine) typhus transmitted by fleas from rats, not lice.
• R. akari: Causes rickettsialpox transmitted by mites and typically produces an eschar at the bite site.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A state health worker applies indoor spray insecticide for adult mosquito control. The most commonly used indoor spray insecticide is selected. Simultaneously, for space spraying during a dengue outbreak, a different agent is chosen. What is the correct pairing and why is DDT being phased out despite its effectiveness?
options: Indoor: DDT; Space: Malathion; DDT phased out due to cost
Indoor: Malathion; Space: Cyfluthrin; DDT phased out due to resistance and toxicity
Indoor: Cyfluthrin; Space: DDT; DDT phased out due to resistance only
Indoor: Malathion; Space: DDT; DDT still first line for indoor spray
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Indoor: Malathion; Space: Cyfluthrin; DDT phased out due to resistance and toxicity

Anti-adult measures:

| Method | Agent

| ------ | -----

| Indoor spray (IRS) | Malathion (M/C used), DDT (being phased out)

| Space spray | Cyfluthrin, Malathion

Why DDT phased out: DDT problems:

• Resistance developed in vectors
• Environmental toxicity (persistent organic pollutant — biomagnification)
• Human toxicity (carcinogenic, endocrine disruptor)
• Banned under Stockholm Convention on persistent organic pollutants

DDT still used for Kala Azar vector control (sandfly) — DDT = insecticide of choice for Kala Azar because sandfly only hops and rests on walls.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A stool sample from a patient with chronic abdominal discomfort shows brown, spherical eggs with a thick, radially striated shell. When subjected to a modified Ziehl–Neelsen stain, the egg wall appears acid-fast. This finding is most consistent with:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Taenia saginata

Taenia species eggs are brown, spherical with a thick radially striated shell (embryophore) and contain a hexacanth embryo with hooklets.

Special staining property:

• On modified Ziehl–Neelsen stain, the egg wall of Taenia saginata may show acid-fast staining.

Diagnostic points:

• Eggs indicate Taenia infection.
• Species differentiation usually requires proglottids or scolex examination:

o    T. saginata: 15–30 uterine branches, unarmed scolex

o    T. solium: 7–13 uterine branches, armed scolex

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A technician wants to sterilize the material of the laboratory. Which of the following is a correct combination for him to use?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Liquid paraffin- Hot air oven

Different laboratory materials require specific sterilization methods depending on their heat stability and composition.

• Hot air oven (dry heat sterilization) is used for oils, fats, waxes, and powders that cannot be sterilized by moist heat. Therefore, liquid paraffin is sterilized using a hot air oven.

Why not other options:

B. Heat-sensitive vaccine – Pasteurization: Pasteurization reduces microbial load but does not sterilize; vaccines require cold storage or filtration, not pasteurization.

C. LSS medium – Autoclave: Loeffler’s serum slope (LSS) contains serum, which is damaged by autoclaving; it is sterilized by inspissation, not autoclave.

D. Catgut sutures – Autoclave: Catgut is heat sensitive and is sterilized by chemical methods (e.g., iodine/alcohol) or irradiation, not autoclaving.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: All are true about cephalosporins except:
options: Cefazolin is a first generation parenteral cephalosporin
Cefixime has poor activity against Staph aureus
Cefoxitin has no activity against anaerobes
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Cefoxitin has no activity against anaerobes

Cephalosporins are β-lactam antibiotics classified into generations based on their antimicrobial spectrum.

• Cefazolin

• First-generation cephalosporin
• Given parenterally
• Good activity against gram-positive cocci
• Commonly used for surgical prophylaxis

• Cefoperazone

• Third-generation cephalosporin
• Has antipseudomonal activity

• Cefixime

• Third-generation oral cephalosporin
• Poor activity against Staphylococcus aureus

• Cefoxitin

• A second-generation cephamycin
• Good activity against anaerobes, especially Bacteroides fragilis
• Used in intra-abdominal and pelvic infections

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: All are true about Mission AIDS Suraksha except:
options: India has upgraded to 95-95-99 targets, aiming for viral suppression by 1 December 2027
Viral suppression is defined as HIV RNA ≤ 200 copies/mL, targeted in 99% of those on treatment
219 high-priority districts are classified into 4 tiers via Suraksha Sankalp Karyashala workshops
'Surakshit' status requires all of 95-95-99 plus zero mother-to-child transmission of HIV, syphilis and Hep B
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 'Surakshit' status requires all of 95-95-99 plus zero mother-to-child transmission of HIV, syphilis and Hep B

None

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: All of the following are true regarding the 2025 updates in drug-sensitive TB treatment in adults, except:
options: The new regimen duration is 4 months
Moxifloxacin replaces ethambutol in the intensive phase
Rifapentine is included in both intensive and continuation phases
Pyrazinamide is continued in the continuation phase
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Pyrazinamide is continued in the continuation phase

The updated shorter regimen for drug-sensitive tuberculosis (DS-TB) in adults is a 4-month regimen based on rifapentine and moxifloxacin.

• Intensive phase:

• Rifapentine
• Isoniazid
• Pyrazinamide
• Moxifloxacin

(Ethambutol is replaced by moxifloxacin)

• Continuation phase:

• Rifapentine
• Isoniazid
• Moxifloxacin

Pyrazinamide is NOT continued in the continuation phase, making option D incorrect.

High-yield facts:

• Rifapentine is a long-acting rifamycin
• The regimen shortens treatment duration from 6 months to 4 months
• Intended for selected adults with drug-sensitive pulmonary TB

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: All of the following are Urease-producing organisms except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. V.cholera

• Urease enzyme:

• Converts urea → ammonia + CO₂
• Leads to alkalinization of medium

• Urease-positive organisms (high-yield list):

• Proteus (strongly positive; classic association with struvite stones)
• Nocardia
• Cryptococcus (important diagnostic clue in CSF)

• Urease-negative (exception):

• Vibrio cholerae → does NOT produce urease

Clinical correlation:

• Urease production → ↑ urine pH → predisposes to renal stones (Proteus)

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: All of the following properties are true with regard to Malassezia species except:
options: It easily grows on fungal isolation media
It is the causative agent of pityriasis versicolor
It is susceptible to Amphotericin B
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. It easily grows on fungal isolation media

Malassezia species are lipophilic yeasts that require lipids for growth, which makes them difficult to culture on routine fungal media.

• Cause pityriasis (tinea) versicolor, a superficial fungal infection of the skin.
• Can cause catheter-related fungemia, especially in neonates receiving lipid-rich parenteral nutrition.
• Generally susceptible to antifungals such as amphotericin B and azoles.

Important laboratory point:

• They do not grow easily on standard fungal isolation media unless lipid supplementation (e.g., olive oil) is provided.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: All of the following statements about Tzanck smear are true except:
options: It is performed by scraping the base of the lesion
It can differentiate HSV from VZV
Sensitivity of the test is only about 60%
It can demonstrate multinucleated giant cells
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. It can differentiate HSV from VZV

A Tzanck smear is a rapid cytological test used in the diagnosis of vesicular viral infections, especially Herpes simplex virus (HSV) and Varicella-zoster virus (VZV)

Procedure:

• The base of a vesicular lesion is scraped.
• The smear is stained (e.g., Giemsa or Wright stain) and examined microscopically.

Findings:

• Multinucleated giant cells
• Ballooning degeneration of epithelial cells

Limitation:

• Although it confirms a herpesvirus infection, it cannot differentiate HSV from VZV.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: All of the following statements regarding antifungal drug toxicity are true except:
options: Long-term itraconazole use may cause cardiomyopathy
Amphotericin B can cause renal tubular acidosis
Echinocandins cause severe bone marrow suppression
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Echinocandins cause severe bone marrow suppression

Key toxicities of major antifungals:

•

Itraconazole

o    Can cause negative inotropic effects with long-term use, leading to cardiomyopathy or worsening heart failure.

•

Amphotericin B

o    Causes nephrotoxicity due to renal tubular damage.

o    May lead to renal tubular acidosis, hypokalemia, and hypomagnesemia.

•

Voriconazole

o    Associated with photosensitivity reactions.

o    Long-term use may increase the risk of cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (skin cancer).

•

Echinocandins (e.g., caspofungin, micafungin, anidulafungin)

o    Generally well tolerated.

o    They do NOT cause severe bone marrow suppression, making this statement false.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: All of the following statements regarding Cryptococcus gattii are true, except:
options: It is endemic in tropical and subtropical regions
It corresponds to serotypes B and C
It is commonly associated with eucalyptus trees
It predominantly causes disease in immunocompromised hosts
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. It predominantly causes disease in immunocompromised hosts

Cryptococcus gattii is an encapsulated yeast that differs from Cryptococcus neoformans in epidemiology and host susceptibility.

• Endemic in tropical and subtropical regions (e.g., Australia, Southeast Asia, parts of Africa and South America).
• Corresponds to serotypes B and C.
• Commonly associated with eucalyptus trees and environmental plant material.
• Often infects immunocompetent individuals, causing pulmonary disease and cryptococcal meningitis.

Contrast:

• Cryptococcus neoformans typically infects immunocompromised patients, especially those with HIV/AIDS.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: An F⁺ strain of E. coli conjugates with an F⁻ strain. During the process, the F factor gets incorrectly excised from the chromosome, carrying along a segment of bacterial DNA. The recipient cell subsequently acquires both plasmid and chromosomal genes and becomes partially diploid. Which of the following best explains this phenomenon?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Formation of F′ (F-prime) plasmid

• F′ plasmid forms when F factor excises imprecisely from chromosome
• It carries adjacent bacterial genes
• Transfer leads to partial diploidy (merozygote) in recipient

Other Options:

Option A. Hfr strain → F factor integrated into chromosome (not excised)

Option B. Transduction → bacteriophage-mediated

Option D. Transformation → uptake of naked DNA

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: An HIV-positive pregnant woman, not on ART, delivers a male baby vaginally at term. What is the next step of management in this baby?
options: Start nevirapine syrup once daily at birth
Start zidovudine syrup only after a positive PCR test at birth
Start nevirapine syrup only after a positive PCR test at 6 weeks
Start nevirapine and zidovudine syrup once daily at birth
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Start nevirapine and zidovudine syrup once daily at birth

This newborn is high-risk for HIV transmission because:

• Mother is HIV-positive
• Not on ART
• Delivered vaginally

Management Principle: All HIV-exposed infants receive antiretroviral prophylaxis at birth, not waiting for PCR results

High-risk infant (this case):

• Mother not on ART / inadequate ART / high viral load

Recommended regimen:

• Dual prophylaxis: Nevirapine (NVP) + Zidovudine (AZT)

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: An investigator is studying an experimental treatment for HIV infection that inhibits the maturation of new HIV virions. Patients who are taking the drug are observed for several years and side effects are recorded. A correlation is established between the drug and the development of impaired glucose tolerance. In addition, a significant portion of the patients who take the drug for several years develop kidney stones and show increased fat accumulation in the neck with loss of subcutaneous fat in the face and extremities. Which of the following processes is most likely targeted by this drug?
options: Viral DNA integration into host DNA
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Viral polypeptide cleavage

The drug described inhibits maturation of newly formed HIV virions, which is the mechanism of HIV protease inhibitors. Protease inhibitors block this polypeptide cleavage, resulting in immature, noninfectious viral particles.

Characteristic adverse effects of protease inhibitors:

• Insulin resistance / impaired glucose tolerance
• Lipodystrophy (buffalo hump, loss of peripheral fat)
• Nephrolithiasis (especially with indinavir)

Why not other options:

A. Viral entry into host cell: Blocked by entry inhibitors (eg, maraviroc, enfuvirtide); they do not cause lipodystrophy or nephrolithiasis.

C. Viral DNA integration into host DNA: Targeted by integrase inhibitors (eg, raltegravir); not associated with lipodystrophy syndrome.

D. Reverse transcription of viral RNA: Targeted by NRTIs/NNRTIs; side effects differ (eg, lactic acidosis, neuropathy).

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Anti-larval measures are being taken for a pond in a city. Which of the following synthetic insecticides are not recommended for such measures?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. DDT

Anti-larval measures target the larval stages of mosquitoes in water bodies to prevent adult mosquito emergence.

Common larvicides used:

• Temephos (Abate) – widely used organophosphate larvicide.
• Fenthion – used as a larvicide in water bodies.
• Paris green – copper acetoarsenite historically used against mosquito larvae.

Not recommended for anti-larval control:

• DDT, which is primarily an adulticide used for indoor residual spraying (IRS) to kill adult mosquitoes resting on walls.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Arrange the following in order of being most to least resistant:
options: Spores > Prions > Mycobacterium > Naked virus > Enveloped virus
Prions > Spores > Mycobacterium > Naked virus > Enveloped virus
Mycobacterium > Naked Virus > Spores > Enveloped virus
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Prions > Spores > Mycobacterium > Naked virus > Enveloped virus

Microorganisms vary in their resistance to sterilization and disinfectants. The order from most resistant to least resistant is:

Prions > Bacterial spores > Mycobacteria > Naked (non-enveloped) viruses > Enveloped viruses

• Prions are most resistant because they are misfolded proteins without nucleic acids, resistant to heat, radiation, and many disinfectants.
• Bacterial spores (e.g., Bacillus, Clostridium) resist heat and chemicals due to thick protective coats and low metabolic activity.
• Mycobacteria are moderately resistant because of their lipid-rich mycolic acid cell wall.
• Naked viruses are more resistant than enveloped viruses since they lack a fragile lipid envelope.
• Enveloped viruses are least resistant because their lipid envelope is easily destroyed by detergents, alcohol, and drying.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Arrange the stages of spore formation (sporulation) in correct order:
options: Axial filament formation ➔ Septum formation ➔ Asymmetric division ➔ Engulfment ➔ Cortex formation ➔ Maturation and lysis
Engulfment ➔ Cortex formation ➔ Septum formation ➔ Asymmetric division ➔ Axial filament formation ➔ Maturation and lysis
Septum formation ➔ Asymmetric division ➔ Engulfment ➔ Cortex formation ➔ Maturation and lysis ➔ Axial filament formation
Asymmetric division ➔ Engulfment ➔ Cortex formation ➔ Septum formation ➔ Axial filament formation ➔ Maturation and lysis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Axial filament formation ➔ Septum formation ➔ Asymmetric division ➔ Engulfment ➔ Cortex formation ➔ Maturation and lysis

Sporulation (endospore formation) occurs in certain bacteria such as Bacillus and Clostridium when environmental conditions become unfavorable.

Correct sequence of sporulation:

1. Axial filament formation – Chromosomal DNA aligns along the cell axis.
2. Septum formation – A transverse septum begins to form.
3. Asymmetric division – Formation of a smaller forespore and larger mother cell.
4. Engulfment – The mother cell membrane engulfs the forespore.
5. Cortex formation – A thick peptidoglycan cortex develops around the forespore.
6. Maturation and lysis – The spore matures and the mother cell lyses, releasing the resistant endospore.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Choose the correct statement regarding CMV:
options: Ganciclovir resistance is due to mutation in UL97 phosphotransferase gene
CMV can be cultured in vitro in any mammalian cell
Commonest manifestation of CMV associated disease is watery diarrhea
UL54 mutated CMV strains do not show cross resistance to Foscarnet
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ganciclovir resistance is due to mutation in UL97 phosphotransferase gene

Cytomegalovirus (CMV) is a β-herpesvirus (Human herpesvirus-5) that causes opportunistic infections, especially in immunocompromised patients and transplant recipients.

First-line drug: Ganciclovir / Valganciclovir

Mechanism of resistance:

• Mutation in the UL97 gene prevents phosphorylation of ganciclovir.
• As a result, the drug cannot be activated, leading to ganciclovir resistance.

Other important points:

B. CMV can be cultured in vitro in any mammalian cell: CMV grows best in human fibroblast cell cultures, not in all mammalian cells.

C. Commonest manifestation of CMV associated disease is watery diarrhea: Common CMV disease manifestations include retinitis, colitis, esophagitis, and pneumonitis, not watery diarrhea as the most common symptom.

D. UL54 mutated CMV strains do not show cross resistance to Foscarnet: UL54 gene mutations (viral DNA polymerase) can cause cross-resistance to ganciclovir, cidofovir, and sometimes foscarnet.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: During conjugation experiments, a donor strain transfers antibiotic resistance and lactose fermentation genes to a recipient cell. However, the recipient rarely becomes F⁺ after mating. Which type of donor strain is most likely involved?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hfr strain

Hfr (High-frequency recombination) strains are bacterial donor cells in which the F (fertility) plasmid is integrated into the bacterial chromosome.

Mechanism during conjugation:

• DNA transfer begins from the integrated F factor.
• Chromosomal genes adjacent to the F factor (e.g., antibiotic resistance, lactose fermentation genes) are transferred to the recipient.
• Because the entire F factor is rarely transferred, the recipient usually remains F⁻ even though it acquires some donor chromosomal genes.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: During the production of a viral vaccine using embryonated hen’s eggs, which site is specifically utilised for the cultivation of yellow fever virus?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Allantoic Sac

• Embryonated hen’s eggs are commonly used for cultivation of viruses for vaccine production and laboratory isolation. Different viruses grow in specific compartments of the egg.
• Yellow fever virus is cultivated in the allantoic sac, where it multiplies efficiently and can be harvested for vaccine preparation.
• Common egg inoculation sites:

| Site | Viruses commonly grown

| ---- | ----------------------

| Chorio-allantoic membrane (CAM) | Poxviruses, herpes viruses

| Allantoic sac | Influenza virus vaccine, Rabies vaccine, Yellow fever virus

| Amniotic sac | Primary isolation of influenza

| Yolk sac | Chlamydia, arbovirus, rickettsiae "CAR"

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Enzyme derived from a bacteria that acts by converting plasminogen to plasmin, thereby promoting clot lysis. The enzyme was originally isolated from β-hemolytic streptococci belonging to Lancefield Group C. The most likely bacterial source of this enzyme is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Streptococcus equisimilis

• Streptokinase = fibrinolysin enzyme (activates plasminogen → plasmin)
• Historically obtained from Group C β-hemolytic streptococci
• The key species is Streptococcus equisimilis
• Streptokinase is used clinically as a thrombolytic agent

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Identify the correct agent-disease pairings from the list provided: 1. Lyme disease — Borrelia burgdorferi 2. Cat-scratch disease — Bartonella henselae 3. Glanders — Burkholderia mallei 4. Rat bite fever — Borrelia recurrentis 5. Trench fever — Bartonella bacilliformis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 2, 3

Correct agent–disease associations are important for identifying zoonotic and vector-borne infections.

Correct pairs:

1. Lyme disease — Borrelia burgdorferi

• Transmitted by Ixodes ticks and causes erythema migrans and multisystem disease.

2. Cat-scratch disease — Bartonella henselae

• Transmitted via cat scratches or bites, causing regional lymphadenopathy.

3. Glanders — Burkholderia mallei

• Zoonotic infection transmitted from infected horses or donkeys, causing pulmonary or septic disease.

Incorrect pairs:

4. Rat bite fever is caused by Streptobacillus moniliformis (common) or Spirillum minus\, not Borrelia recurrentis.

5. Trench fever is caused by Bartonella quintana\, not Bartonella bacilliformis (which causes Carrion’s disease).

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Identify the correct statements about malaria control: 1. Urban malaria scheme is based on anti-larval measures where SPR >5% 2. Anti-adult measures include ITBN and LLIN 3. Most efficient to control urban malaria is environmental control of diseases 4. Synthetic pyrethroids are agents of choice for Sandfly
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 3, 4

Malaria control programs involve vector control measures and environmental management, especially in urban areas.

• Urban Malaria Scheme (UMS): Focuses mainly on anti-larval measures when Slide Positivity Rate (SPR) > 5%.
• Environmental control: The most effective method in urban malaria control is source reduction, such as eliminating stagnant water where mosquitoes breed.
• Insecticides: Synthetic pyrethroids are commonly used insecticides for sandfly control (important in vector control programs).

Note:

• ITBN/LLIN are personal protective measures against mosquito bites but are not classified as anti-adult mosquito control strategies in this context.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: In a busy OPD at a District hospital, you are evaluating a 5-year-old boy who presents with fever, generalized malaise, and a distinctive rash. The child's clinical presentation strongly suggests a diagnosis of measles. The mother, anxious about the contagious nature of the disease and the risk it poses to her other kids and family members, inquires about the recommended period of isolation for her infected child. What would be your most appropriate recommendation for the duration of isolation?
options: From onset of rash to 3 days after rash
2 weeks before rash to 1 week after rash
From onset of rash to 5 days after rash
From catarrhal stage to 4 days after rash
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. From catarrhal stage to 4 days after rash

Measles is highly contagious, with the maximum infectivity during the catarrhal (prodromal) stage, when symptoms such as fever, cough, coryza, and conjunctivitis appear.

Period of infectivity:

• Begins during the catarrhal stage (about 4 days before rash onset)
• Continues until 4 days after the appearance of the rash

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: In a dengue-prone zone, 300 houses were inspected. 120 breeding containers were found, of which 90 were Aedes-positive. What is the Breteau Index?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 30

The Breteau Index (BI) is an entomological indicator used in dengue surveillance to measure the density of Aedes mosquito breeding.

Calculation in this case:

• Houses inspected = 300
• Aedes-positive containers = 90

A higher Breteau Index indicates a greater risk of dengue transmission in the community.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: In a patient presented with a fever and a positive filarial antigen test, what is the next best step of management?
options: Detection of microfilariae in the blood smear
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Detection of microfilariae in the blood smear

This question tests the diagnostic approach to filariasis, especially how to proceed after a positive circulating filarial antigen (CFA) test.

• Filarial antigen test (CFA):

• Detects adult worm antigen (commonly Wuchereria bancrofti)
• Can be positive even when microfilariae are not yet demonstrated

• Next step after positive antigen test:

• Confirm infection by demonstrating microfilariae in peripheral blood smear
• Blood should ideally be collected at night (nocturnal periodicity)

This Confirms active infection and parasitemia and Helps in:

• Disease staging
• Monitoring treatment response

Why other options are incorrect:

• Bone marrow biopsy → not relevant
• DEC provocation test → outdated, rarely used now
• Scrotal ultrasound → useful for detecting “filarial dance sign” but not first confirmatory step

questions.subject: Microbiology
