questions.text: In a patient with HIV, which of following is correct statement for prophylaxis of opportunistic infections?
options: Prophylaxis for Pneumocystis carinii Pneumonia (PCP) is indicated when CD4 count is <500/ul
Stop prophylaxis for PCP if CD4 count is >350/ul on two occasions 6 months apart
Prophylaxis for MAC is indicated when CD4 count is <350/ul
Prophylaxis for Cryptococcus is indicated when CD4 count is <150/pl
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Stop prophylaxis for PCP if CD4 count is >350/ul on two occasions 6 months apart

Prophylaxis against opportunistic infections in HIV is guided by the CD4 cell count.

Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP):

• Start prophylaxis: when CD4 <200 cells/µL.
• Stop prophylaxis: when CD4 count rises above \~200–350 cells/µL for at least 3–6 months on effective ART.

Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC):

• Prophylaxis indicated when CD4 <50 cells/µL (e.g., azithromycin or clarithromycin).

Cryptococcal infection:

• Routine primary prophylaxis is not generally recommended, even at low CD4 counts.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: In a region, health officials report that the prevalence of a certain infectious disease is greater than 5% among high-risk populations but less than 1% among pregnant women. How should this region be classified in terms of disease prevalence?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Moderate prevalence region

This question tests epidemiological classification of disease prevalence, commonly applied to infections like HIV. Key classification criteria:

• High prevalence:

• 5% in high-risk groups AND
• ≥1% in antenatal (pregnant women)

• Moderate prevalence:

• 5% in high-risk groups
• <1% in antenatal population ✅

• Low prevalence:

• <5% in high-risk groups
• <1% in antenatal population

Application to this case:

• High-risk group prevalence >5%
• Pregnant women <1%

→ Moderate prevalence region

Core concept:

• Antenatal prevalence reflects general population spread
• High-risk group prevalence reflects concentrated epidemic

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Match the following mycobacterium with characteristic feature: List I (Organism) A. Mycobacterium kansasii B. Mycobacterium scrofulaceum C. Mycobacterium avium complex D. Mycobacterium fortuitum E. Mycobacterium marinum List II (Characteristic) 1. Rapid grower (<7 days) 2. Photochromogen (pigment on light exposure) 3. Nonchromogen, AIDS-associated infection 4. Scotochromogen (pigment in dark) 5. Fish tank granuloma, grows at lower temp
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. A-2, B-4, C-3, D-1, E-5

Atypical (non-tuberculous) mycobacteria are identified by integrating Runyon classification with clinical context.

Key classification principles:

• Photochromogens → pigment only after light exposure (M. kansasii)
• Scotochromogens → pigment even in dark (M. scrofulaceum)
• Nonchromogens → no pigment (Mycobacterium avium complex)
• Rapid growers → grow within 7 days (M. fortuitum)

Clinical correlations:

• MAC → disseminated disease in immunocompromised (AIDS)
• M. marinum → fish tank granuloma, grows at lower temperatures
• M. kansasii → TB-like pulmonary disease

| Runyon Group | Organism | Key Feature | Clinical Association

| ------------ | -------- | ----------- | --------------------

| Photochromogen | Mycobacterium kansasii | Pigment only on light exposure | TB-like pulmonary disease

| Mycobacterium marinum | Grows at low temp (30–32°C) | Fish tank granuloma |

| Scotochromogen | Mycobacterium scrofulaceum | Pigment even in dark | Cervical lymphadenitis in children

| Nonchromogen | Mycobacterium avium complex | No pigment | Disseminated disease in AIDS

| Mycobacterium ulcerans | Mycolactone toxin | Buruli ulcer (chronic skin ulcer) |

| Rapid growers | Mycobacterium fortuitum | Growth <7 days | Wound infections, post-surgical infections

| Mycobacterium chelonae | Rapid growth | Skin/soft tissue infections |

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Match the type of motility (List I) with the organism (List II): List I (Motility Pattern) A. Darting motility B. Tumbling motility C. Swarming motility D. Corkscrew motility E. Umbrella motility (at 25°C) List II (Organism) 1. Proteus mirabilis 2. Vibrio cholerae 3. Listeria monocytogenes 4. Treponema pallidum 5. Campylobacter jejuni
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. A-2, B-3, C-1, D-4, E-3

| Motility Type | Correct Organism | Key Point

| ------------- | ---------------- | ---------

| Darting | Vibrio > Campylobacter | Rapid, corkscrew-like darting motion (o)

| Tumbling | Listeria monocytogenes | Seen in broth culture

| Swarming | Proteus mirabilis | Concentric rings on agar

| Corkscrew | Treponema pallidum | Spirochete movement

| Umbrella (25°C) | Listeria monocytogenes | Characteristic lab pattern

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Mazzotti test is the name given to:
options: Complement fixation test for Loa loa
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Provocation test for Onchocerca volvulus

The Mazzotti test is a provocation test used in the diagnosis of onchocerciasis, caused by Onchocerca volvulus.

Principle:

• The patient is given a small oral dose of diethylcarbamazine (DEC).
• In individuals infected with Onchocerca volvulus, the drug causes rapid killing of microfilariae, which triggers a localized allergic reaction.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Mission AIDS Suraksha aims to achieve HIV epidemic control in India by December 1, 2027. Regarding its targets and district performance categories, all of the following are correct except:
options: The “99” target refers to suppressed viral load
Surakshit+ districts have zero vertical transmission of HIV, Syphilis, and Hepatitis B
Saksham districts have achieved all three 95:95:99 targets
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Saksham districts have achieved all three 95:95:99 targets

Mission AIDS Suraksha is India’s strategy to achieve HIV epidemic control by 2027 through expanded testing, treatment, and viral suppression.

The “95:95:95” targets mean:

• 95% of people living with HIV know their status
• 95% of diagnosed individuals receive ART
• 95% of those on ART achieve viral suppression

In updated national goals, the final target may be extended to “99” for viral suppression performance indicators in specific program metrics.

District performance categories:

• Surakshit+ districts → elimination of vertical transmission of HIV, syphilis, and hepatitis B
• Saksham districts → progressing districts with strong HIV program implementation, but not necessarily achieving all 95:95:99 targets

Therefore, saying Saksham districts have achieved all three 95:95:99 targets is incorrect.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: New Delhi metallo-beta-lactamase (NDM-1) confers resistance to which class of antibiotics?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Carbapenems

New Delhi metallo-β-lactamase-1 (NDM-1) is a metallo-β-lactamase enzyme produced by certain gram-negative bacteria (e.g., Klebsiella pneumoniae, Escherichia coli). It hydrolyzes β-lactam antibiotics, particularly carbapenems, which are usually considered last-line drugs for multidrug-resistant infections.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Regarding mechanisms of genetic exchange in bacteria, which of the following statements are correct? 1. Transduction is mediated by bacteriophages and may be generalized or specialized 2. Conjugation requires direct cell-to-cell contact and is mediated by sex pili 3. Transformation requires viable donor bacteria for DNA transfer 4. Specialized transduction transfers only specific portions of bacterial DNA 5. F factor integration into bacterial chromosome converts F⁺ cell into Hfr strain 6. Conjugation can occur between Gram-positive bacteria via pili formation
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2, 4, 5

Bacterial genetics is driven by horizontal gene transfer, which enables rapid spread of antibiotic resistance and virulence factors.

Key mechanisms:

• Transformation → uptake of naked DNA from environment (no live donor needed)
•

Transduction → bacteriophage-mediated DNA transfer

• Generalized → random DNA
• Specialized → specific genes near prophage site

•

Conjugation → direct cell-to-cell transfer via plasmids

• F⁺ cell → transfers plasmid
• Hfr strain → transfers chromosomal genes due to F-factor integration

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Several residents of a jail develop febrile illness within a short period of time. Symptoms include fever, nonproductive cough, myalgia, rigors, dyspnea, and diarrhea. Organisms found in induced sputum samples stain poorly with Gram stain but are visualized easily using silver stain. Urine testing for bacterial antigens is positive in most of the affected individuals. Which of the following is the most likely source of this outbreak?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Building water-distribution system

This question tests recognition of Legionella infection (Legionnaires’ disease) and its environmental source.

• Causative organism: Legionella pneumophila
• Transmission:

• Inhalation of aerosolized contaminated water
• Common in closed settings (jails, hotels, hospitals)

• Source (high-yield):

• Building water-distribution systems
• Air conditioners, cooling towers, showers

• Diagnostic clues:

• Poor Gram stain visualization
• Seen with silver stain
• Urinary antigen test positive (important rapid test)

• Clinical features:

• Atypical pneumonia + systemic features
• Fever, dry cough, dyspnea
• GI symptoms (diarrhea) and myalgia (classic clue)

• Differentiation:

• Not spread person-to-person
• Not foodborne

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Solvent/Detergent (SD) plasma destroys lipid-enveloped viruses. So, on SD plasma transfusion, which of the following infection is likely to occur?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hepatitis A Virus (HAV)

Solvent/detergent (SD) treatment of plasma inactivates lipid-enveloped viruses by disrupting their lipid membrane. Therefore, it effectively eliminates viruses such as HIV, hepatitis B virus (HBV), and hepatitis C virus (HCV). However, non-enveloped viruses lack a lipid membrane and are resistant to this process. Hepatitis A virus (HAV), a non-enveloped RNA virus, can therefore still be transmitted through SD-treated plasma.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Terizidone acts mainly by inhibiting:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Cell wall synthesis

Terizidone is a second-line antitubercular drug used in the treatment of multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB). It is a prodrug of cycloserine.

• Inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis by blocking enzymes involved in peptidoglycan formation, particularly:

• Alanine racemase
• D-alanine–D-alanine ligase

This prevents formation of D-alanine, an essential component of the mycobacterial cell wall.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: The following are types of rapid molecular tests under NTEP except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. MGIT960

Under the National Tuberculosis Elimination Programme (NTEP), rapid molecular diagnostic tests are used for early detection of Mycobacterium tuberculosis and drug resistance. Rapid molecular tests include:

• CBNAAT (Cartridge-Based Nucleic Acid Amplification Test / GeneXpert)
• TrueNAAT (chip-based real-time PCR test)
• LPA (Line Probe Assay) for detecting resistance to rifampicin and isoniazid

These tests detect mycobacterial DNA and resistance mutations quickly.

MGIT 960, however, is a liquid culture system used for mycobacterial culture and drug susceptibility testing, not a rapid molecular test.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: The most common organism causing diarrhea associated with shellfish ingestion in adults is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Norovirus

Norovirus is the most common cause of acute gastroenteritis associated with shellfish ingestion, particularly raw or undercooked oysters and other seafood contaminated with sewage.

• Causes acute onset vomiting, watery diarrhea, abdominal cramps, and nausea
• Highly contagious, often causing outbreaks in cruise ships, restaurants, and institutions
• Leading cause of foodborne viral gastroenteritis in adults

Why not other options:

A. Astrovirus: Causes mild diarrhea mainly in children, not typically linked to shellfish outbreaks.

C. Echovirus: An enterovirus causing meningitis or febrile illness, not common foodborne gastroenteritis.

D. Rotavirus: Major cause of severe diarrhea in infants and young children, not shellfish-associated outbreaks.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: The most effective intervention to reduce mother-to-child HIV transmission is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Maternal ART during pregnancy

Maternal antiretroviral therapy (ART) during pregnancy is the most effective intervention to prevent mother-to-child transmission (MTCT) of HIV.

• ART suppresses maternal viral load, which is the most important determinant of transmission.
• Lower viral load significantly reduces intrauterine, intrapartum, and postpartum transmission.

Additional preventive measures include:

• Infant antiretroviral prophylaxis
• Safe infant feeding practices
• Elective cesarean section in selected cases with high viral load

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: The symmetric protein shell which encloses the viral genome is called:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Capsid

The capsid is the protein coat that surrounds and protects the viral nucleic acid (genome).

• The capsid is composed of repeating protein subunits called capsomeres.
• Together, the capsid and viral genome form the nucleocapsid.

Functions of the capsid:

• Protects viral genetic material
• Helps in attachment and entry into host cells
• Determines the shape and symmetry of the virus (icosahedral, helical, complex)

Virion = complete virus particle (capsid ± envelope + genome)

Peplomers = glycoprotein spikes on enveloped viruses

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: The tissue of origin of HeLa cell line is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Carcinoma cervix

The HeLa cell line is derived from cervical carcinoma cells obtained from Henrietta Lacks in 1951. It was the first immortal human cell line successfully cultured in the laboratory.

Characteristics of HeLa cells:

• Derived from cervical cancer tissue
• Immortal cell line with rapid growth in culture
• Widely used in virology, cancer research, vaccine development, and molecular biology

Why not other options:

A. Epithelioma of larynx (HEp-2): Derived from epithelioma of larynx cell line.

B. Carcinoma of nasopharynx (KB): Derived from carcinoma of nasopharynx.

D. Monkey kidney (Vero): Derived from African green monkey kidney cells.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Toxorhynchites mosquitoes are used in biological control because:
options: Adult females suck large quantities of human blood
Larvae prey upon larvae of container-breeding mosquitoes
Adults are strong fliers that transmit arboviruses efficiently
They sterilize other mosquitoes through mating interference
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Larvae prey upon larvae of container-breeding mosquitoes

Toxorhynchites mosquitoes (also called “elephant mosquitoes”) are used in biological control of disease-transmitting mosquitoes because their larvae are predatory.

• Larvae feed on the larvae of other mosquitoes, especially Aedes and Culex species that breed in containers.
• Adult Toxorhynchites mosquitoes do not suck blood; they feed on nectar, so they do not transmit diseases.

Because of their larval predation, they help reduce populations of vector mosquitoes that transmit diseases such as dengue, chikungunya, and Zika.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: What concentration of tetanus antitoxin in the blood is considered clinically protective against tetanus?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. >0.01 IU/ml

Protection against tetanus depends on the presence of neutralizing antibodies against tetanus toxin.

• A serum tetanus antitoxin level ≥0.01 IU/mL is considered the minimum protective level against tetanus.
• This level is achieved after complete immunization with tetanus toxoid–containing vaccines (e.g., DPT, Td).
• Individuals with antibody levels below 0.01 IU/mL are considered susceptible and may require tetanus prophylaxis (vaccine ± tetanus immunoglobulin) after injury.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: What is the most likely mode of transmission of Q fever in humans?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Aerosol inhalation

Q fever is caused by Coxiella burnetii, an obligate intracellular bacterium transmitted mainly from infected livestock (sheep, goats, cattle).

Primary mode of transmission:

• Inhalation of contaminated aerosols containing organisms from animal birth products, urine, feces, or milk.

Key features:

• Highly infectious organism
• Can survive in the environment as spore-like forms
• Occupational risk in farmers, veterinarians, abattoir workers

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: What is the primary function of the CRISPR system in bacteria?
options: To facilitate horizontal gene transfer between bacterial cells
To enable bacteria to resist viral infections through sequence-specific DNA cleavage
To allow the incorporation of viral DNA into the bacterial genome
To protect bacteria from the eukaryotic immune system
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. To enable bacteria to resist viral infections through sequence-specific DNA cleavage

CRISPR (Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats) is a bacterial adaptive immune system that protects bacteria against bacteriophage (viral) infections and foreign genetic elements.

Mechanism:

1. Adaptation (Spacer acquisition): When bacteria are infected by a virus, fragments of viral DNA are incorporated into the CRISPR locus as “spacers”.
2. Expression: The CRISPR region is transcribed into CRISPR RNA (crRNA).
3.

Interference:

4.

CRISPR-associated (Cas) proteins use the crRNA as a guide to recognize complementary viral DNA.

5. The Cas enzyme then cleaves the invading viral DNA, preventing infection.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which among the following is false regarding Mollaret’s meningitis?
options: Diagnosed by demonstration of HSV abs in CSF
Persistence of HSV DNA in CSF
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Neurologic sequelae common

Mollaret’s meningitis is a form of benign recurrent lymphocytic meningitis; most commonly associated with Herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV-2).

• Recurrent episodes of aseptic meningitis
• Lymphocytic pleocytosis in CSF
• Episodes last 2–5 days and resolve spontaneously
• HSV DNA may be detected in CSF by PCR

Important characteristic:

• The disease is self-limiting and typically does not cause permanent neurological sequelae.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which among the following is not a sexual spore?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Sporangiophore

Fungi reproduce through sexual and asexual spores.

Sexual spores are formed after fusion of nuclei (karyogamy) and meiosis. Examples include:

• Zygospore – seen in Zygomycetes (e.g., Rhizopus).
• Ascospore – produced inside an ascus in Ascomycetes.
• Basidiospore – produced on a basidium in Basidiomycetes.

Sporangiophore is not a spore.

• It is a specialized hyphal stalk that bears the sporangium, which contains asexual spores (sporangiospores).

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which method is considered the gold standard for determining the Minimum Inhibitory Concentration (MIC) of an antibiotic?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Broth dilution method

The Minimum Inhibitory Concentration (MIC) is the lowest concentration of an antibiotic that inhibits visible bacterial growth after incubation.

Broth dilution method (macro- or micro-dilution) is considered the gold standard for determining MIC.

• Helps determine antibiotic susceptibility
• Guides appropriate antimicrobial therapy

Why not other options:

A. Kirby–Bauer disk diffusion: Gives zone of inhibition and categorizes bacteria as sensitive/intermediate/resistant, but does not give exact MIC.

C. E-test strip: Provides an approximate MIC, but it is not the gold standard.

D. Agar dilution method: Can determine MIC but is labor-intensive and less commonly used compared to broth dilution.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following best differentiates mutational from transferable drug resistance?
options: Mutational resistance involves plasmids; transferable resistance involves chromosomes
Mutational resistance commonly affects multiple drugs simultaneously
Transferable resistance is usually associated with high-degree enzyme-mediated resistance
Transferable resistance often results in decreased virulence
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Transferable resistance is usually associated with high-degree enzyme-mediated resistance

| Feature | Mutational Drug Resistance | Transferable Drug Resistance

| ------- | -------------------------- | ----------------------------

| Genetic basis | Chromosome mediated | Plasmid mediated

| Drug spectrum | Resistance to one drug | Resistance to multiple drugs

| Transferability | Resistance non-transferable | Resistance transferable

| Effect on virulence | Virulence of organism lowered | Virulence of organism not lowered

| Degree of resistance | Low-degree resistance | High-degree resistance

| Mechanism | Due to decreased permeability, development of alternative metabolic pathway, or inactivation of drug | Due to production of many degrading enzyme

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following correctly describes the hierarchy of NACO ART centres from highest to lowest level according to their organisational structure?
options: ART Centre → Link ART Centre → ART Plus Centre → Centre of Excellence
Centre of Excellence → ART Plus Centre → ART Centre → Link ART Centre
ART Plus Centre → Centre of Excellence → ART Centre → Link ART Centre
Link ART Centre → ART Centre → ART Plus Centre → Centre of Excellence
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Centre of Excellence → ART Plus Centre → ART Centre → Link ART Centre

Hierarchy (highest to lowest, per NACO):

| Level | Function

| ----- | --------

| Centre of Excellence | Tertiary referral, complicated cases, 2nd/3rd-line ART, research

| ART Plus Centre | 2nd-line ART initiation, higher patient load

| ART Centre | 1st-line ART initiation and follow-up

| Link ART Centre | ART drug refill/dispensing only (no new initiation), peripheral access point

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following drug is an anti pseudomonal penicillin?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Piperacillin

Antipseudomonal penicillins are extended-spectrum penicillins that have activity against Pseudomonas aeruginosa, a common cause of hospital-acquired infections.

Piperacillin belongs to the ureidopenicillin group and has broad gram-negative coverage, including Pseudomonas aeruginosa. It is often combined with a β-lactamase inhibitor (tazobactam) to enhance activity against β-lactamase–producing organisms.

Why other options are incorrect

A. Cephalexin – first-generation cephalosporin, mainly gram-positive coverage, no activity against Pseudomonas.

B. Dicloxacillin and C. Cloxacillin – penicillinase-resistant penicillins used mainly for Staphylococcus aureus, not Pseudomonas.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following drugs does not require dose reduction in patients with renal failure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Doxycycline

• Cef in: Cefoperazone, Ceftriaxone
• The: Tigecycline
• R: Rifampicin
• E: Erythromycin
• N: Nafcillin
• A: Ampicillin
• L: Lincosamide (Clindamycin)
• D: Doxycycline

Why the other drugs require dose adjustment:

A. Gentamicin – eliminated almost entirely by the kidneys; accumulation can cause nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity.

B. Vancomycin – renally excreted, requiring dose adjustment and therapeutic drug monitoring.

C. Amphotericin B – causes significant nephrotoxicity, so dosing must be carefully adjusted and monitored in renal impairment.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following is an inclusion criterion for the shorter bedaquiline regimen in the treatment of tuberculosis?
options: INH resistance with both KatG and inhA mutation
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Rifampicin-resistant but fluoroquinolone-sensitive TB

The shorter bedaquiline-containing regimen is used for the treatment of multidrug-resistant or rifampicin-resistant tuberculosis (MDR/RR-TB) under specific eligibility criteria.

Eligibility Criteria — Shorter (9–11 month) All-Oral MDR/RR-TB Regimen

| # | Criterion

| --- | ---------

| i | Confirmed rifampicin resistance (MDR/RR-TB)

| ii | Fluoroquinolone resistance excluded/not detected (this is the single most important eligibility determinant — FQ resistance = ineligible → goes to longer/BPaLM regimen)

| iii | No prior exposure to second-line drugs for >1 month (i.e., not previously treated with second-line anti-TB drugs, excluding exposure for <1 month or to manage DST-resistant strains)

| iv | No severe extrapulmonary disease — excludes CNS TB, spinal/skeletal TB, miliary TB, disseminated TB, or TB with multi-organ involvement

| v | No additional resistance beyond the rifampicin-resistance-conferring mutation — i.e., not both InhA AND KatG mutations together (since dual mutation suggests broader resistance profile affecting high-dose isoniazid efficacy used in the regimen)

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following is not a characteristic feature of EI Tor vibrio?
options: Resistant to El Tor phage V
Not susceptible to group IV phage
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Resistant to El Tor phage V

Vibrio cholerae biotype El Tor differs from the classical biotype in several microbiological characteristics used for laboratory identification.

Characteristic features of El Tor biotype:

• Sensitive to El Tor phage V
• Resistant to polymyxin B
• Voges–Proskauer (VP) test positive
• Hemolytic activity present
• Resistant to classical cholera phage IV

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following is not true regarding Trench fever?
options: Also known as five day fever
Causative organism is associated with culture negative endocarditis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Cat is the animal reservoir

Trench fever is caused by Bartonella quintana and was historically seen among soldiers living in crowded, unhygienic conditions during World War I.

• Also called “five-day fever” because of recurrent febrile episodes every \~5 days.
• Transmitted by the human body louse (Pediculus humanus corporis).
• Common in homeless populations and people living in poor sanitary conditions.
• Bartonella quintana can cause culture-negative endocarditis.

Why option C is incorrect

• Cats are the reservoir for Bartonella henselae, which causes cat-scratch disease, not trench fever.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following is the most peripheral centre under the Revised National Tuberculosis Control Programme organization structure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Designated Microscopy Centre

Under the Revised National Tuberculosis Control Programme (RNTCP)/National Tuberculosis Elimination Programme (NTEP), the TB control system is organized in a hierarchical structure for diagnosis and management.

Structure (from higher to peripheral level):

1.      Intermediate Reference Laboratory (IRL) – performs advanced testing and quality control.

2.      District TB Centre (DTC) – supervises TB control activities at the district level.

3.      Tuberculosis Unit (TU) – covers a population of \~2.5 lakh and supervises field activities.

4.      Designated Microscopy Centre (DMC) – the most peripheral unit, where sputum smear microscopy for TB diagnosis is performed.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following microbes is also referred to as Friedlander's bacillus?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Klebsiella pneumoniae

Friedländer’s bacillus is the historical name for Klebsiella pneumoniae, a gram-negative, encapsulated, non-motile rod belonging to the Enterobacteriaceae family.

• Prominent polysaccharide capsule → gives colonies a mucoid appearance
• Lactose fermenter on MacConkey agar
• Non-motile
• Urease positive

Klebsiella pneumoniae commonly causes:

• Severe lobar pneumonia, especially in alcoholics, diabetics, and debilitated patients
• Thick “currant jelly” sputum
• Urinary tract infections
• Hospital-acquired infections and multidrug resistance (e.g., ESBL, carbapenemase producers)

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following organisms is not an exception to Koch’s postulates?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Staphylococcus aureus

• Mycobacterium leprae – can grow in animals (armadillos, mouse footpads) but not on artificial culture media.
• Treponema pallidum – can grow in animals (rabbits) but not on artificial culture media.
• Neisseria gonorrhoeae – grows well on artificial culture media (e.g., chocolate agar, Thayer–Martin) but does not reliably produce disease in experimental animals, so it fails the animal-inoculation step.

Therefore, all three are exceptions to Koch’s postulates because Koch required growth both in artificial culture AND in experimental animals.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following protease inhibitors is most associated with QT interval prolongation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Saquinavir

Saquinavir, an HIV protease inhibitor, is most strongly associated with QT interval prolongation, which can predispose to serious ventricular arrhythmias such as torsades de pointes. Saquinavir can interfere with cardiac potassium channels (hERG channels), delaying ventricular repolarization and prolonging the QT interval on ECG.

Why not other options:

A. Atazanavir: Mainly causes indirect hyperbilirubinemia (UGT1A1 inhibition), not significant QT prolongation.

B. Darunavir: Generally well tolerated; main issues are rash and hepatotoxicity, not QT prolongation.

C. Indinavir: Associated with nephrolithiasis and hyperbilirubinemia, not QT prolongation.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following refers to a host in which the larval stage of the parasite remains viable without further development?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Paratenic host

A paratenic host (transport host) is a host in which a parasite remains alive and infective but does not undergo further development. The parasite is simply carried until it reaches the definitive host, where normal development continues. Parasite remains viable and infective. Helps bridge the ecological gap between intermediate and definitive hosts.

Comparison with other hosts:

| Host type | Definition

| --------- | ----------

| Definitive host | Host in which the parasite undergoes sexual reproduction

| Intermediate host | Host in which larval or asexual development occurs

| Paratenic host | Parasite survives without further development

| Reservoir host | Host that maintains the parasite in nature and serves as a source of infection

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following statement is false about biofilms?
options: Bacteria that form biofilms are usually metabolically more active
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Bacteria that form biofilms are usually metabolically more active

A biofilm is a structured community of microorganisms attached to a surface and embedded in a self-produced extracellular matrix (glycocalyx/exopolysaccharide).

Key characteristics of biofilms:

• Glycocalyx-enclosed bacterial communities that adhere to surfaces.
• Commonly form on medical devices and prosthetic materials (eg, prosthetic valves, catheters, joint prostheses).
• Bacterial communication within biofilms occurs through quorum sensing, which regulates gene expression and biofilm formation.
• Bacteria within biofilms are metabolically less active and slow-growing, making them highly resistant to antibiotics and host immune responses.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following statements regarding monkey pox is false?
options: Patient needs to wear a triple layer mask during isolation
Contact monitoring must be done for a period of 21 days from day of contact
It is caused by an enveloped, double-stranded DNA virus
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Requires BSL-4 facilities for isolation

Monkeypox (mpox) is a zoonotic infection caused by an enveloped, double-stranded DNA virus of the Orthopoxvirus genus (family Poxviridae). It spreads through close contact with lesions, respiratory droplets, body fluids, or contaminated materials.

Key public health and infection control points:

• Isolation precautions: Patients should be isolated and wear a triple-layer mask to reduce respiratory droplet transmission.
• Contact monitoring: Individuals exposed to a confirmed case should be monitored for 21 days, which corresponds to the maximum incubation period of the virus.
• Laboratory biosafety: Routine diagnostic testing for monkeypox can be performed in BSL-2 or BSL-3 laboratories with appropriate precautions; BSL-4 is not required.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following tests is a type of ring precipitation test?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ascoli's thermoprecipitation test

Ascoli’s thermoprecipitation test is a ring precipitation test used for the rapid detection of Bacillus anthracis antigen in infected animal tissues (e.g., hides, wool, hair).

Principle:

• Tissue extract containing anthrax antigen is layered over specific anti-anthrax serum in a test tube.
• If antigen is present, an antigen–antibody precipitation ring forms at the interface.

| Test | Type

| ---- | ----

| Ascoli test | Ring precipitation

| VDRL | Flocculation

| Rose Bengal | Agglutination

| Elek test | Gel precipitation (immunodiffusion)

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which test becomes positive earliest in syphilis infection?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Dark-field microscopy

Dark-field microscopy is the earliest test to become positive in syphilis, as it directly demonstrates motile spirochetes (Treponema pallidum) from the exudate of a primary chancre.

• Detects live spirochetes before antibodies are formed.
• Serological tests (VDRL, RPR, TPHA) become positive later after seroconversion.

Order of positivity:

1.  Dark-field microscopy (direct detection)

2.  Nontreponemal tests – VDRL, RPR

3.  Treponemal tests – TPHA, FTA-ABS

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 12-year-old boy has septic arthritis. Synovial fluid culture shows gram-positive cocci in clusters, catalase positive, beta-haemolytic, sensitive to oxacillin and cefoxitin. What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cloxacillin

The organism is Methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA).

• Gram-positive cocci in clusters → Staphylococcus
• Catalase positive
• Sensitive to oxacillin/cefoxitin → MSSA

Drug of choice for MSSA:

Anti-staphylococcal penicillins: “CONDOM”

• Cloxacillin
• Oxacillin
• Nafcillin
• Dicloxacillin
• Oxacillin
• Methicillin

Why not vancomycin?

• Vancomycin is preferred for MRSA, not MSSA when beta-lactams are effective.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 24-year-old otherwise healthy woman presents with a 2-day history of dysuria, increased urinary frequency, and suprapubic discomfort. She has no fever, flank pain, vomiting, or vaginal discharge. Her vital signs are stable, and there is no history of recent antibiotic use or urinary tract abnormalities. She is diagnosed with an uncomplicated lower urinary tract infection, and empirical therapy is planned. Which of the following drugs should not be preferred as first-line empirical treatment in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ciprofloxacin

Uncomplicated acute cystitis in an otherwise healthy, non-pregnant woman is most commonly caused by Escherichia coli. Nitrofurantoin, fosfomycin, and cotrimoxazole (where local resistance is <20%) are the recommended first-line empirical therapies. Fluoroquinolones (e.g., ciprofloxacin) should not be preferred as first-line treatment because of increasing bacterial resistance, risk of collateral damage, and serious adverse effects. They should be reserved for complicated infections or when first-line agents cannot be used.

Why not the other options?

• A. Nitrofurantoin: First-line drug for uncomplicated cystitis; achieves high urinary concentrations but should not be used for pyelonephritis due to poor renal tissue penetration.
• B. Cotrimoxazole: First-line option if local E. coli resistance is <20% and there has been no recent use.
• D. Fosfomycin: First-line agent given as a single oral dose with excellent activity against common uropathogens, including many multidrug-resistant strains.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 24-year-old sexually active male presents to the outpatient department with complaints of painful urination and a thick yellow urethral discharge for the past 3 days. He denies any fever, chills, or flank pain. He reports multiple unprotected sexual encounters in the past month. A urethral swab is sent for Gram stain, which shows intracellular gram-negative diplococci within polymorphonuclear leukocytes. The organism is resistant to penicillins. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ceftriaxone

Disseminated Gonococcal Infection (DGI): Triad:

• Dermatitis
• Tenosynovitis
• Migratory polyarthritis

Resistance Mechanisms for penicillin

1. β-lactamase production (penicillinase)
2. Altered PBPs (↓ binding affinity)
3. Efflux pumps

Penicillins (amoxicillin) become ineffective

Intracellular gram-negative diplococci in urethral discharge indicate Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Penicillin resistance is common due to β-lactamase production. A third-generation cephalosporin like ceftriaxone is the drug of choice for resistant gonorrhea. It provides reliable activity and high cure rates for uncomplicated infection.

| Condition | Treatment

| --------- | ---------

| Uncomplicated gonorrhea | Ceftriaxone IM single dose

| With possible Chlamydia | Ceftriaxone + Azithromycin/Doxycycline

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 25-year-old male presents to the clinic with complaints of burning sensation during urination and a purulent discharge from the penis for the past 5 days. He has had unprotected sexual intercourse with a new partner two weeks ago. On examination, the urethral meatus is erythematous, and there is a noticeable purulent discharge. A Gram stain of the discharge reveals intracellular gram-negative diplococci. The patient is otherwise healthy and has no known drug allergies. What is the most appropriate treatment for this patient?
options: Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million Units intramuscularly
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cefixime 400 mg orally

Urethritis + purulent discharge

↓

Gram stain → GN diplococci

↓

Gonorrhea

↓

Use cephalosporin

↓

Cefixime

Intracellular gram-negative diplococci indicate Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Third-generation cephalosporins are first-line therapy for uncomplicated gonorrhea. Oral cefixime is an accepted alternative when parenteral therapy is not used. Penicillin resistance is common, and doxycycline/metronidazole do not treat gonorrhea.

| Infection | Drug

| --------- | ----

| Gonorrhea | Ceftriaxone / Cefixime

| Chlamydia | Doxycycline / Azithromycin

| Syphilis | Penicillin

| Trichomonas | Metronidazole

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 50-year-old male presents with complaints of leg swelling and pain in the heel, which started a few days after he began an antibiotic course for a lower respiratory tract infection. Examination reveals signs suggestive of Achilles tendinitis. Which of the following best describes the mechanism of action of the drug most likely responsible for his condition?
options: Inhibition of bacterial cell wall synthesis
Inhibition of bacterial folic acid synthesis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Inhibition of bacterial DNA gyrase

Action: Prevents DNA supercoiling and replication

Leads to:

• DNA damage
• Bacterial death

Fluoroquinolone

↓

Inhibits DNA gyrase

↓

DNA replication blocked

↓

Bacterial cell death

Achilles tendinitis after an antibiotic course is a classic adverse effect of fluoroquinolones. These drugs act by inhibiting bacterial DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV, blocking DNA replication. Tendon toxicity is a hallmark clue for this class. Hence the mechanism is DNA gyrase inhibition.

Fluoroquinolones cause:

• Collagen degradation
• Oxidative stress in tendons

Leads to:

• Tendinitis
• Tendon rupture (Achilles most common)
•

| Mechanism | Drug Class | Example

| --------- | ---------- | -------

| DNA gyrase inhibition | Fluoroquinolones | Ciprofloxacin

| Protein synthesis inhibition | Aminoglycosides | Gentamicin

| Cell wall inhibition | β-lactams | Penicillin

| Folate inhibition | Sulfonamides | TMP-SMX

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 63-year-old diabetic woman presents with fever, flank pain, dysuria, and elevated WBC count. Imaging reveals mild hydronephrosis. Urinalysis shows pyuria and bacteriuria. She is diagnosed with a complicated urinary tract infection (UTI). Which of the following is the parenteral drug of choice for empirical treatment of a complicated UTI?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Meropenem

It’s a complicated UTI because of:

• Diabetes
• Systemic signs (fever, ↑WBC)
• Upper tract involvement (flank pain)
• Obstruction (hydronephrosis)

Common organisms:

• E. coli (most common)
• Klebsiella
• Proteus
• Pseudomonas (important in complicated cases)
• ESBL-producing organisms

Complicated UTI with systemic features in a diabetic patient requires broad-spectrum parenteral coverage against resistant Gram-negative bacilli. Meropenem is a carbapenem with excellent activity against ESBL-producing organisms and severe pyelonephritis. Nitrofurantoin is only for uncomplicated cystitis. Carbapenems are preferred empiric therapy in high-risk complicated infections.

A) Ceftriaxone

• Good for moderate infections
• BUT:

• No ESBL coverage
• Limited against resistant organisms

C) Amoxicillin-clavulanate

• Oral / mild infections
• Resistance common

D) Nitrofurantoin

Key concept:

• Acts only in urine (bladder)
• Poor tissue penetration

NOT used in:

• Pyelonephritis
• Complicated UTI

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A pregnant woman presents with urinary tract infection (UTI). Which of the following acts as a urinary antiseptic?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Nitrofurantoin

A urinary antiseptic is a drug that achieves antibacterial concentrations only in urine, with negligible systemic (plasma/tissue) levels — hence it treats lower UTI/cystitis but never pyelonephritis or systemic infection.

Nitrofurantoin is the prototype: it is rapidly absorbed, concentrated by the kidney, and excreted into urine where it is reduced by bacterial nitroreductases into reactive intermediates that damage bacterial ribosomes, DNA and metabolic enzymes — a multi-target action, which explains its remarkably low resistance rate. It is safe in the first and second trimesters and is a preferred agent for asymptomatic bacteriuria/cystitis in pregnancy.

Other options:

• B. Ciprofloxacin → fluoroquinolone; contraindicated in pregnancy (cartilage/arthropathy risk); it is a systemic antibiotic, not an antiseptic.
• C. Doxycycline → contraindicated in pregnancy — teeth staining, enamel hypoplasia, bone growth inhibition, maternal hepatotoxicity.
• D. Cotrimoxazole → avoid in 1st trimester (folate antagonism → neural tube defects) and near term (kernicterus).

Pearl:

• Urinary antiseptics = Nitrofurantoin, Methenamine, Nalidixic acid.
• Avoid nitrofurantoin at term (38 wk onwards) → risk of neonatal hemolysis (G6PD deficiency).

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Infusion of which one of the following antibacterial agents may cause the ‘Red Man Syndrome’ characterized by rapid onset of erythematous rash and pruritus on the head, face, neck and upper trunk?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Vancomycin

Red Man Syndrome is an infusion-related reaction caused by rapid IV administration of vancomycin. It is due to non-IgE-mediated histamine release from mast cells, producing:

• Rapid-onset flushing and erythema
• Pruritus
• Predominantly involving the face, neck, and upper trunk
• Sometimes hypotension and tachycardia

Why not other options?

• A. Vancomycin: Correct. Classic cause of Red Man Syndrome.
• B. Minocycline: Can cause dizziness, pigmentation, and hypersensitivity reactions, but not the classic Red Man Syndrome.
• C. Levofloxacin: Can cause QT prolongation, tendinopathy, CNS effects, and dysglycemia.
• D. Metronidazole: Common adverse effects include GI symptoms and a metallic taste; prolonged use can cause peripheral neuropathy.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Match the following: Organism: 1. Helicobacter pylori 2. Mycobacterium tuberculosis 3. Chlamydia trachomatis 4. Non-penicillinase-producing gonococci Drug: a. Amoxicillin b. Doxycycline c. Clarithromycin d. Streptomycin
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1–c, 2–d, 3–b, 4–a

Knowledge of the drug of choice (DOC) for common bacterial pathogens is essential for selecting appropriate antimicrobial therapy and is frequently tested in examinations.

Correct Match:

• 1. Helicobacter pylori → c. Clarithromycin
• 2. Mycobacterium tuberculosis → d. Streptomycin
• 3. Chlamydia trachomatis → b. Doxycycline
• 4. Non-penicillinase-producing gonococci → a. Amoxicillin (historically susceptible strains)

Why is A correct?

• H. pylori eradication regimens include clarithromycin (where macrolide resistance is low) along with a proton pump inhibitor and other antibiotics.
• Streptomycin is a first-line antitubercular drug (now mainly reserved for selected indications such as drug-resistant TB or when injectable agents are required).
• Doxycycline is the drug of choice for uncomplicated Chlamydia trachomatis infection.
• Non-penicillinase-producing Neisseria gonorrhoeae are susceptible to amoxicillin/penicillin; however, due to widespread resistance, ceftriaxone is now the recommended treatment in current practice.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which antimicrobial shows concentration-dependent killing?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Aminoglycosides

Concentration-dependent killing:

• Higher drug concentration → greater bacterial killing.

Classic drugs:

• Aminoglycosides
• Fluoroquinolones
• Daptomycin

Aminoglycosides also show: Post-antibiotic effect

Beta-lactams / Vancomycin:

• Show time-dependent killing.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following drugs is/are useful in the treatment of Listeria monocytogenes infection? 1. Ceftriaxone 2. Gentamicin 3. Ampicillin 4. Sulfamethoxazole Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 2, 3 and 4 only

Ampicillin is the drug of choice for Listeria monocytogenes infection. Gentamicin is often added for synergistic bactericidal activity in severe infections such as meningitis or endocarditis. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) is the preferred alternative in patients allergic to penicillin.

Why not the other option?

• Ceftriaxone: Listeria is intrinsically resistant to cephalosporins; therefore, ceftriaxone is ineffective despite being commonly used for bacterial meningitis.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following statements are true about diphtheria toxin? a. It inhibits EF-2 b. It is an A-B type exotoxin c. It primarily affects the myocardium and nerves d. Toxin is produced only by strains carrying a plasmid
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. a, b and c

Diphtheria toxin is a phage-encoded A-B exotoxin produced by toxigenic strains of Corynebacterium diphtheriae. It inactivates elongation factor-2 (EF-2) by ADP-ribosylation, thereby inhibiting protein synthesis and causing cell death. The toxin primarily affects the myocardium and peripheral nerves, leading to myocarditis and neuropathy, the major life-threatening complications of diphtheria.

Why is B correct?

• a. Inhibits EF-2 ✓: Blocks protein synthesis by ADP-ribosylation of EF-2.
• b. It is an A-B type exotoxin ✓: The A (active) subunit inhibits protein synthesis, while the B (binding) subunit mediates entry into host cells.
• c. It primarily affects the myocardium and nerves ✓: Responsible for myocarditis, arrhythmias, and peripheral neuritis.
• d. Toxin is produced only by strains carrying a plasmid ✗: The tox gene is carried by a lysogenic β-corynephage, not a plasmid.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following statements regarding ESBL-producing organisms is/are correct? 1. Carbapenems are considered the preferred drugs for serious infections caused by ESBL-producing bacteria 2. ESBL-producing organisms are susceptible to piperacillin-tazobactam combination 3. ESBL-producing E. coli is resistant to 3rd and 4th generation cephalosporins but more susceptible to 1st and 2nd generation cephalosporins like cefazolin 4. Resistance due to ESBL production is commonly acquired through plasmid-mediated gene transfer
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 2 and 4

What are ESBLs?

• Extended spectrum β-lactamase
• Enzymes that destroy beta-lactam antibiotics
• Produced mainly by E. coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae
• Spread hospital to hospital via plasmids (conjugation)

What ESBLs Destroy vs Spare

| Destroys: | Spares:

| --------- | -------

| All penicillins | Carbapenems

| ALL cephalosporins (1st– 4th gen) |

| Aztreonam | —

Key: No cephalosporin generation is safe — all are hydrolyzed

Treatment:

| Severity | Drug

| -------- | ----

| Severe/Bloodstream | Meropenem

| Moderate | Ertapenem

| UTI only (mild) | Nitrofurantoin / Fosfomycin

1. Carbapenems are considered the preferred drugs for serious infections caused by ESBL-producing bacteria: Carbapenems = drug of choice for serious infections
2. ESBL-producing organisms are susceptible to piperacillin-tazobactam combination: Pip-tazo susceptible in vitro but fails clinically in severe infections (MERINO trial showed higher mortality)

• MERINO Trial:

• Meropenem superior to pip-tazo for ESBL bloodstream infections — 30-day mortality 3.7% vs 12.3%

3. ESBL-producing E. coli is resistant to 3rd and 4th generation cephalosporins but more susceptible to 1st and 2nd generation cephalosporins like cefazolin: ESBLs hydrolyze ALL cephalosporins — no 1st gen advantage
4. Resistance due to ESBL production is commonly acquired through plasmid-mediated gene transfer: Spread by plasmids — reason for rapid global spread

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which one of the following groups of drugs is ineffective against gram positive bacteria?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Monobactams

Monobactams (e.g., Aztreonam) are β-lactam antibiotics with activity primarily against aerobic Gram-negative bacteria and have virtually no activity against Gram-positive organisms or anaerobes.

Spectrum of Activity of Monobactams

• Effective against:

• Gram-negative bacilli
• Pseudomonas infection
• Enterobacteriaceae

• Ineffective against:

• Gram-positive cocci
• Anaerobic bacteria

Why the Other Options Are Incorrect

• A. Glycopeptides (e.g., Vancomycin): Excellent activity against Gram-positive organisms, including MRSA.
• C. Fluoroquinolones: Later generations (e.g., levofloxacin, moxifloxacin) have significant Gram-positive coverage.
• D. First-generation cephalosporins: Strong activity against Gram-positive cocci such as streptococci and methicillin-sensitive staphylococci.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 10-year-old child has been diagnosed with diphtheria and is being treated in the ward. His 2.5-year-old brother, who lives in the same house, has received all due vaccinations according to NIS. What is the next best step for the management of the younger sibling?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Erythromycin only

For contacts of diphtheria:

1. Antibiotic prophylaxis → eradicate carriage
2. ± Vaccine (toxoid) depending on immunization status

Why ONLY erythromycin here?

• Child is fully immunized → already has protective antibodies
• So NO need for booster/toxoid immediately
• Only need to eliminate possible colonization

👉 Hence: Erythromycin only

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 24-year-old recreational swimmer develops severe otalgia and purulent otorrhea two days after swimming in the sea. Culture of the ear discharge grows a halophilic, oxidase-positive, curved Gram-negative bacillus. Which of the following Vibrio species is most commonly associated with ear infections?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Vibrio alginolyticus

Vibrio alginolyticus is a halophilic (salt-loving) Vibrio commonly found in marine and coastal waters. It is the most frequent Vibrio species associated with ear infections, especially:

• Otitis externa
• Otitis media (less common)
• Occasionally conjunctivitis and superficial wound infections

Infections typically follow exposure to seawater, particularly in swimmers, divers, and surfers.

Why the other options are incorrect?

• B. Vibrio parahaemolyticus ❌: Primarily causes acute gastroenteritis following consumption of raw or undercooked seafood, especially oysters. Ear infections are uncommon.
•

C. Vibrio vulnificus ❌: Causes:

• Severe wound infections after seawater exposure
• Necrotizing fasciitis
• Primary septicemia after eating raw oysters, especially in patients with chronic liver disease

It is not the common cause of otitis.

* D. Vibrio fluvialis ❌: Associated mainly with gastroenteritis and only occasionally with extraintestinal infections.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 24-year-old woman presents with high fever, hypotension, diffuse erythematous rash and vomiting during menstruation. The diagnosis is confirmed as toxic shock syndrome (TSS). She is using tampon. What is the mechanism of action of the toxin responsible?
options: ADP-ribosylation of elongation factor-2 (EF-2), causing inhibition of protein synthesis
Cross-linking of MHC class II molecules with T-cell receptors
Cross-linking of MHC Class I Molecules with T-Cell receptors
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cross-linking of MHC class II molecules with T-cell receptors

Toxic shock syndrome (TSS) is classically caused by Staphylococcus aureus producing Toxic Shock Syndrome Toxin-1 (TSST-1), a superantigen. Superantigens bypass normal antigen processing by simultaneously binding MHC class II molecules on antigen-presenting cells and the Vβ region of the T-cell receptor (TCR), resulting in massive, nonspecific T-cell activation and a cytokine storm.

• TSST-1 binds directly to:

• MHC Class II on antigen-presenting cells.
• Vβ region of the T-cell receptor.

• This causes excessive release of IL-1, IL-2, TNF-α, and IFN-γ, leading to fever, diffuse erythematous rash, hypotension, and multiorgan dysfunction.

Why not the other options?

• A. ADP-ribosylation of elongation factor-2 (EF-2), causing inhibition of protein synthesis: Mechanism of diphtheria toxin and Pseudomonas exotoxin A.
• C. Cross-linking of MHC Class I Molecules with T-Cell receptors: Incorrect; superantigens bind Class II MHC and the Vβ region of the TCR.
• D. Polyclonal B-cell activation: Seen with Epstein–Barr virus (EBV) infection.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 25-year-old male presents with complaints of urethral discharge and dysuria for the past 1 week. The discharge was scant and mucoid for a few days but he reports profuse and yellowish discharge since 2 days. Gram staining of the urethral discharge reveals gram-negative intracellular monocoсci and diplococci. On further questioning, he gives a history of unprotected sexual intercourse 15 days ago. Which one of the following conditions will be your most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Gonorrhea

The most likely diagnosis is gonococcal urethritis caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae.

• Profuse, thick, yellowish/purulent urethral discharge
• Dysuria
• Gram stain shows gram-negative intracellular diplococci (GNID)
• History of unprotected sexual intercourse

The initial scant mucoid discharge can occur before the typical purulent gonococcal discharge becomes prominent.

Why not other options?

• A. Gonorrhea: Correct. N. gonorrhoeae appears as gram-negative intracellular diplococci and causes profuse purulent urethral discharge.
• B. Chancroid: Caused by Haemophilus ducreyi; presents with a painful genital ulcer and tender inguinal lymphadenopathy.
• C. Syphilis: Caused by Treponema pallidum; classically presents with a painless chancre in primary syphilis.
• D. Lymphogranuloma venereum: Caused by Chlamydia trachomatis L1–L3; typically causes a transient painless genital lesion followed by painful inguinal lymphadenopathy.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 27-year-old individual develops a transient genital lesion that resolves spontaneously. Approximately two weeks later, they present with painful inguinal lymphadenopathy (buboes) and fever. Which Sero-varieties of Chlamydia trachomatis are responsible for this infection?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. L1, L2, L3

Recognize Lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV) as a sexually transmitted infection caused by Chlamydia trachomatis serovars L1, L2, and L3, characterized by a transient painless genital ulcer followed by painful inguinal lymphadenopathy (buboes) and systemic symptoms. Differentiating LGV from other chlamydial serovars is a common exam topic.

Why not the other options?

• A. D–K: Cause urogenital infections (nongonococcal urethritis, cervicitis, PID, neonatal conjunctivitis), not LGV.
• C. M0: Not a recognized serovar of C. trachomatis.
• D. A–C: Cause trachoma, a chronic ocular infection, not genital disease.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 28-year-old foreigner presents with sudden onset of profuse watery diarrhea after returning from a recent trip to Southeast Asia. He reports passing large volumes of pale, “rice-water” stools without blood or mucus. Which of the following toxins is most likely responsible for this patient’s condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cholera toxin

Vibrio cholerae causes profuse “rice-water” diarrhea through the action of cholera toxin, an A-B exotoxin. The toxin ADP-ribosylates the Gs protein, leading to persistent activation of adenylate cyclase, increased intracellular cAMP, and massive secretion of chloride and water into the intestinal lumen. The resulting diarrhea is watery, non-inflammatory, and non-bloody, causing rapid dehydration and electrolyte loss.

Why not the other options?

• A. Shigella toxin: Causes bloody diarrhea (dysentery) by invading the colonic mucosa and inhibiting protein synthesis via the 60S ribosomal subunit.
• B. Cholera toxin: ✔ Correct. Causes profuse rice-water stools by increasing cAMP without invading the intestinal mucosa.
• C. E. coli toxin: Enterotoxigenic E. coli (ETEC) also causes watery diarrhea but is classically associated with traveler’s diarrhea, not the characteristic rice-water stools of cholera.
• D. Botulinum toxin: Produces descending flaccid paralysis by blocking acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction, not diarrhea.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 30-year-old male travels frequently and has food during his travels. He presents to PHC OPD with abdominal pain, fever for 4 days. He has bradycardia too. Test for confirmation of diagnosis:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Blood culture

Enteric fever (typhoid) should be suspected in a patient with prolonged fever, abdominal pain, and relative bradycardia (Faget sign) and is caused by Salmonella typhi.

Blood culture is the best confirmatory test in the first week of illness

Timeline of investigations:

• 1st week → Blood culture (highest yield)
• 2nd week onward → Widal test becomes positive
• Later stages → Stool and urine cultures may become positive

Why not others:

• Widal test → not reliable in early phase
• Stool/urine culture → useful later

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 32-year-old farmer working in rodent-infested rice fields presents with fever, conjunctival suffusion, and signs of liver failure. Which stage of the disease does this presentation correspond to?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Weil's disease

Weil’s disease, the severe immune phase of leptospirosis, characterized by high fever, conjunctival suffusion, jaundice, acute kidney injury, hemorrhagic manifestations, and hepatic dysfunction. It occurs after exposure to water or soil contaminated with the urine of infected animals, especially rats, making farmers, sewage workers, and veterinarians high-risk groups.

Why not the other options?

• A. Leptospirosis: Refers to the overall infection caused by Leptospira interrogans; the severe icteric form is specifically called Weil’s disease.
• C. Convalescent stage: Recovery phase with resolution of symptoms; not associated with acute liver failure.
• D. Weil–Felix: An agglutination test used for the diagnosis of rickettsial infections, unrelated to leptospirosis.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 34-year-old cattle handler presents with gradual onset fever, malaise, weight loss, drenching night sweats, low back pain, and mild hepatosplenomegaly. He frequently assists in animal delivery. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Brucellosis

Brucellosis is a zoonotic infection caused by Brucella species (most commonly Brucella melitensis). It is transmitted through direct contact with infected livestock (cattle, sheep, goats, pigs), exposure to animal placental tissue, or ingestion of unpasteurized milk and dairy products. The disease presents with undulating fever, drenching night sweats, malaise, weight loss, arthralgia, low back pain, and hepatosplenomegaly.

Why not the other options?

• A. Leptospirosis: Acquired through water contaminated with animal urine; presents with fever, conjunctival suffusion, jaundice (Weil disease), and renal failure.
• C. Anthrax: Caused by Bacillus anthracis; presents with a painless black eschar (cutaneous anthrax), inhalational disease, or gastrointestinal anthrax.
• D. Rabies: Transmitted by bites from infected mammals; presents with hydrophobia, aerophobia, and encephalitis, not chronic fever with hepatosplenomegaly.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 34-year-old woman underwent splenectomy following a road traffic accident 3 years ago. She now presents to the emergency department with high-grade fever, hypotension, septic shock, and rapidly deteriorates despite treatment. Which of the following organisms is the target for empirical treatment in such patients?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Streptococcus pneumoniae

Asplenic patients are at lifelong risk of overwhelming post-splenectomy infection (OPSI) due to impaired clearance of encapsulated bacteria. Streptococcus pneumoniae is the most common and most important pathogen, often causing rapidly progressive sepsis, meningitis, or septic shock with a high mortality rate.

• The spleen plays a critical role in opsonization and phagocytic clearance of encapsulated organisms.
• Following splenectomy, Streptococcus pneumoniae is the leading cause of fulminant sepsis, warranting prompt empiric antibiotic coverage.

Why not the other options?

• B. Escherichia coli: Common cause of sepsis but not specifically associated with asplenia.
• C. Mycobacterium tuberculosis: Asplenia does not significantly increase susceptibility.
• D. Clostridium difficile: Causes antibiotic-associated colitis, not overwhelming post-splenectomy sepsis.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 35-year-old female presents with generalized muscle rigidity, difficulty in swallowing and laryngeal spasms for the past one week. She has developed trismus over the past 2 days and has a pulse rate of 130 beats/minute and a respiratory rate of 35 breaths/minute on presentation. She gives a history of getting her ears pierced from a roadside jewellery seller 2 weeks ago. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Tetanus

The patient has classic features of generalized tetanus:

• Trismus (lockjaw) → characteristic early feature
• Generalized muscle rigidity
• Dysphagia and laryngeal spasms
• Autonomic overactivity → tachycardia and tachypnea
• Recent ear piercing with an unsterile instrument → potential inoculation of Clostridium tetani spores

Why not other options?

• A. Enteric fever: Causes prolonged fever, abdominal symptoms, and relative bradycardia—not generalized muscle rigidity or trismus.
• B. Pertussis: Causes paroxysmal cough with inspiratory whoop, not muscle rigidity.
• C. Diphtheria: Causes pharyngitis with a gray pseudomembrane and may cause myocarditis/neuropathy, but not generalized rigidity and lockjaw.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 35-year-old male presents with acute profuse painless “rice-water” diarrhea, severe dehydration, and vomiting after consuming street food. The causative organism produces an enterotoxin. What is its intracellular mechanism of action?
options: SNARE protein cleavage causing blockade of neurotransmission
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Increased cAMP

Cholera, caused by Vibrio cholerae, presents with profuse painless “rice-water” diarrhea, vomiting, and severe dehydration. Its cholera toxin (AB₅ toxin) causes persistent activation of adenylate cyclase, leading to marked elevation of intracellular cAMP. This results in massive chloride secretion (via CFTR channels), followed by sodium and water loss into the intestinal lumen, producing secretory diarrhea.

Mechanism:

• Cholera toxin ADP-ribosylates the Gsα protein
• Gsα remains constitutively active
• ↑ Adenylate cyclase → ↑ cAMP
• ↑ CFTR-mediated chloride secretion → water follows → watery diarrhea

Why not the other options?

• B. Increased cGMP: Seen with heat-stable (ST) toxin of enterotoxigenic E. coli (ETEC).
• C. Inhibition of protein synthesis (EF-2 inactivation): Mechanism of diphtheria toxin and Pseudomonas exotoxin A.
• D. SNARE protein cleavage causing blockade of neurotransmission: Mechanism of botulinum toxin and tetanospasmin.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 35-year-old veterinarian presents with intermittent fever, profuse night sweats, malaise, and arthralgia after assisting in the delivery of goats. Blood culture later grows Brucella melitensis. Which of the following is not considered a significant mode of transmission of brucellosis?
options: Vertical transmission among infected animals through the placenta
Inhalation of infectious aerosols in laboratories or slaughterhouses
Consumption of unpasteurized milk or dairy products
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Routine person-to-person transmission between humans

Brucellosis is a zoonotic infection caused by Brucella species:

• B. melitensis – goats and sheep (most virulent)
• B. abortus – cattle
• B. suis – pigs
• B. canis – dogs

Humans acquire infection mainly through:

• Consumption of unpasteurized milk, cheese, or other dairy products
• Direct contact with infected animal tissues, blood, placenta, or aborted fetuses
• Inhalation of infectious aerosols, especially in laboratories, abattoirs, and farms

Why the other options are correct?

• A. Vertical transmission among infected animals through the placenta ✅: Brucella readily spreads among livestock via infected placentas, aborted fetuses, and reproductive secretions, helping maintain infection within herds.
• B. Inhalation of infectious aerosols ✅: An important occupational route affecting veterinarians, farmers, abattoir workers, and laboratory personnel.
• D. Consumption of unpasteurized milk or dairy products ✅: This is the most common route of human infection worldwide.

Why Option C is incorrect?

• C. Routine person-to-person transmission between humans ❌: Human-to-human transmission is exceptionally rare and is not epidemiologically significant. Rare cases have occurred through:

• Breastfeeding
• Blood transfusion
• Organ transplantation
• Sexual transmission (very uncommon)
• Vertical transmission from mother to fetus

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 40-year-old farmer presented with retro-orbital pain, conjunctival suffusion, night fever and chills, calf tenderness, cervical lymphadenopathy, hypokalemia, and joint pain. What can be the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Leptospirosis

Leptospirosis should be suspected in patients with fever, conjunctival suffusion, and calf muscle tenderness, especially with occupational exposure (e.g., farmers).

• Conjunctival suffusion (redness without discharge)
• Severe calf muscle tenderness (characteristic)
• Fever with chills, myalgia, joint pain
• Retro-orbital pain may be present
• Electrolyte abnormalities (e.g., hypokalemia)

Transmission: Exposure to water/soil contaminated with urine of infected animals (especially rodents)

Severe form: Weil’s disease → jaundice, renal failure, hemorrhage

Differentiation:

• Dengue → retro-orbital pain but no calf tenderness or conjunctival suffusion
• Malaria → periodic fever, no conjunctival suffusion

Filariasis → lymphatic involvement

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 5-year-old boy is brought to the clinic with multiple honey-crusted pustular lesions over both legs. Gram stain from the lesion reveals Gram-positive cocci in chains, and blood agar culture demonstrates β-hemolytic colonies. Which of the following tests would provide the best presumptive identification of the causative organism as Group A Streptococcus?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Bacitracin sensitivity test

The child most likely has streptococcal pyoderma (impetigo) caused by Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A Streptococcus, GAS).

Laboratory clues:

• Gram-positive cocci in chains
• β-hemolytic colonies on blood agar
• Catalase negative
• Bacitracin sensitive (Taxo A disc) → classical presumptive identification test for GAS

Modern laboratories often use the PYR test, which is positive in Group A Streptococcus, but bacitracin sensitivity remains the classic examination answer.

Why the other options are incorrect?

•

A. Catalase test ❌: Catalase differentiates:

• Staphylococci → Catalase positive
• Streptococci → Catalase negative

It does not identify Group A Streptococcus.

* B. Optochin sensitivity test ❌: Used for identification of Streptococcus pneumoniae, which is:

* α-hemolytic

* Optochin sensitive

* Bile soluble

* C. Bile solubility test ❌: Another confirmatory test for Streptococcus pneumoniae.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 52-year-old diabetic farmer from Thailand presents with prolonged fever, weight loss, cough, and multiple lung cavities on chest imaging. He is initially treated for pulmonary tuberculosis, but blood cultures later grow a Gram-negative bacillus isolated from soil and stagnant water. Which of the following statements regarding this disease is incorrect?
options: It is caused by Burkholderia mallei.
It is endemic in Southeast Asia and northern Australia.
It may clinically mimic pulmonary tuberculosis.
The causative organism is considered a potential bioterrorism agent.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. It is caused by Burkholderia mallei.

Melioidosis is caused by Burkholderia pseudomallei, a motile, aerobic Gram-negative bacillus that is a saprophyte in soil and surface water.

It is an important cause of severe community-acquired sepsis in Southeast Asia and northern Australia, particularly in:

• Diabetics (most important risk factor)
• Chronic kidney disease
• Alcoholism
• Immunocompromised patients

Because of its varied presentations, melioidosis is often called the "Great Mimicker."

Why the other options are correct?

• B. It is endemic in Southeast Asia and northern Australia ✅: Correct. The disease is highly endemic in Thailand, Malaysia, Singapore, Vietnam, Myanmar, and northern Australia.
• C. It may clinically mimic pulmonary tuberculosis ✅: Correct. Chronic pulmonary melioidosis may present with:

• Chronic cough
• Weight loss
• Fever
• Cavitary lung lesions making it difficult to distinguish from tuberculosis.

• D. The causative organism is considered a potential bioterrorism agent ✅: Correct. Burkholderia pseudomallei is classified as a Category B bioterrorism agent because it:

• Can be aerosolized
• Causes severe disease
• Persists in the environment
• Is intrinsically resistant to several antibiotics

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 6-week-old infant presents with features of meningitis. Which of the following combinations of organisms are common causes of meningitis in this age group? 1. Listeria monocytogenes 2. Haemophilus influenzae type b 3. Staphylococcus aureus 4. Streptococcus pneumoniae
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 2 and 4 only

The causative organisms of bacterial meningitis vary with age. In young infants (1–3 months of age, including a 6-week-old infant), the common pathogens include Listeria monocytogenes, Haemophilus influenzae type b (where vaccination is incomplete), and Streptococcus pneumoniae. Therefore, empiric therapy must provide adequate coverage for these organisms.

Why is D correct?

• Listeria monocytogenes: Important cause of neonatal and young infant meningitis.
• Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib): Can cause meningitis in infants who are unimmunized or partially immunized.
• Streptococcus pneumoniae: A major cause of bacterial meningitis beyond the neonatal period.
• Staphylococcus aureus is not a common community-acquired cause of meningitis in this age group; it is more often associated with neurosurgical procedures, trauma, or hematogenous spread.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 65-year-old woman underwent elective surgery five days ago and received intravenous clindamycin postoperatively. She now presents with profuse watery diarrhea. Which organism is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Clostridioides difficile

Clostridioides difficile is the most common cause of antibiotic-associated diarrhea and pseudomembranous colitis. Broad-spectrum antibiotics, particularly clindamycin, cephalosporins, fluoroquinolones, and amoxicillin/ampicillin, disrupt the normal colonic flora, allowing C. difficile to proliferate and produce toxins A and B, leading to colonic inflammation and diarrhea.

Why not the other options?

• B. Enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli (ETEC): Causes traveler’s diarrhea after contaminated food or water, not antibiotic-associated diarrhea.
• C. Salmonella enteritidis: Causes inflammatory diarrhea associated with contaminated poultry or eggs, often with fever.
• D. Staphylococcus aureus: Causes rapid-onset food poisoning (1–6 hours) due to ingestion of preformed enterotoxin, presenting with vomiting rather than post-antibiotic diarrhea.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 67-year-old man develops high-grade fever, non-productive cough, diarrhea, and confusion 5 days after staying at a hotel. Chest radiograph shows multilobar pneumonia. Which of the following statements regarding this infection is correct?
options: Aspiration of contaminated water is an important route of infection
Detection of urinary Legionella antigen is the gold standard for diagnosis
Pontiac fever is the pneumonic form of Legionella infection
Person-to-person transmission is common during outbreaks
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Aspiration of contaminated water is an important route of infection

Legionella pneumophila is acquired from environmental water sources such as cooling towers, air-conditioning systems, showers, and hospital water supplies. Infection occurs by aspiration or inhalation of contaminated water droplets, with aspiration being an important mechanism, particularly in susceptible individuals.

Typical features of Legionnaires' disease

• High fever
• Dry cough
• Diarrhea
• Hyponatremia
• Confusion
• Multilobar pneumonia

Why the other options are incorrect?

• B. Detection of urinary Legionella antigen is the gold standard for diagnosis ❌: Urinary antigen testing is rapid and commonly used, but the reference (gold standard) test is culture on Buffered Charcoal Yeast Extract (BCYE) agar. PCR is also highly sensitive and increasingly used.
• C. Pontiac fever is the pneumonic form of Legionella infection ❌: Pontiac fever is a self-limited, influenza-like illness without pneumonia. The pneumonic illness caused by Legionella is called Legionnaires' disease.
• D. Person-to-person transmission is common during outbreaks ❌: Human-to-human transmission is exceedingly rare and is not considered an important mode of spread. Infection is acquired from contaminated environmental water sources.

High-Yield Pearl

| Legionnaires' disease | Pontiac fever

| --------------------- | -------------

| Pneumonia present | No pneumonia

| High fever, cough, diarrhea, confusion | Influenza-like illness

| Requires antibiotics (macrolide/fluoroquinolone) | Self-limiting

| Environmental water exposure | Environmental water exposure

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 9-year-old boy from a rural tropical village presents with multiple papillomatous skin lesions over the legs and painless ulcerative plaques. Dark-field microscopy demonstrates spirochetes, and both VDRL and TPHA are positive. Which of the following statements regarding this condition is incorrect?
options: It is primarily transmitted through sexual contact.
It is caused by Treponema pertenue.
Previous infection confers cross-immunity with syphilis.
Routine serological tests cannot distinguish it from syphilis.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. It is primarily transmitted through sexual contact.

Yaws is a non-venereal treponematosis caused by Treponema pallidum subspecies *pertenue (formerly Treponema pertenue*).

Key features:

• Predominantly affects children (5–15 years)
• Endemic in warm, humid tropical regions
• Spread by direct skin-to-skin contact with infectious lesions
• Sexual transmission does not occur
• Produces skin, soft tissue, and later bone involvement

Why the other options are correct?

• B. It is caused by Treponema pertenue ✅: Correct. Yaws is caused by T. pallidum subsp. *pertenue*.
• C. Previous infection confers cross-immunity with syphilis ✅: Correct. The treponemes share common antigens, resulting in cross-immunity.
