• D. Routine serological tests cannot distinguish it from syphilis ✅: Correct. Both non-treponemal tests (VDRL, RPR) and treponemal tests (TPHA, FTA-ABS) are positive in both infections and cannot differentiate yaws from syphilis.

High-Yield Pearl

| Feature | Yaws | Syphilis

| ------- | ---- | --------

| Organism | T. pallidum subsp. pertenue | T. pallidum subsp. pallidum

| Transmission | Direct skin contact (non-sexual) | Sexual and vertical

| Common age | Children | Adults

| Genital lesions | Absent | Present

| Serology | Same as syphilis | Same

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A child presents with pharyngitis, and Group A Streptococcus is isolated from the throat specimen. Which bacterial factor facilitates the binding of fibronectin on host cells, thereby aiding in bacterial attachment?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Lipoteichoic acid

Group A Streptococcus (Streptococcus pyogenes) adheres to host epithelial cells via lipoteichoic acid, which binds to fibronectin on host cells.

• Lipoteichoic acid (LTA) on bacterial surface binds fibronectin
• Fibronectin acts as a bridge to host epithelial cells
• Facilitates colonization of the pharynx

Other virulence factors:

• M protein → anti-phagocytic, major virulence factor
• Capsule (hyaluronic acid) → immune evasion
• Streptolysins → tissue damage

Why not others:

• Lipoprotein → not primary adhesion factor here
• Capsule → prevents phagocytosis, not adhesion

Flagella → GAS is non-motile

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A child was brought with complaints of high fever, multiple seizures, headache, and neck rigidity. CS analysis showed low glucose, high protein, and many polymorphs. The CSF culture showed pleomorphic gram-negative bacilli. What is true about the causative organism?
options: Produces non-lactose fermenting colonies on MacConkey agar
Exhibits satellitism around Staphylococcus aureus colonies
It exhibits alpha hemolysis on sheep blood agar
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Exhibits satellitism around Staphylococcus aureus colonies

The described organism is Haemophilus influenzae,

• A pleomorphic ,Gram-negative bacillus causing pyogenic meningitis in children.
• Characteristically shows satellitism around Staphylococcus aureus on blood agar.
• Requires Factor X (hemin) and Factor V (NAD) for growth (because S. aureus releases NAD (Factor V)

CSF findings in bacterial meningitis:

• ↓ glucose, ↑ protein
• Neutrophilic predominance.

Why not others:

• Bacitracin sensitivity: seen in Group A Streptococcus ( bacitracin and optochin sensitivity)
• Non-lactose fermenter on MacConkey: applies to some Gram-negative bacilli like salmonella, shigella, proteus, not H. influenzae
• Alpha hemolysis: seen in Streptococcus pneumoniae

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A farmer presents with fever, jaundice, and conjunctival hemorrhage, and later succumbs to the illness. What is the most likely disease responsible for this clinical presentation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Weil's disease

Weil’s disease is the severe form of leptospirosis caused by Leptospira interrogans, typically seen in individuals exposed to contaminated water (e.g., sewage workers). Key clinical triad:

• Fever
• Jaundice
• Hemorrhage (classically conjunctival suffusion/hemorrhage)

Important features:

• Exposure to contaminated water or animal urine (especially rodents)
• Biphasic illness → septicemic phase followed by immune phase
• Severe disease → hepatic dysfunction, renal failure, hemorrhage

Differentiation:

• Brucellosis → undulant fever, no hemorrhage
• Hepatitis A → jaundice without hemorrhagic features
• Dengue hemorrhagic fever → thrombocytopenia, no prominent jaundice

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A female patient presents with swollen Bartholin glands. Discharging pus showed Gram-negative intracellular diplococci. Which is the organism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Neisseria gonorrhoeae

Gram-negative intracellular diplococci seen in pus from an infected Bartholin gland are characteristic of Neisseria gonorrhoeae.

• Appears as kidney-shaped Gram-negative diplococci inside neutrophils
• Causes gonorrhea, a sexually transmitted infection
• Commonly presents with urethritis, cervicitis, and can involve Bartholin glands
• Culture on selective media (e.g., Thayer-Martin) confirms diagnosis

Differentiation:

• Chlamydia trachomatis → intracellular but not visible on Gram stain
• Chancroid (Haemophilus ducreyi) → Gram-negative coccobacilli (“school of fish”)
• Treponema pallidum → spirochete, not seen on Gram stain

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A microbiologist demonstrates the biphasic life cycle of Chlamydia trachomatis. After entering a host epithelial cell, the infectious particle transforms into a larger metabolically active form that multiplies by binary fission within a cytoplasmic inclusion before reverting to the infectious form. Which of the following statements is correct?
options: The reticulate body is the infective extracellular form.
The elementary body is metabolically active and undergoes binary fission.
The reticulate body exists only within host cells.
The elementary body is the replicative form.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. The reticulate body exists only within host cells.

Chlamydia trachomatis is an obligate intracellular bacterium with a biphasic developmental cycle involving two morphologically and functionally distinct forms.

• Elementary Body (EB):

• Infectious form
• Extracellular
• Metabolically inactive
• Enters host cells by endocytosis

• Reticulate Body (RB):

• Non-infectious
• Metabolically active
• Exists only intracellularly
• Replicates by binary fission within membrane-bound inclusion bodies
• Converts back to elementary bodies before release

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A microbiologist is reviewing the mechanisms by which bacteria acquire antibiotic resistance. Which of the following statements is incorrect?
options: Enzymatic inactivation of antibiotics is the most common mechanism of bacterial resistance.
Resistance genes carried on plasmids are transmitted only by vertical inheritance during bacterial cell division.
Loss or modification of the vancomycin-binding target contributes to resistance in some enterococci.
Altered penicillin-binding proteins are responsible for β-lactam resistance in Streptococcus pneumoniae.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Resistance genes carried on plasmids are transmitted only by vertical inheritance during bacterial cell division.

Plasmid-mediated resistance is not restricted to vertical transmission.

Plasmids are primarily disseminated through horizontal gene transfer, allowing rapid spread of resistance genes within and between bacterial species.

Mechanisms of horizontal gene transfer

• Conjugation (most important) → transfer of plasmids through sex pili
• Transformation → uptake of free DNA
• Transduction → bacteriophage-mediated transfer

Although plasmids are passed to daughter cells during bacterial division (vertical transmission), this is not their exclusive mode of spread.

Why the other options are correct?

• A. Enzymatic inactivation of antibiotics is the most common mechanism ✅: Correct. Examples include:

• β-lactamases
• Extended-spectrum β-lactamases (ESBLs)
• Carbapenemases
• Aminoglycoside-modifying enzymes

•

C. Loss or modification of the vancomycin-binding target contributes to resistance in enterococci ✅: Correct. VanA/VanB genes replace:

• D-Ala–D-Ala → D-Ala–D-Lac

This markedly reduces vancomycin binding.

* D. Altered penicillin-binding proteins cause resistance in Streptococcus pneumoniae ✅: Correct. Resistance develops due to modified PBPs, resulting in decreased affinity for β-lactam antibiotics.

High-Yield Pearl: Mechanisms of Antibiotic Resistance

| Mechanism | Example

| --------- | -------

| Enzymatic destruction | β-lactamases, ESBLs, carbapenemases

| Altered target site | MRSA (PBP2a), S. pneumoniae (altered PBPs), VRE (D-Ala→D-Lac)

| Reduced permeability | Loss of porins in Gram-negative bacteria

| Efflux pumps | Tetracycline, macrolide resistance

| Horizontal gene transfer | Conjugation (plasmids), transformation, transduction

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A microbiologist isolates a small pleomorphic Gram-positive coccobacillus from the blood culture of a pregnant woman with fever. On incubation at 25°C, the organism demonstrates characteristic tumbling motility, but this motility is absent at 37°C. Which of the following organisms is the most likely isolate?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Listeria monocytogenes

Listeria monocytogenes is a small, pleomorphic Gram-positive coccobacillus with the following characteristic features:

• Tumbling motility at 20–25°C (umbrella motility in semisolid agar)
• Non-motile at 37°C
• Facultative intracellular pathogen
• Catalase positive
• Narrow zone of β-hemolysis
• Able to grow at 4°C (cold enrichment)

It is an important foodborne pathogen causing:

• Neonatal sepsis and meningitis
• Maternal infection during pregnancy
• Meningitis in elderly and immunocompromised patients

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A microbiology resident is comparing the major diarrheagenic pathotypes of Escherichia coli. One of the following statements incorrectly describes the mechanism of disease. Identify the false statement.
options: Enteroaggregative E. coli (EAEC) produces the heat-stable enterotoxin EAST-1.
Enterohemorrhagic E. coli (EHEC) infection may be complicated by hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS).
Enteropathogenic E. coli (EPEC) causes diarrhea by invading intestinal epithelial cells.
Enterotoxigenic E. coli (ETEC) is a common cause of traveler's diarrhea.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Enteropathogenic E. coli (EPEC) causes diarrhea by invading intestinal epithelial cells.

Enteropathogenic E. coli (EPEC) is non-invasive. It causes diarrhea by producing attaching and effacing (A/E) lesions, leading to:

• Intimate attachment to enterocytes (via intimin)
• Destruction of microvilli
• Formation of actin-rich pedestals
• Malabsorption and watery diarrhea

Unlike Enteroinvasive E. coli (EIEC), EPEC does not invade intestinal epithelial cells.

Why the other options are correct?

• A. EAEC produces heat-stable enterotoxin EAST-1 ✅: Correct. Enteroaggregative E. coli (EAEC) characteristically exhibits stacked-brick adherence and may produce EAST-1 (Enteroaggregative Heat-Stable Toxin-1), contributing to persistent diarrhea.
• B. EHEC can be complicated by HUS ✅: Correct. Enterohemorrhagic E. coli (EHEC) (e.g., O157:H7) produces Shiga-like toxin (verotoxin), which may lead to:

• Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia
• Thrombocytopenia
• Acute kidney injury (Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome)

• D. ETEC is a common cause of traveler's diarrhea ✅: Correct. Enterotoxigenic E. coli (ETEC) produces:

• Heat-labile toxin (LT) → ↑ cAMP
• Heat-stable toxin (ST) → ↑ cGMP

causing secretory watery diarrhea.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient presented with abdominal pain since 4 days with a history of remitting fever and bradycardia after having meals outside frequently. Which test can be done in the patient to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Blood culture

Enteric (Typhoid) fever – Salmonella typhi/paratyphi: presents with step-ladder fever, abdominal pain, and relative bradycardia (Faget sign) after outside food intake.

| Week of Illness | Test of Choice

| --------------- | --------------

| 1st week | Blood culture

| 2nd week | Agglutination (Widal test)

| 3rd week | Stool culture

| 4th week | Urine culture

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient presented with complaints of diarrhea and vomiting for >3 hours after consuming salads and milk at a picnic. Which of the following organisms is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Staphylococcus aureus

Staphylococcus aureus food poisoning is caused by ingestion of preformed enterotoxin in contaminated food, leading to rapid-onset gastroenteritis.

Incubation period: short (1–6 hours) → symptoms within a few hours

Food sources: salads (e.g., mayonnaise), milk, cream-based foods, pastries

Mechanism: ingestion of heat-stable enterotoxin (toxin formed in food before consumption).

Clinically presents with:-

• Prominent vomiting ; Diarrhea ; Usually no fever
• Self-limiting --> resolves within 24 hours

Why not others:

• Bacillus cereus: can cause rapid vomiting type, but classically associated with reheated rice/ Chinese food consumption
• Salmonella enterica: longer incubation (12–48 hours); Presents as inflammatory diarrhea with fever
• Clostridium perfringens: incubation 8–16 hours, mainly diarrhea with minimal vomiting

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient presents with step-ladder fever, rose spots, and intestinal ulcers for 3 days and is diagnosed clinically with enteric fever. What is the ideal test to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Blood culture

• Blood culture is the investigation of choice during the first week of enteric fever.
• Bacteremia is highest early in the illness, giving blood culture the highest sensitivity.
• Widal test detects antibodies and usually becomes positive only after 7–10 days.
• Stool culture becomes positive mainly during the second and third weeks.
• Urine culture has lower sensitivity and becomes positive later.
• Bone marrow culture is the most sensitive test overall, even after antibiotics.
• Salmonella Typhi is isolated using blood culture before antibody production.
• Blood should ideally be collected before starting antibiotics.
• Early diagnosis allows prompt antimicrobial therapy.
• Timeline: Week 1–Blood culture → Week 2–Widal → Week 2–3–Stool/Urine culture.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient was injured with a rusted metal object. What is the mechanism of action of tetanus toxin in such cases?
options: Inhibit the release of GABA and glycine
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Inhibit the release of GABA and glycine

Tetanus toxin (tetanospasmin) causes spastic paralysis by blocking inhibitory neurotransmission. Inhibits release of inhibitory neurotransmitters GABA and glycine from interneurons in the spinal cord

Loss of inhibitory control → continuous motor neuron excitation → muscle rigidity and spasms

Clinical features:

• Trismus (lockjaw)
• Opisthotonus
• Generalized muscle spasms

Differentiation:

• Botulinum toxin inhibits acetylcholine release → flaccid paralysis
• Tetanus causes spastic paralysis due to inhibition of inhibitory neurotransmitters

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient with atypical pneumonia is started on ceftriaxone, but shows no clinical improvement. Further evaluation identifies the causative organism as one that lacks a cell wall, making it intrinsically resistant to all β-lactam antibiotics. Which of the following organisms does not contain peptidoglycan in its cell wall?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Mycoplasma pneumoniae

Mycoplasma is unique among bacteria because it completely lacks a cell wall. Consequently:

• No peptidoglycan is present
• Cell membrane contains sterols (cholesterol), which provide structural stability
• It is intrinsically resistant to β-lactam antibiotics (penicillins, cephalosporins, carbapenems)

Why the other options are incorrect?

• A. Chlamydia trachomatis ❌: Chlamydia is an obligate intracellular bacterium. Although it lacks a classical peptidoglycan cell wall, it possesses peptidoglycan involved in cell division and is not classified as a naturally cell wall-deficient bacterium. In older entrance examinations, it is not considered the correct answer.
• C. Rickettsia prowazekii ❌: Rickettsia is a Gram-negative obligate intracellular bacterium with a thin peptidoglycan layer and an outer membrane.
• D. Virus ❌: Viruses do not possess a cell wall at all. Since the question pertains to organisms with bacterial cell wall characteristics, viruses are not the intended answer.

High-Yield Pearl

| Organism | Cell wall | Peptidoglycan | Important feature

| -------- | --------- | ------------- | -----------------

| Mycoplasma | ❌ Absent | ❌ Absent | Contains cholesterol; β-lactam resistant

| Chlamydia | Atypical | Minimal peptidoglycan (division ring) | Obligate intracellular

| Rickettsia | Present | ✅ Thin layer | Obligate intracellular Gram-negative bacterium

| Virus | No cell wall | ❌ Absent | Acellular

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A sewage worker presented with abdominal pain, jaundice, conjunctival suffusion, and blood in the urine for the past 5 days. Which of the following is the investigation of choice?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Microscopic agglutination test

Leptospirosis (e.g., in sewage workers exposed to contaminated water) is best confirmed by the Microscopic Agglutination Test (MAT)--> is the gold standard serological test.

Etiology: Leptospira interrogans (spirochete)

Risk factors: exposure to water contaminated with animal urine (rats, sewage) Enters via: Skin cuts, eyes, nose (mucosal surface)

Clinical features (Weil disease):

• High fever, chills
• Severe muscle pain (calf tenderness )
• Conjunctival suffusion (red eyes without pus → classic clue)
• Jaundice (liver involvement)
• AKI (kidney injury)
• Bleeding tendencies (platelets ↓, capillary damage)

Diagnosis:

MAT (Microscopic Agglutination Test) → detects antibodies against leptospira (gold standard)

Early phase: PCR may be used

Why not others:

• Widal test: Done for typhoid fever
• Weil-Felix reaction: Done for rickettsial infections
• Paul-Bunnell test: Done for infectious mononucleosis (EBV)

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A traveler consumed oysters. He later presented with bloody diarrhea, abdominal pain, and vomiting. The organism seen on microscopy exhibited Kanagawa phenomenon. The likely causative organism is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Vibrio parahaemolyticus

Vibrio parahaemolyticus is a marine, halophilic organism that causes acute gastroenteritis after ingestion of raw or undercooked seafood (especially oysters).

• Bloody diarrhea, abdominal pain, vomiting
• Exposure to seafood (oysters, shellfish)
• Gram-negative, curved rod

Diagnostic hallmark:

• Kanagawa phenomenon → β-hemolysis on Wagatsuma agar
• Due to thermostable direct hemolysin (TDH) → virulence factor

Differentiation:

• Vibrio cholerae → profuse watery “rice water” diarrhea, not bloody
• Staphylococcus aureus → toxin-mediated, rapid onset vomiting
• Salmonella typhi → enteric fever, not seafood-associated diarrhea

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A woman presents with high-grade fever and signs of shock. She has a history of prolonged tampon use. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Toxic shock syndrome toxin

Toxic Shock Syndrome (TSS) : an acute, life-threatening illness caused by toxin-producing Staphylococcus aureus.

• Classically associated with prolonged tampon use.

Causative toxin: TSST-1 (toxic shock syndrome toxin-1)

Mechanism: acts as a super antigen → massive T-cell activation → cytokine storm → shock

Clinically presents as:

• High-grade fever
• Hypotension (shock)
• Multiorgan involvement (renal, hepatic, CNS)

Why not others:

• Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome: exfoliative toxin causing flaccid blisters and skin peeling mainly in neonates and children; no shock
• Septic shock: may occur, but tampon use + toxin-mediated features point to TSS
• Streptococcal pharyngitis: localized throat infection; No shock.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: After heavy rainfall and flooding in Mumbai, several patients develop high fever, severe cough, myalgia, headache, conjunctival suffusion, jaundice, and acute kidney injury. They had walked barefoot through floodwater contaminated with animal waste. Dark-field microscopy shows tightly coiled spiral organisms with hooked ends. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Leptospirosis

Leptospirosis is a zoonotic infection caused by Leptospira interrogans, a thin, tightly coiled spirochete with characteristic hooked ends (“question mark” appearance). Humans acquire the infection through contact with water or soil contaminated with the urine of infected animals (especially rats). It commonly occurs after heavy rainfall and flooding, particularly when people walk barefoot through contaminated floodwater. Severe disease (Weil disease) is characterized by jaundice, acute kidney injury, hemorrhage, and conjunctival suffusion.

• Dark-field microscopy showing tightly coiled spirochetes with hooked ends

Why not the other options?

• A. Borrelia infection: Causes Lyme disease or relapsing fever; transmitted by ticks or lice, not floodwater.
• B. Treponema pallidum infection: Causes syphilis; transmitted sexually and lacks the typical floodwater exposure and Weil disease.
• C. Spirillum minus infection: Causes rat-bite fever (sodoku) following a rat bite, not water exposure.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: An abattoir worker develops a cutaneous ulcer on the dorsum of the hand. Culture of the lesion yields a Gram-positive organism that shows a positive McFadyean’s reaction. What is the most likely causative organism in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Bacillus anthracis

Bacillus anthracis causes cutaneous anthrax, classically seen in individuals handling animal products (e.g., abattoir workers).

• McFadyean reaction → demonstrates capsule (polypeptide capsule) using special staining
• Appears as blue bacilli with a pink capsule
• Painless ulcer → progresses to black eschar with surrounding edema

Key microbiological features:

• Gram-positive, spore-forming rod
• Non-motile
• Forms characteristic “Medusa head” colonies

Differentiation:

• Leptospira → spirochete (not Gram-positive rod)
• Clostridium perfringens → gas gangrene, not eschar
• Listeria → intracellular pathogen, no capsule demonstration by McFadyean

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: An animal handler presents with a black, necrotic eschar on his back. Which of the following organisms is the most likely causative agent?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Bacillus anthracis

A black necrotic eschar with surrounding edema in a person exposed to contaminated animal products (e.g., hides, meat, street handling) --> characteristic of cutaneous anthrax, caused by Bacillus anthracis.

Lesion progression:

• Painless papule → vesicle → black eschar (malignant pustule)
• Marked surrounding edema (disproportionate to lesion)

Transmission: spores from infected animals or contaminated animal products entering through skin cuts

Virulence factors:

• Poly-D-glutamate capsule (antiphagocytic)
• Anthrax toxin (edema toxin + lethal toxin)

Why not others:

• Rickettsia typhi: causes endemic typhus (no eschar)
• Scrub typhus: eschar present, but smaller with systemic features; caused by Orientia, not associated with this occupational exposure
• Coxiella burnetii: Q fever (no eschar)

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: An elderly resident of an old-age home consumed raw milk along with other residents. Shortly after, several individuals developed abdominal pain, bloody diarrhea, and vomiting. Microscopic examination of the stool revealed Gram-negative curved rods. What is the most likely causative organism responsible for this outbreak?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Campylobacter jejuni

Campylobacter jejuni is a common cause of foodborne gastroenteritis associated with consumption of unpasteurized milk and presents with bloody diarrhea.

• Gram-negative, curved or “comma-shaped” rods
• Microaerophilic organism
• Transmitted via contaminated food (especially unpasteurized milk, poultry)

Important complications:

• Guillain-Barré syndrome
• Reactive arthritis

Differentiation:

• Clostridium perfringens → toxin-mediated watery diarrhea, no blood
• Staphylococcus aureus → rapid-onset vomiting due to preformed toxin

Vibrio parahaemolyticus → seafood-associated diarrhea

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Assertion - Reason: (A) Myocarditis is the common known complication of faucial diphtheria (R) It is due to bacteremia by diphtheria
options: Assertion is true, reason is true; reason is the correct explanation for the assertion
Assertion is true, reason is true; reason is not the correct explanation for the assertion
Assertion is false and reason is true
Assertion is true and reason is false
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Assertion is true and reason is false

Myocarditis is a well-known and serious complication of faucial diphtheria, but it is not due to bacteremia.

• Corynebacterium diphtheriae produces a potent exotoxin
• The toxin spreads hematogenously and causes damage to distant organs, especially the heart and nerves
• Myocarditis occurs due to toxin-mediated inhibition of protein synthesis (via EF-2 inactivation), not due to direct bacterial invasion

Concept clarification:

• Diphtheria is primarily a toxemia, not a bacteremia
• Local infection remains in the throat, while systemic effects are toxin-mediated

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Cat-scratch disease is caused by infection of which of the following organisms?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Bartonella henselae

Cat-scratch disease is a zoonotic infection caused by Bartonella henselae, a Gram-negative bacillus transmitted through cat scratches, bites, or flea exposure. It typically presents with a papule at the inoculation site, followed by painful regional lymphadenopathy. The disease is usually self-limiting but may cause disseminated infection in immunocompromised individuals.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A. Chlamydia trachomatis: Causes trachoma, urogenital infections, lymphogranuloma venereum, and neonatal conjunctivitis.
• B. Coxiella burnetii: Causes Q fever, transmitted by inhalation of aerosols from infected animals.
• C. Trypanosoma cruzi: Causes Chagas disease, transmitted by the triatomine (reduviid) bug.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Chocolate agar is primarily used to culture which of the following organisms?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Haemophilus influenzae

Chocolate agar is an enriched medium used to culture fastidious organisms, especially Haemophilus influenzae.

·    Prepared by heating blood agar, which lyses RBCs → releases growth factors:

o    Factor X (hemin)

o    Factor V (NAD)

·         Haemophilus influenzae requires both X and V factors, hence grows well on chocolate agar

·         Also supports growth of Neisseria species (e.g., N. gonorrhoeae, N. meningitidis)

Why not others:

·         Listeria monocytogenes: grows on standard media (e.g., blood agar)

·         Staphylococcus aureus: grows on simple media (blood agar)

·         Escherichia coli: grows on routine media (e.g., MacConkey agar)

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Choose the correct statements from the following options: a. Widal test done in first week of illness b. Microscopic agglutination test in Leptospira c. Weil Felix test in typhus fever d. Standard agglutination test in Brucellosis e. VDRL used for Treponema pallidum
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. b, c, d, e

Understanding the appropriate serological tests for different infections is essential for diagnosis and exam questions.

Correct associations:

• Leptospira → Microscopic agglutination test (MAT)
• Typhus (rickettsial infections) → Weil-Felix test
• Brucellosis → Standard agglutination test (SAT)
• Treponema pallidum → VDRL (non-treponemal screening test)

Incorrect statement:

• Widal test is not useful in the first week of illness; it becomes positive only after 7–10 days

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: In a rural village, several residents report finding a sudden large number of dead rats around their houses. A few days later, villagers develop fever, painful lymph node swelling, and severe weakness. A rodent-associated epidemic transmitted by rat fleas is suspected. Residents are at highest risk of which disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Bubonic plague

Bubonic plague is caused by Yersinia pestis, a Gram-negative bipolar (“safety pin”) staining coccobacillus. It is transmitted to humans through the bite of infected rat fleas (Xenopsylla cheopis). A sudden die-off of rats often precedes human outbreaks because infected rodents succumb to the disease, causing infected fleas to seek human hosts. The hallmark clinical feature is painful, enlarged regional lymph nodes (buboes) associated with high fever and systemic toxicity.

Why not the other options?

• A. Dengue fever: Transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes, not rat fleas, and presents with fever, myalgia, rash, and thrombocytopenia.
• C. Typhoid fever: Caused by Salmonella Typhi, transmitted by contaminated food or water; does not cause buboes or follow rat die-offs.
• D. Hepatitis A: Spread by the fecal-oral route, causing acute hepatitis without lymph node swelling.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: In the modified Duke criteria for infective endocarditis, which one of the following is not a major criterion?
options: New partial dehiscence of prosthetic valve
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Roth’s spots

The modified Duke criteria diagnose infective endocarditis using major and minor criteria.

Major criteria include:

• Positive blood cultures with typical organisms
• Evidence of endocardial involvement on echocardiography (vegetation, abscess, new partial dehiscence of a prosthetic valve)
• New valvular regurgitation

Why not the other options?

• A. New partial dehiscence of prosthetic valve ✔️: Major criterion (echocardiographic evidence).
• B. Positive blood culture ✔️: Major criterion.
• C. Roth’s spots ❌: Minor criterion (an immunologic phenomenon).
• D. New valvular regurgitation ✔️: Major criterion.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Match each disease with the correct causative agent from the options provided: A. Donovanosis B. Oroya fever C. Rat bite fever D. Pinta 1. Treponema carateum 2. Klebsiella granulomatis 3. Bartonella bacilliformis 4. Streptobacillus moniliformis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. a-2, b-3, c-4, d-1

| Condition | Organism

| --------- | --------

| Donovanosis | Klebsiella granulomatis

| Oroya fever | Bartonella bacilliformis

| Rat bite fever | Streptobacillus moniliformis

| Pinta | Treponema carateum

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: The Kanagawa phenomenon, demonstrated using Wagatsuma agar, is characteristic of which bacterial organism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Vibrio parahaemolyticus

The Kanagawa phenomenon is a hemolysis reaction seen on Wagatsuma agar and is characteristic of Vibrio parahaemolyticus.

• Demonstrates beta-hemolysis due to thermostable direct hemolysin (TDH)
• TDH is a major virulence factor responsible for enterotoxic effects
• Associated with seafood-related gastroenteritis (especially raw/undercooked seafood)

Differentiation:

• Vibrio cholerae → causes rice-water diarrhea via cholera toxin (no Kanagawa phenomenon)
• ·       Shigella → invasive dysentery, no hemolysis on Wagatsuma agar
• Burkholderia pseudomallei → causes melioidosis, unrelated

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: The neuropsychiatric manifestations of the infections caused by which one of the following infectious agents presents as ‘Muttering Delirium’ or ‘Coma Vigil’ in which patients pick randomly at bed clothes or imaginary objects?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Salmonella typhi

• Muttering delirium (coma vigil) is a classical neuropsychiatric manifestation of enteric (typhoid) fever, particularly in severe disease.
• The patient may appear confused, drowsy, and withdrawn, with characteristic “picking at bedclothes” or imaginary objects.

Why not the other options?

• A. Neisseria gonorrhoeae: Causes gonorrhea and disseminated gonococcal infection, not the classic typhoid delirium.
• B. Cardiobacterium hominis: Causes infective endocarditis, not muttering delirium.
• D. Campylobacter jejuni: Primarily causes acute inflammatory gastroenteritis; may rarely have neurological complications such as Guillain-Barré syndrome.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: The virulence factor of Bacillus anthracis responsible for resistance to phagocytosis is its capsule. Which of the following is the correct biochemical composition?
options: pXO1 plasmid and poly-α-glutamic acid capsule
pXO2 plasmid and poly-γ-glutamic acid capsule
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. pXO2 plasmid and poly-γ-glutamic acid capsule

Bacillus anthracis is unique among bacteria because its antiphagocytic capsule is composed of poly-γ-D-glutamic acid, not polysaccharide. Capsule synthesis is encoded by the pXO2 plasmid, while the pXO1 plasmid encodes the anthrax toxin components.

Why is D correct?

• pXO2 plasmid → Encodes the poly-γ-D-glutamic acid capsule, which prevents phagocytosis.
• The capsule is an important virulence factor responsible for immune evasion.

Why not the other options?

• A. pXO2 plasmid and polysaccharide capsule: Incorrect; the capsule is poly-γ-D-glutamic acid, not polysaccharide.
• B. pXO1 plasmid and poly-α-glutamic acid capsule: Incorrect; pXO1 encodes toxins, not the capsule, and the capsule is γ, not α, glutamic acid.
• C. pXO1 plasmid and polysaccharide capsule: Incorrect for both the plasmid and capsule composition.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Two patients present with flaccid paralysis and hypotonia—one after consuming canned food and the other after eating unprocessed puffer fish. Which of the following correctly matches the mechanisms responsible for their paralysis, respectively?
options: Botulinum toxin blocks Na⁺ channels; Tetrodotoxin blocks ACh release
Botulinum toxin prevents ACh release; Tetrodotoxin blocks Na⁺ channels
Botulinum toxin blocks nicotinic receptors; Tetrodotoxin blocks Ca²⁺ channels
Botulinum toxin increases ACh release; Tetrodotoxin blocks K⁺ channels
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Botulinum toxin prevents ACh release; Tetrodotoxin blocks Na⁺ channels

Botulinum toxin and tetrodotoxin both produce flaccid paralysis, but by different mechanisms. Botulinum toxin acts at the presynaptic neuromuscular junction, where it cleaves SNARE proteins, preventing acetylcholine (ACh) release. In contrast, tetrodotoxin binds to and blocks voltage-gated sodium (Na⁺) channels, preventing action potential generation and propagation in nerves and muscles.

Why not the other options?

• A. Botulinum toxin blocks Na⁺ channels; Tetrodotoxin blocks ACh release: The mechanisms are reversed.
• C. Botulinum toxin blocks nicotinic receptors; Tetrodotoxin blocks Ca²⁺ channels: Nicotinic receptor blockade is the mechanism of non-depolarizing neuromuscular blockers (e.g., vecuronium); tetrodotoxin does not block calcium channels.
• D. Botulinum toxin increases ACh release; Tetrodotoxin blocks K⁺ channels: Both statements are incorrect.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: What does ‘H’ indicate in a patient presenting with a history of EHEC O157:H7?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Flagella

| Antigen | Represents | Location / Structure

| ------- | ---------- | --------------------

| O antigen | Somatic antigen | LPS (cell wall)

| H antigen | Flagellar antigen | Flagella (motility)

| A antigen | Fimbrial (pili) antigen | Surface pili or fimbriae

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: What is the primary mechanism of action of botulinum toxin?
options: Inhibition of release of acetylcholine from presynaptic nerve terminals
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Inhibition of release of acetylcholine from presynaptic nerve terminals

Botulinum toxin causes flaccid paralysis by blocking the presynaptic release of acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction. It cleaves SNARE proteins (e.g., SNAP-25, synaptobrevin, syntaxin), preventing fusion of acetylcholine-containing vesicles with the presynaptic membrane and thereby inhibiting neurotransmitter release.

Why not the other options?

• A. Irreversible inhibition of acetylcholinesterase: Mechanism of organophosphate poisoning, which causes excess acetylcholine and cholinergic toxicity.
• B. Blockade of postsynaptic nicotinic receptors: Mechanism of non-depolarizing neuromuscular blockers (e.g., vecuronium, rocuronium).
• D. Competitive antagonism at muscarinic receptors: Mechanism of atropine and other antimuscarinic drugs.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which among the following is the most specific disease caused by Streptococcus agalactiae?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Neonatal sepsis

Streptococcus agalactiae (Group B Streptococcus) is classically associated with neonatal infections.

• Most specific disease: neonatal sepsis (early- and late-onset)
• Also causes neonatal meningitis and pneumonia
• Transmitted from colonized maternal genital tract during delivery

Clinical relevance:

• Screening of pregnant women (35–37 weeks) is recommended
• Intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis prevents neonatal infection

Differentiation:

• Streptococcus pyogenes → pharyngitis, rheumatic fever
• Streptococcus mutans → dental caries
• Infective endocarditis → more commonly due to viridans streptococci or Staphylococcus aureus

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which among the following organism is the cause of necrotizing fasciitis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Streptococcus pyogenes

Necrotising fasciitis is a Life-threatening soft tissue infection

• Most commonly caused by Group A β-hemolytic Streptococcus.

• Infection through skin microcuts/ surgical wounds--> Has enzymes like Hyaluronidase, streptokinase--> these help s. pyogenes travel / spread rapidly along tissue/ fascial planes--> rapid tissue destruction.
• Produces exotoxins (streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxins) → Massive T-cell activation --> Cytokine storm --> Tissue destruction + shock.

Clinical features:

• Severe pain out of proportion to findings ; spread along fascial planes
• Skin necrosis, bullae, crepitus (late)
• Systemic toxicity (fever, shock)

Why not others :

• Streptococcus pneumoniae → causes pneumonia, meningitis; not necrotising fasciitis. ( respiratory route; not via skin)
• Clostridium perfringens → gas gangrene (myonecrosis), not classic necrotizing fasciitis
• Clostridium tetani → tetanus (neurotoxin-mediated disease).

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which bacterial toxin acts by interfering with EF-2 function?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Diphtheria

Diphtheria toxin inhibits protein synthesis by inactivating elongation factor-2 (EF-2).

• Catalyzes ADP-ribosylation of EF-2
• Blocks translocation step in protein synthesis → cell death

Key points:

• Produced by Corynebacterium diphtheriae
• Responsible for systemic complications such as myocarditis and neuropathy
• Acts as an exotoxin (A-B toxin)

Differentiation:

• Clostridium toxins → neurotoxins (tetanus, botulinum) affecting neurotransmitters
• Bacillus (e.g., anthrax) → edema and lethal toxins
• Vibrio cholerae → activates adenylate cyclase → ↑ cAMP

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which extracellular cell adhesion is disrupted by Vibrio cholerae?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Occludens

Vibrio cholerae disrupts tight junctions between intestinal epithelial cells, specifically affecting zonula occludens.

• Cholera toxin → ↑ cAMP via activation of adenylate cyclase
• Leads to massive chloride and water secretion
• Also disrupts tight junction proteins (occludens), increasing intestinal permeability

Key concept:

• Tight junctions (zonula occludens) maintain paracellular barrier integrity
• Their disruption contributes to profuse watery diarrhea

Differentiation:

• Integrins → cell–matrix adhesion
• Cadherins → adherens junctions (cell–cell adhesion)

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following are correct in respect of Diphtheria? 1. The incubation period is 14 to 28 days. 2. Diphtheria antitoxin is used in treatment of cases. 3. It is one of the diseases protected from by the Pentavalent vaccine given in National Program. Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 2 and 3 only

Diphtheria is an acute toxin-mediated infection caused by Corynebacterium diphtheriae. It primarily affects the upper respiratory tract and can lead to severe complications due to the diphtheria exotoxin, including myocarditis and neuritis. Early administration of diphtheria antitoxin (DAT) is lifesaving.

• Statement 1: The incubation period is 14–28 days. ❌

• The incubation period is 2–5 days (range 1–10 days), not 14–28 days.

• Statement 2: Diphtheria antitoxin is used in treatment of cases. ✅

• Diphtheria antitoxin (DAT) neutralizes circulating toxin and should be administered as early as possible, without waiting for culture confirmation.
• It is given along with antibiotics (erythromycin or penicillin).

• Statement 3: It is one of the diseases protected from by the Pentavalent vaccine given in the National Programme. ✅

• The Pentavalent vaccine protects against:

• Diphtheria
• Pertussis
• Tetanus
• Hepatitis B
• Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib)

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following correctly denote(s) the clinical manifestations of diphtheria? 1. Dermatosis characterized by punched-out ulcerative lesions with necrotic sloughing 2. Dysphonia, dysphagia and headache 3. Myocarditis, cardiac arrhythmias and congestive heart failure 4. Massive tonsillar, submandibular and paratracheal oedema presenting as ‘bull-neck’ appearance Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 2, 3 and 4

1. Dermatosis with punched-out ulcerative lesions and necrotic slough: Correct

• Cutaneous diphtheria can cause ulcerative lesions with necrotic slough.

2. Dysphonia, dysphagia and headache: Correct

• Pharyngeal/laryngeal diphtheria may cause dysphagia and dysphonia, while systemic toxin effects can produce headache and malaise.

3. Myocarditis, cardiac arrhythmias and congestive heart failure: Correct

• Diphtheria toxin can cause myocarditis, potentially leading to conduction abnormalities, arrhythmias and heart failure.

4. Bull-neck appearance: Correct

• Severe pharyngeal diphtheria can cause extensive tonsillar, submandibular and cervical edema, producing the characteristic “bull-neck” appearance.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following has two circular DNA segments?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Vibrio cholerae

Vibrio cholerae is unique among the listed bacteria because it possesses two circular chromosomes (DNA segments):

• Chromosome I (\~3 Mb): Contains most essential housekeeping genes and major virulence genes.
• Chromosome II (\~1 Mb): Contains genes involved in adaptation, environmental survival, and accessory functions.

Why not the other options?

• A. Escherichia coli: Has a single circular chromosome (may also carry plasmids, which are not considered chromosomes).
• C. Mycobacterium leprae: Has a single circular chromosome with a highly reduced genome.
• D. Mycoplasma genitalium: Has one of the smallest single circular bacterial genomes.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following is an obligate intracellular organism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ehrlichia chaffeensis

Obligate intracellular organisms are bacteria that must live and multiply inside host cells because they lack the ability to generate sufficient energy independently.

•

Ehrlichia chaffeensis is an obligate intracellular bacterium

•

→ Infects monocytes

→ Forms morulae (intracytoplasmic inclusions)

→ Transmitted by tick bite

Other obligate intracellular organisms:

• Chlamydia
• Rickettsia
• Coxiella
• Ehrlichia
• Anaplasma

Why not others:

• Campylobacter jejuni → extracellular
• Tropheryma whipplei → intracellular but not obligate
• Serratia marcescens → extracellular

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following statements are correct regarding brucellosis? 1. Fever may develop into an undulating pattern that persists for weeks. 2. Associated musculoskeletal symptoms are a feature of the disease. 3. Brucellae behave as facultative intracellular parasites. Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 2 and 3

Brucellosis is a zoonotic infection caused by Brucella spp., acquired through unpasteurized dairy products, direct contact with infected animals, or inhalation. It classically presents with undulating fever, night sweats, malaise, and musculoskeletal involvement (arthralgia, arthritis, sacroiliitis, spondylitis). Brucella are facultative intracellular gram-negative coccobacilli, allowing persistence and chronic infection.

Why are the statements correct?

• 1. Fever may develop into an undulating pattern that persists for weeks ✔️: Fever is characteristically undulating, recurring over weeks.
• 2. Associated musculoskeletal symptoms are a feature of the disease ✔️: Musculoskeletal symptoms are common and are the most frequent focal complication.
• 3. Brucellae behave as facultative intracellular parasites ✔️: Brucellae are facultative intracellular organisms, surviving within macrophages.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following statements are correct regarding UTI? 1. Urine is an excellent culture medium for bacteria. 2. Atrophic urethritis in postmenopausal women is a risk factor. 3. Antibiotics are recommended in all cases of asymptomatic bacteriuria. 4. Certain strains of E. coli have a particular propensity to invade the urinary tract. Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 2 and 4

Urinary tract infection (UTI) occurs when uropathogens, most commonly uropathogenic Escherichia coli (UPEC), colonize and invade the urinary tract. Risk factors include female sex, urinary stasis, catheterization, sexual activity, and postmenopausal atrophic urethritis/vaginitis due to estrogen deficiency.

Why not statement 3?

• Asymptomatic bacteriuria should not be treated routinely. Antibiotics are recommended only in pregnancy and before invasive urological procedures associated with mucosal bleeding (and selected recent renal transplant patients), not in all cases.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following statements are correct regarding Weil’s disease? I. It is caused by a virus named leptospira II. Acute kidney injury can lead to oliguria in this disease III. Microscopic agglutination is the investigation of choice IV. Ceftriaxone given parenterally is effective treatment Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. II, III and IV

Weil’s disease is the severe icteric form of leptospirosis, a zoonotic infection caused by the spirochete Leptospira interrogans. It is transmitted through contact with water or soil contaminated with urine of infected animals, especially rats.

The disease is characterized by the triad of:

• Jaundice
• Acute kidney injury (AKI)
•

Hemorrhagic manifestations

•

I. It is caused by a virus named leptospira. ✘

• Incorrect. Leptospira interrogans is a spirochete bacterium, not a virus.

• II. Acute kidney injury can lead to oliguria in this disease. ✔

• AKI is a major complication of Weil’s disease and may present with oliguria or non-oliguric renal failure.

• III. Microscopic agglutination is the investigation of choice. ✔

• The Microscopic Agglutination Test (MAT) is the gold standard serological test for diagnosing leptospirosis. ⭐

• IV. Ceftriaxone given parenterally is effective treatment. ✔

• IV ceftriaxone or IV penicillin G is recommended for severe leptospirosis.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following test is used for antibiotic sensitivity?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. E-test ( Epsilometertest )

The E-test (Epsilometer test) is used to determine antibiotic sensitivity by providing a quantitative measure of the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC).

• A plastic strip impregnated with a gradient of antibiotic is placed on an inoculated agar plate
• An elliptical zone of inhibition forms after incubation
• The MIC is read where the ellipse intersects the strip

Why not others:

• Elek’s test detects diphtheria toxin production
• Latex agglutination is used for antigen detection
• CAMP test identifies Group B Streptococcus

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which one of the following is a manifestation of vascular phenomenon in the modified Duke criteria for infective endocarditis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Janeway lesions

In the modified Duke criteria for infective endocarditis, vascular phenomena are minor criteria and include:

• Janeway lesions
• Major arterial emboli
• Septic pulmonary infarcts
• Mycotic aneurysm
• Intracranial hemorrhage
• Conjunctival hemorrhages

Why not the other options?

• A. Roth’s spots: Immunologic phenomenon (minor criterion).
• B. Osler’s nodes: Immunologic phenomenon (minor criterion).
• D. Positive rheumatoid factor: Immunologic phenomenon (minor criterion).

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which one of the following is the causative organism of Erythrasma, a mild, localized and superficial skin infection?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Corynebacterium minutissimum

Erythrasma is a superficial bacterial skin infection caused by Corynebacterium minutissimum. It commonly affects intertriginous areas such as the groin, axillae, inframammary folds, and toe webs, especially in diabetic, obese, and immunocompromised individuals.

The infection presents as well-demarcated, reddish-brown patches with fine scaling and is often mistaken for fungal infections. The organism produces porphyrins, which fluoresce coral-red under Wood’s lamp examination, a classic diagnostic feature.

Why not the other options?

• A. Corynebacterium pseudotuberculosis: Causes caseous lymphadenitis in animals and is a rare human pathogen.
• C. Corynebacterium diphtheriae: Causes diphtheria, characterized by pseudomembrane formation and toxin-mediated systemic disease.
• D. Corynebacterium matruchotii: Part of the normal oral flora and associated with dental plaque formation.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which organism moves transcellularly by utilizing actin filaments?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Listeria

Listeria monocytogenes spreads from cell to cell by polymerizing host actin filaments.

• Uses ActA protein to induce actin polymerization
• Forms “actin comet tails” that propel the bacterium within and between cells
• Allows transcellular spread without exposure to extracellular immune defenses

Key points:

• Facultative intracellular organism
• Causes meningitis and sepsis in neonates, elderly, and immunocompromised
• Shows tumbling motility and grows at low temperatures

Differentiation:

• EIEC → intracellular but does not use actin-based motility
• Salmonella → resides in vacuoles (no actin comet tails)
• Vibrio → extracellular organism

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 34-year-old HIV-positive male presented with low-grade fever, cough, night sweats, and weight loss for the past 3 weeks. In view of TB investigations, the Mantoux test was negative, chest X-ray showed non-specific findings and an adequate amount of sputum could not be collected for slide examination. Which of the following is used to diagnose latent TB infection in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Interferon gamma release assay

The test used to diagnose latent TB infection in this patient is the Interferon-gamma release assay(IGRA).

TB test done on a whole blood sample is IGRA. In this test, sensitized T lymphocytes (from whole blood) of suspected individuals, are exposed to highly specific M. tuberculosis antigens such as CFP –10 and ESAT 6. This releases the cytokine IFN- gamma into the blood, which is then measured. It has been evaluated for the diagnosis of latent tuberculosis in HIV patients (who frequently have a negative Mantoux test.

IGRAs that have been approved by the US (FDA) are

* QuantiFERON-TB Gold In-Tube test (QFT-GIT): It quantitates the amount of interferon-gamma produced by CD4+ T cells in response to the antigens from Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

* T-SPOT.TB test (T-Spot): It determines the total number of individual effector T cells expressing Interferon-gamma.

* QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus (QFT- Plus)

IGRAs are more specific than Tuberculin Skin Testing (TST) because of less cross-reactivity to BCG vaccination and sensitization by nontuberculous mycobacteria.

There are 3 described methods for tuberculin skin testing (TST):

* Mantoux test, also known as the Pirquet test (preferred method)

* Heaf test

* Tine test

The TrueNat TB test is a new molecular test that can diagnose TB and resistance to rifampicin in one hour. This test uses a sputum sample and only about 0.5 ml of the sample is required.

Urine lipoarabinomannan (LAM) assay is used for the diagnosis of tuberculosis. Lipoarabinomannan (LAM) antigen is a lipopolysaccharide present in the mycobacterial cell wall, released from metabolically active cells or degenerating cells of patients having tuberculosis. Urine LAM is a useful tool in diagnosing tuberculosis, especially in patients with HIV and a low CD 4 count.

QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus (QFT- Plus) is an improved version of the QuantiFERON-TB Gold test. QuantiFERON-TB Gold detects only TB-specific CD4+ responses. However, QuantiFeron-TB Gold Plus detects both CD8+ and CD4+ T cell responses to TB specific antigens.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 4-year-old boy presents with complaints of fever and sore throat. On examination, he has extensive cervical swelling and a well-demarcated white-gray exudative substance adherent to his oropharynx and attempts to remove this pseudomembranous result in bleeding. The parents report that all his childhood vaccines were skipped due to religious beliefs. A throat swab under Albert's staining is as below. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Diphtheria

This is a classic clinical description, oral examination with pseudomembrane and the image given above is of a patient with diphtheria.

Corynebacterium diphtheria (also called Klebs- Loeffler bacillus) is a gram-positive bacillus with clubbing at both ends. They possess characteristic polymetaphosphate granules also called metachromatic granules.

The diphtheria toxin is an extremely potent protein toxin that acts by inhibiting protein synthesis by inactivating the elongation factor (EF-2).

Clinically, patients with diphtheria present with fever, sore throat, and pseudomembranous lesions on the tonsillar, pharyngeal, or nasal mucosa. The pseudo-membrane in diphtheria is tightly adherent to the underlying tissues and attempts to remove them result in bleeding. A few patients develop massive edema of the tonsils, submandibular and paratracheal region causing a characteristic bull-neck. It is associated with foul breath, thick speech, and stridor.

The systemic manifestations of diphtheria are due to diphtheria toxin and not due to bacteremia. It has a special affinity for myocardium, adrenal glands, and nerve endings and therefore, causes weakness as a result of neurotoxicity, cardiac arrhythmias, or congestive heart failure due to myocarditis.

Treatment of diphtheria includes administration of diphtheria anti-toxin. Recommended antibiotics include penicillin G and erythromycin for two weeks. Patients are placed in an isolation room and droplet precautions should be maintained for all cases of respiratory diphtheria. Although patients are not contagious starting 48 hours after antibiotic therapy, droplet precautions are typically maintained until the completion of the antibiotic course and are culture-negative on two cultures taken 24 hours apart. Droplet precautions include the use of masks, gowns, gloves, and protective eye gear when providing direct patient care.

While the development of an effective vaccine has nearly eradicated the disease in many countries, failure to undergo routine vaccination leaves some patients at risk. Vaccination with diphtheria toxoid is recommended for all cases of diphtheria after convalescence, as natural infection may not induce an adequate level of protective immunity.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 55-year-old man comes with complaints of fever and increasing fatigue for the past week. On examination, he is febrile at 40°C, hypotensive, and has tachycardia. The blood smear of this patient is given below. What is the causative agent?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Plasmodium falciparum

The given clinical history and the blood smear show multiple ring forms in RBCs suggestive of Plasmodium falciparum.

It shows a very high percentage of RBCs containing ring forms. This high-level parasitemia is more often seen in Plasmodium falciparum infection than in infection by the other plasmodia.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A chronic asthmatic patient who is on inhaled steroids presents with a history of a burning sensation on eating hot or spicy food and the following findings are seen. What is the most possible diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Candida infection

The clinical vignette of inhaled steroid use along with a lesion on the tongue points towards a diagnosis of Candida infection.

Erythematous (atrophic) candidiasis appears as a red, raw-looking lesion. It may or may not be related to pseudomembranes. On the tongue, there is a loss of the lingual papillae, leaving a smooth area. It can occur after long-term corticosteroid or antibiotic usage or those with HIV. Other names for this condition include acute atrophic oral candidiasis and antibiotic sore tongue.

Cutaneous and mucosal infections manifest as thrush affecting the tongue, lips, gums, and palate. It is seen as a patchy to confluent whitish pseudomembranous lesion and is commonly associated with AIDS. Candida may also invade the vaginal mucosa, leading to vulvovaginitis, and the nails, and around the nail plate, leading to onychomycosis. Mucocutaneous manifestations are managed with topical nystatin or oral ketoconazole.

Other options:

Burning mouth syndrome (BMS) is a burning sensation in the mouth with no underlying dental or medical cause, where no related signs of disease are found in the mouth.

Migratory glossitis/geographic tongue is due to the rapid loss and regrowth of filiform papillae of the tongue. It is a benign inflammatory condition of the tongue associated with psoriasis and reactive arthritis. Geographic tongue, though consistent with the clinical image, is not the best fit considering the clinical history. It is usually asymptomatic but can be occasionally associated with a sore tongue.

Oral lichen planus is associated with Wickham striae in the oral cavity. They are fine white lines in a lacy or fern-like pattern that cross the plaques in lichen planus.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: An AIDS-positive patient came with a history of fever, vomiting, and meningismus. Which of the following tests help in the rapid diagnosis of cryptococcal meningitis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Blood assay for cryptococcal antigen

Blood assay for cryptococcal antigen help in the rapid diagnosis of cryptococcal meningitis.

Latex agglutination tests are mainly used for the detection of carbohydrate antigens of encapsulated microorganisms. In latex agglutination tests, an antigen-specific antibody (either polyclonal or monoclonal) is fixed to latex beads. When the clinical specimen from the patient is added to a suspension of the latex beads, the antibodies bind to the antigens on the microorganism forming a lattice structure, and agglutination of the beads occurs.

Cryptococcal meningitis is the most common cause of meningitis in an immunocompromised HIV patient. It generally occurs in untreated patients, with CD4+ T cell counts <100/μL.

It presents with subacute meningoencephalitis with fever, nausea, vomiting, altered mental status, headache, and meningeal signs. The CSF profile shows elevations in WBC with lymphocyte predominance, elevated protein levels, and reduced to normal levels of glucose. The CSF opening pressure is usually elevated

Diagnosis is made by demonstration of yeast cells or cryptococcal antigen in CSF. India ink stain is used to demonstrate capsulated budding yeast cells in CSF as they have a distinctive appearance because their capsules exclude ink particles. But its very much subjective and hence is less preferred over other methods for rapid diagnosis. Rapid detection of cryptococcal antigen in CSF and blood can also be done. Colonies develop within a few days on most media at room temperature or 37°C.

Treatment

*  Induction – IV or Liposomal Amphotericin B with Flucytosine for at least 2 weeks, continuing with Amphotericin alone ideally until the CSF culture turns negative.

*  Maintenance -  Oral Fluconazole until the CD4+ T cell count has increased to >200 cells/μL for 6 months in response to cART.

*  Primary Prophylaxis - Oral Fluconazole when CD4+ T cell count is <100/μL.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: An unknown disease of suspected infectious origin has come up in your town. As a microbiologist, you collect the relevant samples and detect the etiological cause. Which of the following types of PCR would you do?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Multiplex PCR

Multiplex PCR can be used to identify an unknown infectious agent.

Types of PCR:

* Multiplex PCR: Primers to more than one pathogen are used simultaneously and hence multiple products are obtained.

* Nested PCR: It involves the sequential use of two primer sets. The first primer set is used for amplification and the amplicon obtained is then used as a target sequence for second amplification. This ensures specificity. Used in GeneXpert to detect Mycobacterium TB and resistance to rifampicin.

* Quantitative PCR: Apart from just detecting the target sequences, it also tells the number of such target sequences. We can quantify the HIV viral load with this technique.

* Reverse transcriptase PCR: The enzyme reverse transcriptase (RT) is used to synthesize a complimentary copy of DNA (cDNA) from RNA and this cDNA is then used as a template for PCR. Unlike conventional PCR which can only amplify DNA, this one can even amplify RNA. It is used to detect H1N1 from the Nasopharyngeal swab.

* Real-time PCR: This helps quantify the PCR and gives an estimate of the pathogen DNA load in the specimen. It uses fluorescent dyes or specific DNA probes. It is also known as qPCR (Quantitative PCR).

questions.text: Identify the dermatophyte based on the macroconidia shown in the image below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Epidermophyton

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: New A 33-year-old male comes with complaints of dry cough, fever, and shortness of breath for 2 days along with a loss of taste and smell. He is a social worker who has been traveling a lot. What would be the investigation of choice for this patient to confirm the diagnosis of COVID-19?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. RT-PCR

The patient with the above clinical scenario is most likely suffering from COVID-19. RT-PCR (reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction) is the investigation of choice to confirm an acute infection of COVID-19.

There are two major types of tests for COVID-19:

* Nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs; eg, RT-PCR) –
RT-PCR for SARS-CoV-2 is the primary test used to diagnose active COVID-19. The test is typically performed on nasopharyngeal swabs, but can also be performed on other respiratory tract specimens (eg, oropharyngeal swabs, lower respiratory tract samples).

* Serology –
Serologic tests measure antibodies to SARS-CoV-2 and are primarily used to identify patients who have had COVID-19 in the past. While some serologic assays can help identify patients with acute infection, they are not as reliable as RT-PCR and not recommended for this purpose.

Basic protective measures against the new coronavirus: (SARS CoV 2)

* Wash your hands frequently for at least 20 seconds.

* Maintain social distancing- Maintain at least 1-meter distance between yourself and anyone who is coughing or sneezing

* Avoid touching eyes, nose, and mouth

* Practice respiratory hygiene- cover your mouth and nose with your bent elbow or tissue when you cough or sneeze, then dispose of the used tissue immediately.

* If you have fever, cough, and difficulty breathing, seek medical care early

* Stay informed and follow the advice given by your healthcare provider

Treatment: There is no specific antiviral treatment recommended for COVID-19. People with COVID-19 should receive supportive care to help relieve symptoms. For severe cases, treatment should include care to support vital organ functions.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Oral hairy leukoplakia is associated with which of the following infections?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Epstein Barr virus

Oral hairy leukoplakia (OHL) is due to the reactivation of Epstein Barr Virus (EBV) infection and usually occurs in association with immunodeficiency due to HIV infection.

Oral hairy leukoplakia in HIV-infected patients presents with white corrugated plaque over the lateral border of the tongue, which cannot be rubbed off.

Other conditions associated with EBV infection are

* Glandular fever: fever, pharyngitis, and posterior cervical lymphadenopathy

* Rash triggered by Ampicillin

* Burkitt's Lymphoma

* Nasopharyngeal carcinoma

* EBV‐associated lymphoproliferative disease

* Age‐related EBV‐associated B‐cell lymphoma

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: The egg shown below belongs to _____
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Whipworm

The given egg is of whipworm i.e, Trichuris trichiura.

The characteristic features of whipworm eggs are:

* Eggs are barrel-shaped in the middle with a projecting mucus plug at each pole containing an unsegmented ovum. The plugs are colorless.

* They float in the saturated salt solution.

* It has a triple shell, the outermost layer of which is stained brown.

The infection is acquired by the ingestion of foods contaminated with infected eggs. Adult whipworm colonizes the caecum and colon of humans where a male and female mate and the female worm lays the eggs. They are passed in feces and become infective after 3 months. Clinical features can vary from asymptomatic infection in mild cases to lower abdominal pain and diarrhea in moderate infection. In severe cases, it can cause profuse bloody diarrhea and rectal prolapse.

The image below shows the life cycle of Trichuris trichiura.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: What is the average incubation period of plasmodium falciparum ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 12

The average incubation period of Plasmodium falciparum is around 12 days.

The average incubation period of Plasmodium is:

* P.vivax-14 days

* P.falciparum-12 days

* P.ovale-14 days

* P.malariae-30 days

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following is the mechanism of action of cholera toxin?
options: Toxin causes Increased guanyl cyclase activity
The toxin causes continued activation of adenylate cyclase
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. The toxin causes continued activation of adenylate cyclase

The toxin causes continued activation of adenylate cyclase.

Mechanism of action of cholera toxin:

* The cholera toxin molecule consists of 1 A and 5 B subunits. The B (binding) units attach to the GM1 ganglioside receptors on the surface of jejunal epithelial cells. The A (active) subunit, on being transported into the enterocyte, dissociates into A1 and A2.

* A1 causes prolonged activation of cellular adenylate cyclase and accumulation of cAMP, leading to outpouring into the small intestinal lumen, of large quantities of water and electrolytes, and the consequent watery diarrhea that is isotonic with plasma but contains much more potassium and bicarbonate.

* The toxin also inhibits intestinal absorption of sodium and chloride.

* All clinical manifestations and complications in cholera result from the massive water and electrolyte depletion thus caused.

Pearl PF0802: Mechanism of action of various bacterial toxins

The mechanism of action of various bacterial toxins are as given below:

Increase in cAMP

* Bordetella pertusis

* Bacillus anthracis

* Vibrio cholerae - Cholera toxin

* Enterotoxigenic E.coli (ETEC) - heat labile toxin

Increase in cGMP

* Enterotoxigenic E.coli (ETEC) - heat stable toxin

Inhibition of protein synthesis

* Diptheria toxin: inhibit elongation factor-2 (EF-2)

* Pseudomonas: inhibit elongation factor-2 (EF-2)

* Clostridium difficile

* Enterohemorrhagic E.coli (EHEC)-Shiga-like toxin: inhibit 60S

* Shigella dysenteriae- Shiga toxin: inhibit 60S

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: While collecting a blood sample for investigations, you accidentally drop and spill a 5 ml tube of blood. Which among the following is the best solution to clean it?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1:100 Sodium hypochlorite

Sodium hypochlorite solution in 1:100 dilution is used to clean a blood spill of less than 10 ml.

Blood spills may occur because a laboratory sample breaks during the procedure or during transport, or because there is excessive bleeding during the procedure. In such cases, clean up the spill and record the incident, using the following steps:

* Wear a pair of non-sterile gloves or appropriate PPE.

* Use appropriate instruments (like tongs or a pan and brush) to sweep up any broken glass (or container) as
possible. Do not pick up pieces with your hands.

* Discard the broken glass in a sharps container. If not possible due to the size of the broken glass, wrap it in several layers of paper and discard it carefully in a separate container. It should not be discarded in the regular waste container.

* Use disposable paper towels to absorb as much of the body fluids as possible.

* Wipe the area with water and detergent until it is visibly clean.

* Saturate the area again with 5.25-6.15% sodium hypochlorite, which should be prepared daily.

* Spills < 10ml are cleaned with 1:100 dilution sodium hypochlorite

* Spills >10ml or involving a culture spill in the laboratory are cleaned with 1:10 dilution sodium hypochlorite.

* Follow this decontamination process with terminal disinfection, using a 1:100 dilution of sodium hypochlorite.

* Rinse off the tongs, brush, and pan.

* Remove and discard the gloves.

* Wash hands carefully with soap and water, and dry with a disposable towel.

* Record the incident if a specimen was lost, or persons were exposed to blood and body fluids.

Shigella species do not ferment lactose with the exception of S.sonnei which is a late lactose fermenter.

Mannitol fermentation is of importance in the classification of Shigella.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 40-year-old nurse presents to the clinic requesting an HIV test. She had a needle prick injury while at work from an HIV positive patient. Antibodies against which of the following will be detected first by ELISA or Western blot?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. gp 41

Antibodies against gp41 will be detected first by ELISA or Western blot.

Antibodies to HIV usually appear within 3–6 weeks of primary infection. The appearance of HIV-binding antibodies occurs prior to the appearance of neutralizing antibodies. The only viral proteins that elicit neutralizing antibodies are the envelope proteins gp120 and gp41.

The order of appearance of antibodies is as follows:

Antibody to envelope gp41 > Antibodies to gag protein (p24 and p55) > Antibodies to envelope gp120 > Antibodies to gag protein p17 > Antibodies to pol gene products (p31 and p66).

Note: The earliest antigen to appear in the blood following HIV infection is p24.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 54-year-old farmer from Ohio presents to a physician with a chronic cough. A chest X-ray demonstrates a mass lesion with hilar lymphadenopathy. Biopsy of the mass and staining with lactophenol cotton blue demonstrates multiple, tiny yeast forms within macrophages as below. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Histoplasmosis

The given clinical history and the presence of tiny yeast forms within macrophages are suggestive of Histoplasmosis.

Histoplasmosis is also known as Darling's disease, Cave's disease or Ohio disease. It is endemic in USA i.e. it has specific geographical distribution.

The causative agent is Histoplasma capsulatum, a dimorphic fungus. It is a facultative intracellular parasite. Yeast form occurs mainly in tissues at a temperature of 37oC and mycelial form occurs in soil at 25oC. Spores are found in bird or bat droppings in the soil which acts as reservoir of infection. Transmission occurs via inhalation of conidia. Person-to-person transmission or animal-to-man transmission is not yet known.

After inhalation, the conidia develop into yeast cells and are engulfed by alveolar macrophages. Within macrophages, the yeasts may disseminate to reticuloendothelial tissues, such as the liver, spleen, bone marrow, and lymph nodes. Biopsy reveals tiny (2-4 microns) oval-shaped yeast cells inside macrophages.

On culture and microscopy, tuberculate macroconidia and hyaline septate mould with microconidia are seen.

Itraconazole is the treatment for mild to moderate infection, while in disseminated disease, systemic treatment with amphotericin B may be required.

Pearl PF0827: Systemic fungi - Histopathological findings

Histoplasma: Tiny oval yeast cells (2- 4 μm size) with narrow-based budding within the macrophages with an underlying granulomatous response.

Blastomyces : Thick-walled round yeast cells of 8- 15 μm size with single broad-based budding (figure of 8 appearance)

Coccidoides : Mature spherules of coccidioidomycus is seen in the above image. Spherules which are large sac like structures (20--80 μm size), have thick, double refractile wall, and are filled with endospores.

Paracoccidioides : Round thick-walled yeasts, with multiple narrow-necked buds attached circumferencially giving rise to Mickey mouse or pilot wheel appearance.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 55-year-old man comes with complaints of fever and increasing fatigue for the past week. On examination, he is febrile, hypotensive and tachycardic. The findings of microscopic examination of his peripheral blood smear is given below. What is the causative agent?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Plasmodium falciparum

The given clinical history and the blood smear shows multiple ring forms in RBCs are suggestive of Plasmodium falciparum.

Falciparum malaria shows a very high percentage of RBCs containing ring forms. This high-level parasitemia is more often seen in Plasmodium falciparum infection than in infection by the other plasmodia.

Binucleate rings (double chromatin) are common resembling stereo headphones in appearance.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 6-year-old boy presents with lower abdominal pain and diarrhea. The stool examination finding is shown below. Which of the following is most likely to cause this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Entamoeba histolytica

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of amoebic dysentery caused by Entamoeba histolytica and the given image shows hematophagous trophozoite of Entamoeba histolytica.

Clinical features of intestinal amebiasis:

* Acute intestinal amebiasis- dysentery, lower abdominal discomfort, and flatulence.

* Chronic amebiasis- low-grade symptoms such as occasional diarrhea, weight loss, and fatigue.

A granulomatous lesion called an ameboma may form in the cecal or rectosigmoid areas of the colon which can resemble an adenocarcinoma of the colon.

Option A - Giardia is often asymptomatic, but in some cases can lead to fat malabsorption, dull epigastric pain, and flatulence.

Option B - Shigella causes bacillary dysentery which is characterised by fever and generalised abdominal tenderness.

Option D - Campylobacter presents with fever, pain, and watery diarrhea. The stool contains leucocytes and blood.

Metronidazole is used in the treatment of amoebiasis like amoebic colitis and amoebic liver abscess. It is well absorbed from the small intestine and only a small amount of the unabsorbed drug reaches the colon, which is insufficient to kill the cysts.

Hence, luminal agents like diloxanide furoate, nitazoxanide or iodoquinol are required for the eradication of cysts and trophozoites in the intestine.
