questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 60-year-old male presents with painless cervical lymphadenopathy and right-sided deafness. On examination, the tympanic membrane was dull on the right side. Moreover, decreased mobility of the soft palate was also noted. What is the viral etiological agent associated with the diagnosis of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. EBV

The given clinical condition is nasopharyngeal carcinoma and Epstein–Barr Virus (EBV) is one of the closley associated etiological agents of this condition.

Specific viral markers are being developed to screen people in high-incidence areas. EB virus has two important antigens: Viral capsid antigen (VCA) and Early antigen (EA).

IgA antibodies of EA are highly specific for nasopharyngeal cancer but have a sensitivity of only 70–80% while IgA antibodies of VCA are more sensitive but less specific. IgA antibodies against both EA and VCA should be done for screening of patients for nasopharyngeal cancer.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A child presents with the complaint of perianal itching which occurs predominantly at night and disturbs sleep. Eggs of the causative organism have been shown in the following image. Which of the following is the causative organism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Enterobius vermicularis

Enterobius vermicularis or pinworm infection presents as itching (pruritus) and restless sleep (due to nocturnal perianal or perineal pruritus).

Enterobius vermicularis completes its entire life cycle in the human host. They are oviparous. Man acquires infection by ingesting embryonated eggs containing larva through contaminated fingers and by autoinfection.

At night, the gravid female worm comes out through the anus and lays its sticky eggs on the perianal skin. This leads to pruritus and the patient scratches the affected perianal area. The worm can crawl into the vulva and vagina causing irritation and a mucoid discharge. It can also cause chronic salpingitis, cervicitis, peritonitis, recurrent urinary tract infections, and appendicitis.

Since pinworms are rarely released in faeces, stool examination is not useful in the diagnosis. The NIH swab (National Institutes of Health, USA) consists of a glass rod with a piece of transparent cellophane attached at one end with a rubber band. The cellophane part is used for swabbing by rolling over the perianal area. The cellophane piece is spread over a glass side and examined microscopically.

Plano-convex eggs containing a tadpole-shaped embryo, are deposited by the gravid female worm on perianal skin which causes pruritis.

Frequent hand washing, fingernail cleaning, regular bathing, and frequent washing of night clothes, and bed linen should be done. Treatment is with albendazole 400mg or mebendazole 100mg

Pearl PF1690: Eggs in parasitology

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: An 8-year-old boy was brought to the emergency department with complaints of continuous diarrhoea that started 20 hours ago and is rice watery in consistency.He is drowsy and unresponsive. His eyes are sunken and skin turgor is poor.What is the likely causative agent?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Vibrio cholerae

The rice watery stools along with the other clinical features are suggestive of Vibrio cholerae infection.

Vibrio cholerae is a comma-shaped, gram-negative bacillus with darting motility. It has a single polar flagellum. It causes cholera, an acute diarrheal disease. It is marked by painless, profuse, rice water stools- watery diarrhoea with flecks of mucus, associated with effortless vomiting. Pulmonary oedema and arrhythmias are some of the complications.

Infection is acquired by ingestion of contaminated food and water. The organisms produce an enterotoxin known as cholera toxin (CT). It has 1 A and 5 B subunits. The B subunit (binding units) fixes to the GM1 ganglioside receptors on jejunal epithelial cells. The A subunit dissociates into the A2 fragment, which attaches the A1 fragment to the B subunit. This results in prolonged accumulation of cAMP, which causes an outpouring of large amounts of water and electrolytes into the intestinal lumen. Ultimately, it results in profuse watery diarrhoea.

The characteristic darting mobility and its hindrance by antiserum can be used for rapid microscopic diagnosis.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Identify the fungus shown in the image given below which is stained by india ink dye.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Cryptococcus

The image above shows the fungus cryptococcus.

The image shows India ink preparation which is employed to detect the presence of capsulated yeast, cryptococcus neoformans. It induces negative staining by creating a black, semi-opaque background that makes the capsule of the yeast clearly visible. Cryptococcus has a polysaccharide capsule which is demonstrated as clear halos against a black background.

Cryptococcus neoformans is an opportunistic fungus that is found worldwide as a saprophyte in soil enriched with pigeon droppings. It may cause infection in immune-competent people, resulting in a flu-like illness with complete recovery.

Infection in immunocompromised people like AIDS patients or patients with hematological malignancies results in meningoencephalitis.

Mucicarmine stain can also be used in the identification of cryptococcus. The image given below shows mucicarmine stained specimen of lung tissue containing cryptococci.

Culture on Sabouraud dextrose agar (SDA) at 37'C appears as smooth, mucoid, and creamy white. The cryptococcal antigen(in serum and CSF) is sensitive and specific and can be demonstrated by the latex agglutination test.

Treatment of cryptococcal meningitis involves a combination therapy of amphotericin B with flucytosine. Fluconazole can be added with these drugs in AIDS patients to prevent relapse.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Identify the organism in the given slide stained with Gomori methenamine silver stain which shows acute angle branching and septate hyphae.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Aspergillus

The given slide stained with GMS shows acute-angled (45o) uniform, branching septate hyphae which is suggestive of Aspergillus species.

Aspergillus species grow rapidly, producing aerial hyphae that bear characteristic conidial structures. Long aseptate conidiophores are seen with terminal vesicles on which phialides are arranged in basipetal chains.

The following image shows LPCB mount of Aspergillus fumigatus showing the long conidiophores with terminal vesicles.

Option A: Mucor produces nonseptate, broad hyphae with aerial sporangiophores which end in a sporangium.

Option B: Penicillium produces septate hyphae with branched, septate and brush-like conidiophores.

Option D: Rhizopus appears similar to Mucor but it has rhizoids with sporangiophores arising in groups directly above the rhizoids.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which among the following is a high-level disinfectant?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Glutaraldehyde

Glutaraldehyde is an example of a high-level disinfectant.

High-level disinfectant- This is a chemical that kills all microbial pathogens except a large number of spores. It may have some activity against a smaller number of spores if the contact time is increased. Eg- Glutaraldehyde, hydrogen peroxide.

Intermediate level disinfectant: A chemical that kills all microbial pathogens including mycobacteria and non enveloped viruses except spores. Eg- Alcohol, iodophors.

Low-level disinfectants:They kill only vegetative bacteria, fungi, and lipid enveloped viruses, e.g Benzalkonium chloride

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following is amplified in an RT-PCR test for the COVID-19 virus?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. DNA

In an RT-PCR test for the COVID-19 virus DNA is amplified.

COVID-19 virus (Coronavirus) is a single-stranded linear RNA virus. RT-PCR is used to identify the RNA of this virus by generating complementary DNA (cDNA) copies of the mRNA using the reverse transcriptase enzyme.

The steps of RT-PCR can be explained as follows:

* Isolation of RNA

* Reverse transcription- Synthesis of DNA from RNA by using an RNA-dependent DNA polymerase

* Polymerase chain reaction- Using heat-stable DNA polymerase, such as Taq polymerase, DNA is amplified

* Separation of the PCR products-  by agarose gel electrophoresis

* Visualisation of the amplified DNA (with ethidium bromide)

(Note again that it is the DNA that is amplified and not RNA even though we are trying to detect an RNA virus)

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following is the vector for Zika virus?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Aedes albopictus

Aedes albopictus is a vector for Zika virus transmission. Aedes aegypti is also a vector for zika virus.

Zika virus (RNA virus) is a flavivirus and the infection is characterized by influenza-like clinical signs including fever, headache, and malaise.

A maculopapular rash, conjunctivitis, myalgia, and arthralgia usually accompany or follow those manifestations. Petechial rashes are not seen.

Complications: Guillian-Barre syndrome and microcephaly and intracranial calcification in infants born to mothers infected with Zika virus. Pregnant women should consider postponing travel to areas where Zika virus transmission is ongoing.

Diagnosis:

* Trioplex Real-Time RT-PCR (rRT-PCR) assay

*  Zika MAC-ELISA.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 12-year-old boy is brought to the OPD with complaints of fever, ear pain, and difficulty in swallowing for 1 week. On examination, there is testicular swelling and his jaw is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Mumps

The given clinical scenario with fever, ear pain, parotid swelling, and testicular swelling is suggestive of mumps.

Mumps is caused by RNA paramyxovirus. It is spread from person to person via droplets from clinical and subclinical cases. The incubation period is 12-21 days. The virus appears in the saliva from up to 7 days before to as long as 7 days after the onset of parotid swelling.

The patient presents with prodrome lasting 1-2 days consisting of fever, headache, and vomiting. After the prodrome, unilateral or bilateral parotitis develops, which is tender. It may be associated with ipsilateral ear pain. Ingestion of sour or acidic foods may enhance pain.

It can be prevented by administering the live attenuated MMR vaccine at 15-18 months and 5 years.

Complications of mumps:

* Aseptic meningitis or meningoencephalitis

* Epididymo-orchitis which is usually unilateral. Seen in post-pubertal males

* Oophoritis

* Other complications include pancreatitis and myocarditis

Neurological complications such as meningoencephalitis or aseptic meningitis may develop before, during, or following parotitis, typically emerging about 5 days after its onset.

most often appearing around 5 days after the onset of parotitis. It can present with headaches, neck stiffness, and drowsiness.

*Note: Non-mumps parotitis can be caused by:

* Epstein-Barr virus - causes infectious mononucleosis

* Coxsackievirus - causes herpangina

* Parainfluenza virus - causes croup

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 13-year-old girl has had 4 episodes of meningitis over the last 4 years, with the disease lasting a few days at a time, leaving slowly resolving neurological symptoms such as visual and memory loss. A CSF cytology shows lymphocytic pleocytosis and a diagnosis of Mollaret’s meningitis is made. Which organism is implicated here?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Herpes simplex virus

Mollaret’s meningitis or benign recurrent lymphocytic meningitis is most commonly caused by the herpes simplex virus (HSV). Demonstration of HSV antibodies in CSF or persistence of HSV DNA in CSF can establish the diagnosis.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 21-year-old girl who presented with multiple beefy-red painless ulcers over the vulval region is diagnosed with granuloma inguinale. What is the causative organism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Klebsiella granulomatis

The causative organism of granuloma inguinale is Klebsiella granulomatis, a gram-negative bacillus.

Granuloma inguinale begins as a painless nodule that later ulcerates to form multiple beefy red painless ulcers. These ulcers tend to coalesce. There will be minimal adenopathy and progressive destruction of the vulva.

Microscopic examination of smears from the lesion/biopsy specimens reveals pathognomonic intracytoplasmic Donovan bodies and clusters of bacteria with a bipolar (safety-pin) appearance.

The microscopic image below shows the pathognomonic intracytoplasmic Donovan bodies. It also shows clusters of gram-negative bacteria with a bipolar/safety-pin appearance.

Management:

* Tetracycline 500 mg every 6 h for 2–3 weeks

* Gentamycin 1 mg/kg IM 8 h for 2 weeks

Other options:

Option A - Chlamydia trachomatis causes Lymphogranuloma Venereum.

Option C - Haemophilus ducreyi causes Chancroid.

Option D - Herpes simplex virus causes genital herpes.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 24-year-old woman presents with pruritic hypopigmented macules and confluent patches over the chest. Skin scraping and KOH preparation show an abundance of yeast-like cells and short branched filaments like a 'Spaghetti and meatball appearance'. What is the most likely causative organism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Malassezia

The clinical scenario is suggestive of  Pityriasis Versicolor and the causative agent is the lipophilic, yeast-like fungus Malassezia furfur (Pityrosporum orbiculare).

Pityriasis Versicolor is a chronic, usually asymptomatic, involvement of the stratum corneum, characterized by discrete or confluent macular areas of discoloration or de-pigmentation of the skin.

The areas involved are mainly the chest, abdomen, upper limbs, and back.

Skin scraping and KOH preparation show an abundance of yeast-like cells and short branched filaments (Spaghetti and meatball appearance).

Treatment includes topical azoles or terbinafine for 2 weeks.

The image below shows the hypopigmented lesions of P. versicolour over the chest.

Electron microscopic image of Malassezia furfur

Other options:

* Tinea corporis/ ringworm infection is caused by the dermatophyte Trichophyton rubrum. It results from invasion and proliferation of the causal fungi in the stratum corneum with lesions on the trunk and limbs.

* Candida, the causative agent for candidiasis, appear as budding gram-positive cells on wet films and smears. Mycelial forms suggest colonization. Culture colonies are creamy-white and have a yeasty odor. Candida albicans, the most commonly implicated pathogenic species, form chlamydospores on corn meal agar.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 3-year-old male child was brought to your clinic with an erythematous rash on the cheek which later spread downwards to involve his trunk and limbs. He has also had a low-grade fever, headache, and mild upper respiratory tract infection for the past few days. The suspected organism contains single-stranded DNA. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Erythema infectiosum

The given clinical scenario and image are strongly suggestive of erythema infectiosum. It is caused by Parvoviruses. Parvovirus B19 is a non-enveloped single-stranded DNA virus.

Clinically, parvovirus B-19 infection may have several presentations-

* Erythema infectiosum- Also known as the fifth disease. The incubation period after infection is typically around 4-14 days. The hallmark of erythema infectiosum is the characteristic rash, which appears initially as erythematous facial flushing, often described as a “slapped cheek” appearance. Later the rash spreads rapidly or concurrently to the trunk and proximal extremities as diffuse macular erythema. The child may be febrile.

* Transient aplastic crisis- It may be seen in patients with underlying chronic hemolytic anaemia like sickle-cell disease, thalassemia, hereditary spherocytosis, and RBC enzyme deficiencies like pyruvate kinase deficiency. Patients with aplastic crisis appear ill with fever, malaise, and pale with tachycardia and tachypnea due to profound anaemia. The rash may or may not be present. Children with sickle-cell disease may also develop vaso-occlusive crises.

* Pure red cell aplasia- Persistent B19V infection that results in pure red cell aplasia has been reported in a wide variety of immunosuppressed patients, including patients with congenital immunodeficiency, AIDS, and lymphoproliferative disorders and transplant recipients.

* Primary maternal infection is associated with non-immune fetal hydrops and intrauterine fetal demise.

It is a clinical diagnosis that usually does not require investigations. However, in the case of pregnant women or with other manifestations an IgM ELISA or PCR assay may be done.

It is self-limited and resolves on its own.

questions.text: A 45-year-old man presents with fever, headache, photophobia, and neck rigidity for the last 2 days. He had undergone a heart transplant one year back and is on immunomodulatory drugs. A lumbar puncture was taken in view of meningitis which showed reduced glucose, increased protein, and increased leukocytes with predominant neutrophils. On microscopy, differential motility was seen, non-motile at 37 degrees and tumbling motility at 25 degrees. What is the most likely organism causing this?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Listeria

The clinical scenario and LP findings are suggestive of meningitis. Differential motility with risk factors of immunosuppression suggests a Listeria infection.

Risk factors for Listeria meningitis include:

* Age>50

* Diabetes

* Chronic illness

* Malignancy

* Immunosuppressive therapy

Listeria monocytogenes shows slow tumbling motility when grown at 25 °C.

But at 37°C, it is non-motile because the peritrichous flagella are produced by the bacillus optimally between 20°C and 30°C. This is known as differential motility as motility pattern changes with a change in temperature.

Listeria moves from cell-to-cell using host cell actin framework.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 55-year-old man comes with complaints of fever and increasing fatigue for the past week. On examination, he is febrile, hypotensive and tachycardic. The findings of his peripheral blood smear are given below. What is the causative agent?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Plasmodium falciparum

The given clinical history and the blood smear showing multiple ring forms in RBCs are suggestive of Plasmodium falciparum.

Plasmodium falciparum causes malignant tertian malaria. This means that the fever has a periodicity of 48 hours corresponding to one cycle of erythrocytic schizogony. Malignant because it is a more severe and fatal type of malaria.

Major manifestations of severe falciparum malaria include unarousable coma/ cerebral malaria (failure to localize or respond appropriately to stimuli or coma persisting for >30 min after generalized convulsion), acidosis, severe normocytic normochromic anemia, renal failure, pulmonary edema, hypoglycemia, shock, and disseminated intravascular coagulation. Other manifestations include hemoglobinuria, hyperparasitemia, jaundice, and extreme weakness.

Falciparum malaria shows a very high percentage of RBCs containing ring forms. This high-level parasitemia is more often seen in Plasmodium falciparum infection than in infection by other plasmodia. After the ring form in the peripheral blood, the rest of the erythrocytic cycle occurs in the capillaries of the brain and internal organs. So, only ring forms can be seen in the peripheral blood and not the late trophozoites and schizonts. The gametocytes of P. falciparum are crescent-shaped or “banana-shaped” (as shown below), whereas those of the other plasmodia are spherical.

The treatment of choice is artesunate given at a dose of 2.4 mg/kg stat IV, followed by 2.4 mg/kg at 12 and 24 hours, and then daily if necessary.

In Plasmodium falciparum, recrudescence can be seen which is defined as the recurrence of asexual parasitemia. It usually occurs within 8 weeks of treatment and is due to incomplete treatment or drug resistance.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 70-year- old woman was diagnosed with right leg cellulitis and was admitted in hospital for 3 days. She was prescribed clindamycin. Two days after her discharge, she developed diarrhoea and abdominal pain. Her temperature was 38.8 degrees. Her blood reports revealed a Hb level of 12g/dl; WBC count of 18,000/mm3; CRP of 160mg/l. What is the most probable etiological agent?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Clostridium difficile

The given clinical vignette of a patient with diarrhoea following antibiotic administration is suggestive of pseudomembranous colitis due to Clostridium difficile.

Clostridium difficile is the most common cause of infectious diarrhoea in nosocomial infections. It is the most common antibiotic-associated diarrhoea. It is commonly seen in individuals who receive a prolonged antibiotic course, which causes a change in the composition of gastrointestinal microbial flora, leading to the colonization of C. difficile.

Clinical features:

* Lower abdominal pain with loose watery diarrhea.

* Fever, leukocytosis

* In some patients, the disease may progress to life-threatening pseudomembranous colitis.

Investigations:

* Nucleic acid amplification tests, including PCR assays, for C. difficile toxin A or B gene in stool

* Stool culture in selective media

* Demonstrating toxin by Hep-2 cell cultures

* Toxin gene identification by enzyme immunoassay

* Colonoscopy or sigmoidoscopy reveals a characteristic appearance, with erythema, white plaques, or an adherent pseudomembrane.

Nucleic acid amplification tests, including PCR assays, for C. difficile toxin A or B gene in the stool are used as they are both rapid and sensitive while retaining high specificity.

Oral vancomycin, metronidazole, and fidaxomicin are used for the treatment of pseudomembranous colitis, depending on its severity.

First choice treatment of C. difficile colitis:

Severity
Treatment

Mild to moderate
Oral Vancomycin

Severe (WBC >15,000/cu.mm, Creatinine >1.5 times baseline)
Oral Vancomycin

Severe, Complicated (Shock, Ileus, Toxic Megacolon)
Oral Vancomycin + IV Metronidazole ± Rectal Vancomycin

Recurrent/ multiple episodes
Fecal Microbiota Transplantation (FMT)

Fidaxomicin is an alternative in all cases. Metronidazole is now reserved for non-severe infections in settings where access to first-line drugs is limited or cost is an issue.

Recent update: Harrison's 20th edition recommends the use of vancomycin over metronidazole in the treatment of initial episodes which are mild to moderate in severity. Metronidazole is recommended only if vancomycin or fidaxomicin are not accessible. Oral metronidazole is less effective than the other options and may necessitate a longer treatment course for response.

Other options: Escherichia coli, Norovirus, Rotavirus are all causes of Traveller's diarrhea.

Other causes for Nosocomial diarrhea:

* Clostridium perfringens,

* Klebsiella oxytoca,

* Staphylococcus aureus.

Pearl PF1578: Diagnostic criteria for Clostridium difficile infection

The diagnosis of CDI is based on a combination of clinical criteria:

1.Diarrhea (≥3 unformed stools per 24 h for ≥2 days) with no other recognized cause

2.Detection of toxins A or B in the stool by PCR or culture

or

Detection of pseudomembranes in the colon

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A farmer with a history of flea bite in a godown presents with the features of high fever, painful inguinal lymphadenopathy, vomiting and diarrhea and hypotension. Smears prepared from the discharge of these swellings revealed bacteria with bipolar staining. Which stain will help in the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Wayson’s stain

The given clinical scenario of fever, chills, lymphadenopathy, and a smear showing bipolar staining of bacteria is highly suggestive of bubonic plague caused by Yersinia pestis. The stain used for this organism is the Wayson stain containing methylene blue.

Plague is a zoonotic disease caused by Yersinia pestis. It is a gram-negative, non-motile, coccobacillus. The reservoirs of infection are wild rodents like field mice, gerbils, skunks, etc. In India, the gerbil (Tatera indica) is the main reservoir. The important vector of plague is rat flea (Xenopsylla cheopis).

Humans contract the disease through contact with the infected animal's tissues, flea bites, or droplet infection from pneumonic plague cases.

Human plague mainly presents as:

Bubonic plague- Most common form. The patient experiences excruciating lymphadenitis, headache, chills, and an abrupt fever. The lymph nodes in the neck, axilla, or groin enlarge and become known as "buboes". This is followed by the suppuration of the buboes. Bubonic plague cannot spread from person to person as the bacilli are locked up in the buboes and do not find a way or easy exit.

Pneumonic plague- It develops as a complication of bubonic-septicemic plague.

Septicemic plague- It occurs when the infection spreads to the blood.

Laboratory diagnosis- Microscopy reveals bacteria that show characteristic bipolar staining or safety pin appearance when stained with Wayson's stain. Antibodies to the F1 antigen of the bacteria can also be demonstrated by passive hemagglutination. PCR is used for a rapid presumptive diagnosis.

Treatment- Streptomycin, doxycycline, and chloramphenicol can be used.

Pearl PF1012: Rat Fleas

* Rat fleas belong to the genus Xenopsylla.

* Their morphology includes a conical head, no neck, a thorax that has 3 segments and an abdomen with 10 segments.  They have three pairs of legs and no wings.

* The four stages in their life cycle are egg, larva, pupa and adult.

* They cannot fly but can leap up to 6 inches horizontally.

* They transmit diseases by biting, mechanical transmission and feces.

* Flea indices that are used in flea surveys are general flea index, specific flea index, percentage incidence of flea species and rodent infestation rate.

* Rat fleas are vectors for endemic typhus (murine typhus), chiggerosis, bubonic plague and hymenolepis diminuta.

* Insecticidal control is mainly 10% DDT.

* Resistance to DDT, gamma-HCH and dieldrin has been recorded.

* Repellants like diethyltoluamide and benzyl benzoate are efficient.

* Rodent control also aims to reduce flea infestation.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient has complaints of fever with a mild headache associated with some difficulty in swallowing. A throat examination reveals swollen glands and a thick, whitish membrane over his tonsils which bleeds on scraping the lesion. A sample is taken from the exudate and a gram stain is done, which is as shown below. What is the organism associated with the disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Corynebacterium diphtheriae

The history of white membrane over the tonsils and gram stain image showing gram-positive bacilli in Chinese letter arrangement points towards the diagnosis of faucial diphtheria caused by Corynebacterium diphtheriae.

Corynebacterium diphtheria is a gram-positive bacillus with clubbing at both ends. They possess characteristic polymetaphosphate granules also called metachromatic granules or Babes-Ernst granules. On microscopy, the bacilli are arranged at angles to each other which is seen as the Chinese letter or cuneiform pattern.

Albert’s stain or Neisser’s stain or Loeffler's methylene blue are used to demonstrate the metachromatic granules of Corynebacterium diphtheria. These granules are called as polar bodies as they are situated at the ends of the bacilli.

The systemic manifestations of diphtheria are due to diphtheria toxin. It is an exotoxin that consists of two fragments - A and B. It acts by inhibiting protein synthesis. Fragment B helps in binding of the toxin to the cells and fragment A inactivates the elongation factor (EF-2) responsible for protein synthesis.

The clinical manifestation of diphtheria depends on the site of infection. Pharyngeal/faucial diphtheria is the most common presentation. The patient has marked adenitis, a bull neck, and severe toxemia. Pseudomembrane over the tonsils are characteristic. Bleeding from the tonsils can occur. It leads to life-threatening complications such as asphyxia, circulatory failure, post-diphtheritic paralysis, and toxemia.

Cutaneous diphtheria is due to non-toxigenic strains of diphtheria. It may present as a diphtheritic whitlow or skin ulcer.

The image below shows the pseudomembrane over the tonsil typically seen in diphtheria.

Image below shows bull neck.

Isolation of corynebacterium from patient or close contact confirms the diagnosis. Specimen collection for culture should be done from nose, throat and if possible from below the membrane. It grows readily on Loeffler's serum slope and confirmation can be done by growing on potassium tellurite agar which serves as a selective medium.

Image below shows Loeffler's serum slope.

Treatment of diphtheria consist of administering diphtheria anti-toxin (20,000 - 100,000 units) and supplementing with antibiotics (penicillin and erythromycin).

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient presented with a black, foul-smelling discharge from the nose. On examination, blackish necrotic mass filling the nasal cavity and eroding the septum and hard palate were seen. What is the most important risk factor for this disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Diabetes

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of mucormycosis and the most important risk factor among these is diabetes.

Mucormycosis is an opportunistic mycosis. It is typically seen in patients with diabetes mellitus and/or diabetic ketoacidosis, and immunocompromised patients. Mucormycosis recently emerged as an important superinfection in COVID-19 patients, especially in India. The surge in cases is most likely due to diabetes mellitus and steroid use.

Risk factors for the infection include the following:

* Uncontrolled diabetes

* Acidosis (especially diabetic ketoacidosis)

* Steroid treatment

* Lymphomas and leukemias

* Immunodeficiencies

* Severe burns

The rhino-orbital-cerebral is the most common form of mucormycosis. Patients present with rhinitis, eye or facial pain, and facial numbness followed by the onset of conjunctival suffusion and swelling along with blurry vision.

Patients can have local tissue destruction with blackish nasal discharge typically resembling the presentation of invasive mucormycosis. The blackish discoloration is due to direct fungal invasion causing arterial and venous thrombosis leading to gangrene.

Diagnosis is made by biopsy with histopathologic examination. The biopsy shows characteristic wide, ribbon-like aseptate hyphal elements that branch at right angles.

The below image shows biopsy findings seen in mucormycosis.

Treatment includes intravenous administration of amphotericin B and wide excision of necrotic tissues. Along with the reversal of underlying conditions and risk factors.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient presented with complaints of fever for 3 days and general fatigue. On examination, splinter hemorrhages were seen. Echocardiography revealed vegetations on the valves and thus a blood culture was done. The organism in the culture was seen as cocci in chains that showed alpha hemolysis on blood agar and was resistant to optochin and bile. Which of the following bacteria is most commonly implicated in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Streptococcus sanguis

The clinical scenario of fever, splinter haemorrhages, and vegetations on echocardiography is suggestive of infective endocarditis. The bacteria seen as cocci with alpha hemolysis and resistant to optochin and bile are most suggestive of Streptococcus viridans and in the following options, Streptococcus sanguis is a type of viridans bacteria.

Streptococcus sanguis belong to the viridans group of streptococci and they cause subacute bacterial endocarditis.

Streptococci that show alpha hemolysis on blood agar are again classified on the basis of optochin sensitivity and bile solubility.

* Alpha hemolysis: Streptococcus pneumoniae is sensitive to optochin and is bile soluble. Viridians streptococci are resistant to optochin and are bile insoluble.

* Beta hemolysis: Group B is resistant to bacitracin and Group A is sensitive to it.

* Gamma hemolysis: Enterococcus grows in 6.5% NaCl and non-enterococcus does not.

Viridans streptococci show alpha hemolysis on blood agar and are resistant to optochin. They contain:

* Streptococci sanguis causes subacute bacterial endocarditis

* Streptococci mitis

* Streptococci mutans

* Streptococci salvarius

Other options:

Option A- Streptococcus pyogenes are beta-hemolytic and bacitracin sensitive.

Option C- Enterococcus does not show hemolysis.

Option D- Streptococcus agalacticae shows beta hemolysis and is bacitracin resistant.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient was diagnosed with Tuberculosis and while testing for resistance he was found to be resistant to Isoniazid, Rifampicin, Amikacin, and Ofloxacin. What is this type of TB called?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Extensively Drug-Resistant TB

This patient having resistance to first-line drugs rifampicin and isoniazid along with resistance to amikacin and ofloxacin is a case of Extensively Drug-Resistant TB

XDR-TB (extensively drug-resistant TB) is defined as multi-drug resistant(MDR) TB (resistant to rifampicin and isoniazid) which is also resistant to one fluoroquinolone (eg. ofloxacin) AND resistant to one second-line injectable drug (amikacin or kanamycin or capreomycin).

It is usually seen in patients who have previously received treatment for TB and have either failed to complete treatment or relapsed.

Pearl PF0266: ATT Regimen for TB Patients

As per the latest recommendations from National Tuberculosis Elimination Programme (NTEP), treatment of TB is now based primarily on drug susceptibility testing. This is irrespective of new cases, previously treated cases or recurrent TB cases.
All cases of TB are treated with Drug Sensitive TB Regimen, as long as the patient is sensitive to isoniazid and rifampicin. (No classification into category I or II)

Classification based on drug resistance

* Mono-resistant (MR): A TB patient, who is resistant to one 1st line anti-TB drug only.

* Poly-Drug Resistant (PDR): A TB patient, who is resistant to more than one 1st line anti-TB drug, other than Rifampicin.

* Rifampicin Resistant (RR): A TB patient, who is resistant to rifampicin with or without resistance to other drugs. Patients, who have rifampicin resistance, should be managed as if they are an MDR TB case.

* Multi Drug Resistant (MDR): A TB patient, who is resistant to both isoniazid and rifampicin.

* Extensively Drug Resistant (XDR): A MDR TB patient who is additionally resistant to a fluoroquinolone (ofloxacin, levofloxacin, or moxifloxacin) and a second-line injectable anti TB drug (kanamycin, amikacin, or capreomycin).

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A truck driver came with complaints of a painless indurated genital ulcer after unsafe intercourse. Which of the following can be used to diagnose the condition in a low-resource setting when an active ulcer is present?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Dark field microscopy

The clinical vignette of a painless, indurated genital ulcer in a truck driver is most likely suggestive of syphilitic chancre / hard chancre caused by Treponema pallidum. The motility of the organism can be demonstrated by dark ground/ field microscopy which can be used in a low economic, low resource setting.

Dark ground microscopy can be used to diagnose syphilis when an active chancre or condyloma lata is present to visualize Treponema pallidum. Dark-field microscopy images have a dark background with a refractile organism. The dark ground microscope has an optical system that enhances the contrast of unstained bodies. It is generally less sensitive.

Various types of Spirochetes and their appearances under a dark ground microscope:

* Treponemes generally are short, slender with regular and sharp spirals.

* Leptospira have a large number of closely wound spirals and characteristic hooked ends.

* Borrelia is large with irregular and wide open coils.

The image given below shows Treponema pallidum demonstrated by dark ground microscopy and the various appearances of other spirochetes respectively.

Other options:

Option B: Fluorescent treponema antibody absorption test (FTA-ABS) is an indirect immunofluorescence test used to detect specific treponemal antibodies. It is not available for routine testing as it is done only in suitably equipped labs.

Option C: VDRL test is a slide flocculation test in which the serum is inactivated at 56°C for 30 minutes and a measured volume of serum is placed on a special cavity slide. The cardiolipin antigen after preparation is added to the serum sample on a slide and is rotated on a VDRL rotator for a specified period of 4 minutes. In a positive test, the cardiolipin antigen reacts with reagin antibodies present in the infected serum and forms visible clumps. In a negative test, cardiolipin continues to remain as uniform crystals in the serum.

Option D: Treponema pallidum immobilization (TPI) test detects the presence of treponemal antibodies in the serum. Similar to the FTA-ABS test, it is also not available for routine testing.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Condyloma Accuminata is most commonly caused by ___.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. HPV 6,11

Human papillomavirus 6 & 11 (6 >11) are the most common cause of anogenital warts ,also known as Condyloma Accuminata.

* Giant Anogenital warts are known as Buschke Lowenstein Tumor.

* It is more common in males than in females.

* Most common site:

* In males: Frenulum, corona, glans penis

* In females: Posterior fourchette

* On histology koilocytes are seen.

These are squamous epithelial cells which have nuclear enlargement, irregular nuclear membrane, hyperchromasia, perinuclear halo.

* Most of these warts resolve spontaneously.

* Persistent warts might transform into malignancy most commonly when infected with HPV 16 and 18.

Treatment:

Provider administered:

* Podophyllin (25%) - Antimitotic drug

* Trichloroacetic acid

* Cryotherapy

Both trichloroacetic acid and cryotherapy are safe in pregnancy.

Patient administered:

* Purified podophyllin called podophyllotoxin

* Imiquimod - Immunomodulator which acts on toll-like receptor 7 and 8

Correct answer: D. Mac-Conkey agar

E.coli can be grown best in MacConkey agar.

MacConkey agar is used to distinguish lactose fermentators (seen as pink colonies) from non-lactose fermentators(seen as colourless or pale). It is selective and differential media.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: One of the effector mechanisms in cell-mediated immunity involves identifying and lysing target cells whose membrane surface antigens are bound by specific antibodies.NK cells are one of the effector cells capable of this process. What other cells are capable of this process?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Neutrophils and eosinophils

Neutrophils and Eosinophils are capable of the effector mechanism described along with NK cells.

The effector mechanism being described refers to Antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC). Antibody dependent cellular cytotoxicity is seen with NK cells. However, it is also seen in macrophages,neutrophils and eosinophil killing certain parasitic worms like helminths via IgE antibodies.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following stains is used for the diagnosis of Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ziehl-Neelsen stain

Ziehl-Neelsen stain is used for staining M. tuberculosis.

Steps involved in Ziehl-Neelsen stain are:

* Place sample on slide evenly spread it with rotational movement

* Air-dry the slide and fix it by passing it over a flame

* Apply carbol fuchsin stain

* Wash with water to remove excess stain

* Decolourise with alcohol

* Apply methylene blue stain

* Wash with water to remove excess stain

* View under microscope

Kinyoun modified it so that heat fixing is not required, it is called the cold method. It involves increasing the concentration of phenol acid and the duration of staining. It is then washed with water and decolourised with acid alcohol. Counterstaining with Loeffler's methylene blue or malachite green is done for a minute and viewed under a microscope.

The image below shows the steps of Ziehl-Neelsen staining.

The best diagnostic procedure for M. tuberculosis is sputum culture.

* Sputum microscopy is the most dependable and conventional method for demonstration of AFB(Acid-fast bacteria) by ZN staining method.

* The smears are made from the thick purulent parts of the sputum and then are air-dried, fixed by heating, and finally stained by ZN technique.

* The stained smear is examined under oil immersion lens (100). Acid-fast bacteria in a stained smear appear bright red against a blue background.

* At least 10,000 bacilli should be present per mL of sputum in order to be demonstrable in direct smears.

* At least 300 fields should be examined taking about 10 minutes before giving a negative report.

* The presence of at least two or more typical bacilli in the smear is reported as positive for AFB (Acid-fast bacteria).

The smears are graded depending on the number of tubercle bacilli present in a stained smear on examination by oil immersion lens.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 45-year-old man with multiple sexual partners presents with a palmoplantar rash as seen below. On examination, he has epitrochlear lymphadenopathy. Which of the following is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Secondary syphilis

This clinical scenario of maculopapular rash with flu-like symptoms and epitrochlear lymphadenopathy points to secondary syphilis.

Secondary syphilis occurs within 6 weeks to 8 weeks of the onset of the primary chancre.

It is characterized by the following:

* Onset of systemic manifestations includes symptoms such as malaise, headache, loss of appetite, sore throat

* Generalized symmetric, asymptomatic maculopapular rash on the palms and soles.

* Generalized adenopathy in 50% of cases

* Condyloma lata is the classic finding. They are highly contagious exophytic broad excrescences that ulcerate. These are commonly seen on the vulva, perianal area, and upper thighs.

The image below shows mucosal and cutaneous lesion of secondary syphilis.

Other options:

Option A: Psoriasis presents with itching and a papulosquamous rash commonly on the scalp, trunk, and extensor surfaces of the limbs. The lesions are red, scaly, and have well demarcation from the normal skin. They can also be encircled by a clear peripheral zone called the Woronoff ring.

Option C: Meningococcemia caused by Neisseria meningitidis presents as acute fever with chills, malaise, and prostration. A petechial rash is seen early in the disease. Metastatic involvement of the joints, ears, eyes, lungs, and adrenals may occur.

Option D: Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS) and toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN) are severe mucocutaneous reactions, usually to drugs, characterized by blistering and epithelial sloughing. The two terms describe phenotypes within a severity spectrum, where SJS is the less extensive form and TEN is the more extensive.

Pearl PF1554: Stages of syphilis

* Primary Syphilis:

Chancre- Painless, indurated, usually single

Lymphadenopathy- Painless, unilateral or bilateral, shotty and rubbery inguinal nodes

Dory flop sign- As the chancre is too hard to fold, it will flip over once the prepuce is retracted back.

The chancre self heals in 1-4 months.

Secondary Syphilis:

A & B: Generalized rash(non-itchy, no vesicles, and palm and sole involvement).

This is the most common lesion.

C & D: Condyloma lata.

E: Moth-eaten alopecia (Non-scarring)

F: Mucous patches(Flat erosions on the tongue which can coalesce and form snail track ulcers).These are the most infectious lesions.

G: Pigmentary plaques

H: Psoriasiform syphilitic lesions

Generalized diffuse non-tender lymphadenopathy

Gummatous syphilis(deep punched-out ulcers, with gum-like secretions on the floor)

Pseudo-chancre redux is a gumma occurring at the site of a previously healed ulcer

CVS-Aortitis and aneurysm of the ascending aorta

CNS-General paresis of the insane and tabes dorsalis

Latent Syphilis-Period between secondary and tertiary syphilis, when the patient is asymptomatic clinically, and only serological evidence of infection is present.

* Early latent- Within 1 year of infection

* Late latent- After 1 year of infection

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A cattle farmer presented with a lesion on the arm. Gram staining showed gram-positive rods with square ends with a central spore. Identify the organism.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Bacillus anthracis

The diagnosis based on the given clinical scenario is cutaneous anthrax caused by Bacillus anthracis.

Bacillus anthracis is a gram-positive rod with square ends giving it a characteristic box car appearance/bamboo stick appearance.

Bacillus anthracis is a large, gram-positive, endospore-forming (non-bulging spores), rod-shaped bacterium. It causes zoonotic infections in humans. It is non-motile and capsulated with a characteristic polypeptide capsule.

The image shows the characteristic box car appearance/bamboo stick appearance of bacillus anthracis on Gram staining.

Bacillus anthracis is a category A bioterrorism agent which can cause:

* Cutaneous anthrax: It is caused by contact with infected animal/ animal products. It is seen in tanners and hide-porters. At the site of entry of organism or spores, a papule develops in about 1–7 days. This develops into a vesicle that later breaks down into an ulcer with a black, central, necrotic eschar surrounded by edematous skin. The lesion is also called a malignant pustule. The majority of the patients recover spontaneously, but a few may succumb to septicemia or meningitis.

* Pulmonary anthrax: It is caused by inhaling spores. It is seen in wool sorters. The infection from the lung spreads to the mediastinal lymph nodes and causes hemorrhagic mediastinitis and sepsis.

* Intestinal anthrax: It is caused rarely, by ingesting infected animals.

The image below shows necrotic eschar seen in anthrax:

Laboratory diagnosis:

* Microscopy of the smears shows bacilli arranged end to end in the form of long chains. This is called bamboo stick appearance.

* Under the low-power microscope, the edge of the colony is composed of long, interlacing chains of bacilli, resembling locks of matted hair, called Medusa head appearance.

Fluid or pus from cutaneous lesions, pleural fluid, blood, or CSF can be cultured on:

* Nutrient agar- frosted glass appearance

* Gelatin stab culture- Inverted fir tree appearance

* Blood agar- Non-hemolytic colonies

* Solid medium with penicillin- String of pearls appearance

Other options:

Option A: Infection with Bacillus cereus causes food poisoning with a longer incubation period of 8-16 hours. But patients usually have a history of consumption of fried rice.

Option C: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a gram-negative, catalase-positive, oxidase-positive, non-lactose fermenting bacteria that shows swarming motility. Diseases caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa:

* Burns infections

* Opportunistic and nosocomial infections

* Shanghai fever: severe enteric disease and sepsis

* Malignant otitis externa in diabetics

* Jacuzzi syndrome (Hot tub folliculitis)

* Ecthyma gangrenosum

* Green-nail syndrome

Option D: Brucellosis is a zoonotic infection transmitted to humans from contact with or consumption of contaminated products from goats, sheep, cattle, pigs, and other animals. Clinically, patients may present with an acute infection comprised of undulant fever (Rising and falling fever). They may also have arthralgia, muscular pain, sweating, loss of weight, and appetite. CNS symptoms such as fatigue, irritability, and depression might also occur. Chronic infection tends to be episodic with non-specific symptoms.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A truck driver comes with complaints of a painless indurated genital ulcer after unsafe intercourse. Which of the following investigations can be used to diagnose the causative organism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Dark field microscopy

The clinical vignette of a painless, indurated genital ulcer in a truck driver is most likely suggestive of syphilitic chancre / hard chancre caused by Treponema pallidum. The motility of the organism can be demonstrated by dark ground/ field microscopy which can be used in a low economic, low resource setting.

Dark ground microscopy can be used to diagnose syphilis when an active chancre or condyloma lata is present to visualize Treponema pallidum. Dark-field microscopy images have a dark background with a refractile organism. The dark ground microscope has an optical system that enhances the contrast of unstained bodies. It is generally less sensitive.

Various types of Spirochetes and their appearances under a dark ground microscope:

* Treponemes generally are short and slender with regular and sharp spirals.

* Leptospira have a large number of closely wound spirals and characteristic hooked ends.

* Borrelia is large with irregular and wide open coils.

The image given below shows Treponema pallidum demonstrated by dark ground microscopy.

Other options:

Option B: HSV 2 antibody is used in the diagnosis of herpes genitalis. It is an infection of the genital skin or mucosa caused by  HSV 2 predominantly. It presents as painful genital ulcers and dysuria. It is usually preceded by a prodrome of general malaise.

Option C: The granules of Corynebacterium diphtheria take up bluish purple color when stained with Albert's stain. Albert’s stain, Neisser’s, and Ponder’s stain are used to demonstrate the metachromatic granules of Corynebacterium diphtheria.

Option D: Acid-fast stain is used in the Ziehl–Neelsen staining technique for the identification of acid-fast microorganisms such as M. tuberculosis, M. leprae, and Nocardia.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: The image shown here is a smear, which is used for the diagnosis of which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Herpes simplex virus

The image given below shows the Tzanck smear which is a rapid, diagnostic method. It is used for the diagnosis of the Herpes simplex virus (HSV).

Tzanck cells are multinucleated giant cells with faceted nuclei and homogenously stained ground-glass chromatin. Tzanck smear is a cytological examination of skin blisters. After rupturing the roof of the blister, the floor is scraped with a blade and the material is transferred onto a microscopic slide and fixed. Slides are stained with Giemsa, Wright’s stain, or toluidine blue and examined under the microscope. Tzanck smear is also used in the diagnosis of Hailey-Hailey disease, Darier’s disease, hand-foot-and-mouth disease, etc.

Other options:

Option A: HIV can be detected by virus isolation, detection of antibodies to various antigens of the virus, and by detection of viral DNA, RNA, or antigens.

Option B: Hepatitis B virus is usually detected by viral markers in the serum.

Option C: Koilocytes are characteristically seen in HPV infections, such as Condyloma acuminatum. Koilocytes are lining cells that have perinuclear cytoplasmic vacuolization.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: The stain used for identifying Cryptococcus is _____
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. India ink stain.

The stain used for identifying Cryptococcus is India ink stain.

Indian ink is a negative staining method that provides a uniformly coloured background. The unstained organisms stand out in contrast to the background. It is useful in the demonstration of organisms with capsules that do not take simple stains. It is also used to stain slender bacteria like spirochetes.

The India ink preparation is employed to detect the presence of Cryptococcus neoformans. It is seen as a globular, encapsulated yeast cell with or without budding, between 5 to 20 μm in diameter in size. Cryptococcus has a polysaccharide capsule which is seen against a black background.

Cryptococcus can be cultured from biologic samples like the CSF, sputum, and skin biopsy on routine fungal and bacterial culture media. Colonies are opaque, white-to-cream coloured, and may turn orange-tan or brown after prolonged incubation. They have a mucoid appearance due to the presence of the capsule around the yeast cells.

The image below shows the fungus Cryptococcus, stained with Indian ink.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which among the following culture media is used in the identification of Salmonella?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Wilson and Blair medium

Wilson and Blair bismuth sulphite medium is used for the identification of Salmonella. It is a type of selective and indicator media.

Salmonella typhi reduces sulphite to sulphide in the presence of glucose and produces jet black colonies with a metallic sheen due to the production of H2S on Wilson and Blair bismuth sulphite medium. It is an example of indicator media. It is also a selective media because inhibiting substances are added to inhibit the growth of unwanted bacteria.

On the Wilson-Blair medium, S. paratyphi A produces green colonies due to the absence of H2S production.

On Deoxycholate citrate media and XLD (xylose lysine deoxycholate), colonies show blackheads due to H2S production.

Other options:

Option 1) PLET medium is used to isolate B. anthracis. It is a selective medium consisting of polymyxin, lysozyme, ethylene diamine tetraacetic acid (EDTA), and thallous acetate added to heart infusion agar.

Option 2) BCYE medium (Buffered charcoal yeast extract agar) is used to culture Legionella.

Option 4) Stuart Transport Medium is recommended for the preservation and transportation of Neisseria species and other fastidious organisms from the clinic to the laboratory.

The image below shows black colonies of Salmonella.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which among the following parasites directly invade the skin?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Schistosoma mansoni

The parasite that directly invades the skin is Schistosoma mansoni.

Adult worms of S. mansoni live in the inferior mesenteric vein and their infective form is fork-tailed cercaria. Following skin penetration by cercariae, a pruritic rash termed cercarial dermatitis or swimmers itch develops locally which is self-limiting.

After 4- 8 weeks of the cercarial invasion, high worm load, and egg antigen stimuli lead to the formation of immune complexes which result in a serum sickness-like illness termed Katayama fever. They present with high-grade fever, rash, arthralgia, and hepatosplenomegaly.

When eggs get deposited in the small intestine, patients develop abdominal pain and blood dysentery for a long time called intestinal bilharziasis. The drug of choice is praziquantel 40mg/kg single oral dose. Oxamniquine 15mg/kg single oral dose is also an effective dose.

A yellowish-brown egg with a lateral spine near the rounded posterior end is suggestive of Schistosoma mansoni. In Schistosoma hematobium, the egg has a terminal spine. In Schistosoma japonicum, the egg has no spine but shows a lateral small rudimentary knob.

The life cycle of schistosomes is represented below:

Other options:

Option B: Dracunculiasis/Guinea worm disease is a vector-borne parasitic disease caused by Dracunculus medinenesis. Transmission occurs by consumption of water containing cyclops harboring infective stages of the parasite. This disease is totally a water-based disease and has no alternate way of transmission.

Option C: Wuchereria bancrofti causes filariasis. The adult worms block the lymphatic vessels leading to inflammation and granuloma formation. This causes hard pitting or brawny edema. It can present as lymphadenitis, lymphedema, hydrocele, and elephantiasis. The disease spreads from person to person through mosquito bites.

Option D: Onchocerca volvulus is a tissue nematode. The life cycle of Onchocerca volvulus is completed partly in humans, the definitive host, and partly in female blackflies, the intermediate host. During a blood meal, the female blackfly ingests the microfilariae from the skin and lymphatics of an infected person. Within the vector, the microfilariae develop into the infective stage. When the infected black fly bites another person, it introduces third-stage filarial larvae into the skin of the human host.

Pearl PF1690: Eggs in parasitology

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following dimorphic fungi causes subcutaneous mycosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Sporothrix schenckii

The dimorphic fungus that causes subcutaneous mycosis is Sporothrix schenckii.

Sporotrichosis is caused by Sporothrix schenckii, a thermally dimorphic fungus that lives on vegetation. The infection occurs following traumatic inoculation.

The lesion initially develops as a granulomatous nodule that may progress to form a necrotic or ulcerative lesion. The infection from the lesions in the skin and subcutaneous tissue can spread via the lymphatic channels to the lymph nodes. This condition is known as lymphocutaneous sporotrichosis. This disease is commonly encountered among gardeners and forest workers.

The image below shows lymphocutaneous sporotrichosis.

Other options:

Option B: Histoplasmosis is a systemic fungal infection caused by the dimorphic fungi Histoplasma capsulatum. It is acquired by inhalation and causes a disease similar to tuberculosis and may present as fever, chills, headache, dry cough, dyspnea, and chest pain.

Option C: Blastomycosis is caused by Blastomyces dermatitidis. It is contracted through the inhalation of contaminated soil. Primary infection usually presents as pneumonia.  Chest X-ray reveals consolidation. Disseminated disease may lead to multiple abscesses. Cutaneous lesions present as papules and nodules which progress into large ulcerative lesions.

Option D: T. marneffei is a dimorphic fungus that causes talaromycosis (penicilliosis). It is commonly seen in individuals with advanced AIDS. Clinical features include fever, weight loss, lymphadenopathy, and hepatosplenomegaly. Umbilicated papules that resemble molluscum contagiosum may also be seen.

Hepatitis A has feco-oral transmission. Transmission of Hepatitis B, C, and D can occur sexually.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following immunoglobulins shows the highest concentration in serum?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. IgG

Immunoglobulin G(IgG) shows the highest concentration in serum.

It constitutes about 80 percent of the total immunoglobulin in the serum. It is distributed approximately equally between the intravascular and extravascular compartments

IgG is the only maternal immunoglobulin that is normally transported across the placenta and provides natural passive immunity to the newborn.

Pearl PF1700: Properties of immunoglobulin classes

IgG:

* Half-life- 23 days

* Appears late, indicates chronic infection

* It is the only maternal Ig to cross the placenta.

* Has 4 subclasses.

* Causes complement fixation, precipitation, and neutralization of toxins and virus.

IgM:

* Half-life- 5 days

* Has the highest molecular weight and is a pentamer.

* Polysaccharides and lipids mainly stimulate IgM secretion.

* Intravascular distribution.

* Appears early, indicates recent infection.

* Acts as surface immunoglobulin on the B cells.

* It causes agglutination, hemolysis, complement fixation and opsonization.

IgD:

* Half-life- 2-8 days.

* Acts as a surface immunoglobulin on the B cells.

* Serves as recognition receptors for antigens.

IgE:

* Half-life- 1-5 days

* Causes type I hypersensitivity.

* It is the only heat labile antibody.

* Levels are raised in helminthic infections.

IgA:

* Half-life- 6 days

* It is of 2 types- Serum IgA and Secretory IgA

* Secretory IgA (A dimer) results in mucosal immunity.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following is an acid-fast organism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Mycobacterium avium

Mycobacterium avium is an acid-fast organism.

Acid-fast staining is based on the principle that tubercle bacilli resist decolourization with acids after staining with aniline dyes. Acid fastness is attributed to the variety of fatty acids, alcohols, and lipids in the tubercle bacilli. Acid-fast organisms usually contain mycolic acid, which is acid-fast in the free state.  The steps to carry out acid-fast staining as modified by Ziehl and Neelsen are:

* The slide is stained with carbol fuchsin along with the application of heat.

* It is then decolourized with 20% sulphuric acid. Later methylene blue is used for counterstaining.

* The acid-fast bacteria retain the fuchsin colour, while other organisms take up the counterstain.

Mycobacterium avium complex consists of multiple nontuberculosis mycobacterial species (NTM), which cannot be distinguished in the microbiology laboratory and requires genetic testing. M. avium and Mycobacterium intracellulare are the two original members of the complex. It is a nonmotile, non-spore-forming, gram-positive acid-fast bacillus.

MAC infection is an AIDS-defining opportunistic infection, occurring predominantly at CD4+ T cell counts of <50/μL. The most common presentation is disseminated disease with fever, weight loss, and night sweats. Treatment consists of Clarithromycin / Azithromycin with Ethambutol/ Rifabutin.

Other options:

Option A: Streptococcus pneumoniae is a gram-positive, capsulated, flame-shaped, or lanceolate-shaped diplococcus.

Option B: E. coli is a gram-negative, flagellated rod. It is a lactose fermenter and hence, grows on MacConkey medium to produce pink colonies.

Option D: Actinomyces are gram-positive, anaerobic, and filamentous bacteria that are non-acid-fast.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 16-year-old boy presented with fever, headaches, myalgia, and drowsiness. He later developed dizziness and altered consciousness. His mother reports that he had consumed palm fruit on their recent trip to Kerala and has not been feeling well since then. Keeping the patient's history in mind, which of the following viruses should be considered in your differential diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Nipah virus

This patient with fever, headaches, myalgia, drowsiness, dizziness and altered consciousness, with a history of consuming palm fruit is likely to have been infected with the Nipah virus.

Nipah virus is a zoonotic virus, which is transmitted by animals to humans.

It is an emerging paramyxovirus that belongs to the genus Henipavirus. It has caused disease in humans who have had contact with infected animals.

It has a wide range of hosts and is associated with high mortality rates. Its natural host is a certain species of fruit bat while pigs may be an intermediate host for transmission to humans.
Its transmission can occur by the following methods:

* Unprotected exposure to the secretions from the pigs, or unprotected contact with the tissue of a sick animal.

* Consumption of fruits or fruit products (such as raw date palm juice) contaminated with urine or saliva from infected fruit bats of the family Pteropodidae.

* Human-to-human transmission through close contact with people's secretions and excretions.

* The incubation period ranges from 4 to 14 days.

Patients present with symptoms of headaches, myalgia, vomiting, and sore throat. This is followed by the onset of encephalitis, which manifests as dizziness, drowsiness, and altered consciousness. Patients may also present with acute respiratory distress. Encephalitis and seizures occur in severe cases, progressing to coma within 24 to 48 hours.

Diagnosis is by means of real-time polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) from bodily fluids and antibody detection via enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) methods. The virus can be isolated by cell culture.

There is no treatment or vaccine available for either people or animals. The primary treatment for humans is supportive care.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 28-year-old woman presented to your OPD with complaints of non-foul-smelling curdy white vaginal discharge accompanied by itching and burning. Microscopic examination revealed gram-positive budding yeast and pseudohyphae. What is the causative organism in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Candida albicans

In the given clinical scenario, symptoms of non-foul smelling curdy white vaginal discharge and budding yeast cells and pseudohyphae on microscopy are suggestive of vulvovaginal candidiasis caused by Candida albicans.

Candida species are yeast-like fungi, which normally inhabit the skin and mucosa. Vulvovaginal candidiasis occurs in conditions that decrease the normal genital microbiota(e.g., long-term antibiotic use), allowing the yeasts to proliferate and produce symptoms.

Candida albicans is an ovoid or spherical budding cell, which produces pseudohyphae both in tissues and in culture. Unlike other species of candida, yeast cells of Candida albicans will begin to form germ tubes after incubation in serum maintained at 37°C for about 90 minutes. This is known as the Reynolds-Braude phenomenon.

The clinical symptoms of vulvovaginal candidiasis include curdy white vaginal discharge, dysuria, and intense itching with vaginal pH <4.5.

Diagnosis includes:

* Wet smear with 10% KOH solution- shows budding yeast cells and pseudohyphae as seen in the image below:

* Gram staining - Gram-positive budding cells with pseudohyphae

* Sabouraud agar culture - Creamy white smooth colonies with yeasty odour.

* Corn meal agar culture - Candida albicans form chlamydospores.

* CHROMagar - Candida albicans colonies appear green.

Treatment involves oral fluconazole 150 mg single dose or local intravaginal application of antifungal agents such as imidazole miconazole, clotrimazole, vaginal pessaries or creams used for 3-6 days is effective.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 30-year-old male presents with continuous discomfort in the right hypochondrium. Upon examination, an enlarged liver 8cm below the costal margins is noted. The image below displays his CT radiograph. Additionally, he reports a history of spending a significant amount of time around pet dogs. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Echinococcus granulosus

The given clinical scenario along with  CT scan of the liver showing a hydatid cyst seen as a hypodense lesion with internal septation, suggests a diagnosis of Echinococcus granulosus. It is the most common causative agent in hydatid cysts, while Echinococcus multilocularis and Echinococcus ligartus account for a small number of cases.

Hydatid cysts result from infection by the Echinococcus, and can result in cyst formation anywhere in the body.

Dogs are the definitive hosts of E. granulosus. Sheep are the usual intermediate hosts, but humans are accidental intermediate hosts. Humans are end-stage hosts of the parasite since there is no human-to-human transmission.

Approximately 75% of hydatid cysts are located in the right lobe of the liver and are solitary. The clinical presentation of a hydatid cyst is largely asymptomatic until complications occur. The most common presenting symptoms are abdominal pain, dyspepsia, and vomiting. The most frequent sign is hepatomegaly.

Investigation:

* CT examination reveals a fluid density cyst, with frequent peripheral focal areas of calcification, which usually indicates no active infection if completely circumferential.

* Septation and daughter cysts may be visualised. The water-lily sign indicates a cyst with a floating, undulating membrane, caused by a detached endocyst.

* May also show hyperdense internal septa representing a spoke wheel pattern within a cyst.

The life cycle of Echinococcus is depicted in the image below:

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 40-year-old man with a history of poor dental hygiene undergoes tooth extraction and develops low-grade fever with a new-onset heart murmur two weeks later. Blood cultures show alpha-hemolytic gram-positive cocci arranged in chains. Which organism is most likely responsible for his condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Streptococcus viridans

Streptococcus viridans is a group of gram-positive cocci arranged in chains, often a common cause of infective endocarditis, particularly in cases of subacute bacterial endocarditis.

Streptococcus viridans is a part of the normal flora of the human mouth, throat, and upper respiratory tract. They are alpha-hemolytic, meaning they cause partial hemolysis on blood agar, resulting in a greenish colouration of the agar, hence the name "viridans," which means "green" in Latin.

Although Viridans streptococci are typically susceptible to penicillin, certain strains may exhibit resistance. Therefore, it is crucial that when dealing with endocarditis, the specific strain responsible is identified, and its sensitivity to antibiotics is assessed. This ensures the selection of suitable antibiotics at effective bactericidal levels for treatment.

Other options:

Option A) Staphylococcus aureus is  Beta-hemolytic, and appears in grape-like clusters, not chains. It causes acute endocarditiswith rapid valve destruction, usually in IV drug users.

Option B) Streptococcus pyogenes is also beta-hemolytic, not alpha. It is the Group A Streptococcus causing pharyngitis, impetigo, and rheumatic fever.

Option C) Streptococcus pneumoniae is Alpha-hemolytic but appears as lancet-shaped diplococci, not chains. It is optochin sensitive and causes pneumonia, meningitis, and otitis media.

Pearl PF1994: Modified Duke's criteria for diagnosis of infective endocarditis

Diagnosis of Infective endocarditis is by Duke's Criteria, which requires either:

* Pathologic criteria

* Clinical criteria

If clinical criteria are used, definitive endocarditis is defined by the presence of 2 major or 1 major + 3 minor or 5 minor criteria.

The presence of single pathological criteria is definitive of infective endocarditis.

Note: The diagnosis of endocarditis is rejected if an alternative diagnosis is established either when:

* Symptoms resolve and do not recur with <4 days of antibiotic therapy OR

* If surgery or autopsy yields no pathologic or macroscopic evidence of endocarditis in <4 days of antimicrobial therapy.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A wildlife photographer presents with a blackish lesion at the site of a mite bite from a few days back. He also gives a history of fever and rash. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Scrub typhus

In the above clinical scenario, a history of mite bite followed by the development of a characteristic eschar at the bite site along with fever and rash suggests a diagnosis of scrub typhus.

Scrub typhus, also known as chigger-borne typhus, is caused by Orientia tsutsugamushi. The vector is trombiculid mite. Humans are infected when they are bitten by the mite larvae known as chiggers. The incubation period is 1-3 weeks. Patients develop a characteristic eschar at the site of the mite bite, along with regional lymphadenopathy and maculopapular rash. It can be associated with fever, headache, and conjunctival injection. Meningoencephalitis, myocarditis, and pneumonia can be seen in severe cases.

Serologic assays are used for diagnosis. Weil-Felix reaction is a heterophile agglutination reaction used for diagnosis, wherein the sera are tested for agglutinins to the O antigens of certain Proteus strains OX19, OX2, and OXK. OXK is agglutinated only in scrub typhus. Doxycycline is the treatment of choice for both adults and children.

In Scrub typhus both the adult and nymphal stages of mites are free living in nature, hence they do not feed on vertebral hosts. The larval stage(chigger) feeds on the vertebrate host and pick up the rickettsiae. Rodents are the mammalian reservoir for scrub typhus. Eschar can be seen in the image below:

Other options:

Option A: Anthrax- Cutaneous anthrax (Hide Porter’s disease) present as a black eschar at the site of entry. At the site of entry of organism or spores, a papule develops in about 1–7 days. This develops into a vesicle that later breaks down into an ulcer with a black, central, necrotic eschar surrounded by edematous skin. The disease used to be common in dock workers, carrying loads of hides and skins on their bare backs. Renal involvement is unlikely to be seen in this condition.

The image below shows its characteristic rash:

Option C : Rocky Mountain spotted fever is a rickettsial infection transmitted by ticks (Dermacentor andersoni). It is the most serious type of fever. Symptoms include fever, headache, Rash, muscle pain and lack of appetite. Early treatment with doxycycline is recommended to prevent death and severe illness.

The rash is shown in the image below:

Option D : Epidemic typhus: Epidemic typhus is caused by Rickettsia prowazekii and the vector is louse. Its incubation period is 10 to 14 days. The disease starts with fever and chills. A characteristic rash appears on the fourth or fifth day, starting on the trunk and spreading over the limbs but sparing the face, palms, and soles.
