questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Relative bradycardia is seen in which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Brucellosis

Among the given options, relative bradycardia is seen in brucellosis.

Brucellosis is a zoonotic infection caused by the Brucella species, typically contracted through direct contact with infected animals or consumption of unpasteurized dairy products. The clinical presentation includes undulating fever, relative bradycardia, musculoskeletal symptoms like arthritis and myalgia, general malaise, hepatosplenomegaly, neurological symptoms in neuro brucellosis, presenting as meningitis or encephalitis. In men, epididymal-orchitis can occur, presenting as testicular pain and swelling.

Laboratory diagnosis of brucellosis includes:

* Polymerase chain reaction

* Blood culture with the Castaneda method

* Serological methods include standard agglutination test (SAT), complement fixation test, Coomb’s antiglobulin test, and enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA).

* Tests for animals and animal products: Milk ring tests and Rose Bengal card tests.

Treatment includes antimicrobial therapy with IM streptomycin and oral doxycycline. The prevention of brucellosis can be achieved by pasteurizing milk and other milk products.

Relative bradycardia, also known as Faget's sign, is observed when patients exhibit a lower heart rate than anticipated in relation to an increase in body temperature. Body temperature is commonly regarded as a factor that independently influences heart rate. It is estimated that for each 1°C (1.8°F) rise in temperature, the heart rate typically increases by approximately 15-20 beats per minute.

While this pulse-temperature dissociation is not highly sensitive or specific for establishing a diagnosis, it can still prove beneficial in resource-limited settings due to its easy accessibility and simplicity.

Infectious causes of relative bradycardia include:

* Salmonella typhi

* Brucella (brucellosis)

* Francisella tularensis

* Coxiella burnetii (Q fever)

* Leptospira interrogans

* Legionella pneumophila

* Rickettsia spp.

* Orientia tsutsugamushi (scrub typhus)

* Corynebacterium diphtheriae

* Plasmodium spp. (malaria)

Noninfectious causes include:

* Drug fever

* Beta-blocker use

* Central nervous system lesions

* Malignant lymphoma

* Factitious fever

It was found that relative bradycardia as a feature of a specific disease only occurs in diseases caused by organisms that are both gram-negative and intracellular.

Other options:

Shigellosis, pertussis, and dengue show tachycardia on clinical examination. ( Option A, B & C)

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following is the most common bacteria found as part of the normal flora of the conjunctiva?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Staphylococcus epidermidis

Staphylococcus epidermidis is present as a normal flora of conjunctiva.

The normal flora of the conjunctiva consists of a variety of microorganisms that exist harmlessly and help maintain ocular health by preventing the colonization of pathogenic organisms. The most commonly found bacteria in the conjunctiva include:

Staphylococcus epidermidis (most common), staphylococcus aureus, corynebacterium species, streptococcus viridans, propionibacterium acnes, etc.

Staphylococcus epidermidis is a novobiocin-sensitive, coagulase-negative, non-pigmented, non-hemolytic cocci. It also doesn't ferment mannitol.

It is present on normal skin flora and mucous membranes and has the following virulence factors:

* Biofilms

* Adhesive proteins

* Teichoic acids

* Lipases and DNAses

Among the Coagulase negative staph species, Staph epidermidis is the most common cause of:

* Healthcare-associated bloodstream infections

* Early prosthetic valve endocarditis

* Peritonitis in dialysis patients

* Infections of orthopedic prosthesis

* CSF shunt infections

S. epidermidis is more resistant than Staph aureus to methicillin and the treatment of choice is Vancomycin.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following vectors is associated with Orientia Tsutsugamushi?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Trombiculid mite

Trombiculid mite is the vector responsible for the transmission of scrub typhus caused by Orientia tsutsugamushi.

Scrub typhus, also known as chigger-borne typhus, is caused by Orientia tsutsugamushi. The vector is trombiculid mite. Humans are infected when they are bitten by the mite larvae known as chiggers. The incubation period is 1- 3 weeks. Patients develop a characteristic eschar at the site of the mite bite, along with regional lymphadenopathy and maculopapular rash. It can be associated with fever, headache, and conjunctival injection. Meningoencephalitis, myocarditis, and pneumonia can be seen in severe cases.

Serologic assays are used for diagnosis. Weil-Felix reaction is a heterophile agglutination reaction used for diagnosis, wherein the sera are tested for agglutinins to the O antigens of certain Proteus strains OX19, OX2, and OXK. OXK is agglutinated only in scrub typhus. Doxycycline is the treatment of choice for both adults and children.

The below image shows the trombiculid mite which is responsible for the transmission of Orientia tsutsugamushi.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 10-year-old child presents to the paediatric OPD with complaints of abdominal pain and loose stools for the past two days. Upon further questioning, his mother reveals that they ate pani-puri at a roadside stall three days ago. Which of the following organisms is most likely to be the cause of this disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Escherichia coli

The most likely causative organism in the given clinical scenario is Escherichia coli.

Abdominal pain and loose stools following the consumption of street food, such as pani-puri, are classic signs of gastroenteritis. Escherichia coli is a common cause, particularly through contaminated food and water.

E. coli is a gram-negative, flagellated rod. It is a lactose fermenter and hence, grows on MacConkey medium to produce pink colonies.

Clinical infections are of four main types:

* Urinary tract infection

* Diarrhea

* Septicemia, neonatal sepsis and neonatal meningitis

* Pyogenic infections

There are mainly six types of diarrheagenic E. coli:

* Enteropathogenic E. coli (EPEC)

* Enterotoxigenic E. coli (ETEC)

* Enteroinvasive E. coli (EIEC)

* Enterohemorrhagic E. coli (EHEC)

* Enteroaggregative E. coli (EAEC)

* Diffusely adherent E. coli (DAEC)

Enteropathogenic E. coli (EPEC): It causes diarrhea mainly in infants and children. EPEC adherence factor (EAF), a plasmid-encoded protein, is responsible for adherence. Another mechanism is adherence to the enterocyte membrane by a locus of enterocyte effacement (LEE), which is regulated chromosomally. This promotes tight adherence of the pathogen, with loss of microvilli leading to effacement.

Enterotoxigenic E. coli (ETEC) is endemic in developing countries of the tropics and seen in all age groups. Its severity varies from mild, watery diarrhea to a fatal disease indistinguishable from cholera. It has an incubation period of >16 hours. Demonstration of the enterotoxins is helpful to establish the diagnosis. It causes traveler's diarrhea in people from non-endemic areas visiting endemic areas.

The Enterobacteriaceae family is classified based on their action on lactose present in MacConkey's medium:

* Lactose fermenters – Escherichia, Klebsiella

* Late lactose fermenters – Shigella sonnei

* Non-lactose fermenters—Salmonella species, Shigella species

Other options:

Option A: Campylobacter are motile, non-spore-forming, microaerophilic, curved, Gram-negative rods. It is most commonly transmitted by raw or undercooked food products: ingestion of contaminated poultry (most common), raw (unpasteurized) milk, or untreated water. It is characterized by inflammatory diarrhea, abdominal pain, and fever. The degree of diarrhea varies from several loose stools to grossly bloody stools. It is typically self-limiting, and fluid and electrolyte replacement is the mainstay of treatment. For diarrheal disease, oral macrolides are the drugs of choice (erythromycin or azithromycin). Ciprofloxacin or doxycycline can be used as alternatives.

Option B: The rice-water stools are characteristic of Vibrio cholerae infection.

Option C: Bacillus cereus presents with symptoms of recurrent bouts of vomiting and abdominal cramps within 1-5 hours after consumption of fried rice.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 28-year-old HIV patient presents with a non-productive cough and difficulty in breathing, which was progressively increasing. A chest X-ray shows diffuse bilateral interstitial infiltrates along with pneumatocele. Gomori’s methenamine silver staining of the bronchoalveolar lavage shows the following. The most probable causative organism is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Pneumocystis jirovecii

The given clinical picture and the GMS stain showing the black-coloured stained cysts resembling the crushed ping pong balls are suggestive of pneumocystis pneumonia, which is caused by Pneumocystis jirovecii.

Patients with PCP generally present with fever and cough that is usually non-productive. Pneumocystis jirovecii causes pneumocystis pneumonia (PCP) in AIDS patients with CD4 counts below 200 cells/mm³ and usually presents with fever, dry cough, and dyspnoea. Inspiratory crackles are heard on auscultation.

The most common finding on chest x-ray if the disease is suspected early is either a normal film or a faint bilateral interstitial infiltrate. The classic finding of a dense perihilar infiltrate is unusual in patients with AIDS.

The chest radiograph given below shows ground-glass opacities in PCP.

Treatment: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and pentamidine isethionate.

Other options:

Option B: Pulmonary histoplasmosis – The acute form presents with a mild flu-like illness and pulmonary infiltrates in the chest X-ray, with hilar or mediastinal lymphadenopathy. Chronic cavitary histoplasmosis may be seen in smokers with underlying structural lung disease.

Option C: Cryptococcosis: Cryptococcus neoformans typically presents as a lung infection or meningitis in immunocompromised individuals. On SDA, Cryptococcus forms mucoid colonies, and lactophenol blue would show encapsulated yeast.

Option D: Aspergillomas are mass-like fungus balls that are typically composed of Aspergillus fumigatus and are a non-invasive form of pulmonary aspergillosis. Aspergillomas occur in patients with normal immunity but structurally abnormal lungs with pre-existing cavities. The most common underlying condition is pulmonary tuberculosis.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 30-year-old man vomits and has diarrhoea within three hours of eating salad and custard at a picnic. There is no fever present. Which organism is most likely to be the cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Staphylococcus aureus

The above clinical scenario is suggestive of acute food poisoning most likely caused by Staphylococcus aureus.

Food poisoning by Staphylococcus aureus is caused by the ingestion of preformed enterotoxin. The preformed enterotoxin is heat-stable. Eight antigenic types of enterotoxin are currently known, of which type A toxin is responsible for most cases. It contaminates food products such as meat, fish, milk products, mayonnaise, cream pastries, etc. when left at room temperature for a long time.

Enterotoxin acts directly on the autonomic nervous system to cause food poisoning, rather than on the gastrointestinal mucosa. It stimulates the vagus nerve and vomiting center of the brain and also stimulates intestinal peristaltic activity. Staphylococcal food poisoning has a very short incubation period of about 1 - 8 hours. Patients usually present with nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea 2-6 hrs after the consumption of contaminated food.

Other options:

Option A: Gas gangrene is caused by Clostridium perfringens. These gram-positive, anaerobic, spore-bearing bacilli are widely found in soil and feces.

Option B: Salmonella enterica are further divided into two clinical groups: typhoidal salmonellae and non-typhoidal salmonellae, or NTS. Infection with NTS most often results in gastroenteritis—characterized by nausea, vomiting, watery diarrhea, fever, and onset of abdominal cramps 6–48 hours after the ingestion of contaminated food (gastroenteritis is uncommon in typhoidal salmonellae).

Option C: Food poisoning after consumption of fried rice or Chinese street food is suggestive of Bacillus cereus. Food poisoning caused by B. cereus is of two types: Diarrheal type (incubation period 8-16 hours) and Emetic type (incubation period 1-5 hours)

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 32-year-old woman is admitted to the ICU with fever and hypotension. She has rigours, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhoea. Her BP is 70/50 mmHg, with a pulse of 140 bpm and a temperature of 39.5°C. Skin examination reveals generalised erythroderma but no signs of skin infection. She has a history of using tampons for extended periods of time. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome

The above presentation of fever, hypotension, erythroderma, vomiting, and the finding of a retained vaginal tampon point towards a likely diagnosis of staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome.

Toxic shock syndrome (TSS) is a toxin-mediated disease that is most commonly associated with staphylococcal and group A streptococcal infections. Staphylococcal TSS, on the other hand, is associated with the toxic shock syndrome toxin-1 (TSST-1), which binds directly to the MHC II complex and T-cell receptors. This results in a massive increase in the cytokines interleukin-2 (IL-2), interferon γ, and tumor necrosis factor (TNF), leading to a cytokine storm.

Staphylococcal TSS is associated with the use of a highly absorbent tampon. Nonmenstrual cases are seen in patients with surgical or postpartum wound infections, with nasal and wound packing.

Clinical features include fever >102°F, hypotension, widespread macular erythroderma and subsequent desquamation after 7-14 days, and the involvement of multiple organ systems (liver, kidneys, gastrointestinal tract, and/or CNS).

Patients should be managed aggressively with fluids and systemic antibiotic therapy. They can be started on drugs like intravenous vancomycin/daptomycin initially to allow for MRSA (methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus) coverage. Antibiotics can later be changed based on culture sensitivity reports.

The T-cell activation that produces the cytokine storm in TSS can be seen in the image below:

Other options:

Option A: Sepsis is a potentially fatal condition resulting from the body’s abnormal response to an infection, leading to organ dysfunction. It is diagnosed by the presence of infection with an increase of 2 or more points according to the SOFA score. Septic shock occurs in patients with sepsis who need vasopressors to keep MAP >= 65 mmHg and have a lactate level of >2 mmol/L, even after sufficient fluid therapy.

Option B: PID is the inflammation of the upper genital tract, involving the uterus, fallopian tubes, and ovaries. The most common cause of PID is sexually transmitted diseases (STDs) resulting from ascending Chlamydia & gonococcus infections.

Option D: Option D: Streptococcal TSS is associated with pyrogenic exotoxin and other toxins that act as superantigens and mediate the release of proinflammatory cytokines. In contrast to patients with staphylococcal TSS, the majority with streptococcal TSS are bacteremic. The most common associated infection is a soft tissue infection—necrotizing fasciitis, myositis, or cellulitis. It can also be seen in pneumonia, peritonitis, osteomyelitis, and myometritis. The general features of the illness include fever, hypotension, renal impairment, and respiratory distress syndrome. A rash usually does not develop. In the given situation, the source of infection is the retained vaginal tampon; streptococcal TSS is not the correct answer.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 4-year-old child presents to the paediatric OPD with complaints of a low-grade fever, poor appetite, and a sore throat for the past two days. Upon examination, the palms, soles, and oral mucosa show numerous vesicular lesions. The child attends daycare, and several other children have similar complaints. The neurological examination is normal. Which of the following is the most likely causative agent?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Coxsackievirus A16

The presence of vesicular lesions on the palms, soles, and oral cavity and the images showing the characteristic lesions are suggestive of hand-foot-and-mouth disease (HFMD), which is commonly caused by coxsackievirus A16.

Hand-foot-and-mouth disease:

It is commonly caused by Coxsackievirus A16, which is a subgroup of enteroviruses. In large outbreaks, it is also caused by enterovirus 71, coxsackie A viruses 5, 6, 7, 9, and 10, and coxsackie B viruses 2 and 5.

Clinical features:

* Usually, a mild illness

* Vesicular lesions may be seen on the tongue, posterior pharynx, buccal mucosa, palate, lips, etc.

* Maculopapular, vesicular, or pustular lesions may be present on the hands and fingers, buttocks, and groin.

* Lesions are more commonly seen in the hands than in the feet.

* These vesicles resolve in 1 week.

* Infections with enterovirus 71 are more severe and are associated with neurological and cardiopulmonary manifestations.

* Infections with coxsackievirus A16 can occasionally produce complications like encephalitis, acute flaccid paralysis, myocarditis, pericarditis, and shock.

* Coxsackievirus A6 produces atypical HFMD, which is a severe form.

Diagnosis:

* HFMD is usually diagnosed clinically by the characteristic lesions.

* Viral culture can be done to confirm the presence of an enterovirus. Blood, CSF, urine, and mucosal swabs can be cultured.

* RT-PCR testing to detect the viral genome is more sensitive and specific. PCR testing of CSF in children with meningitis is frequently positive even when the cultures are negative.

Treatment:

* No specific antiviral agent is a proven agent for enteroviruses. Supportive care is the mainstay of treatment.

* Milrinone is suggested as an effective agent for enterovirus 71 cardiopulmonary disease.

* Immunoglobulins have been used to manage severe cases, but with varying outcomes.

Other options:

Option A: Roseola infantum, also known as sixth disease, caused by human herpesvirus 6 (HHV-6), is associated with a non-pruritic, pink, morbilliform rash on the trunk and back, which appears after the fever has subsided and disappears after two days. It is also typically associated with ulcers at the uvulo-palatoglossal junction called Nagayama spots.

Option B: Fifth disease, or erythema infectiosum, is an exanthematous fever caused by parvovirus B19 in children, which is also self-limiting and generally requires supportive care only. Its symptoms include a classical slapped cheek rash, which can evolve into a papular purpuric glove and stocking syndrome. There is usually no prodrome or minimal symptoms before the abrupt onset of rash. The virus is known to cause transient myelosuppression and anemia. In very severe disease, IVIG has been tried in some cases.

Option D: Adenovirus is a non-enveloped, double-stranded DNA virus. They are associated with infections of the respiratory tract, eye, and intestines.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 41-year-old dairy worker presents with intermittent fever, night sweats, fatigue, joint pains, and lower backache for the past 3 weeks. He admits to drinking unpasteurised milk from the dairy where he works on a regular basis. On examination, he has mild hepatosplenomegaly and tenderness over his lumbar spine. Blood cultures reveal a slow-growing gram-negative coccobacillus. What is the most appropriate treatment for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Doxycycline + Rifampicin

The given clinical scenario of a 41-year-old dairy worker with intermittent fever, fatigue, joint pains, and lower backache, with frequent consumption of unpasteurised milk, is suggestive of brucellosis, which is treated with doxycycline and rifampicin.

Brucella is a gram-negative, obligate aerobic coccobacillus that causes brucellosis (undulant fever), a zoonotic febrile illness. Humans typically acquire it through occupational or domestic exposure to infected animals (like sheep, goats, and cattle) or their unpasteurised products.

Monocytes and macrophages of the reticuloendothelial system are the primary target cells for brucellosis. Brucellae are intracellular pathogens with a particular affinity for mononuclear phagocytic cells (macrophages and monocytes) found in the reticuloendothelial system (lymph nodes, spleen, liver, and bone marrow). These bacteria proliferate within the reticuloendothelial system, which accounts for its resistance to simple antimicrobial therapy.

The milk ring test (MRT) is positive for Brucella. It is used for the detection of infected animals on dairy farms. In the milk ring test, whole milk is mixed with stained Brucella antigen and incubated at 70°C for 40–50 minutes

* Positive test: Antibodies agglutinate the antigen, forming a blue ring at the cream layer.

* Negative test: No ring forms; the milk remains uniformly blue.

Brucellosis can be acute or chronic. Acute brucellosis presents with muscular and articular pains, asthmatic attacks, nocturnal drenching sweats, exhaustion, anorexia, constipation, nervous irritability, and chills. Chronic brucellosis presents with sweating and joint pain with minimal or no pyrexia, and the illness lasts for years.

Rifampicin interrupts RNA synthesis by binding to a subunit of mycobacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase. Apart from being used to treat leprosy, it is used in the management of tuberculosis, brucellosis, and prophylaxis of meningococcal meningitis. Hepatitis is a major adverse effect. Other side effects include pruritus with rash, redness and watering of eyes, flu-like symptoms, and abdominal cramps. Urine and secretions may become orange-red.

Doxycycline binds to the 30S ribosome and inhibits attachment of aminoacyl tRNA to a site of the ribosome. Photosensitivity, gastrointestinal irritation, mottling of teeth, and suppression of bone growth in children are common adverse effects of tetracycline. Doxycycline is used for prophylaxis of leptospirosis infection following exposure to contaminated water in agricultural workers following floods and natural disasters. Doxycycline is primarily eliminated through the gastrointestinal tract, making it safe for use in renal impairment, as it does not require dose adjustment in renal failure. This antibiotic avoids accumulation in patients with decreased kidney function, reducing the risk of nephrotoxicity or adverse effects related to renal impairment.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A diabetic patient develops whitish plaques in the oral cavity. A KOH mount reveals the presence of budding yeast containing pseudohyphae. Which of the following is the most suitable culture medium for the isolation of this microorganism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Sabouraud's dextrose agar

The most likely diagnosis for the given clinical scenario is oral candidiasis, with Sabouraud's dextrose agar (SDA) being the most suitable culture medium for Candida albicans.

Candida albicans is an opportunistic pathogen that causes candidiasis. It is a yeast when part of the normal flora of mucous membranes but forms pseudohyphae and hyphae when it invades tissue. They are not dimorphic. It forms germ tubes when incubated at 37 degrees Celsius. It is gram-positive and forms colonies of yeasts on Sabouraud's dextrose agar.

Oral candidiasis, or oral thrush, is a patchy, pseudomembranous lesion that can be scraped off, and it develops over the tongue, lips, gums, or palate. It is composed of epithelial cells, yeasts, and pseudohyphae.

It occurs in almost all individuals with AIDS. Other risk factors include high levels of glucose, cellular immunodeficiency, and corticosteroids or antibiotics. It is treated with topical nystatin, oral ketoconazole, or fluconazole.

Other options:

Option A: Chocolate agar: When blood agar is heated to 80-90°C for 15-20 minutes, the V factor is released from within the erythrocytes.

Option C: Thayer-Martin medium is a selective media used to isolate Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Neisseria meningitides.

Option D: Loeffler's serum slope is a medium for the growth of Corynebacterium diphtheriae.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A farmer reports fever, malaise, and diarrhoea. There is a history of contact with livestock. Which of the following organisms is most likely to be the cause of the disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Coxiella burnetii

The most likely diagnosis is Q fever, which is caused by Coxiella burnetii.

The given clinical vignette describes a farmer with fever, malaise and diarrhoea along with previous exposure to livestock. This implies that the illness may be zoonosis-associated.

Q fever, or query fever, is caused by the pathogen Coxiella burnetii, which is a small, pleomorphic, gram-negative coccobacillus that was previously thought to be a Rickettsia but now has its own genus. It can be found in ticks, but it is a zoonosis transmitted to humans either through inhalation of aerosols or through contaminated milk.

It is an occupational hazard among abattoir workers, shepherds, cowherds, and other individuals in close contact with animals, especially during or immediately after their parturition. Acute Q-fever presents with nonspecific signs and symptoms, such as fever, cough, vomiting, diarrhoea, photophobia, pneumonia, and less commonly, anaemia, myocarditis, etc.

The disease can result in a state of chronic fatigue called "Q-fever fatigue syndrome". Chronic Q fever tends to occur months or years after the initial infection and can manifest as Q fever endocarditis, infected prostheses, infected aneurysms, and bone infections.

On TEE, endothelium-covered nodules are seen as vegetations on the valves, and new-onset valve regurgitation may be seen. Diagnosis requires a high index of clinical suspicion due to non-specific features and must be considered in all cases of culture-negative endocarditis.

Diagnostic methods include culture, which requires a level 3 biosafety cabinet and hence is not done in routine practice, or DNA detection using PCR. IFA (indirect fluorescent antibody test) is the most preferred test that identifies antibodies and can differentiate acute and chronic infections.

The treatment of choice is with doxycycline, which may be substituted for trimethoprim-sulphamethoxazole in pregnancy. Doxycycline is given for acute Q fever as 100 mg BD for 14 days. For chronic Q fever, doxycycline and hydroxychloroquine are given. Minimum treatment for native valve endocarditis is 18 months.

Due to the low minimum infective dose of Coxiella, it is a bioterrorism agent, Category B.

Other Options:

Option B: Rickettsia rickettsii is the causative agent for Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever (RMSF). Ticks act as a vector.

Option C: Endemic typhus is caused by Rickettsia typhi and transmitted by Xenopsylla, the flea. The reservoir of the infection is rats. It is a mild, sporadic fever that is not of great public health importance. The disease presents with fever and chills. A characteristic rash appears on the fourth or fifth day, which starts on the trunk and spreads over the limbs but spares the face, palms and soles. By the second week, the patient becomes stuporous and delirious.

Option D: Scrub typhus, also known as chigger-borne typhus, is caused by Orientia tsutsugamushi. The vector is a trombiculid mite.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A gardener presents with multiple vesicles on the hands and multiple eruptions along the lymphatic distribution. The lesions are limited to cutaneous tissues. Which of the following will be observed on microscopy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Asteroid bodies

The presence of multiple vesicles on the hands and multiple eruptions along lymphatics in a gardener is suggestive of sporotrichosis caused by Sporothrix schenckii, which is characterised by asteroid bodies.

Sporotrichosis is a type of subcutaneous mycosis caused by S. schenckii, a dimorphic fungus that lives on vegetation such as grasses, trees, rose bushes, etc. It occurs in the yeast phase in tissues and in cultures at 37°C and in the mycelia phase in nature and cultures at 25°C. The septate hyphae appear very thin and carry flower-like clusters of small conidia borne on delicate sterigmata. Asteroid bodies seen in sporotrichosis consist of a central basophilic yeast cell surrounded by radiating extensions of eosinophilic material.

Following traumatic inoculation into the skin, as in a thorn prick, S. schenckii causes sporotrichosis, a chronic granulomatous infection. The initial lesion appears following a trauma or a thorn prick. The infection then spreads via the lymphatic channels to the lymph nodes. This results in secondary ulcers on the lymph nodes.

Treatment:

* Cutaneous form can be treated with oral or topical potassium iodide

* Lymphocutaneous form—Itraconazole is effective in over 90% of patients with lymphocutaneous infection

* For disseminated infection, amphotericin B is the drug of choice.

The image below shows the asteroid body and flower-like clusters of small conidia seen in sporotrichosis:

The given image shows the distribution of the nodules along lymphatics.

Other options:

Option B: Chromoblastomycosis (chromomycosis) is a subcutaneous mycotic infection that is usually caused by traumatic inoculation. Over months to years, the primary lesion becomes verrucous and wart-like with extension along the draining lymphatics. Histopathology shows sclerotic bodies or medlar bodies.

Option C: Michaelis-Gutmann bodies are PAS-positive basophilic concretions due to iron and calcium deposits in lysosomes seen in malakoplakia. Malakoplakia is a chronic inflammatory reaction resulting from acquired defects in phagocyte function affecting the urinary bladder.

Option D: Henderson–Patterson bodies are seen in molluscum contagiosum, caused by poxvirus.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient presents to the hospital with a history of high fever and chills. On examination, a maculopapular rash was observed over the neck, with a positive tourniquet test. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Dengue haemorrhagic fever

The clinical features are suggestive of dengue haemorrhagic fever.

Dengue, also known as break-bone fever, manifests after an incubation period of 3-14 days. Dengue fever is an acute febrile illness with two or more of the following manifestations: headache, retroorbital pain, myalgia, arthralgia, and rash.

Dengue haemorrhagic fever, or dengue shock syndrome, can occur in individuals with preexisting non-neutralising heterologous dengue antibodies caused by previous infection with a different serotype of the virus or passively acquired maternal antibodies in children. Initially, symptoms simulate normal dengue; however, the patient’s condition worsens.

The virus–antibody complexes are formed within a few days of the second dengue infection, and the non-neutralising enhancing antibodies promote infection of higher numbers of mononuclear cells followed by the release of cytokines, vasoactive mediators, and procoagulants, leading to the disseminated intravascular coagulation seen in the haemorrhagic fever syndrome.

The most important pathology of dengue haemorrhagic fever is increased vascular permeability with plasma leakage into the interstitial spaces associated with increased levels of vasoactive cytokines, which can lead to life-threatening shock in some patients. The clinical criteria of dengue haemorrhagic fever are dengue fever with haemorrhagic tendencies evidenced by one b more of the following:

* Positive tourniquet test

* Petechiae, ecchymoses or purpura

* Bleeding from the mucosa, gastrointestinal tract, injection sites or other sites

* Thrombocytopenia, a more than 20% drop in haematocrit following volume replacement treatment compared to baseline

* Signs of plasma leakage (pleural effusion, ascites, hypoproteinaemia)

Dengue shock syndrome is characterised by all the above criteria for dengue haemorrhagic fever with evidence of circulatory failure manifested by rapid, weak pulse and narrow pulse pressure or hypotension for age, cold, clammy skin and restlessness.

Other options:

Option B: Quartan fever, which occurs on the first and fourth days, is typically associated with Plasmodium malariae infection.

Option C: The disease can present as classical filariasis or occult filariasis. Clinical features include:

* Classical filariasis – Fever, lymphangitis, lymphadenitis, lymphedema, lymphangiovarix, hydrocele, lymphorrhagia, elephantiasis

* Occult filariasis – Massive eosinophilia, hepatosplenomegaly, dyspnoea, arthritis, glomerulonephritis, etc.

Option D: Chikungunya fever is due to infection with the chikungunya virus, spread by mosquitos. The Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus mosquitoes are the most common vectors. It presents as an acute onset of fever, arthralgia, and myalgia with other flu symptoms such as headache, loss of appetite, and nausea. A progressive maculopapular rash develops, which is more pronounced on the trunk.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient presents with a fever and altered sensorium. The peripheral smear shows multiple rings in the RBC. A diagnosis of chloroquine-resistant Plasmodium falciparum was made. What is the most likely course of treatment?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Artesunate

Severe Plasmodium falciparum malaria is diagnosed, and the recommended treatment is artesunate.

Major manifestations of severe falciparum malaria include more than two convulsions in 24 hours, unarousable coma/cerebral malaria (failure to localise or respond appropriately to stimuli or coma persisting for >30 min after generalised convulsion), acidosis, severe normocytic normochromic anaemia, renal failure, pulmonary oedema, hypoglycaemia, shock, and disseminated intravascular coagulation.

Other manifestations include haemoglobinuria, hyperparasitaemia, jaundice, and extreme weakness.

The treatment of choice is artesunate given at a dose of 2.4 mg/kg stat IV, followed by 2.4 mg/kg at 12 and 24 hours, and then daily if necessary. If artesunate is unavailable, artemether is given at a dose of 3.2 mg/kg stat IM, followed by 1.6 mg/kg QD, or quinine dihydrochloride is given at a dose of 20 mg of salt/kg infused over 4 hours, followed by 10 mg of salt/kg infused over 2–8 hours.

Plasmodium falciparum causes malignant tertian malaria. This means that the fever has a periodicity of 48 hours, corresponding to one cycle of erythrocytic schizogony. Malignant because it is a more severe and fatal type of malaria.

Falciparum malaria shows a very high percentage of RBCs containing ring forms. This high-level parasitemia is more often seen in Plasmodium falciparum infections than in infections by other plasmodia. After the ring forms in the peripheral blood, the rest of the erythrocytic cycle occurs in the capillaries of the brain and internal organs. So, only ring forms can be seen in the peripheral blood and not the late trophozoites and schizonts. The gametocytes of P. falciparum are crescent-shaped or “banana-shaped” (as shown below), whereas those of the other plasmodia are spherical.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient with HIV presents with diarrhoea. Stool microscopy reveals 11-12 micron oocysts with two sporocysts each. Which of the following is the most likely causative organism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Cyclospora cayetanensis

The organism with oocysts of size 11-12 μm is Cyclospora cayetanensis.

Cyclospora is a coccidian parasite. The sporulated oocysts are infectious to humans. They reside in the enterocytes in the small intestine. The infection causes prolonged diarrhoea, abdominal pain, and vomiting, which is more severe in immunocompromised individuals.

On a wet mount of the faeces, oocysts are seen as red spheres when stained with acid-fast stain. Sporulated oocysts of Cyclospora are 11-12 μm in size, round, and contain 2 sporocysts, each having two sporozoites. Treatment is by giving cotrimoxazole twice daily for seven days.

Other options:

Option A: Oocysts of Cystoisospora are 23-36 μm, oval, and contain two sporocysts, each having four sporozoites. They are uniformly acid-fast.

Option B: Sporulated oocysts of Cryptosporidium are spherical, 4-5 μm in size, and acid-fast. It is implicated in causing traveller's diarrhoea and chronic persistent diarrhea in immunocompromised patients. The two Cryptosporidium species responsible are Cryptosporidium hominis and Cryptosporidium parvum.

Option D: Ingestion of cysts in non-chlorinated water can contract infection from parasites such as Giardia lamblia.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A respiratory illness outbreak is reported in a paediatric ward, primarily affecting infants under the age of 12 months. The majority of patients present with fever, cough, and tachypnea, as well as wheezing and signs of respiratory distress. Hyperinflation is frequently seen on chest radiographs. What is the most likely cause of the outbreak?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Respiratory syncytial virus

The given clinical features with a radiograph showing hyperinflated lungs and respiratory distress in patients aged 12 months or younger suggest bronchiolitis, which is most commonly caused by respiratory syncytial virus (RSV).

Acute bronchiolitis is predominantly a viral disease in children younger than 2 years. Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is responsible for more than 50% of cases. Bronchiolitis occurs due to viral lower respiratory tract infection, most commonly by the RSV (respiratory syncytial virus). It is common in children less than 12 months of age.

Acute bronchiolitis refers to airway inflammation and obstruction of the lower respiratory tract. Commonly, symptoms of bronchiolitis begin with rhinitis or congestion and cough and may progress to signs of increasing respiratory distress (tachypnoea, wheezing, and accessory muscle use).

Clinical features of bronchiolitis include fever, cough, fine inspiratory crackles, expiratory wheezes, and breathing difficulty. Cyanosis may be seen in severe cases. Radiographs may be normal in some patients. In the majority of them, there will be interstitial infiltrates, hyperexpansion of the chest, and peribronchial thickening. It is more common in boys, in those who have not been breastfed, and in those who live in crowded conditions. The risk is higher for infants with young mothers or mothers who smoked during pregnancy.

Management is mainly conservative. Hypoxemic children should receive cool, humidified oxygen. Rarely, a child might develop respiratory failure and require hospitalisation and invasive ventilation.

Other options:

Option A: Influenza belongs to the Orthomyxovirus family. It presents with fever, myalgia, and respiratory symptoms.

Option B: The most common causative organism for croup is the parainfluenza virus.

Option C: Rotavirus is the most common identifiable viral cause of diarrhoea in children below the age of 5 years and is most frequent between 6 and 24 months of age

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A woman presents with fever after returning from a forest trip. On examination, a black eschar is seen on the abdomen/trunk. What is the drug of choice in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Doxycycline

In the above clinical scenario, a history of a forest trip followed by the development of a characteristic eschar at the bite site along with fever suggests a diagnosis of scrub typhus, which is treated with doxycycline.

Humans are infected when they are bitten by the mite larvae known as chiggers. The incubation period is 1-3 weeks. Patients develop a characteristic eschar at the site of the mite bite, along with regional lymphadenopathy and maculopapular rash. It can be associated with fever, headache, and conjunctival injection. Meningoencephalitis, myocarditis, and pneumonia can be seen in severe cases.

Oral doxycycline is given in uncomplicated scrub typhus. In pregnancy, oral azithromycin is preferred.

In scrub typhus, both the adult and nymphal stages of mites are free-living in nature; hence, they do not feed on vertebrate hosts. The larval stage (chigger) feeds on the vertebrate host and picks up the rickettsiae. Rodents are the mammalian reservoir for scrub typhus. Eschar can be seen in the image below:

Serologic assays are used for diagnosis. The Weil-Felix reaction is a heterophile agglutination reaction used for diagnosis, wherein the sera are tested for agglutinins to the O antigens of certain Proteus strains, OX19, OX2, and OXK. OXK is agglutinated only in scrub typhus.

Scrub typhus:

* Most widespread Rickettsial disease

* A mite is a vector

* Vector – Trombiculid Mite

* Causative agent – Rickettsia tsutsugamushi

* Incubation period – 10–12 days

* Typical clinical feature – Eschar

* Weil-Felix reaction is strongly positive with Proteus strain OXK

* Treatment – Tetracycline

Renal involvement is a common systemic manifestation of scrub typhus. The severity of renal involvement can range from minor urinary abnormalities such as albuminuria and active urinary sediments such as cellular casts, pyuria, and hematuria to acute kidney injury (AKI), necessitating the immediate initiation of renal replacement therapies.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A woman was attacked by a rabid dog. The dog develops symptoms and passes away within a week. Which method is most effective for diagnosing rabies antemortem?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. DFAT - Direct fluorescent antibody test

The most effective method for diagnosing rabies antemortem is DFAT (direct fluorescent antibody test).

Direct immunofluorescence test (direct-IF), also called a direct fluorescent antibody (DFA) test, can be performed to detect rabies nucleoprotein antigens in specimens by using specific monoclonal antibodies tagged with fluorescent dye. Because of its high sensitivity and specificity, the DFA test is considered the “gold standard” method for rabies diagnosis. The best specimen is the hair follicle of the nape of the neck of the dog (most sensitive). Corneal impression smear can also be used. It is usually positive in the late stage with a sensitivity of 30%.

Negri bodies are pathognomonic of rabies virus infection. These are spherical-shaped cytoplasmic inclusion bodies. They contain an eosinophilic matrix, basophilic granules, and viral antigens. Negri body detection in histopathological staining of brain biopsies (hippocampus)—for postmortem diagnosis of rabies.

Rabies is a fatal infection of the central nervous system transmitted by the bite of a rabid animal. It is caused by rhabdoviruses. These viruses are enveloped, rod- or bullet-shaped, and contain single-stranded RNA.

Clinical features of rabies can be categorised into three phases: prodromal, encephalitic phase, and coma. The prodromal phase is characterised by malaise, anorexia, headache, and irritability. This is followed by the encephalitic stage, characterised by abnormal behaviour and seizures. They develop hydrophobia. Attempts to drink liquids cause painful spasms of the pharynx and larynx, producing a choking sensation. Therefore, the patients develop a phobia of even the sight or sound of water. Finally, seizures, coma, and death occur.

Laboratory diagnosis can be done on a postmortem or antemortem basis. Postmortem diagnosis is done by the demonstration of Negri bodies. These bodies are common in the pyramidal neurons of the hippocampus and Purkinje cells of the cerebellum. Antemortem diagnosis is done from corneal scrapings, saliva, or skin biopsy. Demonstration of the virus is done using direct immunofluorescence.

Other methods used in the diagnosis are intracerebral inoculation in the mice, tissue culture, ELISA (enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay), and PCR (polymerase chain reaction). Seller's technique (basic fuchsin and methylene blue in methanol) is used to stain brain impression smears, which has the advantage of allowing for simultaneous fixation and staining.

Reducing the stray dog population and vaccinating all dogs is the most cost-effective and logical way to reduce the incidence of rabies. The Animal Birth Control initiative by the Government of India is aimed at achieving this goal.

Rabies is a highly fatal viral disease caused by the Lyssavirus type 1, which affects the central nervous system. Dogs are considered the major source of rabies infection. Thus, immunization of dogs at the age of 3-4 months and booster doses at regular intervals are recommended to control rabies.

The spread of rabies can be:

* Centripetal:

* The virus enters the peripheral neurons, and it moves via retrograde fast axonal transport towards the spinal cord or brainstem at a speed of up to 250 mm/day

* Once within the CNS, it spreads quickly to other regions in the CNS through fast axonal transport. It infects neurons primarily but may rarely infect astrocytes.

* Centrifugal:

* After CNS infection is established, it spreads along the sensory and autonomic nerves to the salivary glands, adrenal glands, and skin.

* The rabies virus replicates in acinar cells of the salivary glands and is secreted in the saliva of rabid animals that serve as vectors.

External examination of the brain shows intense edema and vascular congestion. Neuronal dysfunction associated with an inflammatory reaction is seen, which is most severe in the brainstem involving the basal ganglia, spinal cord, and dorsal root ganglia.

questions.text: A 12-year-old girl presents with severe headache, photophobia and high fever of 101°F. On examination, papilledema and nuchal rigidity was present. Kernig's and Brudzinski signs were positive. CSF examination shows reduced glucose, increased protein, and increased leukocytes with the predominance of neutrophils. Gram staining of the CSF is shown below. Causative organism is
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Neisseria meningitidis

History and physical examination findings are suggestive of bacterial meningitis. The given image shows intracellular gram-negative diplococci which is  Neisseria meningitidis.

Fever, convulsions, and signs of meningeal irritation (nuchal rigidity, Kernig's sign, Brudzinski's signs) in a child, with CSF showing reduced glucose, increased protein, and increased leukocytes levels is a typical presentation of bacterial meningitis.

Pathogenesis & clinical features:

* The organism enters the body through the nasopharynx by attaching to the epithelial cells with the help of pili. From nasopharynx, they enter the bloodstream producing bacteremia, and the symptoms may resemble upper respiratory tract infection.

* Fulminant meningococcemia is the severe form, where the patient presents with high-grade fever and hemorrhagic rash. There is thrombosis of several small blood vessels in various organs with perivascular infiltration and petechial haemorrhages.

* Some patients with fulminant meningococcemia may also develop disseminated intravascular coagulation, and circulatory collapse, a condition known as Waterhouse–Friderichsen syndrome.

* Droplet precautions are recommended for patients with Neisseria meningitidis and Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib) meningitis until they have received 24 hours of effective therapy.

* Chemoprophylaxis is indicated for the household and close contacts. The preferred antibiotics are rifampin, ciprofloxacin, and ceftriaxone.

Option a: Haemophilus influenzae type B is a gram-negative bacillus. In CSF, long bacillary filamentous forms predominate. H. influenzae b grows on chocolate agar (which supplies necessary nutrients from lysed red blood cells) or as satellite colonies surrounding β-hemolytic colonies of S. aureus on blood agar.

Option c: Streptococcus pneumoniae is a gram-positive, capsulated, flame-shaped or lanceolate-shaped diplococcus.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A middle-aged man presents with a genital ulcer, as shown below. Microscopy of a sample from the lesion is also shown below. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Granuloma inguinale

The image of a red beefy genital ulcer along with the micropscopic findings of Donovan bodies are charachteristic of donovanosis or granuloma inguinale.

Granuloma inguinale is a sexually transmitted infection caused by Calymmatobacterium granulomatis / Klebsiella granulomatis. The incubation period varies from 8-80 days, the average being 50 days.

Four types of lesions have been described in this condition:

* Ulcerogranulomatous - most common type with painless beefy red ulcers. They are also highly vascular and bleed on touch.

* Hypertrophic - usually with a raised irregular edge

* Necrotic - offensive smelling ulcer that causes tissue destruction

* Sclerotic or cicatricial - with fibrous or scar tissue

Primary lesions can occur on genital and extragenital sites. Untreated genital ulcers are followed by genital disfigurement and have the potential for malignant change.

Donovan bodies refer to the Gram-negative rod-shaped or oval organisms that show bipolar staining or safety‐pin appearance, present intracellularly in the cytoplasm of large mononuclear cells.

Treatment(first line):

* Azithromycin 1 g orally once weekly or 500 mg daily for 3 weeks.

The second-line drugs are as follows:

* Doxycycline 100 mg orally BD

* Erythromycin base 500 mg orally QID

* Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 160 mg/800 mg orally BD

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: An elderly patient was rushed to the casualty following bouts of severe breathlessness. He reported a history of fever and cough for the past 3 days. Lab tests were done and the report is interpreted as shown below. "Target sequences for the RdRp gene, E gene, N gene and ORF1ab were detected in the individual." Which of the following test was performed in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. RT-PCR

The given clinical scenario, along with the identification of target sequences for RdRp, E gene, N gene and ORF1ab is suggestive of COVID-19. The test performed here is the gold standard test reverse transcriptase polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) for diagnosis and identification of virus.

RT-PCR involves the reverse transcription of the genetic material of the virus (RNA) to complementary DNA (cDNA), followed by amplification of some regions of the cDNA. Four regions of the SARS CoV2 genome are used as targets:

* RdRp gene (RNA-dependent RNA polymerase)

* Genes from structural proteins

* E (virus envelope)

* N (virus nucleocapsid),

* ORF1ab gene (open reading frame 1a and 1b)

Options A and B: Antibody testing- Antibodies of IgA, IgM, and IgG isotypes specific to different virus proteins are detected by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) or chemiluminescence immunoassays (CLIA). CLIA is more sensitive compared to ELISA.

Option C: CBNAAT (cartridge-based nucleic acid amplification test) uses small, chip-based, portable, battery-operated devices that detect target genetic material of SARS CoV2. Examples include TrueNat and Cepheid Xpert Xpress SARS CoV-2

Note: Rapid antigen test (RAT)- Antigen-based assays are used as point-of-care tests for early detection of SARS-CoV-2. They are used at the field level for early detection of infection and quick containment. Most of such tests have relatively moderate sensitivity but high specificity. They are used for diagnosis along with RT-PCR.

ICMR has approved CoviSelf (nasal swab) for home testing of COVID-19 by RAT. It is advised only in symptomatic individuals and immediate contacts of laboratory confirmed positive cases. All individuals who test positive may be considered as true positives and no repeat testing is required.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Based on the disease shown in the image, which of the following specimens would the filarial worms be absent?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Saliva

The image is suggestive of lymphatic filariasis, and the filarial worms cannot be demonstrated in saliva.

Lymphatic filariasis occurs due to the transmission of W.bancrofti by the bite of Culex mosquitoes. The third stage larval forms from the mosquito enter the lymphatics and lymph nodes where they develop into adult worms. The adult worms become sexually mature and mate to release microfilariae which enter the peripheral circulation.

The disease initially causes acute attacks of lymphangitis and lymphadenitis. Early treatment may even cure the disease. The lymphedema may gradually worsen and get associated with the thickening of the skin and fibrosis of lymph vessels or blockage by adult worms. Hydrocele is another common manifestation that occurs due to lymphatic obstruction.

Microfilaria can be demonstrated in blood, chylous urine, exudate of lymph varix, and hydrocele fluid, however, peripheral blood is the preferred choice. The examination of a thick and thin blood smear stained with Giemsa stain shows the microfilaria. Other methods are by examining the unstained blood under a microscope for the actively motile microfilariae and by acridine orange-microhematocrit tube technique.

The best time to collect the blood samples is at night, between 10 pm and 4 am as they are nocturnally periodic.

DEC provocation test: In this test, a small dose of DEC is given 20-50 minutes before sample collection so that the microfilaria appears in the blood even during the daytime.

The image below shows the life cycle of Wuchereria bancrofti.

*Note:

* W.bancrofti causes Bancroftian filariasis and is transmitted by Culex quinquefasciatus (C. fatigans). In India, Wuchereria bancrofti is the commonest cause of filariasis.

* B. malayi causes Burgian filariasis and the vector is the Mansonia mosquito.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Gamma radiation is used for sterilization of ____?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Syringes, needles and catheters

Gamma radiation is used for the sterilization of articles such as syringes, needles, catheters, and gloves.

Gamma particles show maximum penetration and since there is no increase in temperature during the process it is called as cold sterilisation.

* When a nucleus disintegrates, it will emit radiation either as photons (X or gamma rays) or as high velocity particles.

* Gamma rays are a form of electromagnetic radiation (EMR) similar to X-rays, however, distinguished from the latter by the fact that they are emitted from an excited nucleus.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Identify the class of immunoglobulin shown in the image below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ig A

The above image shows a dimeric structure, characteristic of secretory IgA.

IgA immunoglobulin is the major antibody responsible for mucosal immunity. Its serum levels are usually low. It is predominantly present in the extravascular secretions. It is present in secretions such as milk, saliva, and tears, and in secretions of the respiratory, intestinal, and genital tracts.

When present in the serum, it exists as a monomer similar to IgG. However, when it is secreted, it exists as a dimer. The dimeric structure consists of two monomers, which are stabilized by two additional polypeptides:

* J chain, which stabilizes the molecule.

* Secretory component, which is incorporated into the IgA when transported through the epithelial cell.

Pearl PF0787: Properties of immunoglobulin classes

IgG:

* Half-life- 23 days

* Appears late, indicates chronic infection

* It is the only maternal Ig to cross the placenta.

* Has 4 subclasses.

* Causes complement fixation, precipitation, and neutralization of toxins and virus.

IgM:

* Half-life- 5 days

* Has the highest molecular weight and is a pentamer.

* Polysaccharides and lipids mainly stimulate IgM secretion.

* Intravascular distribution.

* Appears early, indicates recent infection.

* Acts as surface immunoglobulin on the B cells.

* It causes agglutination, hemolysis, and opsonization.

IgD:

* Half-life- 2-8 days.

* Acts as a surface immunoglobulin on the B cells.

* Serves as recognition receptors for antigens.

IgE:

* Half-life- 1-5 days

* Causes type I hypersensitivity.

* It is the only heat labile antibody.

* Levels are raised in helminthic infections.

IgA:

* Half-life- 6 days

* It is of 2 types- Serum IgA and Secretory IgA

* Secretory IgA (A dimer) results in mucosal immunity.

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Giardia lamblia

Image shows trophozoite form of Giardia lamblia.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Identify the virus given in the image below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. HIV

The image shows an HIV virus.

The human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) virus is a spherical, enveloped RNA virus. The nucleocapsid has an icosahedral shell and a cone-shaped core, enclosing the ribonucleoproteins. The genome comprises two identical single-stranded, RNA copies, with the reverse transcriptase enzyme, which is a characteristic feature of retroviruses.

The viral core is surrounded by a matrix protein called p17, which lies underneath the virion envelope. It contains

* Major capsid protein p24

* Nucleocapsid protein p7/p9

* Two copies of viral genomic RNA

* Three viral enzymes (protease, reverse transcriptase, and integrase).

The viral envelope is studded by two viral glycoproteins, gp120 and gp41, which are critical for HIV infection of cells.

questions.text: The causative organism of bull neck diphtheria is
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Corynebacterium diphtheriae

The causative organism of bull neck diphtheria is Corynebacterium diphtheriae.

Faucial diphtheria is the most common type of diphtheria and may vary from mild catarrhal inflammation to very widespread involvement.

According to the clinical severity, diphtheria may be classified as

* Malignant or hypertoxic, in which there is severe toxemia with cervical edema and cervical lymphadenopathy produce a bull's neck appearance in this child.

* Septic, which leads to ulceration, cellulitis, and even gangrene around the pseudomembrane.

* Hemorrhagic, which is characterized by bleeding from the edge of the membrane, epistaxis, conjunctival hemorrhage, purpura, and generalized bleeding tendency.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A boy, upon disturbing a bee hive, received several stings. After a few minutes, he developed symptoms of shock, respiratory failure, and vascular collapse. This is an example of ______.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. IgE-mediated reaction

Anaphylaxis following a bee sting is an example of IgE-mediated reaction or type 1 hypersensitivity. Injurious immune reactions are called hypersensitivity reactions.

Immediate (type I) hypersensitivity:

* These are also called allergic reactions or allergies.

* They are induced by environmental antigens (allergens) that stimulate strong TH2 responses and IgE production in genetically susceptible individuals

* IgE coats mast cells by binding to Fcεg receptors; reexposure to the allergen leads to cross-linking of the IgE and FcεRI, activation of mast cells, and release of mediators.

* The principal mediators are histamine, proteases, and other granule contents; prostaglandins and leukotrienes; as well as cytokines.

* The mediators are responsible for the immediate vascular and smooth muscle reactions and the late-phase reaction (inflammation).

* The clinical manifestations may be local or systemic and range from mildly annoying rhinitis to fatal anaphylaxis.

* It occurs in two phases: immediate phase and late phase.

Sequence of events in immediate hypersensitivity:

Pearl PF0858: Disorders Caused by Immediate Hypersensitivity

Clinical Syndrome

Clinical and Pathologic Manifestations

Anaphylaxis (may be caused by drugs, bee sting, food)

Fall in blood pressure (shock) caused by vascular dilation; airway obstruction due to laryngeal edema

Bronchial asthma

Airway obstruction caused by bronchial smooth muscle hyperactivity; inflammation and tissue injury caused by late-phase reaction

Allergic rhinitis, sinusitis (hay fever)

Increased mucus secretion; inflammation of upper airways, sinuses

Food allergies

Increased peristalsis due to contraction of intestinal muscles

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A child is infected with a negative sense RNA virus which also contains neuraminidase receptors. What is the causative organism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Influenza virus

Influenza virus is a segmented, negative-sense/negative-strand RNA virus with neuraminidase receptors/peplomers projecting from the envelope. It belongs to the family of orthomyxoviruses. The hemagglutinin and neuraminidase receptors are present as two different spikes on the envelope.

Parainfluenza virus, Newcastle disease virus, and Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) are negative-sense single-stranded RNA viruses with a linear genome. No neuraminidase is seen.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A farmer presents with a swollen foot and multiple sinuses as shown in the below image. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Mycetoma

The most likely diagnosis here is Mycetoma which is caused by Eumycetoma.

Mycetoma:-

* Mycetoma is a chronic, granulomatous infection of the skin, subcutaneous tissues, fascia and bone, which most often affects the foot or the hand. It is, therefore, commonly known as Maduramycosis or Madura foot. Mycetoma occurs worldwide.

* Etiology:  It can be divided into three types, eumycetomas, actinomycetomas and botryomycosis.

Pathogenesis:-

* Triad of symptoms: Infection follows traumatic inoculation of the organism into the subcutaneous tissue from soil or vegetable sources, usually on thorns or splinters and results in tumefactions, deformities and draining sinuses discharging fungal colonies called grains or granules (triad of symptoms).

* Subcutaneous tissues of the feet, lower extremities, hands, and exposed areas are most often involved.

* Grains: Within host tissues the organisms develop to form compacted colonies (grains) 0.5–2 mm in diameter, the color of which depends on the organism responsible.

Laboratory Diagnosis

* A. Direct Examination: The presence of grains in pus collected from draining sinuses or in biopsy material is diagnostic.

* B. Culture Samples should also be cultured, at both 25–30°C and 37°C, on brain-heart infusion agar or blood agar for actinomycetes and on Sabouraud agar (without cycloheximide) for fungi.

Treatment:-

The management of eumycetoma is difficult, involving surgical debridement or excision and chemotherapy. Actinomycetoma responds well to rifampicin in combination with sulfonamides or cotrimoxazole.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A farmer presents with a warty cutaneous growth on his foot. Histopathological image of the growth is given below. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Chromoblastomycosis

This patient is likely a case of chromoblastomycosis.

It is a subcutaneous infection caused by fungi belonging to the genera fonsecaea. It enters the skin by traumatic inoculation. Hence, seen in woodcutter and farmers. It appears as sclerotic bodies on histopathology examination and copper penny bodies on KOH mount. Treatment with antifungals are given.

Other options:

Mycetoma:

* It is caused by various types of Fungi (Eumycetoma) or filamentous bacteria (actinomycetes).

* It presents with a painless nodule but with time, papules and pustules may form which breaks down to form draining sinuses, with the discharge of granules.

Image: Mycetoma of Foot.

Sporotrichosis: Nodules generally develop along the draining lymphatics.

Phaeohyphomycosis : it is a chronic fungal infection involving the skin and subcutaneous tissue. The lesions maybe plaques which are verrucous, hypertkeratotis or ulcerated. The fungi implicated are usually of the class Phialophora or Cladophora or other demetacious fungi.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient came to the gynecology OPD with complaints of foul-smelling frothy vaginal discharge and intense itching. On examination, the cervix appeared strawberry-like. Which of the following statements is false regarding the causative organism?
options: It exists in cyst and trophozoite form
The gold standard for diagnosis is culture on CPLM or PEM
The treatment of choice is metronidazole
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. It exists in cyst and trophozoite form

The given clinical picture is suggestive of Trichomonas vaginalis infection.

Trichomonas vaginalis is the only protozoa with one stage in its life cycle ie., trophozoite form (No cyst stage is seen).

It is an obligate parasite and cannot live without close association with vaginal, urethral, or prostatic tissues. Sexual transmission is the main route of infection.

Trichomonas vaginalis has a jerky or twitching type of mobility on the wet saline mount.

The gold standard for diagnosis is culture on CPLM (cystine-peptone-liver infusion-maltose) or PEM.

The treatment of choice  is the oral dose of metronidazole 500 mg twice daily for 7 days.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient has presented with blister on hand followed by axillary lymphadenopathy. What will you ask the patient with regard to history?
options: History of similar complaint in family members
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. History of exposure to cat

Patient with blister on the hand followed by axillary lymphadenopathy is more suggestive of Cat scratch disease, a disease caused by Bartonella henselae, hence we should ask about the history of exposure to cat.

Cat-scratch disease is also known as subacute regional lymphadenitis. It is acquired following contact with infected animals, commonly cats.

Regional lymph nodes demonstrate:

* Follicular hyperplasia with circumscribed central stellate necrosis with neutrophils

* Surrounded by palisading histiocytes (suppurative granulomas)

* Sinuses packed with monocytoid B cells

* Usually, there are no perifollicular and intrafollicular epithelioid cells

Bartonella henselae also causes bacillary angiomatosis and bacillary peliosis in HIV-infected people.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient presents with pain abdomen, diarrhea, and a stepladder pattern fever. He also complains of a headache and malaise. His symptoms were gradually worsening over the past 2 weeks. Which of the following is the best screening test?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Widal test

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of typhoid fever and the best test to screen for a patient symptomatic for 2 weeks is the Widal test.

Enteric fever (typhoid fever) is caused by Salmonella species. The patient presents with stepladder pyrexia (fever), abdominal pain, diarrhea, headache, and malaise.

Diagnosis of enteric fever:

*

Blood culture: It is more sensitive during 1st week than in the subsequent weeks. It rapidly becomes negative on treatment with antibiotics.

* Antibody testing: WIDAL test to detect rising titers of H and O agglutinins against salmonella typhi and paratyphi. Agglutinins appear by the end of the first week and rise steadily up to the 3rd or 4th week, after which they disappear.

*

Stool culture: It yields positive results from the 3rd week onwards.

*

Urine culture: Results may be positive after the 2nd week.

* In the first week of illness, bone marrow culture offers the highest sensitivity and can remain positive for up to 5 days after initiation of antibiotic therapy.

Widal Test: This is a test for the measurement of H and O agglutinins for typhoid and paratyphoid bacilli in the patient's serum. In this test, the agglutination titer depends on the stage of the disease. It is performed by mixing equal volumes (0.4 ml) of serial dilutions of the serum (from 1/10 to 1/640) with fixed volumes of H and O antigens in the Dreyer's and Felix agglutination tubes, respectively. These tubes are incubated overnight and the agglutination titres are read. H agglutination leads to the formation of cotton woolly clumps while O agglutination is seen as a disc-like pattern at the bottom of the tube.
The antigens used in Widal's test include:

* O antigens of S. typhi (TO)

* H antigens of S. typhi (TH)

* H antigens of S. paratyphi A (AH)

* H antigens of S. paratyphi B (BH)

Interpretation:

* The agglutination titer will depend on the stage of the disease:

* Agglutinins usually appear by the end of the first week.

* The titer increases steadily till the third or fourth week, after which it declines gradually.

* The H agglutinins persist longer than O agglutinins.

* H antibodies appear earliest after infection and persist for several months.

* The O antibodies follow the appearance of H antibodies and disappear in a few weeks.

* The 4-fold rise in titers between 1st and 3rd week is highly significant as compared to a single high titer:

* This is because, in persons who had a prior enteric fever, there is a transient rise of titer due to unrelated infections (malaria, dengue), known as an anamnestic reaction.

* Therefore, after a one-week interval, if the titer increases, it indicates true infection. If the titer decreases, it indicates an anamnestic reaction.

* Cases treated early with antibiotics may show poor agglutinin response.

* Interpretation of Widal test:

* Demonstration of a rise in titre of antibodies by testing two or more serum samples is more meaningful than a single test.

* H agglutinin titer > 1/160 and O agglutinin titer >1/80 is considered significant.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: If a sample is cultured in LJ media, what would be the staining characteristic of the organism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Acid fast

Mycobacterium tuberculosis exhibits an acid-fast property when stained with a differential stain such as the Ziehl-Neelsen method. Lowenstein-Jenson medium is a selective medium used for Mycobacterium tuberculosis culture. The presence of malachite green imparts a green colour and makes Lowenstein Jenson medium a selective media by inhibiting other bacteria.

Mycobacterium tuberculosis resists decolorisation by 20% sulphuric acid and is therefore called acid-fast.

Colony characteristics on LJ Medium:

Mycobacterium tuberculosis colonies on LJ medium are dry, rough, raised, irregular colonies with a wrinkled surface, tenacious, difficult to emulsify, creamy white and buff-colored (rough, tough, buff).

Mycobacterium bovis forms moist, smooth, flat, white colonies on LJ media that break up easily when touched.

Components of LJ medium:

* Egg: Provide fatty acids and protein required for the metabolism.

* Malachite green: Prevents growth of contaminants.

* Mineral salt solution: Buffer.

* Glycerol: Source of carbon, Favours growth of M. tuberculosis, but not M. bovis.

* L-asparagine: Source of Nitrogen.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Of the following, which organism cannot be grown on an artificial culture media?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Mycobacterium leprae

Mycobacterium leprae cannot be grown in a pure culture medium. It does not obey Koch's postulates and cannot be grown in vitro.

Mycobacterium leprae is an obligate intracellular bacillus confined to humans, armadillos, and in some locales, sphagnum moss. It is the only bacterium which invades peripheral nerves.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which among the following methods is used to sterilize a glass petri dish?
options: Autoclaving at 121 degree Celsius for 30 – 60 minutes
Hot air oven at 160 degree Celsius for 120 minutes or less
Flash autoclaving at 134 degree Celsius for 3 minutes
Hot air oven at 121 degrees Celsius for 30 – 60 minutes
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hot air oven at 160 degree Celsius for 120 minutes or less

Hot air oven at 160 degree Celsius for 2 hours is used to sterilize glasswares like petri dish.

Exposure to dry heat in a sterilizing hot air oven at temperatures of 160° Celsius for 2 hours ensures carbonization of organic material and destruction of microorganisms and spores.

* This method can be used for metals, glassware, some heat-resistant and/or water-immiscible oils, powders and waxes.

* One of the drawback of  sterilization with hot air is that it has no penetrating power, and hence not suitable for disinfection of bulky articles such as mattresses.

* Because it employs very high temperatures it destroys plastic, rubber and other delicate substances.

options: There is a gradual sequential change in antigenic structure
It doesn’t account for the periodic epidemics of influenza

Antigens to the predecessor viruses do not neutralise the new variants

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A microbiology resident is revising heterophile antibody-based agglutination tests used in infectious diseases. Which of the following tests is NOT based on the detection of heterophile antibodies?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Rose–Waaler test

Heterophile agglutination tests detect cross-reacting antibodies produced against one antigen that agglutinate unrelated antigens because of shared epitopes.

The Rose–Waaler test is not a heterophile test. It is an autoantibody test used for the detection of Rheumatoid Factor (RF).

In this test:

• Sheep RBCs are coated with rabbit anti-sheep erythrocyte antibodies.
• Rheumatoid factor (IgM against the Fc portion of IgG) causes agglutination.

Thus, it detects an autoantibody, not a heterophile antibody.

Why the other options are heterophile tests?

• A. Paul–Bunnell test ✅: Detects heterophile antibodies produced in infectious mononucleosis (EBV) that agglutinate sheep or horse erythrocytes.
• B. Weil–Felix test ✅: Detects antibodies in rickettsial infections that cross-react with Proteus OX strains (OX2, OX19, OXK).
• D. Cold agglutination test ✅: Detects cold-reacting IgM antibodies produced in Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection that agglutinate human red blood cells at low temperatures.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A neurologist evaluates a patient with rapidly progressive dementia, myoclonus, and periodic sharp-wave complexes on EEG. MRI shows hyperintensity in the caudate nucleus and putamen, raising suspicion for Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease (CJD). Which of the following best describes the causative agent?
options: An infectious protein lacking nucleic acid
A hybrid infectious particle composed of bacterial and viral components
An infectious agent containing abundant DNA responsible for replication
An organism that can be propagated on routine cell-free culture media
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. An infectious protein lacking nucleic acid

Prions are proteinaceous infectious particles composed of an abnormal isoform (PrPS) of the normal cellular prion protein (PrPC).

Key characteristics:

• No DNA or RNA
• Infectious despite lacking nucleic acid
• Propagate by inducing misfolding of normal prion proteins
• Resistant to heat, proteases, formalin, UV radiation, and standard sterilization methods
• Cause transmissible spongiform encephalopathies (TSEs)

Major Prion Diseases:

• Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease (CJD)
• Variant CJD
• Kuru
• Gerstmann–Sträussler–Scheinker syndrome
• Fatal familial insomnia
• Bovine spongiform encephalopathy ("Mad cow disease")

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient from a military background presented with rash, fever, and altered sensorium. There is also a deficiency of the membrane attacking complex. The likely cause can be:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Neisseria meningitides

Neisseria meningitidis causes meningococcemia ± meningitis, presenting with fever, rash, and altered sensorium.
