Option D: Toxoplasma is transmitted through various routes, including ingestion of contaminated food or water, contact with infected cat feces, and transplacental transmission from mother to fetus. However, it is not primarily transmitted through blood

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following is transmitted by walking barefoot in soil?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Madurella mycetomatis

Madurella mycetomatis is transmitted by walking barefoot in soil. It causes Eumycetoma.

Mycetoma is a chronic, granulomatous infection of the skin, subcutaneous tissues, fascia, and bone, which most often affects the foot or the hand. It can be divided into three types- eumycetomas, actinomycetomas, and botryomycosis.

Infection follows traumatic inoculation of the organism into the subcutaneous tissue from soil or vegetable sources. Within host tissues, the organisms develop to form compacted colonies (grains) 0.5–2 mm in diameter, the colour of which depends on the organism responsible. It results in tumefactions, deformities, and draining sinuses, discharging these grains or granules.

Laboratory Diagnosis:

A. Direct Examination: The presence of grains in pus collected from draining sinuses or in biopsy material is diagnostic.
B. Culture Samples should also be cultured, at both 25–30°C and 37°C, on brain-heart infusion agar or blood agar for actinomycetes and on Sabouraud agar (without cycloheximide) for fungi.

Treatment:

The management of eumycetoma is difficult, involving surgical debridement or excision and chemotherapy. Actinomycetoma, on the other hand, responds well to rifampicin in combination with sulfonamides or cotrimoxazole.

Curvularia, Coccidioides immitis, and Aspergillus fumigatus are not transmitted by walking barefoot in soil.

The image below shows a mycetoma of the foot:

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following is true with respect to the organism shown below?
options: Associated with budding yeast cells and pseudohyphae
Opportunistic infections are seen in patients with CD4 count < 900
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Most commonly involves the lungs

The above image shows Cryptococcus neoformans stained with India ink and its infection most commonly involves the lungs. Indian ink is a type of negative stain that is not picked up by the capsule, making it evident. Although Cryptococcosis usually presents clinically as chronic meningo-encephalitis, the primary infection always involves the lungs.

Cryptococcus is an opportunistic fungus that is found worldwide as a saprophyte in soil enriched with pigeon droppings.

Pathogenesis:

• Infection is initiated by inhalation of the yeast cells.
• The primary pulmonary infection may be asymptomatic or may mimic an influenza-like respiratory infection, often resolving spontaneously.
• In immunocompromised, the yeasts may multiply and disseminate to other parts of the body, but preferentially to the CNS, causing cryptococcal meningoencephalitis.
• Other common sites of dissemination include the skin, adrenals, bone, eye, and prostate gland.

Clinical findings:

• Chronic meningitis (Headache, nuchal rigidity, disorientation)
• CSF pressure, protein concentration and cell count are elevated
• Cutaneous ulcers, granulomata.

Diagnosis:

• Specimens - CSF, tissue, exudates, sputum, blood, urine, skin scrapings
• Microscopy - Gram staining shows gram-positive round budding yeast cells
• India ink preparation reveals capsulated budding yeast cells; capsules are prominent in this staining.
• Culture - Colonies on SDA at 37°C appear as smooth, mucoid and creamy white.
• Serology - Demonstration of cryptococcal antigen by latex agglutination test is a sensitive, specific and rapid method for identificcation of cryptococcal meningoencephalitis.

Treatment:

• Cryptococcosis without CNS involvement: Fluconazole is the drug of choice
• HIV patient with CNS involvement: Induction: Liposomal Amphotericin B with Flucytosine for at least 2 weeks
Maintenance: Oral Fluconazole

Other Options:

Option B: Cryptococcus neoformans is a round or ovoid budding yeast cell, 4-20 μm in diameter, with a prominent polysaccharide capsule.Although the fungus grows primarily as a yeast, hyphae are produced during the sexual phase and during a process called monokaryotic fruiting, which is also believed to involve sexual reproduction, but no pseudohyphae are produced during normal circumstances.

Option C: C.neoformans is frequently found in soils contaminated with avian excreta and can easily be recovered from shaded and humid soils contaminated with pigeon droppings. Hence, can be found in more than one reservoir other than man.

Option D: C.neoformans usually affects patients with advanced HIV infection and CD4+ T lymphocyte counts of as low as <200/μL .

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following parasites reproduce directly from egg to larva without fertilisation through parthenogenesis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Strongyloides stercoralis

The females of Strongyloides stercoralis are known to be parthenogenetic i.e. capable of generating offspring without the need for fertilisation by a male.

Strongyloides stercoralis has a parasitic cycle and a free-living cycle in soil. Humans are the natural host but morphologically indistinguishable strains may be seen in dogs and cats. Filariform larvae are the infective form and there are two modes of infection: penetration of the skin by 3rd stage filariform larva, and autoinfection (external and internal).

The female worms present in the intestine lay eggs in the mucosa which hatches immediately, releasing the rhabditiform larva. The larva migrates into the lumen of the intestine and passes down to be released into the faeces. The rhabditiform larva may change into a filariform larva while passing through the bowel.

The filariform larvae in the bowel do not leave the host and become a source of autoinfection as they penetrate the colonic mucosa or perianal skin. The rhabditiform larvae passed in the faeces may undergo two types of development in the soil:

1. Direct development: The rhabditiform larva moults twice on reaching the soil to become the infective filariform larva. The filariform larva can penetrate the skin and enter the circulation.
2. Indirect development: The rhabditiform larvae develop into free-living males and females in the soil.

Other options :

Option B: Ancyclostoma duodenale are dioecious parasites, there is no multiplication within the host, and a single infective larva matures into either a male or a female adult to undergo mating through copulation. It typically takes around 6 weeks from the point of infection for the adult worms to reach sexual maturity and initiate egg-laying.

Option C: Enterobius vermicularis is dioecious.The male is usually unseen as it does not migrate from caecum or appendix. It usually dies after mating and is passed in the faeces. The gravid female migrates down the colon to the rectum and a single worm lays from 5000 to 17,000 eggs

Option D: Trichuris trichuria or the whipworm has a distinct male and female parasite and is typically dioecious. The fertilised female lays about 5000 eggs per day.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following pathological features is incorrectly matched with the disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Suppurative and purulent lesions: Syphilis

Syphilis is not known to cause suppurative and purulent lesions. It causes macular, papular or mixed maculopapular lesions.

Syphilis presents with the following lesions as it progresses through different stages :

• Primary syphilis - Hard chancre, which is painless papule that becomes eroded and indurated.
• Secondary Syphilis - Skin rashes on palms and soles which may be macular, papular, papulosquamous and nodular, but never vesicular or bullous.

• Condylomata lata- mucocutaneous papules that coalesce to form large pink to grey lesions in warm moist intertriginous areas)
• Generalized lymphadenopathy is seen

• Tertiary Syphilis - Gummas, which are locally destructive granulomatous lesions. They are most commonly seen in bone and skin.

Other options :

Option A - Immunodeficient individuals lack the normal response to antigens. This is the reason for the false negative Mantoux test seen in such individuals.

Option B - Chickenpox belongs to the alpha subfamily of herpes group of viruses which has a cytopathic effect of formation of multinucleated giant cells, with rounding and ballooning of infected cells

Option C - Berryliosis is an occupational lung disease, causing a chronic granulomatous inflammatory disease similar to sarcoidosis. Biopsy reveals non-caseating granulomas with monocytic infiltration.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text:
Which of the following statements is true about Cryptococcus?

1. Seen when CD4 < 500

2. Extra pulmonary cryptococcosis is an AIDS-defining illness

3. C.gatti associated with the bird Guano

4. Pathogenic species are urease positive
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 2,4

Statements 2,4 are true about Cryptococcus.

Cryptococcus is an opportunistic fungus that is found worldwide as a saprophyte in soil enriched with pigeon droppings. C.gatti sources from Eucalyptus trees, not bird Guano. (Statement 3)

Pathogenesis:

• Infection is initiated by inhalation of the yeast cells.
• The primary pulmonary infection may be asymptomatic or may mimic an influenza-like respiratory infection, often resolving spontaneously.
• In immunocompromised, the yeasts may multiply and disseminate to other parts of the body, but preferentially to the CNS, causing cryptococcal meningoencephalitis.
• Other common dissemination sites include the skin, adrenals, bone, eye, and prostate gland.
• Extrapulmonary cryptococcosis is an AIDS-defining illness ( Statement 2)
• It is seen when CD4 <200 cells/microliter (Statement 1)

Clinical findings:

• Chronic meningitis (Headache, nuchal rigidity, disorientation)
• CSF pressure, protein concentration, and cell count are elevated
• Cutaneous ulcers, granulomata.

Diagnosis:

• Specimens - CSF, tissue, exudates, sputum, blood, urine, skin scrapings
• Microscopy - Gram staining shows gram-positive, urease-positive (Statement 4) round budding yeast cells
• India ink preparation reveals capsulated budding yeast cells; capsules are prominent in this staining.
• Culture - Colonies on SDA at 37°C appear as smooth, mucoid and creamy white.
• Serology - Demonstration of cryptococcal antigen by latex agglutination test is a sensitive, specific and rapid method for identification of cryptococcal meningoencephalitis.

Treatment:

• Cryptococcosis without CNS involvement: Fluconazole is the drug of choice
• HIV patient with CNS involvement: Induction: Liposomal Amphotericin B with Flucytosine for at least 2 weeks
• Maintenance: Oral Fluconazole

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 35 year old farmer presents with a painless swelling of the foot that has developed gradually over several months. On examination there are multiple discharging sinuses with black granules seen in the discharge. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Madurella mycetomatis

Madurella mycetomatis Causes eumycetoma (fungal mycetoma)

→ Presents with classic triad:

• Painless subcutaneous swelling
• Multiple discharging sinuses
• Black granules in discharge

Common in farmers due to traumatic implantation (thorn/splinter injury)

Granule color differentiation (high-yield):

• Black granules → Madurella mycetomatis (fungal mycetoma)
• White/yellow granules → Actinomyces, Nocardia (actinomycetoma)

Why not others:

• Actinomyces israelii → sulfur granules (yellow), not black
• Chromoblastomycosis → verrucous lesions, not sinus + granules
• Staphylococcus aureus → acute painful abscess, no granules

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 42-year-old man presents with fever, weight loss, and a persistent cough for the past 2 weeks. A lung biopsy is performed, which reveals small yeast forms measuring 2–4 μm in diameter, showing narrow-based budding and predominantly located within macrophages. Which of the following is the most likely causative organism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Histoplasma capsulatum

Identify Histoplasma capsulatum by its characteristic histopathological appearance: small (2–4 μm), oval, narrow-based budding yeast located within macrophages. Histoplasmosis commonly presents with fever, weight loss, cough, and pulmonary infiltrates, particularly in immunocompromised individuals or those exposed to bird or bat droppings. Demonstration of intracellular yeast forms in tissue is highly suggestive of the diagnosis.

Why not the other options?

• A. Cryptosporidium parvum: An intestinal protozoan causing profuse watery diarrhea, not pulmonary disease or intracellular yeast in macrophages.
• B. Mycobacterium tuberculosis: Produces caseating granulomas with acid-fast bacilli, not budding yeast forms.
• D. Blastomyces dermatitidis: Appears as large (8–15 μm), broad-based budding yeast, usually extracellular, unlike the small intracellular narrow-based budding yeast of Histoplasma.

High-yield Pearl

| Fungus | Characteristic Histology

| ------ | ------------------------

| Histoplasma capsulatum | 2–4 μm, narrow-based budding yeast within macrophages

| Blastomyces dermatitidis | Broad-based budding yeast (8–15 μm)

| Cryptococcus neoformans | Encapsulated narrow-based budding yeast (India ink positive)

| Coccidioides immitis | Large spherules containing endospores

Exam Tip:

• Histoplasma = “Hides in Histiocytes (macrophages).”
• Bird/bat droppings + Intracellular 2–4 μm narrow-based budding yeast = Histoplasma capsulatum.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 50-year-old male patient with a history of chronic pulmonary aspergillosis is being treated with voriconazole. He has been on the medication for two weeks and comes to the clinic for a follow-up. During the visit, he asks about the specific guidelines and considerations for taking voriconazole to ensure its effectiveness and safety. Which of the following statements is false about voriconazole?
options: It should not be given with pyrazinamide
It should be taken empty stomach
It is given as a loading dose
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. It should not be given with pyrazinamide

Let's take into consideration this controversial PYQ about Voriconazole:

A) "It should not be given with pyrazinamide." There is no specific contraindication against combining voriconazole with pyrazinamide; this is false. (The known contraindications involve rifampin and certain other CYP-inducing TB drugs.)

B) "It should be taken on an empty stomach." This is true: voriconazole's absorption is reduced by food, so patients are instructed to dose it at least 1 hour before or 2 hours after meals.

C) "It is given as a loading dose." This is true: clinical guidelines recommend an initial loading dose (e.g., 6 mg/kg IV or 400 mg PO twice on day 1) to achieve therapeutic levels rapidly.

(D) "It requires therapeutic drug monitoring." This is true: because of voriconazole's narrow therapeutic window and variable metabolism, TDM is recommended to ensure efficacy and avoid toxicity.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 56-year-old gardener presents with an ulcerative nodule with purulent discharge on his right index finger. He had a prick with a thorn at the same site around a month back. Which one of the following infections is most likely?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Sporotrichosis

Sporotrichosis is a subcutaneous fungal infection caused by Sporothrix schenckii, a dimorphic fungus. It is classically associated with traumatic inoculation by thorns, splinters, or plant material, earning it the name “Rose gardener’s disease.”

The infection typically presents as a painless papule or ulcerative nodule at the site of inoculation, followed by nodular lesions along the draining lymphatics (lymphocutaneous sporotrichosis).

Why not the other options?

• A. Chromoblastomycosis: Presents as slow-growing verrucous (cauliflower-like) plaques, usually on the lower limbs after traumatic implantation.
• B. Mycetoma (Madura foot): Characterized by the triad of swelling, multiple draining sinuses, and colored granules, commonly involving the foot.
• C. Phaeohyphomycosis: A heterogeneous group of infections caused by dematiaceous fungi, presenting as subcutaneous cysts or abscesses, but not classically associated with thorn injury and lymphatic spread.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 65-year-old patient with uncontrolled diabetes developed severe rhino-orbito-cerebral mucormycosis following a severe COVID-19 infection. Surgical debridement of the affected area has been done. Which of the following drugs is not used in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Voriconazole

Mucormycosis is a life-threatening opportunistic fungal infection caused by fungi of the order Mucorales (e.g., Rhizopus). Management requires urgent surgical debridement, correction of underlying risk factors (e.g., diabetes, ketoacidosis), and prompt initiation of active antifungal therapy.

• Voriconazole has no reliable activity against Mucorales and should not be used for the treatment of mucormycosis. It is active against Aspergillus, but not Rhizopus or other Mucor species.

Why not the other options?

• A. Liposomal Amphotericin B ✓: Drug of choice (first-line therapy) for mucormycosis.
• B. Posaconazole ✓: Used as step-down (oral) therapy or salvage therapy after initial control.
• D. Isavuconazole ✓: Effective against Mucorales; an alternative first-line agent or step-down therapy.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 68-year-old man with poorly controlled diabetes mellitus presents with rapidly progressive orbital cellulitis, panophthalmitis, facial swelling, and black necrotic nasal eschar. Direct microscopy of the periorbital exudate demonstrates broad, ribbon-like, aseptate hyphae with irregular branching. Which of the following fungi is the most likely etiological agent?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Apophysomyces species

The patient has rhino-orbito-cerebral mucormycosis, a rapidly invasive fungal infection seen classically in:

• Uncontrolled diabetes mellitus (especially diabetic ketoacidosis)
• Immunocompromised patients
• Iron overload/deferoxamine therapy
• Neutropenia

The hallmark microscopic finding is:

• Broad (5–15 μm), ribbon-like hyphae
• Aseptate (pauci-septate)
• Irregular branching at right or obtuse angles (≈90°)

Apophysomyces is a member of the order Mucorales and produces these characteristic aseptate hyphae.

Why the other options are incorrect?

• A. Candida albicans ❌: Appears as budding yeast cells with pseudohyphae, not broad aseptate hyphae.
•

B. Aspergillus fumigatus ❌: Produces:

• Septate hyphae
• Acute-angle (\~45°) dichotomous branching

This is the classic morphology of aspergillosis, not mucormycosis.

* C. Penicillium (Talaromyces) marneffei ❌: A dimorphic fungus causing opportunistic infections in HIV patients. It does not produce broad aseptate hyphae in tissue.

High-Yield Pearl

| Fungus | Hyphae

| ------ | ------

| Mucor/Rhizopus/Apophysomyces | Broad, aseptate, right-angle branching

| Aspergillus | Thin, septate, acute-angle (45°) branching

| Candida | Budding yeast with pseudohyphae

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A bronchial asthma patient who is on inhalational steroids presented with white patchy lesions on the tongue and buccal mucosa. What is the drug that can be used to treat this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Clotrimazole

Inhaled corticosteroids predispose to oral candidiasis, presenting as white patchy plaques on tongue and buccal mucosa.

Clotrimazole (topical azole) is first-line treatment for uncomplicated oral thrush.

Griseofulvin and terbinafine are used for dermatophyte infections, not Candida.

Flucytosine is reserved for severe systemic fungal infections, not oral candidiasis.

| Drug | Class | Use

| ---- | ----- | ---

| Clotrimazole | Azole | Oral candidiasis ✔️

| Griseofulvin | Microtubule inhibitor | Dermatophytes (skin, hair)

| Terbinafine | Squalene epoxidase inhibitor | Dermatophytes

| Flucytosine | DNA/RNA inhibitor | Systemic (with amphotericin)

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A diabetic patient presented with rhinitis and swelling of the face. Intranasal biopsy revealed the presence of broad-based aseptate hyphae with right-angle branching. There was evidence of vascular invasion. What will be the preferred treatment for this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Amphotericin B

Broad, aseptate hyphae with right-angle branching indicate mucormycosis, an angioinvasive fungal infection seen in diabetics. Especially in DKA-

High glucose + acidic environment

→ Fungal growth ↑

→ Impaired immunity

The treatment of choice is amphotericin B, which is rapidly fungicidal.

Amphotericin B

↓

Binds ergosterol

↓

Membrane pores form

↓

Cell contents leak

↓

Fungal death

Azoles like fluconazole and ketoconazole are ineffective against Mucor. Early aggressive amphotericin therapy is lifesaving.

| Fungus | Morphology | Drug

| ------ | ---------- | ----

| Mucor | Broad, aseptate, 90° | Amphotericin B

| Aspergillus | Septate, 45° | Voriconazole

| Candida | Budding yeast | Fluconazole

| Dermatophytes | Septate | Griseofulvin

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A microbiology student is revising organisms in which the capsule serves as a major virulence factor by inhibiting phagocytosis. One organism in the list has a misleading name because, despite its species epithet, it does not possess a true capsule. Identify the organism.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Histoplasma capsulatum

Despite its name, Histoplasma capsulatum does not possess a true capsule. The term "capsulatum" refers to the capsule-like clear halo seen around the yeast in tissue sections due to shrinkage artifact, not a polysaccharide capsule.

Why the other options are correct?

• A. Streptococcus pneumoniae ✅: Possesses a thick polysaccharide capsule, which is its major virulence factor. Capsule types form the basis of pneumococcal vaccines and serotyping.
• B. Neisseria meningitidis ✅: Has a polysaccharide capsule essential for invasive disease. Serogroups (A, B, C, W, Y, etc.) are based on capsular polysaccharides.
• D. Cryptococcus neoformans ✅: Possesses a large polysaccharide capsule composed mainly of glucuronoxylomannan (GXM). The capsule is demonstrated by:

• India ink preparation
• Mucicarmine stain
• Cryptococcal antigen detection

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A middle-aged woman from Assam presents with chronic cough, fever, weight loss, and cavitary lesions in the lungs. Lung biopsy shows granulomatous inflammation with caseous necrosis and histiocyte-rich infiltrates. Which of the following should be strongly considered in the differential diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Histoplasmosis

Histoplasmosis, caused by Histoplasma capsulatum, is a dimorphic fungus acquired by inhalation of microconidia from soil contaminated with bird or bat droppings. It produces chronic granulomatous inflammation with caseating necrosis, closely mimicking tuberculosis, and may disseminate to organs such as the liver, spleen, and bone marrow, especially in immunocompromised individuals or patients with diabetes.

• Chronic cough, weight loss, cavitary lung lesions, granulomatous inflammation with necrosis, and hepatic involvement are characteristic of disseminated histoplasmosis.

Why not the other options?

• B. Sarcoidosis: Causes non-caseating granulomas without necrosis or cavitary lung lesions.
• C. Granulomatosis with polyangiitis: Characterized by necrotizing granulomatous vasculitis involving the upper airway, lungs, and kidneys; liver involvement is uncommon.
• D. Aspergillosis: Typically causes aspergilloma, allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis, or invasive disease in severely immunocompromised patients; granulomatous liver lesions are not typical.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient presents with fever, headache, neck stiffness, and features suggestive of meningitis. CSF examination is performed, and Nigrosin stain demonstrates budding yeast with an unstained halo. Which of the following organisms is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cryptococcus

Cryptococcus neoformans is an encapsulated budding yeast that commonly causes subacute or chronic meningitis, especially in immunocompromised patients (e.g., HIV/AIDS, transplant recipients). The polysaccharide capsule is demonstrated by Nigrosin (India ink) stain, which shows budding yeast surrounded by a clear unstained halo due to negative staining.

• Cryptococcus has a thick polysaccharide capsule, producing the characteristic clear halo on Nigrosin/India ink preparation of CSF.

Why not the other options?

• A. Candida: Budding yeast with pseudohyphae; no capsule and therefore no halo on India ink.
• C. Histoplasma: Small intracellular yeast found within macrophages; diagnosed with fungal stains, not India ink.
• D. Pneumocystis: Causes pneumonia in immunocompromised patients; diagnosed by Gomori methenamine silver (GMS) stain, not CSF India ink.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient with bronchial asthma on long-term inhaled corticosteroid therapy presents with whitish plaques over the tonsils. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Oral Candidiasis

Inhaled corticosteroids (ICS) are a common cause of oropharyngeal candidiasis (oral thrush) due to local immunosuppression, allowing overgrowth of Candida albicans. Patients typically present with white, curd-like plaques over the oral mucosa, tongue, or tonsils that can be scraped off, leaving an erythematous base. The risk can be minimized by using a spacer and rinsing the mouth after each inhalation.

Why not the other options?

• A. Oral candidiasis: ✔ Correct. Characterized by scrapable white plaques, commonly associated with ICS use, HIV infection, diabetes, and prolonged antibiotic therapy.
• B. Aphthous ulcer: Presents as painful, shallow ulcers with a yellow base and erythematous halo, not white plaques.
• C. Leukoplakia: A non-scrapable white patch, considered a premalignant lesion, commonly associated with tobacco use.
• D. Lichen planus: Presents with lacy white reticular lesions (Wickham striae) or erosive lesions, not removable plaques.

| White Oral Lesion | Characteristic Feature

| ----------------- | ----------------------

| Oral candidiasis | Scrapable white plaques, erythematous base; ICS, HIV, diabetes

| Leukoplakia | Non-scrapable white patch, premalignant

| Oral lichen planus | Lacy white Wickham striae

| Aphthous ulcer | Painful ulcer with yellow base, not a white plaque

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient’s tissue biopsy reveals asteroid bodies on histopathological examination. Which of the following culture medium is most appropriate for isolating the causative organism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Sabouraud’s dextrose agar

Asteroid bodies on histopathology are classically seen in sporotrichosis, caused by the dimorphic fungus Sporothrix schenckii.

·         Asteroid bodies: central yeast surrounded by eosinophilic radiating material (Splendore–Hoeppli phenomenon)

·         Disease: Sporotrichosis (“rose gardener’s disease”)

·         Transmission: traumatic inoculation via thorns, splinters

·   Culture:

o    Sabouraud’s dextrose agar (SDA) is the medium of choice for fungal isolation

o    Shows mold form at 25°C and yeast form at 37°C (dimorphic fungus)

Why not others:

·         Blood agar / Chocolate agar / Nutrient agar: used for bacteria, not fungi

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: An elderly woman with diabetes mellitus develops a black necrotic eschar over the nose and face, facial pain, and ophthalmoplegia following corticosteroid therapy. Which microorganism is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Rhizopus

Rhizopus (order Mucorales) is the most common cause of rhino-orbito-cerebral mucormycosis, an aggressive opportunistic fungal infection seen in patients with uncontrolled diabetes mellitus (especially diabetic ketoacidosis), prolonged corticosteroid therapy, or severe immunosuppression. The fungus is angioinvasive, causing vascular thrombosis, tissue infarction, and the characteristic black necrotic eschar.

• Rhizopus causes rhino-orbito-cerebral mucormycosis, presenting with:

• Black necrotic nasal/facial eschar
• Facial pain and swelling
• Ophthalmoplegia
• Cranial nerve palsies
• Rapid progression to cerebral involvement

Why not the other options?

• B. Aspergillus: Causes invasive pulmonary disease and aspergilloma; histology shows acute angle (\~45°), septate hyphae.
• C. Candida: Causes mucocutaneous infections and candidemia, not black necrotic facial eschar.
• D. Cryptococcus: Causes meningitis in immunocompromised patients, especially HIV; encapsulated budding yeast.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: An HIV-positive patient presents with dysphagia and odynophagia. Endoscopic examination of the esophagus reveals plaques. What is the most likely causative organism?
options: Thin septate hyphae with acute angle branching
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Budding yeast cells with pseudohyphae

In an HIV-positive patient, dysphagia and odynophagia with white esophageal plaques is characteristic of Candida esophagitis.

• Caused by Candida albicans
• Microscopy shows budding yeast cells with pseudohyphae
• Occurs in advanced immunosuppression (low CD4 count)
• Endoscopy shows white, adherent plaques in the esophagus

Differentiation:

• Thin septate hyphae with acute angle branching → Aspergillus (lung disease, not esophagus)
• Acid-fast bacilli → tuberculosis
• Squamous cell cancer → irregular mass/ulcer, not fungal plaques

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: An immunocompromised patient presents with a unilateral, painful, black necrotic lesion on the right side of the face. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Mucormycosis

Mucormycosis is a rapidly progressive, angioinvasive fungal infection seen in immunocompromised patients (especially uncontrolled diabetes/DKA), characterized by black necrotic eschar due to vascular invasion and tissue infarction.

·         Most common presentation: rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis

·         Hallmark feature: unilateral facial pain + black necrotic lesion (eschar)

·         Pathogenesis: invasion of blood vessels → thrombosis → ischemic necrosis

·         Microscopy: broad, aseptate hyphae with right-angle branching

·         Management: Immediate IV amphotericin B + aggressive surgical debridement + correction of underlying immunosuppression

Why not others:

·         Aspergillosis → septate hyphae, acute-angle branching

·         Histoplasmosis → intracellular yeast in macrophages

·         Candidiasis → superficial mucocutaneous infection (no necrotic eschar)

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Consider the following statements with regard to coccidioidomycosis: 1. It is a primary systemic mycosis caused by dimorphic fungi Coccidioides immitis and Coccidioides posadasii. 2. Primary pulmonary coccidioidomycosis presents with cough, fever, chest pain and arthritis. 3. Progressive pulmonary coccidioidomycosis presents with constitutional symptoms like fever, weight loss, anorexia and features of lobar pneumonia. 4. Coccidioides meningitis is a mild disease, not warranting any treatment. Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2 and 3

Coccidioidomycosis (Valley fever) is a primary systemic fungal infection caused by the dimorphic fungi Coccidioides immitis and Coccidioides posadasii. Infection occurs by inhalation of arthroconidia from contaminated soil and is endemic in the southwestern United States, northern Mexico, and parts of Central and South America.

• Statement 1. It is a primary systemic mycosis caused by dimorphic fungi Coccidioides immitis and Coccidioides posadasii: Correct. Coccidioides immitis and Coccidioides posadasii are dimorphic fungi causing primary systemic mycosis.
• Statement 2. Primary pulmonary coccidioidomycosis presents with cough, fever, chest pain and arthritis: Correct. Primary pulmonary coccidioidomycosis typically presents with fever, cough, pleuritic chest pain, arthralgia/arthritis, fatigue, and sometimes erythema nodosum (“desert rheumatism”).
• Statement 3. Progressive pulmonary coccidioidomycosis presents with constitutional symptoms like fever, weight loss, anorexia and features of lobar pneumonia: Correct. Progressive pulmonary disease presents with persistent fever, weight loss, anorexia, chronic cough, and may mimic lobar pneumonia, tuberculosis, or lung malignancy.
• Statement 4. Coccidioides meningitis is a mild disease, not warranting any treatment: Incorrect. Coccidioidal meningitis is the most serious extrapulmonary complication and is fatal if untreated. It requires long-term (often lifelong) antifungal therapy, usually with fluconazole.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Desert rheumatism is caused by:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Coccidioides immitis

Desert rheumatism refers to the arthralgia and erythema nodosum seen in primary infection with Coccidioides immitis

• Caused by Coccidioides immitis (dimorphic fungus)
• Endemic in desert regions (Southwestern USA)
• Infection acquired by inhalation of arthroconidia (spores)
• Tissue → spherules filled with endospores
• Culture → mold with arthroconidia

Clinical features:

• Primary pulmonary infection (flu-like illness)
• Desert rheumatism triad:

o    Fever

o    Arthralgia (joint pains)

o    Erythema nodosum

Differentiation:

• Histoplasma → intracellular yeast in macrophages
• Mucor → broad, aseptate hyphae
• Paracoccidioides → “pilot wheel” budding

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: In a patient in the ICU, an infection in the central venous catheter is noted. Staining showed a gram-positive oval-shaped organism that reproduces by budding. Identify the organism.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Candida

A central venous catheter–associated infection with Gram-positive, oval organisms showing budding indicates Candida species.

• Candida is a yeast → appears as oval, budding cells on microscopy
• Can form pseudohyphae in tissue
• Common cause of catheter-related bloodstream infections (CRBSI), especially in ICU patients

Risk factors:

• Indwelling catheters
• Immunocompromised state
• Broad-spectrum antibiotic use
• Total parenteral nutrition

Differentiation:

• E. coli → Gram-negative rod
• Staphylococcus aureus / epidermidis → Gram-positive cocci (not budding)

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Match the following: 1. Leprosy 2. Tinea capitis 3. Contact dermatitis 4. Lupus vulgaris a. Biopsy b. Patch test c. KOH mount d. Slit smear
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1-d, 2-c, 3-b, 4-a

Match the Following:

A. Leprosy → D. Split skin smear

• Caused by Mycobacterium leprae
• Diagnosis depends on demonstrating bacilli

Split Skin Smear

• Taken from ear lobes, lesions, or cooler areas
• Stained with Ziehl–Neelsen (modified)
• Shows acid-fast bacilli (AFB)
• Helps calculate Bacillary Index (BI) → classification (PB vs MB)

B. Tinea capitis → C. KOH Wet Mount

• Fungal infection of scalp (dermatophytes: Trichophyton, Microsporum)

KOH Preparation

• Hair/skin scrapings + 10–20% KOH
• KOH dissolves keratin → leaves fungal elements
• Shows:

• Hyphae
• Spores (endothrix/ectothrix)

C. Contact Dermatitis → B. Patch Test

• Type IV hypersensitivity reaction (delayed)

Patch Test

• Standard allergens applied on back for 48 hours
• Reading at 48–72 hours
• Identifies specific allergen

D. Lupus vulgaris → A. Biopsy

• Cutaneous tuberculosis (paucibacillary)

Biopsy Findings

• Granulomas with epithelioid cells + Langhans giant cells
• Caseation may be minimal
• AFB often not easily seen

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Thorn prick injury is a common mode of infection in all except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Dermatophytosis

Thorn prick / traumatic implantation infections (subcutaneous mycoses):

• Sporotrichosis → caused by Sporothrix schenckii

→ Classic: “rose gardener’s disease” (thorn injury)
• Chromoblastomycosis → traumatic implantation of dematiaceous fungi
• Mycetoma → entry via soil-contaminated thorn/splinter injuries

These infections:

→ Occur after minor trauma (thorn prick, splinter)

→ Involve skin + subcutaneous tissue

Dermatophytosis (EXCEPTION):

• Caused by dermatophytes (Trichophyton, Microsporum, Epidermophyton)
• Spread by direct contact (person, animal, fomites)
• Limited to keratinized tissues (skin, hair, nails)
• No trauma or thorn prick required

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: What type of budding is described by a broad base with a small bud coming off of it, often associated with a figure of 8 appearances?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Blastomycosis

Blastomyces dermatitidis is identified by broad-based budding yeast, often giving a characteristic figure-of-8 appearance.

• Broad-based budding = hallmark of blastomycosis
• Thick-walled yeast seen in tissue

Clinical features:

• Pulmonary infection (pneumonia-like illness)
• Cutaneous and bone involvement in dissemination

Differentiation:

• Cryptococcus → narrow-based budding + capsule (India ink)
• Candida → budding yeast with pseudohyphae
• Histoplasma → intracellular yeast in macrophages (narrow-based budding)

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following fungal infections is caused by dermal inoculation of the fungal agent, usually from a thorn?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Sporotrichosis

Sporotrichosis is a subcutaneous mycosis caused by the dimorphic fungus Sporothrix schenckii complex. Infection occurs through traumatic inoculation of the fungus into the skin, classically following injury with a rose thorn, splinter, or contaminated plant material. Hence, it is also known as “Rose gardener’s disease.”

• A. Mycetoma ✗: A chronic subcutaneous infection caused by fungi (eumycetoma) or filamentous bacteria (actinomycetoma), characterized by the triad of swelling, multiple draining sinuses, and granules.
• B. Aspergillosis ✗: Caused by Aspergillus spp., acquired by inhalation of spores, primarily affecting the lungs.
• C. Mucormycosis ✗: Caused by Mucorales fungi, usually seen in uncontrolled diabetes, diabetic ketoacidosis, or immunocompromised patients, acquired by inhalation.
• D. Sporotrichosis ✓: Acquired by dermal inoculation through a thorn prick or similar injury.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following opportunistic systemic mycoses is characterized by rapid development of severe tissue necrosis and emerged as a specific complication associated with COVID-19 infection in India?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Mucormycosis

Mucormycosis is an opportunistic invasive fungal infection caused by fungi belonging to the order Mucorales (most commonly Rhizopus arrhizus/oryzae). It is characterized by angioinvasion, leading to vascular thrombosis, tissue ischemia, and rapidly progressive tissue necrosis. During the COVID-19 pandemic, India witnessed a large surge in COVID-19-associated mucormycosis (CAM), particularly in patients with uncontrolled diabetes and corticosteroid use.

Why not the other options?

• A. Histoplasmosis ✗: Caused by Histoplasma capsulatum; acquired by inhalation of spores from bird/bat droppings; does not typically cause rapidly progressive tissue necrosis.
• C. Coccidioidomycosis ✗: A dimorphic fungal infection endemic to the southwestern United States; not associated with COVID-19-related outbreaks in India.
• D. Sporotrichosis ✗: A subcutaneous fungal infection acquired by traumatic inoculation (e.g., rose thorn injury).

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following organism is intrinsically resistant to the given drug?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Candida krusei: Fluconazole

Candida krusei is intrinsically resistant to fluconazole due to altered ergosterol pathway enzymes and reduced drug affinity. This resistance is predictable and clinically important. Other listed organisms are generally susceptible to their respective drugs. Fluconazole resistance is a classic hallmark of C. krusei.

| Drug | Mechanism

| ---- | ---------

| Fluconazole | ↓ Ergosterol synthesis

| Amphotericin B | Pore formation

| Micafungin | ↓ β-glucan (cell wall)

| Voriconazole | Ergosterol inhibition

Candida krusei = resistant to fluconazole

Candida glabrata = dose-dependent sensitivity

Voriconazole = DOC for Aspergillus

Amphotericin B = broad-spectrum

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following organisms is not classified as a dimorphic fungus?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Cryptococcus neoformans

Dimorphic fungi exist in two forms depending on temperature: mold form at 25°C and yeast (or tissue) form at 37°C. “mold in the cold, yeast in the heat”

• Histoplasma capsulatum, Coccidioides, and Talaromyces marneffii are dimorphic fungi
• Cryptococcus neoformans is not dimorphic; it exists only as an encapsulated yeast with polysaccharide capsule seen in India ink preparation.

Key points:

• Histoplasma → intracellular yeast in macrophages
• Coccidioides → spherules with endospores in tissue
• Talaromyces marneffii → yeast with transverse septum

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Bacterial transduction occurs by
options: Uptake of genetic material by other bacteria.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Bacteriophage

Bacterial transduction occurs by bacteriophages.

Transduction is a process of acquiring bacterial DNA from a bacteriophage (virus) that has incorporated bacterial DNA from previous host bacteria.

Other methods of exchange of genetic material are transformation and conjugation. Transformation involves the uptake of genetic material from the environment, which is released by other bacteria. Conjugation is the direct transfer of DNA from one bacterial cell to another bacterial cell through a sex pilus or bridge. The transferred DNA is a plasmid, a circle of DNA that is distinct from the main bacterial chromosome.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Cutaneous larva migrans is most commonly caused by which organism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ancylostoma braziliense

Cutaneous larva migrans is most commonly caused by Ancylostoma braziliense.

Cutaneous larva migrans or ground itch or creeping eruption is caused by nematode larvae that infect by skin penetration.

The most common cause is non-human species of Hookworm Ancylostoma braziliense and A. caninum.

Necator americanus and Strongyloides sp also cause cutaneous larva migrans, and Toxocara canis usually causes viscreal and ocular larva migrans.

Differences between cutaneous larva migrans and visceral larva migrans:

Cutaneous larva migrans
Visceral larva migrans

Tissue involved
Skin
Various organs of the body like the liver, lungs, and eyes

Infecting Organism
Mostly by non-human nematodes
Mostly by non-human nematodes (mainly by dog and cat)

Portal of Entry
Penetration of skin
Ingestion of infected eggs

Eosinophilia
Mild
Persistent high

Serodiagnosis
Not developed
Well developed

Treatment
Thiabendazole
Diethylcarbamazine and prednisolone

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Multiple abscesses with discharging sinuses, demonstrating sulphur granules in pus, are caused by
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Actinomyces

Multiple abscesses with discharging sinuses, demonstrating sulfur granules in pus, are characteristic of actinomycosis caused by Actinomyces.

Actinomycosis is a chronic granulomatous infection characterized by indurated swellings in the connective tissue with suppuration and discharge of sulfur granules. The most common causative agent is Actinomyces israelli.

Various clinical forms of actinomycosis include cervicofacial, thoracic, abdominal, and pelvic actinomycosis. Among them, oral-cervicofacial actinomycosis is most common, presenting as a soft tissue swelling, abscess, or mass lesion involving the angle of the jaw.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Mycoplasma is inherently resistant to which of the following antibiotics?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Beta lactam antibiotics

Mycoplasma are inherently resistant to beta-lactam antibiotics.

Mycoplasma lack cell wall, and are therefore inherently resistant to antibiotics acting on the bacterial cell wall e.g. beta-lactams (penicillins, cephalosporins).

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Nude mice are not resistant to xenograft due to the absence of _______
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. T cell

Nude mice are not resistant to xenograft due to absence of T cell.

A xenograft is a tissue graft or organ transplant from a donor of a different species.

Nude mice lack body hair, hence the name. They lack a thymus and thus cannot generate mature T lymphocytes. The absence of T-lymphocytes makes them unable to mount adaptive immune responses requiring helper T cells and cytotoxic T cells. The absence of functioning T cells also prevents the rejection of allografts & xenografts.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Pasteurization is done at ______.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 63 degree Celsius for 30 minutes

Pasteurization: Milk is heated at either

• 63°C for 30 minutes: the Holder method or
• 72°C for 15–20 seconds: the flash process

followed by cooling quickly to 13°C or lower.

All the non-sporing pathogens are killed except Coxiella burnetti, which may survive in Holder method.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Sabin-Feldman dye test is used for diagnosis of which of the following condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Toxoplasmosis

Sabin-Feldman dye test is used for the diagnosis of toxoplasmosis.

It is based on the principle that the presence of anti-toxoplasma antibodies in the patient's serum inhibits the staining of trophozoites by alkaline methylene blue dye. Toxoplasma trophozoites and complement are added to the patient's serum which is then incubated for an hour at 37°C. After incubation, methylene blue dye is added.

• If anti-toxoplasma antibodies are present in the serum, these are activated by complement and the parasite membrane is lysed. Thus, the trophozoites are not stained (positive result).
• If there are no antibodies, trophozoites will take up the stain and appear blue under the microscope (negative result).

The dilution of the test serum at which 50% of the tachyzoites are not stained is reported as the antibody titer of the test serum. The test is highly sensitive and specific. However, it cannot differentiate between recent or past infections as it detects only IgG antibodies.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: TB test done only on whole blood sample is ___________.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Interferon gamma release assay

TB test done on a whole blood sample is the interferon-gamma release assay. It has been used for the diagnosis of latent tuberculosis in patients with HIV(who frequently have a negative Mantoux test).

Interferon-gamma release assays include:

• QuantiFERON-TB Gold
• T-SPOT.TB

QuantiFERON-TB Gold quantitates the amount of IFN-γ produced by CD4+ T cells in response to the antigens from Mycobacterium tuberculosis. QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus (QFT- Plus) is an improved version of the QuantiFERON-TB Gold test. QuantiFERON-TB Gold detects only TB-specific CD4+ responses. However, QuantiFeron-TB Gold Plus detects both CD8+ and CD4+ T-cell responses to TB-specific antigens.

T-SPOT.TB determines the total number of individual effector T cells expressing IFN-γ.

The TrueNat TB test is a new molecular test that can diagnose TB in one hour as well as test for rifampicin resistance. This test uses a sputum sample taken from the patient. Only about 0.5 ml of the sample is required. Gene Xpert is also a molecular method of testing that cannot use blood as a sample. (Option A and B)

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: The adult form of echinococcus is seen in which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Dog

The adult form of echinococcus is seen in dogs and other canids, which are its definitive hosts.

The larval stage is passed in intermediate hosts such as sheep, cattle, goat, swine, horses, camels, and man. Man acts as an accidental intermediate host (dead end). Human infection follows the ingestion of eggs due to the intimate handling of dogs or by eating raw vegetables or other food contaminated with dog feces.

Note: Humans can become accidental definitive hosts, second intermediate hosts, or paratenic hosts for spirometra. These are cestodes belonging to the Diphyllobothriidae family. They cause a condition called sparagnosis.

The image below shows the life cycle of Echinococcus granulosus.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: What is the vector for the condition diagnosed by the image shown below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Sandfly

The image shown is of the Leishman-Donovan bodies whose presence are diagnostic of Kala Azar. The vector of Kala Azar is a sandfly.

Leishman-Donovan bodies are amastigotes with a double dot appearance containing a nucleus and small rod-like kinetoplast. They are present inside the macrophage.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which fungus is most commonly associated with orbital cellulitis in patients with diabetic ketoacidosis ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Rhizopus

Rhizopus is the most common fungus associated with orbital cellulitis in patients with diabetic ketoacidosis.

Diabetic patients are immunocompromised and so prone to develop opportunistic infections like mucormycosis - caused by Rhizopus and Mucor spp. Rhino-orbital- cerebral disease is the most common form of mucormycosis. It mostly occurs in diabetics. Patients initially present with eye or facial pain, facial numbness, conjunctival suffusion and swelling, and blurry vision. Infection then spreads from the ethmoid sinus to the orbit, leading to proptosis and orbital cellulitis.

Rhizopus is angioinvasive, and thus the infection may spread to the frontal lobe and cavernous sinus, leading to septicemia and thromboses. The sinus tissue in such patients often develops into a black necrotic eschar.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following can grow in an acidic pH?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Lactobacilli

Among the given options, lactobacilli is the one that can grow in an acidic pH.

It is a gram-positive, facultatively anaerobic, non-motile, non–spore-forming bacterium. Lactobacillus derives lactic acid from glucose, creating an acidic environment, and can grow in an acidic medium. It is found in the vagina as part of its normal microbiota.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following is Burkholderia cepacia resistant to?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Cefotetan

Burkholderia cepacia is resistant to cefotetan.

B. cepacia complex strains are intrinsically resistant to aminoglycosides, polymixin, first and second-generation cephalosporins (e.g. cefotetan) and carboxypenicillins. This antimicrobial resistance is mediated by efflux pumps, antimicrobial degradation, modifying enzymes or altered membrane functions.

B. cepacia is a Gram-negative bacillus which can cause severe necrotizing pneumonia in patients with chronic granulomatous disease. It can lead to fatal septicemia in patients with cystic fibrosis.

Antimicrobial agents that are effective against B. cepacia complex include meropenem, ceftazidime, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, piperacillin and temocillin.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following is called as Australia antigen?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. HBsAg

HBsAg (Hepatitis B surface antigen) is also known as the Australia antigen. It is called so because it was first isolated from the serum of an Australian person.

Sera from hepatitis B patients when observed under an electron microscope show three types of particles:

• A spherical particle: 22nm, most abundant, contains only HBsAg.
• Filamentous or tubular particle: 22nm, contains only HBsAg.
• A double-walled spherical structure: 42nm diameter, is the complete Hepatitis B virus. It was described by Dane and is called Dane particle.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following is the predominant pathogen to infect renal transplant recipients one to four months following transplantation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Cytomegalovirus

The predominant pathogen to infect renal transplant recipients in the period around 1 to 4 months following the transplantation is cytomegalovirus (CMV).

CMV is the most common virus to affect recipients after organ transplantation (kidney, heart, lung etc). The maximal risk occurs between 1 and 4 months after transplantation (in the absence of prophylaxis). The most common CMV presentation in kidney transplant patients includes fever, leukopenia, hepatosplenomegaly, myalgia, and arthralgia. Antiviral prophylaxis with ganciclovir or valganciclovir is used in renal transplant recipients whenever indicated to prevent CMV disease.

Given below are the most common opportunistic infections in renal transplant recipients:

Peritransplant (less than 1 month)
Early (1-6 months)
Late (more than 6 months)

• Wound infection
• Herpes virus
• Oral candidiasis
• Urinary tract infection

• Pneumocystis jiroveci
• Cytomegalovirus
• Hepatitis B
• Listeria

• Aspergillus
• Nocardia
• BK Virus (polyoma)
• Herpes Zoster

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following organisms causes scombroid fish poisoning?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pseudomonas aeruginosa

Scombroid fish poisoning is associated with Pseudomonas aeruginosa.

It follows the consumption of both scombroid (mackerel-like) fish and nonscombroid fish that have not been refrigerated properly. The musculature of these dark- or red-fleshed fish undergoes decomposition by Morganella morganii, Escherichia coli, Proteus species, Klebsiella species, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa. There is consequent decarboxylation of the amino acid L-histidine to form histamine.

A second compound is thought to play a causative role in this intoxication because large doses of oral histamine do not reproduce the affliction. The toxin or toxins involved are heat stable and are not destroyed by cooking or freezing.

Symptoms develop within 15–90 min of ingestion. Most cases are mild, with tingling of lips and mouth, mild abdominal discomfort, and nausea. The more severe and commonly described presentation includes flushing, conjunctival hyperemia, pruritus, urticaria, and angioedema. Without treatment, the symptoms generally resolve within 8–12 h.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following organisms produce urease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Helicobacter pylori

Helicobacter pylori produces urease.

Urease-producing organisms: (Mnemonic-PUNCH)

• Proteus
• Ureaplasma urealyticum
• Nocardia
• Cryptococcus, Corynebacterium urealyticum
• H. pylori

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which type of hypersensitivity reaction is involved in the hyperacute rejection of renal transplants?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Type II

Hyperacute graft rejection is an example of type II hypersensitivity reaction.

It is mediated by preformed antibodies. It is a rare event that occurs in kidney transplantation.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 16-year-old boy is admitted with fever, icterus, conjunctival suffusion, and hematuria for 15 days. Which serological test should be done for diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Microscopic agglutination test

A history of fever with liver and kidney involvement should arouse suspicion of leptospirosis (Weil's disease). A microscopic agglutination test is used for the diagnosis of leptospirosis.

Antibodies against leptospirosis appear in the blood 5-7 days after infection. Serotype-specific tests for leptospirosis includes:

• Microscopic agglutination test
• Macroscopic agglutination test

Other options:

Option A: Widal test is used to screen for typhoid fever

Option C: Weil-Felix reaction is used to diagnose rickettsial fevers

Option D: Paul-Bunnell test is the investigation of choice for infectious mononucleosis.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 23-year-old patient has a history of travel to China and the consumption of pickled crab. He now complains of rusty sputum and cough. What is the most likely causative organism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Paragonimus westermani

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of infection with Paragonimus westermani.

Paragonimus westermani is a trematode. The transmission to humans occurs by eating raw or undercooked crab or crayfish containing metacercariae. The metacercariae excyst in the human gut and young worms migrate to the lungs, where they become encapsulated in lung tissue.

The patient complains of cough, chest pain, and hemoptysis. The viscous sputum is speckled with golden-brown eggs.

Praziquantel (25 mg/ kg TDS for 1-2 days) is the drug of choice.

The image below shows the life cycle of Paragonimus westermani.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 3-year-old child presents with a history of repeated sinopulmonary infections caused by encapsulated organisms. Which of the following is most likely to be deficient in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. IgG2

Deficiency of IgG2 results in recurrent sinopulmonary infections with encapsulated organisms.

IgG is the only maternal immunoglobulin that is normally transported across the placenta and provides natural passive immunity to the newborn. IgG1 is the antibody maximally transported across the placenta, whereas IgG2 has the least transplacental movement.

Deficiencies of other IgG:

• IgG1- bacterial infections (diphtheria, tetanus)(Option A)
• IgG3- viral infections (Option C)
• IgG4- parasitic infections (Option D)

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 30 year old female developed pruritic papules with excoriated plaques in the interdigital web spaces. Later the lesion spread to the groin and under-surface of the breasts. The lady gives a history of intense pruritus which is more severe at night. Given below is the organism responsible for this condition. Identify the wrong statement about the same.
options: The entire life cycle takes about 15 days
Male parasite burrows into the epidermis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Male parasite burrows into the epidermis

The clinical background is probably suggestive Scabies. The given image depicts Itch mite also called Sarcoptes scabiei. The female parasite burrows into the stratum corneum layer of the epidermis and lays eggs in the burrow.

A single female may lay about 30 eggs at a rate of 2 to 3 per day, and ultimately dies at the end of the burrow.

The life cycle has 4 stages: Egg, Larva, Nymph, and Adult. The adult mites live for 1 to 2 months.

Itching is a hypersensitivity reaction to the eggs and dead parasite in the epidermis.

Permethrin cream - 5% is the treatment of choice.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A HIV patient presents with persistent diarrhea. Microscopic examination of the stool is given below. Identify the causative organism:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Cryptosporidium

Diarrhea in an HIV patient is suggestive of a coccidean parasitic infestation. Kinyoun stain - positive oocysts as seen in the given image is suggestive of Cryptosporidium.

Points in favor:

• HIV patient with diarrhea
• Oocysts are round,  contains four sporozites which is uniformly acid fast on staining.

Comparison of coccidian parasites causing diarrhea in an immunocompromised host:

Property
Cryptosporidium
Cyclospora
Isospora

8-12 μm, round contains 2 sporocyst each having two sporozoites
23-36 μm, oval contain two sporocyst, each having four sporozoites.

Acid-fast detection
Uniformly acid fast
Variable acid fast
Uniformly acid fast

Sporulation of the oocyst
Occurs inside host cell
Occurs in soil
Occurs in soil

Sporulated cyst

Unsporulated oocyst

Treatment is fluid replacement and cotrimoxazole.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient is brought to the hospital, with complaints of seizures and the MRI image of the brain is given below. The disease is most probably caused by?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Cysticercosis cellulosae

The given clinical scenario and MRI brain showing scolex within multiple cystic lesions are suggestive of neurocysticercosis caused by the larval form of T. solium called Cysticercosis cellulosae.

Neurocysticercosis is the most common central nervous system parasitic infection.

The clinical features of neurocysticercosis include epilepsy, features of raised intracranial tension, and evident hydrocephalus. Patients can also have psychiatric disturbances, transient paresis, and visual disturbances.

The CT and MRI findings seen in neurocysticercosis are:

• Scolex within a cyst
• Cystic lesions with or without ring enhancement
• Nodular calcifications
• Focal enhancing lesions
• Multilobulated cystic lesions in the subarachnoid space.

Note: About 70% of adult-onset epilepsy is due to neurocysticercosis.

Albendazole is the drug of choice for neurocysticercosis. Glucocorticoid therapy is usually begun before initiating albendazole (an antiparasitic drug). This is continued for several days after the institution of therapy to reduce the incidence of side effects from inflammatory reactions to dead and dying cysticerci of Taenia solium.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient presents with gastrointestinal problems including abdominal pain and distension, bloody and mucus-filled diarrhea, and tenesmus, with rectal prolapse. A stool examination reveals the presence of typical barrel-shaped eggs. What is the possible causative agent?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Trichuris trichiura

The given clinical picture and the barrel-shaped eggs are suggestive of infection with Trichuris trichiura (whipworm).

The characteristic features of whipworm eggs are:

• Eggs are barrel-shaped in the middle with a projecting mucus plug at each pole containing an unsegmented ovum. The plugs are colorless.
• They float in the saturated salt solution.
• It has a triple shell, the outermost layer of which is stained brown.

The below image shows the egg of Trichuris trichiura.

In moderate infections of 20 adult worms or less, the worms are confined to the caecum and ascending colon. The symptoms include epigastric and lower abdominal pain, diarrhea (rarely bloody), vomiting, flatulence and distention, weight loss, and increased blood and iron loss.

In heavy infections of 200 adults worms or more (trichuris dysentery syndrome), the worms are in the distal colon and rectum. The symptoms include bloody diarrhea with profuse mucus, abdominal pain, tenesmus, weight loss leading to cachexia, severe anemia, and rectal prolapse. On examination, clubbing may be present. Blood investigations may show moderate eosinophilia.

Chronic infection leads to growth retardation and nutritional deficiencies. Around 0.005 ml of blood is lost per day per worm. In heavy infections, as much as 4 to 5 ml can be lost per day per worm.

Treatment is mebendazole or albendazole.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A veterinarian developed an ulcer with central black eschar over the forearm as shown in the image. Which of the following is the most probable causative organism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Bacillus anthracis

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of cutaneous anthrax which is caused by Bacillus anthracis.

Human anthrax presents in one of three ways:

• Cutaneous Anthrax(hide porter’s disease)- Black eschar at the base, with a very prominent inflammatory ring around the eschar, is referred to as a malignant pustule.
• Pulmonary Anthrax(Wool sorter’s disease)- Hemorrhagic pneumonia.
• Intestinal Anthrax- Hemorrhagic diarrhoea. It occurs mainly in primitive communities that eat the carcasses of animals dying of anthrax.

Robert Koch validated the germ theory of disease after discovering the anthrax bacillus as the cause of anthrax. He also discovered the causative agents of tuberculosis and cholera. Hence, he is known as the Father of Bacteriology.

Koch's postulates, which link specific microorganisms to specific diseases, state that the microorganism must be:

1. Found in abundance in diseased organisms, but not in healthy organisms.
2. Isolated from a diseased organism and grown in pure culture
3. Able to cause disease when inoculated into a healthy organism
4. Re-isolated from the diseased experimental host and identical to the original specific causative agent

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: An 11-year-old boy was brought to the pediatric OPD with multiple abscesses over his face, chest, and back. The child has a history of recurrent respiratory infections. On examination, he has atopic excoriating skin and multiple cold abscesses on his back. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hyper IgE syndrome

From the above clinical history and examination, the most probable diagnosis is hyper IgE syndrome (Job’s syndrome).

It is an autosomal dominant primary immunodeficiency disease caused by  a mutation of STAT3 gene. Neutrophils do not generate an immune response, probably due to a defect in chemotaxis. Patients present with recurrent staphylococcal skin abscesses, recurrent lung infections (pneumatoceles), eczema, eosinophilia and high serum levels of lgE.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: An 18 year old female presents with severe headache and high fever of 101°F. On examination, papilloedema and nuchal rigidity was present. Gram staining of the CSF is shown below. Causative organism is
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Neisseria meningitidis

History and physical examination findings are suggestive of meningitis.

The given image shows intracellular gram negative diplococci i.e. Neisseria meningitidis.

Option a:Haemophilus influenzae type B is a gram negative bacillus. In CSF, long bacillary filamentous forms predominate.

Option c: Streptococcus pneumoniae is a gram positive, capsulated, flame shaped or lanceolate shaped diplococci.

Option d: Listeria monocytogenes is a gram positive bacillus.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text:
BCYE medium is used to culture:

BCYE - Buffered charcoal yeast extract
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Legionella

BCYE medium (buffered charcoal yeast extract agar) is used to culture Legionella pneumophila.

Legionella pneumophila has fastidious growth requirements and grows on complex media such as  BCYE medium with L-cysteine and antibiotic supplements (e.g., polymyxin B, cefazolin, vancomycin). The charcoal acts as a detoxifying agent. It grows slowly, and the colonies may take 3–6 days to appear.

Other options:

Option A: Leptospira is cultured on EMJH (Ellinghausen, McCullough, Johnson and Harris) medium

Option B: Bacillus cereus is cultured on PEMBA (Polymyxin pyruvate egg-yolk mannitol–bromothymol blue) agar

Option C: Campylobacter is cultured on Skirrow's, Campy BAP or Butzler's agar.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Contact based isolation is employed for which of the following diseases?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. MRSA

Contact based isolation is employed for patients who are infected with MRSA (methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus).

The three categories of transmission-based precautions include:

• Contact-based isolation is used for infections, diseases, or germs that are spread by touching the patient or items in the room. Examples include MRSA, vancomycin-resistant enterococci (VRE), diarrheal illnesses, open wounds, and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV).
• Droplet-based isolation is employed for diphtheria and mumps.
• Airborne precautions are required to protect against conditions like measles, severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS), varicella (chickenpox), and Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Cowdry type A inclusions are seen in:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Herpes simplex

Cowdry type A inclusions are seen in herpes simplex infection.

The classic Cowdry type A (Lipshutz) inclusion appears as a light purple, homogeneous intranuclear structure surrounded by a clear halo. The inclusions stain with antibodies to HSV, permitting a rapid, specific diagnosis of HSV infection.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: In which of the following is the disc diffusion method for antibiotic susceptibility testing applied?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Kirby-Bauer method

The disc diffusion method for antibiotic susceptibility testing is applied in the Kirby-Bauer method.

In Kirby-Bauer’s disc diffusion method, a suitable standard dilution of a broth culture of the test bacterium is inoculated on the surface of a solid medium (Cation-adjusted Mueller-Hinton agar) as a lawn culture. After drying, various antibiotic discs are placed on its surface. Zones of inhibition around the disc are recorded and interpreted according to the zone diameters available in the tables of the Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute (CLSI) guidelines. The results obtained are qualitative (resistant, sensitive, or partially sensitive).

The image below shows Kirby-Bauer disc diffusion method.

Laboratory testing for antibiotic sensitivity can be done by:

• Diffusion methods: The drug diffuses through a solid medium so that a gradient is established. The concentration is highest near the site of drug application and decreases with distance. The test bacterium is cultured on the medium and its sensitivity to the antibiotic is determined by the zone of growth inhibition. Examples include Kirby–Bauer method and Stokes method.
• Dilution methods: Serial dilutions of the drug are prepared and inoculated with bacteria. Examples include tube dilution method and agar dilution method
• Diffusion and dilution method: E–test (Epsilometer)

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Vaccine that requires strain change due to evolving organism is?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Influenza

Influenza vaccine requires periodic strain change due to antigenic change in the surface glycoprotein of the virus.

The change may be gradual (antigenic drift) or drastic (antigenic shift).

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Viral infection mimicking erythroblastosis fetalis is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Parvovirus B19

Parvovirus B19 infection mimics erythroblastosis fetalis.

Parvovirus B19, belonging to the parvovirus group consisting of the smallest animal DNA viruses, primarily infect immature cells of the erythroid lineage. It is associated with erythema infectiosum (fifth disease), transient aplastic crisis, pure red cell aplasia and hydrops fetalis.

During pregnancy, infection with parvovirus B19 can lead to severe anemia, non-immune hydrops fetalis and fetal death. This is because parvovirus preferentially infects RBC progenitor cells. This mimics erythroblastosis fetalis, in which maternal antibodies against fetal RBCs cause varying degrees of anemia and immune-mediated hydrops fetalis in sever cases.

Picornavirus, Epstein-Barr virus and HSV infections do not mimic erythroblastosis fetalis.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: What is the investigation of choice for neurosyphilis?
options: FTA-ABS- Fluorescent Treponemal Antibody Absorption test
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Venereal disease research laboratory (VDRL) test

The investigation of choice for neurosyphilis is VDRL.

The CSF-VDRL test is highly specific and, when reactive, is considered diagnostic of neurosyphilis.

Involvement of the CNS in syphilis is detected by examination of CSF for:

• Mononuclear pleocytosis (>5 white blood cells/μL).
• Increased protein concentration (>45 mg/dL).
• CSF VDRL reactivity.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: What is the stain used for identifying cryptococcus?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Mucicarmine

Mucicarmine stain is used in the identification of cryptococcus.

Mucicarmine stain helps in the detection of the cryptococcal capsule, as it stains mucins of epithelial origin (PAS, alcian blue). Given below is an image of Mucicarmine stained specimen of lung tissue containing cryptococci:

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following is not used as an immediate test in the screening of urinary tract infections (UTI)?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Pour plate culture

Pour plate culture (quantitative test) is not used as an immediate test for screening of UTI. However it is considered the best diagnostic test for confirmation of UTI due it’s high sensitivity and specificity.

The screening tests for UTI are as follows:

• Wet mount examination: It is done to demonstrate pus cells in urine.
• Leukocyte esterase test: It is a rapid and cheaper method, and detects leukocyte esterases secreted by pus cells present in urine.
• Nitrate reduction test (Griess test): Nitrate reducing bacteria like E. coli give a positive result.
• Catalase test: E. coli and other bacteria that produce the enzyme catalase give a positive result.

Quantitative Culture:

• Standardized loop technique
• Pour plate method

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following organisms follow a bird-arthropod-human transmission route?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Japanese encephalitis

Japanese encephalitis follows bird-arthropod-human transmission.

JE virus infects several extra-human hosts, e.g., pigs and birds (like pond herons).  The basic cycles of transmission are:

(a)Pig → Mosquito  → Pig

(b) Bird → Mosquito → Bird

Humans are incidental "dead-end" hosts and are infected by the bite of infected Culex mosquitoes.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following statements is false regarding MHC molecules?
options: MHC class II presents peptide antigen to CD4 T cells
The action of MHC II occurs via endocytic pathway
MHC Class II presents endogenous antigens
MHC II is present on antigen presenting cells
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. MHC Class II presents endogenous antigens

MHC class II presents exogenous antigens while MHC class I presents endogenous antigens.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which type of virus is rubella?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Togavirus

Rubella belongs to the Togaviridae family.

Rubella (German measles)

• Causative organism belongs to family Togaviridae
• Period of infectivity is -5 to +6 days after the onset of the rash
• Incubation period: 2-3 weeks
• Rash appears on day 1
• Forchheimer spots are seen, which are tiny, rose-colored lesions in the oropharynx
• Associated with post infectious thrombocytopenia
• Most serious complication: Encephalitis
• Vaccination: 27/3 live attenuated

Congenital rubella syndrome:

• When a woman in the 1st trimester gets infected with rubella, the resulting complications may include miscarriage, fetal death, premature delivery, or live birth with congenital defects.
• The commonest malformations caused by rubella are cardiac defects, cataract, and deafness, which constitute the classical congenital rubella syndrome.
• Thrombocytopenic purpura present in the babies gave rise to the term “blueberry muffin syndrome.”

Expanded rubella syndrome:

• Some babies present with several other features like hepatosplenomegaly, thrombocytopenic purpura, myocarditis, and bone lesions constituting the expanded rubella syndrome.
• This term also refers to a baby with metastatic neuroblastoma.

Note: Rubella has been reclassified into the family of Matonaviridae in 2020. This is an MCQ from NEET 2019, hence the best answer out of the given options would be Togaviridae.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 14-year-old boy presents with a history of vomiting within 3 hours of consumption of food at a party. Which of the following organism is most likely to cause these symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Staphylococcus aureus

Vomiting 2 hours after the consumption of food is likely food poisoning by Staphylococcus aureus.

Staphylococcus aureus can grow in carbohydrate and protein food sources, producing enterotoxins. There are 15 types, all of which are superantigens. They are preformed toxins that are relatively heat stable. They stimulate the vagus nerve,  vomiting centre of the brain and intestinal peristaltic activity. Type A enterotoxin is responsible for most cases of food poisoning.

The common sources of infection are the foods that are not cooked after handling. These include sliced meats, puddings, pastries, and sandwiches. Ingestion of such contaminated food causes food poisoning within 30 minutes to 6 hours after consumption. Patients present with nausea, vomiting, stomach cramps, and diarrhoea.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 22-year-old student presented with high-grade fever, and purpuric rash as shown in the image below. CSF sample showed gram-negative diplococci. Which of the following is the most likely aetiology?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Neisseria meningitidis

This patient has a high-grade fever and is a student, so he presumably spends a lot of time in crowded areas. The above image shows a purpuric rash. This patient's features are seen in meningococcemia caused by Neisseria meningitidis, which are gram-negative diplococci.

The organism enters the body through the nasopharynx by attaching to the epithelial cells with the help of pili. From the nasopharynx, they enter the bloodstream producing bacteremia, and the symptoms may resemble upper respiratory tract infection.

Fulminant meningococcemia is the severe form, where the patient presents with high-grade fever and hemorrhagic rash. There is thrombosis of several small blood vessels in various organs with perivascular infiltration and petechial hemorrhages. Some patients with fulminant meningococcemia may also develop disseminated intravascular coagulation, and circulatory collapse, a condition known as Waterhouse–Friderichsen syndrome.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 30-year-old female from tribal area presented with fever for the last 3 days. On examination of the peripheral smear, a diagnosis of malaria was made. Which of the following is most likely to be the causative agent?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. P. falciparum
