| Cysticercosis | Eggs of Taenia solium | Larval cysts in tissues (brain, eye, muscle); neurocysticercosis → seizures

Exam Tip:

• Eating pork → Taeniasis (adult worm).
• Swallowing eggs (fecal–oral/autoinfection) → Cysticercosis (larval disease).
• Neurocysticercosis is the leading parasitic cause of epilepsy worldwide.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 40-year-old male, upon returning from a beach holiday, noticed a serpiginous, intensely pruritic linear lesion over the dorsum of foot which moved slowly across the skin to reach up to his toes in 5–6 days. The most likely clinical diagnosis is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Cutaneous larva migrans

The patient has the classic presentation of cutaneous larva migrans (CLM):

• Recent beach exposure
• Serpiginous, intensely pruritic skin lesion
• Gradually advancing over several days
• Commonly affects the feet and lower limbs
• Usually caused by larvae of animal hookworms, especially Ancylostoma braziliense

Why not other options?

• A. Cutaneous larva migrans: Correct. Characteristic creeping eruption caused by migrating hookworm larvae in the epidermis.
• B. Anisakiasis: Caused by ingestion of raw/undercooked marine fish and typically causes gastrointestinal symptoms.
• C. Cutaneous larva currens: Caused by Strongyloides stercoralis and typically migrates much more rapidly, often several centimeters per hour.
• D. Schistosomiasis: Can cause cercarial dermatitis (“swimmer’s itch”), usually presenting as pruritic papules rather than a slowly advancing serpiginous track.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 42-year-old man living in an endemic river basin area of Sub-Saharan Africa presents with generalized pruritus, subcutaneous nodules, and progressive visual impairment. What is the causative organism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Onchocerca volvulus

Onchocerca volvulus is a filarial nematode that causes onchocerciasis (river blindness). It is transmitted by the bite of the female blackfly (Simulium species), which breeds in fast-flowing rivers and streams, making the disease endemic in Sub-Saharan Africa. The disease is characterized by intense pruritus, subcutaneous nodules (onchocercomas), skin depigmentation (“leopard skin”), and progressive ocular involvement leading to blindness.

Why not the other options?

• A. Loa loa: Causes loiasis (African eye worm), transmitted by the deer fly (Chrysops). It presents with Calabar swellings and migration of the adult worm across the conjunctiva, but does not typically cause river blindness.
• C. Wuchereria bancrofti: Causes lymphatic filariasis, presenting with lymphedema, hydrocele, and elephantiasis.
• D. Dracunculus medinensis: Causes Guinea worm disease, characterized by a painful skin blister from which the worm emerges, usually on the lower limb.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 47-year-old businessman returns from a prolonged stay in West/Central Africa and presents with intermittent episodes of foreign-body sensation and redness in one eye. Slit-lamp examination reveals a live, motile adult worm migrating beneath the bulbar conjunctiva. A daytime peripheral blood smear demonstrates sheathed microfilariae with nuclei extending continuously to the tip of the tail. Which of the following parasites is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Loa loa

The patient has loiasis, caused by Loa loa (African eye worm). It is transmitted by the Chrysops (deer fly/mango fly) and is endemic in the rainforests of West and Central Africa.

The classic clinical feature is migration of the adult worm across the subconjunctival tissues, producing the characteristic "eye worm". Patients may also develop Calabar swellings—transient, localized, non-pitting angioedematous swellings due to hypersensitivity reactions.

The microfilariae are:

• Sheathed
• Present in peripheral blood during the daytime (diurnal periodicity)
• Nuclei extend continuously to the tip of the tail

Why not the other options?

• B. Wuchereria bancrofti: Causes lymphatic filariasis (elephantiasis, hydrocele). Its sheathed microfilariae lack nuclei at the tail tip.
• C. Brugia malayi: Also causes lymphatic filariasis. It has two distinct terminal nuclei at the tail tip, not continuous nuclei.
• D. Mansonella perstans: Produces unsheathed microfilariae with nuclei extending to the tail tip but does not cause the characteristic subconjunctival "eye worm" migration.

High-yield pearl

| Parasite | Vector | Microfilariae | Key Clinical Feature

| -------- | ------ | ------------- | --------------------

| Loa loa | Chrysops (deer fly) | Sheathed; nuclei extend to tail tip; diurnal | Eye worm, Calabar swellings

| Wuchereria bancrofti | Mosquito | Sheathed; no nuclei at tail tip; nocturnal | Elephantiasis, hydrocele

| Brugia malayi | Mosquito | Sheathed; two terminal nuclei | Lymphatic filariasis

| Mansonella perstans | Culicoides (biting midge) | Unsheathed; nuclei to tail tip | Mild or asymptomatic filariasis

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A Calabar swelling, which is a short-lived, inflammatory, oedematous swelling close to a limb joint, is characteristically seen in infection caused by which of the following nematodes?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Loa loa

Loiasis is a filarial infection caused by Loa loa, transmitted by the Chrysops (deer fly or mango fly). It is characterized by transient, localized, non-pitting subcutaneous edema (Calabar swellings), which result from a hypersensitivity reaction to migrating adult worms. Migration of the adult worm across the conjunctiva (“African eye worm”) is a classic clinical feature.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A. Onchocerca volvulus: Causes river blindness, subcutaneous nodules, and dermatitis; transmitted by the blackfly (Simulium).
• B. Mansonella perstans: Usually causes mild or asymptomatic filariasis without characteristic Calabar swellings.
• D. Brugia malayi: Causes lymphatic filariasis with recurrent lymphangitis and lymphedema/elephantiasis.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient from a filariasis-endemic region presents with features suggestive of lymphatic filariasis. Peripheral blood examination fails to demonstrate microfilariae. Which of the following is the most likely site where the organisms may be located?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Lung

Key concept: Nocturnal periodicity

• Microfilariae are not constantly present in peripheral blood
• They show nocturnal periodicity:

• Present in peripheral blood at night (10 pm – 4 am)
• Absent during daytime

Where do they go during the day?

During daytime, microfilariae sequester in deep vascular beds, especially: Pulmonary circulation (lungs) ✔

Why lungs?

• Thought to be due to:

• Oxygen tension differences
• Host circadian rhythm
• Adaptation to mosquito feeding habits (night-biting vectors)

Clinical implication

• If blood smear is negative during daytime:

• Repeat at night
• Or use DEC provocation test

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient presents with chronic cough and hemoptysis. Chest X-ray shows ring-shaped opacities in the lung field. CT scan reveals cystic lesions. Sputum examination shows operculated eggs. Which of the following is the drug of choice for this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Praziquantel

Caused by Paragonimus westermani

→ Acquired by eating undercooked crab/crayfish

→ Adults lodge in lungs

Clinical features:

• Chronic cough + hemoptysis (mimics tuberculosis)
• Imaging: ring-shaped opacities / cystic lung lesions
• Sputum: operculated eggs (key diagnostic clue)

Drug of choice: Praziquantel → treatment for most trematode (fluke) infections

Why not others:

• Ivermectin → nematodes (e.g., Strongyloides)
• Diethylcarbamazine → filariasis
• Albendazole → many helminths but not DOC for Paragonimus

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A young woman presents with eye pain, photophobia, and blurred vision. She reports swimming at a beach while wearing contact lenses. Which of the following organisms is the most likely cause of her condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Acanthamoeba spp.

Acanthamoeba keratitis is a vision-threatening corneal infection classically seen in contact lens users exposed to contaminated water (e.g., swimming while wearing lenses)

•

Causative agent: Acanthamoeba (free-living amoeba)

•

Risk factors:

o    Contact lens use (especially poor hygiene)

o    Exposure to freshwater, समुद्र/beach water, or contaminated lens solution

•

Clinical features:

o    Severe eye pain out of proportion to findings

o    Photophobia, blurred vision

o    Ring-shaped stromal infiltrate (classic sign)

•

Diagnosis:

o    Corneal scraping → cysts/trophozoites

o    Confocal microscopy

•

Management: Topical biguanides (PHMB/chlorhexidine) ± diamidines

Why not others:

• Pseudomonas aeruginosa: common in contact lens users but causes rapidly progressive purulent keratitis (not ring infiltrate)
• Aspergillus fumigatus: fungal keratitis with feathery margins
• Herpes simplex virus: dendritic corneal ulcers

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: All of the following statements regarding Toxoplasma gondii are true, except:
options: Transmitted more in third trimester than first
Releases cysts in stool that are immediately infective
Can be grown in peritoneum of mice
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Releases cysts in stool that are immediately infective

Understanding transmission and life cycle of Toxoplasma gondii is essential.

Correct concepts:

• Transmission risk to fetus increases in the third trimester, but severity is higher when infection occurs in the first trimester
• It can be grown in the peritoneum of mice (used in laboratory diagnosis)
• It infects a wide range of mammals and birds (definitive host: cat)

Incorrect statement:

• Oocysts passed in cat feces are not immediately infective; they require 1–5 days in the environment to sporulate and become infective

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: An 18-year-old boy from Rajasthan weighing 50 kg is diagnosed with mixed P. vivax and P. falciparum malaria. What is the appropriate treatment regimen on day 2?
options: Artesunate 50 mg (4 tablets) + Primaquine 2.5 mg (6 tablets)
Artesunate 50 mg (4 tablets) + Primaquine 7.5 mg (6 tablets)
Artesunate 50 mg (4 tablets) + Sulfadoxine/pyrimethamine (750/37.5 mg) (2 tablets) + Primaquine 2.5 mg (6 tablets)
Artesunate 50 mg (4 tablets) + Sulfadoxine/pyrimethamine (750/37.5 mg) (2 tablets) + Primaquine 7.5 mg (6 tablets)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Artesunate 50 mg (4 tablets) + Primaquine 2.5 mg (6 tablets)

Mixed malaria (P. vivax + P. falciparum) is treated as falciparum malaria, using ACT (Artemisinin-based Combination Therapy) along with primaquine.

• Treatment principle:

• Treat as P. falciparum (more severe species)
• Add primaquine for Gametocidal action (falciparum) and Radical cure (vivax hypnozoites)

• Day-wise regimen (ACT-SP in India):

• Day 1–3: Artesunate + Sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine (SP)
• Primaquine: 14-day primaquine course for vivax radical cure

• Artesunate: 4 mg/kg once daily for 3 days.

• For a 50 kg patient: 4 mg/kg × 50 = 200 mg = 4 tablets of 50 mg.

• Primaquine: 0.25 mg base/kg/day for 14 days (after confirming normal G6PD status).

• For a 50 kg patient: 0.25 mg/kg × 50 = 12.5 mg base, rounded to 15 mg = 6 tablets of 2.5 mg.

| INFECTION | DRUGS

| --------- | -----

| P. vivax/ovale | Chloroquine (CQ) 25 mg/kg: DAY 1-3 + Primaquine (PQ) 0.25 mg/kg: DAY 1-14

| P. falciparum/malariae | All Indian States (except northeastern): ACT-SP

• Artesunate 4 mg/kg: DAY 1-3
• Sulfadoxine + Pyrimethamine, 25 mg/kg + 1.25 mg/kg: ONLY DAY 1
• Primaquine 0.75 mg/kg: ONLY DAY 2

Northeastern States: ACT-AL

• Artemether + Lumefantrine: DAY 1-3
• Primaquine 0.75 mg/kg: ONLY DAY 2

| Mixed infections: Vivax + Falciparum

• Aretsunate 4 mg/kg: DAY 1-3
• Sulfadoxine + Pyrimethamine, 25 mg/kg + 1.25 mg/kg: ONLY DAY 1
• Primaquine 0.25 mg/kg: DAY 1-14

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: An HIV-positive patient presents with a history of chronic diarrhea. Stool microscopy reveals cysts measuring 11–22 µm in size, each containing 2 sporocysts. Which of the following parasites is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Cystoisospora belli

Cystoisospora belli is an opportunistic coccidian parasite causing chronic watery diarrhea in immunocompromised patients (especially HIV/AIDS).

• Diagnostic morphology:

• Oocysts (not cysts) measuring \~20–30 µm (≈11–22 µm in some descriptions)
• Contain 2 sporocysts, each with sporozoites → key identifying feature

• Site of infection: small intestine (enterocytes)
• Clinical features:

• Chronic, non-bloody diarrhea
• Malabsorption, weight loss
• Eosinophilia may be present

Why not others:

• A. Cryptosporidium parvum: Smaller oocysts (4–6 µm), no sporocysts seen
• B. Cyclospora cayetanensis: 8–10 µm oocysts, variable acid-fast staining
• D. Toxoplasma gondii: Systemic infection; not a cause of diarrheal illness

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: An ophthalmologist may observe “Snowflake” deposits on the edges of the cornea in a patient infected with which of the following filarial worms?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Onchocerca volvulus

Onchocerciasis (River Blindness) is a filarial infection caused by Onchocerca volvulus, transmitted by the female blackfly (Simulium). Ocular involvement occurs due to migration of microfilariae into the cornea and anterior chamber, leading to punctate keratitis (“snowflake” corneal opacities), which may progress to sclerosing keratitis and irreversible blindness.

Why is D correct?

• D. Onchocerca volvulus✅: Causes snowflake corneal opacities, punctate keratitis, and river blindness. ⭐

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A. Brugia malayi❌: Causes lymphatic filariasis with lymphedema and elephantiasis.
• B. Loa loa❌: Causes Calabar swellings and migration of the adult worm across the conjunctiva (“African eye worm”), but not snowflake corneal deposits.
• C. Mansonella perstans❌: Usually causes mild or asymptomatic filariasis without characteristic ocular disease.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Cholangiocarcinoma is associated with all of the following except?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Hepatitis B

Cholangiocarcinoma (bile duct cancer) is associated with chronic inflammation and biliary tract diseases.

Associated conditions:

• Opisthorchis infection → chronic biliary irritation → strong risk factor
• Primary sclerosing cholangitis → major predisposing condition
• Caroli’s disease → congenital bile duct dilatation → increased risk

Not associated:

• Hepatitis B → primarily associated with hepatocellular carcinoma, not cholangiocarcinoma

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Consider the following statements with regard to cutaneous larva migrans: 1. It is one of the commonest linear lesions seen in travellers. 2. It may be associated with a recent visit to a beach. 3. It is non-pruritic. 4. Track moves across the skin at a rate of 2–3 cm/day. Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 2 and 4

Cutaneous larva migrans (CLM), also known as creeping eruption, is caused by the larvae of animal hookworms (most commonly Ancylostoma braziliense and Ancylostoma caninum). Infection occurs after walking barefoot on contaminated sandy beaches or soil, where the larvae penetrate the skin.

Why are the statements correct/incorrect?

• 1. It is one of the commonest linear lesions seen in travellers ✔️: Correct. CLM is a classic travel-associated dermatosis.
• 2. It may be associated with a recent visit to a beach ✔️: Correct. Exposure to contaminated sand on beaches is a common source.
• 3. It is non-pruritic ❌: Incorrect. Intense itching (pruritus) is the hallmark symptom.
• 4. Track moves across the skin at a rate of 2–3 cm/day ✔️: Correct. The serpiginous track typically advances 2–3 cm/day.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Consider the following statements with regard to giardiasis: 1. Stools should be examined for cysts at 2–3 days interval for its diagnosis. 2. Colonoscopy aspirate gives the highest diagnostic yield. 3. Infection usually occurs by ingesting contaminated water. 4. Giardia has a flagellate trophozoite form. Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 3 and 4

Giardiasis is caused by Giardia lamblia (G. intestinalis, G. duodenalis), a flagellated protozoan.

Why are the statements correct/incorrect?

• 1. Stools should be examined for cysts at 2–3 days interval for its diagnosis ✔️: Correct. Multiple stool examinations increase sensitivity because cyst shedding is intermittent.
• 2. Colonoscopy aspirate gives the highest diagnostic yield ❌: Incorrect. The highest yield is obtained from duodenal aspirate or duodenal biopsy, not colonoscopy aspirate.
• 3. Infection usually occurs by ingesting contaminated water ✔️: Correct. Waterborne transmission is the most common mode.
• 4. Giardia has a flagellate trophozoite form ✔️: Correct. The trophozoite is pear-shaped, bilaterally symmetrical, and flagellated with two nuclei.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Consider the following statements with regard to strongyloidiasis: 1. It parasitizes the mucosa of upper part of small intestine. 2. Larva currens is fast-moving transient rash seen across abdomen and buttocks. 3. Ivermectin is not an effective treatment. 4. Systematic strongyloidiasis is seen in immune competent state. Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1 and 2

Strongyloidiasis is caused by Strongyloides stercoralis. Adult worms live in the duodenum and upper jejunum, and the disease is characterized by autoinfection, which can lead to hyperinfection in immunocompromised patients.

Why are the statements correct/incorrect?

• 1. It parasitizes the mucosa of the upper part of the small intestine ✔️: Correct.
• 2. Larva currens is a fast-moving transient rash seen across the abdomen and buttocks ✔️: Correct.
• 3. Ivermectin is not an effective treatment ❌: Incorrect. Ivermectin is the drug of choice.
• 4. Systemic strongyloidiasis is seen in immunocompetent state ❌: Incorrect. Disseminated disease occurs mainly in immunocompromised patients (e.g., steroids, HTLV-1, transplant recipients, hematologic malignancy).

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: DOC for fasciola hepatica:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Triclabendazole

Triclabendazole is the drug of choice for treating Fasciola hepatica (liver fluke) infections.

| Drug | Primary Uses

| ---- | ------------

| Albendazole | Broad-spectrum: Neurocysticercosis, hydatid disease, ascariasis, hookworm, trichuriasis, strongyloidiasis (with ivermectin).

| Mebendazole | Intestinal nematodes: Enterobius, Ascaris, Trichuris, Hookworm. Less systemic absorption than albendazole.

| Praziquantel | Most trematodes except Fasciola (e.g., Schistosoma) and all cestodes (Taenia, Diphyllobothrium).
Excellent for neurocysticercosis (with steroids).

| Triclabendazole | Fasciola hepatica and Fasciola gigantica (adult + immature flukes).

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Parthenogenesis is seen in which of the following worm?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Strongyloides stercoralis

Parthenogenesis refers to reproduction by females without fertilization.

Strongyloides stercoralis is the only intestinal helminth where parthenogenesis occurs in humans

Mechanism:

• Parasitic female worms in the intestinal mucosa produce eggs without male fertilization
• Eggs hatch into larvae within the intestine

Key points:

• Enables autoinfection and persistent infection
• Important cause of hyperinfection syndrome in immunocompromised patients
• Unique life cycle with both free-living and parasitic forms

Why not others: Trichuris, Ancylostoma, and Enterobius require male and female worms for reproduction

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: The earliest specific cystoscopic appearance of Bilharzial cystitis is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pseudotubercles

Bilharzial cystitis is caused by Schistosoma haematobium, which primarily affects the urinary bladder. Adult worms reside in the vesical venous plexus, and the deposited eggs induce a granulomatous inflammatory reaction in the bladder wall.

The earliest specific cystoscopic finding is the appearance of pseudotubercles, which are tiny yellowish-white granulomatous elevations formed around recently deposited schistosome eggs.

Why not the other options?

• A. Sandy patches: These are a later finding, caused by calcified dead ova deposited in the bladder mucosa. ⭐
• B. Ulcers: Occur later due to chronic inflammation and mucosal damage.
• D. Nodules: A nonspecific finding and not the earliest characteristic lesion.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: The Sabin-Feldman dye test is an indirect fluorescent antibody test which is used to detect antibodies against which of the following organisms?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Toxoplasma gondii

Toxoplasmosis is caused by the intracellular protozoan Toxoplasma gondii. The Sabin–Feldman dye test is the classical reference serological test for detecting IgG antibodies against T. gondii. Although it has largely been replaced by modern ELISA-based assays, it remains an important exam topic.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• B. Leishmania donovani: Diagnosed by rK39 antigen test, demonstration of LD bodies, or PCR.
• C. Coxiella burnetii: Diagnosed by indirect immunofluorescence assay (IFA), the reference test for Q fever.
• D. Trypanosoma cruzi: Diagnosed by serology, PCR, or parasite demonstration in Chagas disease.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which among the following are hepatobiliary flukes (trematodes)? 1. Clonorchis sinensis 2. Mansonella perstans 3. Fasciola hepatica 4. Opisthorchis felineus Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 3 and 4

Hepatobiliary flukes are trematodes that primarily infect the liver and biliary tree, causing cholangitis, biliary obstruction, and chronic hepatobiliary disease. The important human hepatobiliary flukes are Clonorchis sinensis, Fasciola hepatica, and Opisthorchis felineus.

Why is C correct?

• 1. Clonorchis sinensis✅: Chinese liver fluke infecting the intrahepatic bile ducts.
• 3. Fasciola hepatica✅: Sheep liver fluke infecting the liver and biliary tract.
• 4. Opisthorchis felineus✅: A liver fluke causing opisthorchiasis with biliary involvement.

Incorrect option:

• 2. Mansonella perstans❌: A filarial nematode, not a trematode; causes mansonellosis.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which among the following is the first intermediate host for the parasitic fluke Clonorchis sinensis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Snail

Clonorchis sinensis (Chinese liver fluke) is a trematode that infects the biliary tract of humans. Its life cycle requires two intermediate hosts: the freshwater snail as the first intermediate host and freshwater fish as the second intermediate host. Humans acquire infection by eating raw or undercooked freshwater fish containing metacercariae.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A. Dog: Dogs are reservoir/definitive hosts, not intermediate hosts.
• C. Encysts on vegetation: Encystment on aquatic vegetation occurs in Fasciola hepatica, not Clonorchis sinensis.
• D. Sheep: Sheep are the definitive host of Fasciola hepatica, not Clonorchis sinensis.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which among the following parasitic helminths is a nematode and has zoonotic transmission?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Trichinella spiralis

Trichinella spiralis is a zoonotic nematode acquired by eating raw or undercooked pork or wild game meat containing encysted larvae. After ingestion, the larvae mature in the intestine and migrate to striated muscles, producing myositis, fever, periorbital edema, eosinophilia, and muscle pain.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A. Taenia saginata: A cestode (tapeworm) transmitted by undercooked beef.
• C. Fasciola hepatica: A trematode (liver fluke) acquired from aquatic plants (e.g., watercress).
• D. Fasciolopsis buski: An intestinal trematode acquired by eating aquatic plants.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following drugs is not used for uncomplicated falciparum malaria?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Chloroquine

Chloroquine is not used in uncomplicated falciparum malaria due to widespread resistance of Plasmodium falciparum.

Current Treatment (as per NVBDCP guidelines)

• First-line therapy: → Artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT) for 3 days
• Additional drug: → Single dose of primaquine (0.75 mg/kg) on Day 2

(used for gametocyte clearance → reduces transmission)
• North-East India: → Artemether + lumefantrine (3 days)
• Rest of India:→ Artesunate (3 days) + single dose sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine (Day 1)

Key Point

• Chloroquine is ineffective in falciparum malaria → hence not used
• Other options (primaquine, artemether, SP) are part of recommended regimens

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following helminths is known to maintain its life cycle through autoinfection?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Strongyloides stercoralis

Strongyloides stercoralis maintains its life cycle through autoinfection where rhabditiform larvae mature to filariform larvae within the host and penetrate intestinal or perianal mucosa, causing persistent infection especially dangerous in immunocompromised patients.

Organisms causing autoinfection can be remembered as :-

C – Cryptosporidium

H – Hymenolepis nana

E – Enterobius vermicularis

S – Strongyloides stercoralis

T – Taenia solium (via self-ingestion of eggs → cysticercosis)

Hymenolepis nana can also show autoinfection, but Strongyloides is the most characteristic and clinically significant example

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following options is wrong about ascaris lumbricoides?
options: Heavy infection is associated with Rectal prolapse
Fertilised unembronated egg takes time to infect after it goes in soil
Can spread to lungs and cause Asthma like symptoms
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Heavy infection is associated with Rectal prolapse

Understanding the clinical features and life cycle of Ascaris lumbricoides helps identify incorrect statements.

Correct concepts:

• Most infections are asymptomatic
• Fertilized eggs passed in stool are unembryonated and require time in soil to become infective
• Larval migration through lungs can cause cough, wheeze, and eosinophilia (Loeffler syndrome)
• Heavy infection may cause intestinal obstruction, especially in children
• Pulmonary phase causes transient respiratory symptoms

Incorrect statement:

• Rectal prolapse is not associated with Ascaris; it is classically seen in Trichuris trichiura (whipworm) infection

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following pairs of parasites and associated clinical manifestations are correct? 1. Ancylostoma duodenale — Anemia 2. Ascaris lumbricoides — Löffler Syndrome 3. Loa loa — Katayama Fever 4. Trichinella spiralis — Myositis Select the answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2 and 4

1. Ancylostoma duodenale → Anemia — Correct

• Hookworms attach to the intestinal mucosa and cause chronic intestinal blood loss, leading to iron-deficiency anemia.

2. Ascaris lumbricoides → Löffler syndrome — Correct

• Larvae migrate through the lungs, causing transient pulmonary infiltrates with eosinophilia (Löffler syndrome).

3. Loa loa → Katayama fever — Incorrect

• Katayama fever is associated with acute schistosomiasis, particularly Schistosoma mansoni and S. japonicum.
• Loa loa causes Calabar swellings and can cause episodic angioedema.

4. Trichinella spiralis → Myositis — Correct

• Larvae encyst in skeletal muscle, producing myalgia, muscle inflammation, and eosinophilia.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which one among the following vectors transmits the filaria Loa loa?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Chrysops

Loa loa is a filarial nematode that causes Loiasis (African eye worm disease). It is transmitted by the female Chrysops fly (deer fly or mango fly), which is found in the rainforests of West and Central Africa.

The adult worm migrates through subcutaneous tissues and may cross the conjunctiva, producing the characteristic “African eye worm”.

Why not the other options?

• A. Simulium: Vector of Onchocerca volvulus (River blindness). ⭐
• C. Cyclops: Freshwater copepod; intermediate host of Dracunculus medinensis (Guinea worm) and Diphyllobothrium latum, not Loa loa.
• D. Culicoides: Biting midge; vector of Mansonella perstans and certain arboviruses, not Loa loa.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which one of the following is the drug of choice for the treatment of schistosomiasis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Praziquantel

Schistosomiasis (Bilharziasis) is a trematode (fluke) infection caused by Schistosoma species (S. haematobium, S. mansoni, S. japonicum, etc.). Humans acquire the infection when cercariae released from freshwater snails penetrate the skin during contact with contaminated water. Praziquantel is the drug of choice for all major forms of schistosomiasis. Increases parasite membrane permeability to calcium, causing spastic paralysis and death of the worms.

Why not the other options?

• A. Doxycycline ✗: An antibiotic used for bacterial infections and rickettsial diseases; not effective against schistosomes.
• C. Albendazole ✗: Effective against many nematodes (e.g., ascariasis, hookworm, pinworm), but not the drug of choice for schistosomiasis.
• D. Ivermectin ✗: Drug of choice for strongyloidiasis and onchocerciasis; not used for schistosomiasis.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which one of the following statements is correct in the diagnosis of Giardiasis?
options: Stool sample at 2–3 days interval should be examined for cysts
String test is done to find out cysts of Giardia lamblia
Jejunal biopsy samples can show presence of larvae of Giardia lamblia
Cystic form of Giardia lamblia remains viable in water upto 1 week only
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Stool sample at 2–3 days interval should be examined for cysts

Giardiasis is an intestinal protozoal infection caused by Giardia lamblia (G. intestinalis or G. duodenalis). Since cyst excretion in stool is intermittent, multiple stool examinations (usually three samples collected at 2–3 day intervals) significantly increase the diagnostic yield.

Why not the other options?

• B. String test is done to find out cysts of Giardia lamblia: The string test (Entero-Test) is used to obtain duodenal contents containing trophozoites, not cysts.
• C. Jejunal biopsy samples can show presence of larvae of Giardia lamblia: Giardia is a protozoan, not a helminth; it has trophozoite and cyst forms, not larvae.
• D. Cystic form of Giardia lamblia remains viable in water up to 1 week only: Giardia cysts remain viable for several weeks to months in cold water, making waterborne outbreaks common.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which protozoa have 2 or more morphological forms? 1. Naegleria 2. Acanthamoeba 3. Trichomonas 4. Giardia
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 2 & 4

Protozoa can exist in different morphological forms such as trophozoite, cyst, and in some cases additional stages.

• Organisms with more than two forms include:

• Naegleria → trophozoite, cyst, and flagellated form
• Acanthamoeba → trophozoite and cyst (distinct double-walled cyst; functionally considered multiple adaptive forms)
• Giardia → trophozoite and cyst

• Trichomonas has only a trophozoite form (no cyst stage)

Key points:

• Presence of multiple forms helps in survival and transmission
• Cyst form is usually the infective stage (except Naegleria, where trophozoite is infective)
• Trichomonas spreads via direct transmission as it lacks a cyst form

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: ‘Exanthem Subitum’ is caused due to infection of which of the following viruses? 1. Human herpesvirus 6 2. Hepatitis-B virus 3. Human herpesvirus 7 4. Hepatitis-C virus Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1 and 3

Exanthem subitum (roseola infantum) is primarily caused by HHV-6 and can also be caused by HHV-7. It classically presents with high fever followed by the appearance of a maculopapular rash as the fever resolves.

• 1. Human herpesvirus 6 (HHV-6): Correct

• HHV-6 is the classical cause of exanthem subitum (roseola infantum).
• It typically causes high-grade fever for 3–5 days, followed by a maculopapular rash as the fever subsides.

• 2. Hepatitis B virus: Incorrect

• HBV does not cause exanthem subitum.

• 3. Human herpesvirus 7 (HHV-7): Correct

• HHV-7 can also cause roseola, although HHV-6 is the more common cause.

• 4. Hepatitis C virus: Incorrect

• HCV is not a cause of exanthem subitum.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: ‘Slapped-cheek’ rash is caused by infection with which one of the following viruses?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Parvovirus B-19

• Parvovirus B19 causes erythema infectiosum (fifth disease).
• The classic “slapped-cheek” rash appears on the face, followed by a lacy, reticular rash over the trunk and limbs.

Why not the other options?

• A. Zika virus: Can cause maculopapular rash, conjunctivitis, fever, and arthralgia, but not the classic slapped-cheek rash.
• B. HHV-6: Causes roseola (exanthem subitum)—high fever followed by rash as the fever resolves.
• D. Varicella-zoster virus: Causes vesicular lesions in crops at different stages.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: “Man-biting rate”, an important vector index for malaria survey, is correctly defined as:
options: Average number of anopheline bites per day per person
Percentage of female anophelines with sporozoites in their salivary glands
Man-biting rate multiplied by infective sporozoite rate
Proportion of freshly fed female anophelines whose stomach contains human blood
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Average number of anopheline bites per day per person

The man-biting rate (MBR) is the average number of bites by vector mosquitoes received by one person per day.

• (a) Average number of anopheline bites per day per person:  Correct. Represents the frequency of human–vector contact and is expressed as bites/person/day.
• (b) Percentage of female anophelines with sporozoites in their salivary glands: Incorrect. This is the sporozoite rate (infective rate)—the proportion of female mosquitoes carrying sporozoites in their salivary glands.
• (c) Man-biting rate multiplied by infective sporozoite rate: Incorrect. Man-biting rate × sporozoite rate gives the entomological inoculation rate (EIR), not the man-biting rate.
• (d) Proportion of freshly fed female anophelines whose stomach contains human blood: Incorrect. This represents the human blood index, i.e., the proportion of freshly fed mosquitoes containing human blood.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A “slapped cheek” rash is characteristically seen in which of the following infections?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Erythema infectiosum

Erythema infectiosum (Fifth disease) is a childhood exanthematous illness caused by Parvovirus B19. It is characterized by a bright red “slapped cheek” facial rash, followed by a lacy, reticular rash over the trunk and extremities. Although the illness is usually self-limiting in healthy children, it can cause aplastic crisis in patients with hemolytic anemia and hydrops fetalis when acquired during pregnancy.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A. Measles: Presents with fever, cough, coryza, conjunctivitis, Koplik spots, and a maculopapular rash starting behind the ears and spreading downward.
• B. Rubella: Characterized by postauricular and suboccipital lymphadenopathy with a fine pink maculopapular rash.
• C. Chickenpox: Presents with pruritic vesicular lesions in different stages of evolution (“dew drops on a rose petal”).

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 12-year-old boy develops fever and painful axillary lymphadenopathy two weeks after being scratched by a kitten. The clinician suspects cat-scratch disease. Which of the following intradermal skin tests has classically been used for the diagnosis of this infection?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Foshay test

Cat-scratch disease is caused by Bartonella henselae and typically presents with:

• History of cat scratch or bite
• Papule or pustule at the inoculation site
• Regional tender lymphadenopathy
• Mild fever and malaise

Historically, the Foshay intradermal skin test was used to support the diagnosis by demonstrating delayed-type hypersensitivity to Bartonella antigens.

Current practice: The Foshay test is of historical importance and is no longer routinely used. Diagnosis is now primarily based on serology (IFA/ELISA), PCR, or lymph node biopsy when indicated.

Why the other options are incorrect?

• A. Frei test ❌: Used historically for Lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV) caused by Chlamydia trachomatis serovars L1–L3.
• C. Montenegro (Leishmanin) test ❌: Used for cutaneous and mucocutaneous leishmaniasis, indicating cell-mediated immunity to Leishmania.
• D. Schistosomin skin test ❌: Historically used for schistosomiasis; it has no role in diagnosing Bartonella infection.

High-Yield Pearl: Classic Intradermal Tests

| Skin test | Disease

| --------- | -------

| Foshay test | Cat-scratch disease (Bartonella henselae) (historical)

| Frei test | Lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV) (historical)

| Montenegro (Leishmanin) test | Leishmaniasis

| Schick test | Diphtheria susceptibility

| Dick test | Scarlet fever susceptibility

| Mantoux test | Tuberculosis

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 19-year-old college student develops infectious mononucleosis due to Epstein–Barr virus (EBV) infection. During the illness, laboratory tests reveal heterophile antibodies and transient production of several autoantibodies. Which of the following mechanisms best explains the ability of EBV to induce autoimmunity?
options: Aberrant expression of MHC class II molecules
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Polyclonal B-cell activation

Epstein–Barr virus (EBV) infects B lymphocytes by binding to the CD21 (CR2) receptor. Viral proteins, particularly LMP-1 (Latent Membrane Protein-1), promote polyclonal activation of B cells, leading to:

• Hypergammaglobulinemia
• Production of heterophile antibodies
• Generation of multiple autoantibodies
• Increased risk of autoimmune diseases

This non-specific activation of numerous B-cell clones is the classic mechanism by which EBV contributes to autoimmunity.

Why the other options are incorrect?

•

A. Molecular mimicry ❌: Molecular mimicry occurs when microbial antigens resemble self-antigens, leading to cross-reactive immune responses. Classic examples include:

• Rheumatic fever (Streptococcus pyogenes)
• Guillain–Barré syndrome (Campylobacter jejuni)

Although EBV has been implicated in molecular mimicry in some autoimmune diseases, the classic mechanism tested in MBBS entrance exams is polyclonal B-cell activation.

* B. Release of sequestered self-antigens ❌: Seen after trauma to immune-privileged sites such as the eye (sympathetic ophthalmia) or testis, not in EBV infection.

* C. Aberrant expression of MHC class II molecules ❌: May contribute to certain autoimmune conditions but is not the characteristic mechanism associated with EBV.

High-Yield Pearl: Mechanisms of Autoimmunity

| Mechanism | Classic example

| --------- | ---------------

| Polyclonal B-cell activation | Epstein–Barr virus (EBV)

| Molecular mimicry | Rheumatic fever, Guillain–Barré syndrome

| Release of sequestered antigens | Sympathetic ophthalmia

| Bystander activation | Viral infections

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 20–30-year-old man presents with NS1 positivity and has with fever for 5 days. There are no bleeding manifestations. The Hb is 9 gm/dL, platelet count is 20,000, and ALT is 112 U/L. Which of the following should be used in the management of this patient? 1. Paracetamol 2. Platelet transfusion 3. PRBC transfusion 4. Steroids
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1 only

• NS1 positive → early dengue infection
• Day 5 fever → entering critical phase
• Platelets = 20,000 (low but platelet transfusion indicated below 5000/symptoms of bleeding)
• Hb = 9 g/dL → mild anemia
• ALT = 112 → mild hepatic involvement (very common in dengue)

Key clinical clue: NO bleeding manifestations

Dengue virus → Bone marrow suppression + immune destruction

↓

Thrombocytopenia

↓

↑ Capillary permeability (plasma leakage)

↓

Hemoconcentration (↑ Hct, not ↓ Hb initially)

• Platelets fall due to marrow suppression + immune destruction
• Bleeding is NOT directly proportional to platelet count
• Plasma leakage matters more than platelet number

| Feature | Management

| ------- | ----------

| Fever | Paracetamol

| Thrombocytopenia (no bleed) | Observation

| Bleeding | Platelets ± PRBC

| Shock (DSS) | IV fluids (crystalloids first)

| NSAIDs | ❌ Contraindicated

| Steroids | ❌ No role

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 24-year-old male presented with fever and myalgia. On examination, he had a diffuse maculopapular rash. Labs revealed a Hb of 14 g/dL, Hematocrit of 55%, Total WBC count of 4000, and platelet count of 25,000. Which of the following is the best prognostic indicator?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hematocrit

Correct answer is B because rising hematocrit in the setting of thrombocytopenia and leukopenia suggests hemoconcentration due to plasma leakage, which is a key marker of severity and poor prognosis in dengue.

Dengue infection

↓

Endothelial dysfunction

↓

Plasma leakage

↓

Hemoconcentration

↓

↑ Hematocrit

Platelet count helps assess bleeding risk but is not the best prognostic indicator. Leukopenia is common but not predictive of severity. Albumin may fall in plasma leakage but hematocrit rise is the primary monitoring parameter.

| Parameter | Finding

| --------- | -------

| Platelets | ↓↓↓

| WBC | ↓

| Hematocrit | ↑

| Hb | Normal/↑

Dengue severity depends on:

• Capillary permeability, not just platelet count

| Marker | Significance

| ------ | ------------

| Hematocrit ↑ | Plasma leakage (most important)

| Platelets ↓ | Bleeding risk

| AST/ALT ↑ | Liver involvement

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 28-year-old refugee from an overcrowded camp presents with recurrent episodes of high fever separated by afebrile periods. Peripheral blood smear during the febrile episode shows numerous spirochetes. Which of the following Borrelia species is not associated with tick-borne relapsing fever?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Borrelia recurrentis

Relapsing fever is caused by Borrelia species and is characterized by recurrent febrile episodes due to antigenic variation of variable major proteins (Vmps).

There are two epidemiological forms:

• Louse-borne (epidemic) relapsing fever

• Agent: Borrelia recurrentis
• Vector: Human body louse (Pediculus humanus corporis)
• Occurs in overcrowded conditions, refugee camps, wars, and poor sanitation.

• Tick-borne (endemic) relapsing fever

• Transmitted by soft ticks (Ornithodoros spp.)
• Caused by several Borrelia species including:

• B. hermsii
• B. turicatae
• B. duttonii

Why the other options are correct?

• B. Borrelia hermsii ✅: Causes tick-borne relapsing fever, mainly in North America.
• C. Borrelia turicatae ✅: Causes tick-borne relapsing fever and is transmitted by Ornithodoros soft ticks.
• D. Borrelia duttonii ✅: Causes African tick-borne relapsing fever, transmitted by Ornithodoros moubata.

High-Yield Pearl

| Disease | Organism | Vector

| ------- | -------- | ------

| Louse-borne (epidemic) relapsing fever | Borrelia recurrentis | Human body louse

| Tick-borne (endemic) relapsing fever | B. hermsii, B. turicatae, B. duttonii | Soft tick (Ornithodoros)

| Lyme disease | Borrelia burgdorferi | Hard tick (Ixodes)

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 3-year-old child presents with fever and a maculopapular rash that started on the face and spread downward. Examination reveals Koplik spots on the buccal mucosa. The causative organism responsible for this illness belongs to which of the following categories?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Enveloped, negative-sense single-stranded RNA virus

• Diagnosis = Measles (Rubeola)
• Caused by Measles virus (Paramyxovirus family)
• Characteristics:

• Enveloped
• (-) ssRNA virus

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 32-year-old male from rural Bihar presents with a 3-month history of intermittent fever, progressive abdominal distension, and weight loss. On examination, he has marked splenomegaly, pallor, and hyperpigmentation of the skin. Laboratory evaluation reveals pancytopenia. Bone marrow aspiration shows intracellular amastigotes within macrophages. Which of the following is the most likely vector responsible for transmission of this disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Sandfly (Phlebotomus)

Visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar), common in regions like Bihar, is caused by Leishmania donovani and is transmitted by the female sandfly (genus Phlebotomus).

• Vector: Phlebotomus (sandfly)
• Reservoir: humans (in Indian subcontinent)
• Clinical features:

o    Massive splenomegaly

o    Irregular (on-off) fever

o    Anemia, weight loss

o    Hyperpigmentation (“kala-azar”)

• Parasite form:

o    Amastigotes (LD bodies) inside macrophages in spleen, liver, bone marrow

• Diagnosis: Demonstration of LD bodies in tissue aspirate
• Treatment: Liposomal amphotericin B

Why not others:

• Rat flea: plague (Yersinia pestis)
• Chrysops fly: Loa loa (loiasis)
• Black fly (Simulium): Onchocerca volvulus (river blindness)

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 32-year-old male presents to the emergency department with high-grade fever and altered sensorium. He recently returned from a malaria-endemic region. Blood smear confirms Plasmodium falciparum infection resistant to chloroquine. The patient is diagnosed with complicated malaria. What is the most appropriate treatment of choice in this scenario?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Artesunate

Severe (complicated) malaria caused by Plasmodium falciparum, especially chloroquine-resistant strains, should be treated with intravenous artesunate, which is the drug of choice due to its rapid parasite clearance and superior survival benefit compared to quinine.

·         Indications for IV artesunate: altered sensorium (cerebral malaria), severe anemia, acidosis, renal failure, shock, etc.

·         Mechanism: Artemisinin derivatives generate free radicals → rapid killing of parasitized RBCs.

·  Why not others:

o    Quinine: second line; more side effects (cinchonism, hypoglycemia)

o    Sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine: resistance common; not for severe malaria

o    Primaquine: acts on hypnozoites (vivax/ovale), not used in acute severe falciparum malaria

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 32-year-old man returns from a malaria-endemic area with a 5-day history of high-grade fever. On examination, he is drowsy, confused, and has altered sensorium. A peripheral blood smear reveals Plasmodium falciparum. What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Intravenous artesunate

Severe falciparum malaria is a medical emergency requiring immediate intravenous artesunate. Features such as altered sensorium, confusion, drowsiness (cerebral malaria), shock, severe anemia, metabolic acidosis, acute kidney injury, pulmonary edema, hypoglycemia, or hyperparasitemia indicate severe malaria and mandate parenteral therapy, irrespective of the patient’s ability to take oral medications.

• After clinical improvement: Switch to a full course of oral artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT) (e.g., artemether-lumefantrine).
• Mechanism of severe disease: Cytoadherence and sequestration of parasitized RBCs in the microvasculature due to PfEMP1, leading to microvascular obstruction and organ dysfunction.

Why not the other options?

• B. Intravenous artesunate with sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine: Sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine is not recommended as part of initial treatment for severe malaria because of widespread resistance.
• C. Oral artemether-lumefantrine: Used for uncomplicated falciparum malaria, not in patients with severe disease or altered consciousness.
• D. Oral chloroquine: P. falciparum is widely chloroquine-resistant; therefore, chloroquine is not recommended.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 38-year-old man presents with chronic cough, fever, and significant weight loss. Chest X-ray shows right upper lobe infiltrates, and sputum is positive for acid-fast bacilli (AFB). During evaluation, he is found to be HIV positive. What is the most appropriate management plan?
options: Start anti-tubercular therapy (ATT) and ART simultaneously
Start ATT first, and initiate ART after 2 weeks
Start ART first, and add ATT after 2 weeks
Complete ATT first, then start ART
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Start ATT first, and initiate ART after 2 weeks

In patients with HIV–tuberculosis coinfection, the priority is to start anti-tubercular therapy (ATT first), followed by early initiation of ART (within 2 weeks)—especially in those with advanced immunosuppression.

• ATT is started immediately to control active TB (reduces mortality and transmission)
• ART is delayed briefly (≈2 weeks) to:

o    Reduce risk of immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS)

o    Improve drug tolerance and adherence

Timing of ART:

• CD4 < 50 cells/mm³ → start ART within 2 weeks
• CD4 > 50 → start ART within 2–8 weeks

Why not other options:

• Simultaneous start → ↑ risk of severe IRIS
• ART first → worsens untreated TB
• Delay ART till ATT completion → ↑ HIV progression and mortality

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 4-year-old child presents with fever, painful oral ulcers, and vesicular lesions over the palms and soles. What is the most likely causative organism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Coxsackievirus A16

Hand, foot, and mouth disease (HFMD) is a common childhood viral illness caused most commonly by Coxsackievirus A16 (an enterovirus). It is characterized by fever, painful oral ulcers (herpangina), and vesicular lesions on the hands, feet, and occasionally the buttocks. The disease is usually self-limiting and managed with supportive care.

Why not the other options?

• B. Coxsackievirus B: Commonly causes myocarditis, dilated cardiomyopathy, pleurodynia (Bornholm disease), and pericarditis, not HFMD.
• C. Cytomegalovirus (CMV): Causes congenital infections and opportunistic disease in immunocompromised patients, not vesicular lesions on the hands and feet.
• D. Parvovirus B19: Causes erythema infectiosum (fifth disease) with a “slapped cheek” rash and aplastic crisis, not HFMD.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 40-year-old man, newly diagnosed with HIV infection, presents with low-grade fever, productive cough, and weight loss. A chest X-ray reveals nodules suggestive of TB. Sputum GeneXpert reveals Mycobacterium tuberculosis with rifampicin resistance. He is not yet started on ART. His CD4 count is 110 cells/mm³. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Start BPaLM regimen for 6 months and follow up for immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS)
Start HEZ plus levofloxacin for 9 months and monitor for optic neuritis
Start HEZ plus linezolid for 9 months and monitor for hepatotoxicity
Start kanamycin-based MDR regimen for 20 months and continue ART without interruption
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Start BPaLM regimen for 6 months and follow up for immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS)

In HIV patients with rifampicin-resistant (RR/MDR) tuberculosis, the recommended management is an all-oral, shorter regimen such as BPaLM (Bedaquiline + Pretomanid + Linezolid + Moxifloxacin) for \~6 months.

• GeneXpert showing rifampicin resistance = treat as MDR-TB
• BPaLM regimen is now preferred:

o    Shorter duration (≈6 months)

o    Fully oral (no injectables)

o    Higher success rates

HIV considerations:

• Start ATT immediately
• Initiate ART early (within 2 weeks for CD4 <200)
• Monitor for IRIS after ART initiation

Why not other options:

• HEZ regimens → ineffective in rifampicin-resistant TB
• Kanamycin-based regimens → outdated, toxic (ototoxicity), longer duration
• Injectable regimens are no longer preferred

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A doctor receives a telephonic call from the mother of an 8-year-old boy, who informs that the boy has just been bitten by a monkey. The child was playing with his friends when a group of monkeys appeared nearby. Some of the children shouted and threw sticks and stones at the monkeys, who became angry and aggressive. One of the monkeys bit the lady’s son in the forearm and blood is visible over the wound. The nearest health facility is 3 kilometres away. Consider the following statements regarding how the doctor should respond: 1. Advise the mother to rush with the child to the health facility without waiting for anything. 2. Advise the mother to first thoroughly wash the wound with plenty of soap and running water for at least 15 minutes, and then seek treatment. 3. Advise the mother that the animal bite is category I and risk is very low, as the bite was provoked. 4. Advise the mother to seek treatment for the boy’s wound but the boy requires no treatment or prophylaxis for rabies as it is a monkey bite. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 2 only

This is a Category III rabies exposure because the child has sustained a transdermal monkey bite with visible bleeding. Monkey bites are recognized as potential rabies exposures and should not be dismissed because the bite was provoked.

1. Statement 1. Advise the mother to rush with the child to the health facility without waiting for anything: Incorrect.

• The child should certainly reach a health facility promptly, but the first immediate step is thorough wound washing, which should not be delayed while travelling.

2. Statement 2. Advise the mother to first thoroughly wash the wound with plenty of soap and running water for at least 15 minutes, and then seek treatment: Correct.

• The wound should be washed and flushed thoroughly with soap and running water for at least 15 minutes, followed by prompt medical assessment.

3. Statement 3. Advise the mother that the animal bite is category I and risk is very low, as the bite was provoked: Incorrect.

• A bleeding bite is Category III, not Category I.
• Provocation does not eliminate rabies risk. Category III exposure requires rabies vaccination plus rabies immunoglobulin/monoclonal antibodies when indicated.

4. Statement 4. Advise the mother to seek treatment for the boy’s wound but the boy requires no treatment or prophylaxis for rabies as it is a monkey bite: Incorrect.

• Monkey bites can transmit rabies and may also transmit other infections. Therefore, rabies PEP cannot be omitted simply because the animal was a monkey.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A farmer presents with fever, malaise, and diarrhea. There is a history of direct exposure to livestock. Which of the following organisms is the most likely causative agent?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Coxiella burnetii

Coxiella burnetii causes Q fever, a zoonotic infection transmitted from livestock (cattle, sheep, goats), typically via inhalation of contaminated aerosols from animal products (placenta, urine, feces).

·         Risk factor: farmers, veterinarians, slaughterhouse workers

·         Transmission: inhalation (NOT via arthropod bite → important distinction from rickettsiae)

·   Clinical features:

o    Acute: fever, malaise, headache, atypical pneumonia, hepatitis ± diarrhea

o    Chronic: endocarditis (especially in patients with valvular disease)

o    Obligate intracellular organism

o    Survives in harsh conditions (spore-like form)

o    No rash (helps differentiate from rickettsial infections)

Why not others:

·         Rickettsia typhi: flea-borne (endemic typhus)

·         Orientia tsutsugamushi: mite-borne (scrub typhus, eschar present)

·         Rickettsia prowazekii: louse-borne (epidemic typhus)

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A healthcare worker undergoes screening for latent tuberculosis infection (LTBI) using an Interferon-γ Release Assay (IGRA). The assay measures interferon-γ release from sensitized T lymphocytes after stimulation with specific Mycobacterium tuberculosis antigens. Which of the following statements regarding this test is correct?
options: The first-generation QuantiFERON assay used ESAT-6 as the stimulating antigen.
The second-generation QuantiFERON-TB Gold assay employs both ESAT-6 and CFP-10.
IGRAs reliably distinguish latent tuberculosis infection from active tuberculosis disease.
All non-tuberculous mycobacteria are negative in this assay.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. The second-generation QuantiFERON-TB Gold assay employs both ESAT-6 and CFP-10.

Interferon-γ Release Assays (IGRAs) detect cell-mediated immune responses by measuring IFN-γ released from sensitized T cells after stimulation with specific M. tuberculosis antigens.

QuantiFERON evolution:

• First-generation QuantiFERON-TB → Purified Protein Derivative (PPD)
• Second-generation QuantiFERON-TB Gold → ESAT-6 + CFP-10
• QuantiFERON-TB Gold In-Tube (QFT-GIT) → ESAT-6 + CFP-10 + TB7.7
• QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus (QFT-Plus) → ESAT-6 + CFP-10 (optimized CD4⁺ and CD8⁺ T-cell stimulation)

Because ESAT-6 and CFP-10 are absent from BCG vaccine strains and most environmental mycobacteria, IGRAs are more specific than the Mantoux test.

Why the other options are incorrect?

• A. The first-generation QuantiFERON assay used ESAT-6 as stimulating antigen ❌: The original assay used PPD, not ESAT-6.
• C. IGRAs distinguish latent TB from active TB ❌: IGRAs detect immune sensitization only and cannot differentiate latent infection from active tuberculosis.
•

D. All non-tuberculous mycobacteria are negative in this assay ❌: Some NTM species, including:

• Mycobacterium kansasii
• M. marinum
• M. szulgai

possess ESAT-6/CFP-10, leading to possible positive IGRA results.

High-Yield Pearl

| Test | Antigen used | Limitation

| ---- | ------------ | ----------

| Mantoux (TST) | PPD | False positives after BCG vaccination

| QuantiFERON-TB Gold | ESAT-6 + CFP-10 | Cannot distinguish latent from active TB

| T-SPOT.TB | ESAT-6 + CFP-10 | Cannot distinguish latent from active TB

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A microbiologist is preparing a lecture on oncogenic viruses and lists several diseases linked to Epstein–Barr virus (EBV). One of the listed conditions is incorrectly attributed to EBV. Which one is it?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Gastric MALT lymphoma

Epstein–Barr virus (EBV) is a γ-herpesvirus (HHV-4) that infects B lymphocytes via the CD21 (CR2) receptor and is associated with several lymphoid and epithelial malignancies.

Major EBV-associated diseases:

• Infectious mononucleosis
• Burkitt lymphoma (endemic African type)
• Classical Hodgkin lymphoma (especially mixed-cellularity subtype)
• Nasopharyngeal carcinoma
• Post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder (PTLD)
• AIDS-associated primary CNS lymphoma
• Extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma (nasal type)
• Some gastric carcinomas

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A militant living in overcrowded conditions presents with high fever and a centrifugal rash that spares the palms and soles, along with evidence of body louse infestation. What is the most likely causative organism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Rickettsia prowazekii

Rickettsia prowazekii causes epidemic typhus, a severe rickettsial infection associated with overcrowding and poor hygiene, transmitted by the human body louse.

·     Transmission: inoculation of infected louse feces into skin (scratching)

·     Clinical features:

o    High-grade fever, severe headache

o    Centrifugal rash (starts on trunk → spreads outward)

o    Spares palms and soles

o    May progress to delirium, shock

·    Risk factors:

o    Overcrowding (e.g., war zones, refugee camps, prisons)

Why not others:

·         Rickettsia typhi: Endemic (murine) typhus, flea-borne, milder

·         Rickettsia akari: Rickettsial pox (mite-borne, eschar present)

·         Rickettsia conorii: Indian tick typhus (tick-borne, involves palms/soles)

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient addressing from Delhi presents with fever, arthralgia, and extensive petechial rash for 3 days. Lab investigations revealed a hemoglobin of 9 g/dL, a white blood cell count of 9000 cells/mm³, a platelet count of 20000 cells/mm³, and a prolonged bleeding time. The clotting time was normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Dengue

Dengue fever should be suspected in patients with acute fever + severe arthralgia + petechial rash + thrombocytopenia, especially with normal clotting time but prolonged bleeding time.

·         Pathophysiology:

o    Platelet destruction + capillary fragility → bleeding manifestations

o    Coagulation cascade usually intact → normal clotting time

·         Typical lab findings:

o    Thrombocytopenia (↓ platelets)

o    Hemoconcentration (↑ hematocrit in severe cases)

o    Normal or mildly altered WBC count

o    ↑ bleeding time, normal clotting time

·         Clinical features:

o    High fever

o    Severe joint/muscle pain (“breakbone fever”)

o    Petechiae, bleeding manifestations

Why not others:

·         Malaria: anemia, parasitemia, no petechial rash pattern

·         Scrub typhus: eschar + lymphadenopathy

·         Typhoid: step-ladder fever, relative bradycardia, no severe thrombocytopenia

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient being treated for multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB) presents with bilateral tingling and numbness in both lower limbs below the knees. Which of the following drugs is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Linezolid

Peripheral neuropathy (bilateral tingling and numbness) in a patient receiving MDR-TB therapy is classically associated with Linezolid toxicity.

• Linezolid causes dose- and duration-dependent peripheral neuropathy
• It may also cause optic neuropathy with prolonged use
• Mechanism: mitochondrial protein synthesis inhibition (affects neuronal function)
• Neuropathy may be irreversible if not detected early

Differentiation:

• Bedaquiline → QT prolongation
• Levofloxacin → tendinopathy, QT prolongation
• Clofazimine → skin discoloration (reddish-brown pigmentation)

Thus, peripheral neuropathy in MDR-TB treatment strongly suggests linezolid toxicity.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient from Manipur presents to the PHC with fever and chills, and peripheral blood smear confirms Plasmodium falciparum malaria. Which treatment regimen should be administered according to the NVBDCP guidelines?
options: Chloroquine X 3 days + Primaquine X 14 days
Artemether-Lumefantrine X 3 days + Primaquine X Day-2
Artemether-Lumefantrine X 3 days + Primaquine X 14 days
Artesunate Sulfadoxine Pyrimethamine X 3 days + Primaquine X 14 days
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Artemether-Lumefantrine X 3 days + Primaquine X Day-2

Under the NVBDCP/National Malaria Elimination Programme (NMEP) guidelines, Artemether–Lumefantrine (AL) for 3 days is the ACT of choice for uncomplicated Plasmodium falciparum malaria in North-Eastern states (including Manipur) because of high sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine resistance. A single dose of primaquine is given on Day 2 (after excluding G6PD deficiency and contraindications) to reduce transmission by clearing gametocytes.

Why not the other options?

• A. Chloroquine × 3 days + Primaquine × 14 days: Chloroquine is not effective for P. falciparum due to widespread resistance.
• C. Artemether–Lumefantrine × 3 days + Primaquine × 14 days: 14-day primaquine is used for radical cure of P. vivax/P. ovale, not P. falciparum.
• D. Artesunate + Sulfadoxine-Pyrimethamine × 3 days + Primaquine × 14 days: AS+SP is not recommended in North-Eastern states because of SP resistance, and 14-day primaquine is unnecessary for P. falciparum.

| Malaria Type | Region | Treatment | Primaquine

| ------------ | ------ | --------- | ----------

| P. vivax | All India | Chloroquine × 3 days | 14 days (radical cure)

| P. falciparum | Rest of India | Artesunate + Sulfadoxine-Pyrimethamine (AS+SP) × 3 days | Single dose on Day 2 (gametocytocidal)

| P. falciparum | North-Eastern states (Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, Manipur, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland, Sikkim, Tripura) | Artemether-Lumefantrine (AL) × 3 days | Single dose on Day 2

| Mixed infection (P. vivax + P. falciparum) | All India | Treat as P. falciparum (ACT) | 14 days (to eradicate P. vivax hypnozoites)

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient of sickle cell anemia developed aplastic crisis after a viral infection. The agent causing it is
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Parvovirus B19

Parvovirus B19 causes aplastic crisis in patients with hemolytic anemias (e.g., sickle cell disease) by selectively infecting and destroying erythroid precursor cells in the bone marrow.

• Virus type: single-stranded DNA virus (only ssDNA virus)
• Target cells: erythroid progenitors via P antigen (globoside receptor)
• Pathogenesis:

o    Temporary cessation of erythropoiesis

o    Leads to severe anemia (aplastic crisis) in patients with high RBC turnover

• Clinical features:

o    Sudden drop in hemoglobin

o    Reticulocytopenia

o    Fatigue, pallor

• Other manifestations:

o    Erythema infectiosum (slapped cheek rash) in children

o    Hydrops fetalis in pregnant women

Why not others:

• CMV, EBV, HBV: do not specifically target erythroid precursors to cause aplastic crisis

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient presented with retro-orbital pain and rash since the 5 days. Most appropriate test to be done now is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Antibody detectionby ELISA

Selection of dengue diagnostic tests depends on the day of illness.

Key timeline:

• Early phase (Day 1–5):

o    NS1 antigen detection

o    RT-PCR (viral RNA detection)

• Late phase (after Day 5):

o    Antibody detection (IgM ELISA) becomes the test of choice

Clinical application:

• This patient is on Day 5 with retro-orbital pain and rash → entering antibody phase
• IgM antibodies start appearing around Day 5

Key points:

• NS1 and PCR are useful early when viremia is present
• IgM ELISA is preferred after Day 5
• IgG indicates past infection or secondary infection

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient presents with cervical lymphadenopathy, and a peripheral blood smear reveals atypical lymphocytes suggestive of Burkitt lymphoma. The Paul–Bunnell test is performed to further identify the causative organism. This test is used to detect infection by which organism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. EBV

Paul–Bunnell test is a heterophile antibody test used in the diagnosis of infectious mononucleosis caused by Epstein–Barr virus (EBV). During acute EBV infection, patients develop heterophile IgM antibodies that agglutinate sheep or horse red blood cells, making the test positive. EBV infection is also strongly associated with Burkitt lymphoma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma, and several lymphoproliferative disorders.

Why not the other options?

• A. CMV: Can cause a mononucleosis-like syndrome with atypical lymphocytes, but the Paul–Bunnell (heterophile antibody) test is negative.
• C. HHV-6: Causes roseola infantum (exanthem subitum); not detected by the Paul–Bunnell test.
• D. Adenovirus: Causes pharyngoconjunctival fever and respiratory infections; no heterophile antibody production.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient presents with multiple soft, verrucous, exophytic lesions over the external genitalia, giving them a wart-like or cauliflower-like appearance. Which infectious agent is most commonly responsible?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Human papillomavirus (HPV 6,11)

Condyloma acuminata (genital warts) are benign, soft, exophytic, papillomatous (“cauliflower-like”) lesions caused by low-risk Human papillomavirus (HPV) types 6 and 11. They are transmitted through sexual contact and most commonly involve the external genitalia and perianal region.

Why not the other options?

• A. Herpes simplex virus (HSV): Causes painful grouped vesicles that rupture to form shallow ulcers.
• B. Treponema pallidum: Causes syphilis; primary syphilis presents with a painless chancre, while secondary syphilis causes condyloma lata (broad, flat, moist lesions), not cauliflower-like warts.
• D. Haemophilus ducreyi: Causes chancroid, characterized by painful genital ulcers with tender inguinal lymphadenopathy.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient presents with pain in the genital area and a painful vesicle on examination, accompanied by painful lymphadenopathy. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. HSV2

Bottom of Form Painful genital vesicles with tender lymphadenopathy are characteristic of genital herpes caused by HSV-2.

• HSV-2 causes painful vesicular lesions that may rupture to form ulcers
• Associated with painful inguinal lymphadenopathy
• Primary infection may have systemic symptoms (fever, malaise)
• Virus remains latent in sacral ganglia and can reactivate

Differentiation:

• Molluscum contagiosum → painless, umbilicated papules
• HPV → painless genital warts (condyloma acuminata)
• HIV → does not present with localized vesicular genital lesions

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient undergoing antitubercular therapy reports joint pain 10 days after initiation of treatment. Laboratory tests reveal normal AST and ALT levels, a serum creatinine of 0.9 mg/dL, and an elevated serum uric acid level of 10 mg/dL. What is the most appropriate next step in managing this patient's treatment?
options: Stop pyrazinamide and continue the rest of the drugs with kidney function test (KFT) monitoring.
Add uric acid-lowering drugs and continue antitubercular therapy (ATT) as such with liver function test (LFT) and KFT monitoring.
Continue all drugs and monitor serum uric acid level as well as LFT and KFT.
Stop all ATT drugs until laboratory values return to normal.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Stop pyrazinamide and continue the rest of the drugs with kidney function test (KFT) monitoring.

Pyrazinamide commonly causes hyperuricemia by decreasing renal excretion of uric acid, leading to acute gouty arthritis early in ATT.

• Onset within days to weeks of starting therapy
• Joint pain with elevated serum uric acid
• Normal LFT and KFT (isolated hyperuricemia)

Management principle:

• Symptomatic hyperuricemia (with joint pain) → stop pyrazinamide
• Continue remaining ATT drugs
• Monitor renal function
• Asymptomatic hyperuricemia → no need to stop drug

Why not others:

• Adding uric acid–lowering drugs is not first-line
• Continuing drug despite symptoms worsens gout
• Stopping all ATT is unnecessary

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient with XDR-TB is started on BPaL regimen. What is the mechanism of action of pretomanid?
options: Inhibits bacterial cell wall via inhibition of mycolic acid synthesis due to generation of reactive nitrogen species
Inhibits mycobacterial ATP synthase due to reactive nitrogen species
Inhibits arabinogalactan synthesis in mycobacterial cell wall via nitric oxide pathway
Inhibits DNA-dependent RNA polymerase in mycobacteria
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Inhibits bacterial cell wall via inhibition of mycolic acid synthesis due to generation of reactive nitrogen species

Pretomanid is part of the BPaL regimen:

• Bedaquiline
• Pretomanid
• Linezolid

Used for:

• MDR-TB
• XDR-TB

Mechanism:

Pretomanid is a nitroimidazole drug that:

• Releases reactive nitrogen species (including nitric oxide)
• Inhibits mycolic acid synthesis
• Damages mycobacterial cell wall

Other Options:

• B. Mycobacterial ATP synthase inhibition due to reactive nitrogen species → Bedaquiline
• C. Arabinogalactan synthesis inhibition in mycobacterial cell wall via nitric oxide pathway → Ethambutol
• D. DNA-dependent RNA polymerase inhibition in mycobacteria → Rifampicin

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A person has presented with history of dog-bite on the uncovered surface of his right leg. There is a minor abrasion without bleeding. Consider the following statements about management: 1. The bite should be taken as a Category I contact with suspect animal. 2. The bite requires local treatment of the wound. 3. The person requires immediate vaccination. 4. The person requires immediate administration of rabies immunoglobulin. Which of the above statements are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 2 and 3 only

Rabies post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) depends on the WHO exposure category. A minor abrasion without bleeding is classified as Category II exposure, which requires wound management and anti-rabies vaccination, but not rabies immunoglobulin (RIG).

• Statement 1: The bite should be taken as a Category I contact with suspect animal. ❌

• Category I includes touching/feeding animals or licks on intact skin.
• A minor abrasion without bleeding is Category II exposure.

• Statement 2: The bite requires local treatment of the wound. ✅

• Immediate wound washing with soap and running water for at least 15 minutes, followed by application of a virucidal antiseptic (e.g., povidone-iodine), is the most important first step.

• Statement 3: The person requires immediate vaccination. ✅

• Category II exposure requires anti-rabies vaccine (ARV).

• Statement 4: The person requires immediate administration of rabies immunoglobulin. ❌

• Rabies immunoglobulin (RIG) is indicated only for Category III exposures.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A vaccinated dog bites a person and causes bleeding. What is the category of rabies exposure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Category III

Rabies exposure is classified according to the WHO categories based on the type of contact with a suspected rabid animal. Any transdermal bite or scratch causing bleeding is Category III exposure, regardless of whether the dog is vaccinated or unvaccinated.

This is Category III exposure, which requires:

• Immediate wound washing
• Rabies vaccine (PEP)
• Rabies immunoglobulin (RIG) infiltration into the wound (if not previously vaccinated)

The vaccination status of the dog does not change the exposure category. It only influences subsequent management if the dog remains healthy during observation.

Why not the other options?

• A. Category I: Touching/feeding animals or licks on intact skin; no PEP required.
• B. Category II: Minor scratches or abrasions without bleeding; vaccine required but RIG not indicated.
• D. Category IV: No WHO Category IV exists.

| Category | Type of Exposure | Post-Exposure Prophylaxis (PEP)

| -------- | ---------------- | -------------------------------

| Category I | Touching/feeding animals, licks on intact skin | No PEP

| Category II | Minor scratches/abrasions without bleeding, nibbling of uncovered skin | Rabies vaccine

| Category III | Single or multiple transdermal bites/scratches, bleeding, saliva on broken skin or mucosa, bat exposure | Wound washing + Rabies vaccine + RIG

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A wildlife photographer returns from a trip to sub-Saharan Africa and presents with acute fever, jaundice, and hemorrhagic symptoms. Liver biopsy shows intranuclear Councilman/Torres bodies. Which vaccine could have prevented this infection?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 17D

Yellow fever, a viral hemorrhagic disease caused by a Flavivirus, presents with fever, jaundice, and hemorrhage, and is characterized histologically by Councilman bodies (apoptotic hepatocytes) in the liver.

·         Transmission: Aedes mosquito (endemic in sub-Saharan Africa, South America)

·   Clinical features:

o    Fever, myalgia

o    Jaundice + hemorrhage (“yellow” fever)

o    Severe cases → liver failure

·         Prevention: 17D vaccine = live attenuated vaccine → highly effective

Why not others:

·         Nakayama vaccine: Japanese encephalitis

·         Weigl’s vaccine: epidemic typhus

·         Jeryl Lynn strain: mumps vaccine

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A young patient undergoing treatment for multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB) presents with symptoms of weight gain, cold intolerance, and lethargy. Laboratory investigations reveal high levels of thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) and low levels of T3 (triiodothyronine) and T4 (thyroxine). Which of the following drugs is likely responsible for these symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ethionamide

Symptoms point to hypothyroidism:

| Feature | Meaning

| ------- | -------

| Weight gain | ↓ metabolism

| Cold intolerance | ↓ heat production

| Lethargy | ↓ energy

| ↑ TSH + ↓ T3/T4 | Primary hypothyroidism

Ethionamide commonly causes drug-induced hypothyroidism, especially in MDR-TB regimens. It interferes with thyroid hormone synthesis, leading to ↑TSH and low T3/T4. Symptoms include weight gain, cold intolerance, and lethargy. Thyroid dysfunction is a classic adverse effect of ethionamide.

Anti-TB Side Effects Table-

| Drug | Side Effect

| ---- | -----------

| Ethionamide | Hypothyroidism

| PAS | Hypothyroidism

| Isoniazid | Neuropathy

| Rifampicin | Hepatotoxicity

| Pyrazinamide | Hyperuricemia

| Streptomycin | Ototoxicity

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: According to International Health Regulations, yellow fever is unlikely to spread if the Aedes aegypti index is maintained below which percentage?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1%

As per International Health Regulations, the Aedes aegypti house index (percentage of houses/containers with Aedes aegypti larvae) should be maintained below 1% to make yellow fever transmission unlikely.

Why this matters:

| Index Level | Significance

| ----------- | ------------

| <1% | Below this threshold, yellow fever epidemic spread is considered unlikely (IHR standard)

| 1-5% | Increasing risk zone

| >5% | Significant risk of dengue/yellow fever transmission

Key Teaching Point:

• The Aedes aegypti (house) index = percentage of houses/premises showing evidence of Aedes aegypti breeding (larvae/pupae) in a given area.
