• This is distinct from the Breteau Index (number of positive containers per 100 houses), which is considered a more sensitive indicator and is preferred by WHO for dengue vector surveillance — Breteau index <5 is the target for dengue control programs.
• Don't confuse the two indices on the exam:

• House Index <1% → yellow fever (IHR threshold)
• Breteau Index <5 → dengue control target (WHO)

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: All of the following methods are antilarval measures except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Malathion

Malathion is primarily an anti-adult mosquito control measure, not an anti-larval measure. It belongs to the organophosphorus group of insecticides that acts as a nerve/contact poison inhibiting acetylcholinesterase. While malathion can be used for larval control in specific formulations, it is classified under anti-adult measures in mosquito control strategies.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: As per the National Framework for Malaria Elimination in India (2016–2030), which one of the following has to be achieved by the year 2027?
options: The entire country to have less than 1 case due to malaria per 1000 population at risk
The entire country to have less than 1 indigenous case of malaria per 1000 population at risk and less than 1 death due to malaria per 10,000 population at risk
The entire country to have no indigenous case of malaria and no deaths due to malaria
The entire country to have no indigenous cases of malaria and less than 1 death due to malaria per 100,000 population at risk
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. The entire country to have no indigenous case of malaria and no deaths due to malaria

The National Framework for Malaria Elimination (NFME) in India 2016–2030 provides a phased roadmap to eliminate malaria from India in line with the WHO Global Technical Strategy for Malaria. It defines specific milestones and targets to achieve malaria elimination by 2030.

The 2027 target is Entire country to have no indigenous malaria cases and no deaths due to malaria.  This represents the achievement of malaria elimination, after which the country enters the phase of preventing re-establishment of transmission.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: As per the National Vector Borne Disease Control Programme, the first-line agent for treatment of Kala-azar (visceral leishmaniasis) is:
options: Amphotericin B, liposomal, IV, single dose
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Amphotericin B, liposomal, IV, single dose

• Liposomal amphotericin B is the preferred first-line treatment for visceral leishmaniasis (Kala-azar) under India’s national program.
• A single IV dose of 10 mg/kg is used in the Indian elimination program.

Why not other options?

• B. Sodium stibogluconate: Historically used, but no longer preferred because of widespread resistance and toxicity.
• C. Miltefosine: An effective oral antileishmanial drug, but not the first-line regimen for Kala-azar under the current Indian elimination strategy.
• D. Amphotericin B deoxycholate: Effective but more toxic and has largely been replaced by the liposomal formulation.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Consider the following statements about Kyasanur Forest Disease (KFD): 1. It is transmitted by ticks. 2. It was originally called ‘pig disease’ because of the association with dead pigs. 3. It was first recognized in Karnataka State. How many of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Only two of the statements

Kyasanur Forest Disease (KFD), also known as Monkey Fever, is a tick-borne viral hemorrhagic fever caused by the Kyasanur Forest Disease virus (KFDV), a member of the Flavivirus genus. It is endemic to parts of South India, particularly the Western Ghats.

• 1. It is transmitted by ticks. ✓

• KFD is transmitted by the hard tick Haemaphysalis spinigera.

• 2. It was originally called ‘pig disease’ because of the association with dead pigs. ✗

• KFD was originally called “Monkey Fever” because deaths among monkeys (especially black-faced langurs and bonnet macaques) preceded human outbreaks.

• 3. It was first recognized in Karnataka State. ✓

• KFD was first identified in 1957 in the Kyasanur Forest of Shivamogga (Shimoga) district, Karnataka.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Consider the following statements regarding dengue virus: 1. It has four distinct serotypes. 2. Infection with any one serotype confers lifelong immunity for that virus serotype. 3. Secondary infection with dengue serotype 2 leads to severe form of dengue. Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 2 and 3

• 1. It has four distinct serotypes. ✓

• Dengue virus has four serotypes: DENV-1, DENV-2, DENV-3, and DENV-4 (a fifth serotype has been reported experimentally but is not included in routine clinical practice or standard examination questions).

• 2. Infection with any one serotype confers lifelong immunity for that virus serotype. ✓

• Infection produces lifelong, serotype-specific immunity, but only temporary cross-immunity (lasting a few months) against the other serotypes.

• 3. Secondary infection with dengue serotype 2 leads to severe form of dengue. ✓

• Severe dengue is most commonly associated with secondary infection, particularly when DENV-2 is involved. This occurs because of antibody-dependent enhancement (ADE), where non-neutralizing antibodies from a previous infection facilitate viral entry into monocytes, increasing viral replication and disease severity.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Consider the following statements regarding dengue: 1. The mosquito becomes infective after an extrinsic incubation period of 8–10 days. 2. Once it becomes infective, the mosquito remains infective for life. 3. The genital tract of the mosquito does not get infected. Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1 and 2 only

Dengue is transmitted by the female Aedes aegypti mosquito. After feeding on a viremic person, the virus undergoes an extrinsic incubation period (EIP) within the mosquito before it can be transmitted to another human. Once infective, the mosquito remains capable of transmitting the virus for the rest of its life.

• 1. The mosquito becomes infective after an extrinsic incubation period of 8–10 days. ✓

• After ingesting dengue virus, the virus replicates in the mosquito and reaches the salivary glands after an extrinsic incubation period of approximately 8–10 days (temperature-dependent).

• 2. Once it becomes infective\, the mosquito remains infective for life. ✓

• The virus persists in the mosquito’s salivary glands, allowing it to transmit dengue throughout its lifespan.

• 3. The genital tract of the mosquito does not get infected. ✗

• This statement is incorrect because the genital tract can become infected, allowing transovarial (vertical) transmission of dengue virus, although this is not the major mode of transmission.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Daily suppressive therapy for HSV-1 and HSV-2 is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Valacyclovir 1 g once daily

Suppressive antiviral therapy is recommended for patients with recurrent genital herpes (HSV-1 or HSV-2) who experience frequent recurrences, severe symptoms, or wish to reduce the risk of transmission to sexual partners. Long-term suppressive therapy reduces the frequency of recurrences by 70–80% and decreases asymptomatic viral shedding.

• Valacyclovir 1 g orally once daily is a recommended regimen for daily suppressive therapy of recurrent genital herpes. It has better oral bioavailability than acyclovir, allowing once-daily dosing and improving patient compliance.

Why not the other options?

• B. Acyclovir 400 mg once daily

• Dose is inadequate.
• Recommended suppressive dose is 400 mg twice daily.

• C. Acyclovir 400 mg thrice daily

• Not the standard suppressive regimen.
• Used regimens are typically 400 mg twice daily.

• D. Valacyclovir 1 g twice daily

• This dose is used for initial episodes or severe infections, not for routine suppressive therapy.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Digestion and concentration of a sputum sample is done using:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. NaOH–NALC

Sputum specimens for suspected tuberculosis are processed using the NALC–NaOH method, the standard technique for digestion and decontamination before microscopy, culture, or molecular testing.

• N-acetyl-L-cysteine (NALC) acts as a mucolytic agent, liquefying the sputum by breaking down mucus.
• Sodium hydroxide (NaOH) acts as a decontaminating agent, killing contaminating bacteria and fungi while Mycobacterium tuberculosis survives because of its relatively alkali-resistant lipid-rich cell wall.

Why is C correct?

• NaOH–NALC is the standard digestion–decontamination method used for processing sputum samples for mycobacterial diagnosis.

Why not the other options?

• A. HNO₃–NALC: Nitric acid is not used for sputum digestion/decontamination.
• B. HCl–NALC: Hydrochloric acid is not used for TB specimen processing.
• D. H₂SO₄–NALC: Sulfuric acid is not part of the standard NALC digestion protocol.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: During a field visit, an epidemiologist observes mosquito larvae resting parallel to the water surface, without a siphon tube, and having palmate hairs on their abdominal segments. Based on these characteristics, which mosquito species do these larvae most likely belong to?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Anopheles

Anopheles mosquito larvae characteristically rest parallel to the water surface due to the absence of a siphon tube.

They possess palmate hairs on abdominal segments, which help maintain this horizontal position.

In contrast, Aedes and Culex larvae have siphon tubes and hang at an angle, while Mansonia larvae attach to aquatic plants for respiration.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Identify the wrongly matched pair.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. CMV: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma

Knowledge of the association between oncogenic viruses and specific malignancies is essential for diagnosis and frequently tested in examinations.

• Nasopharyngeal carcinoma is strongly associated with Epstein– Barr virus (EBV), not Cytomegalovirus (CMV).

Correct virus– tumor associations:

• EBV → Burkitt lymphoma, Nasopharyngeal carcinoma, Hodgkin lymphoma, Post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder
• HHV-8 → Kaposi sarcoma, Primary effusion lymphoma
• HTLV-1 → Adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma (ATL)
• HPV (16, 18) → Cervical, anal, vulvar, penile, and oropharyngeal cancers
• HBV & HCV → Hepatocellular carcinoma
• Merkel cell polyomavirus → Merkel cell carcinoma

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: In chickenpox, when different stages of the rash appear simultaneously on the same child's body, this phenomenon is known as:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Pleomorphism

Recognize chickenpox (varicella) by its characteristic pleomorphic rash, in which macules, papules, vesicles (“dew drop on a rose petal”), pustules, and crusts coexist simultaneously. This appearance, along with centripetal distribution, is a classic diagnostic feature.

Why not the other options?

• A. Polymorphism: General term meaning “many forms,” but the characteristic term used for the varicella rash in PSM is pleomorphism.
• B. Polymorphous: Descriptive adjective, not the specific term for the rash pattern.
• C. Phytodermatitis: Skin inflammation caused by contact with plants, unrelated to varicella.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: In the National Malaria Control Programme, Indoor Residual Spray (IRS) is the primary method of vector control in rural settings. Which one of the following is the insecticide of choice?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Synthetic pyrethroid

Indoor Residual Spray (IRS) is a key vector control strategy under the National Malaria Control/Elimination Programme. IRS involves spraying the inside walls and ceilings of houses with long-acting insecticides to kill mosquitoes resting indoors after feeding. Synthetic pyrethroids are currently the insecticides of choice for IRS in most areas because of their high efficacy and safety profile.

• Examples: Deltamethrin, Alpha-cypermethrin, Lambda-cyhalothrin
• Advantages:

• Highly effective against Anopheles mosquitoes
• Long residual action
• Lower mammalian toxicity
• Widely used due to increasing resistance to DDT

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A. DDT: Previously the mainstay of IRS but its use has declined due to widespread insecticide resistance in malaria vectors.
• B. Malathion: An organophosphate used mainly where resistance to other insecticides exists or for specific vector control programs; not the current insecticide of choice.
• D. Temephos: A larvicide, used to control mosquito larvae in water bodies, not for indoor residual spraying.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Monkeypox, a viral zoonotic disease, is caused by:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. A double-stranded DNA virus

Monkeypox (Mpox) is a viral zoonotic disease caused by the Monkeypox virus (MPXV), which belongs to the Orthopoxvirus genus of the Poxviridae family. It is a large enveloped double-stranded DNA (dsDNA) virus and is closely related to the smallpox (Variola) virus.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A.  Single-stranded RNA virus ✗
• B. Double-stranded RNA virus ✗
• C. Single-stranded DNA virus ✗

• Monkeypox is not an RNA virus and does not contain single-stranded DNA.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Most common cause of diarrhoea in children:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Rotavirus

The most common cause of acute diarrhoea in children worldwide is Rotavirus.

• Rotavirus is a double-stranded RNA virus (Reoviridae family)
• Primarily affects infants and young children
• Causes severe watery diarrhoea, vomiting, and dehydration
• Transmission is fecal-oral

Clinical relevance:

• Leading cause of severe dehydrating diarrhoea in children under 5 years
• Prevention is by oral rotavirus vaccination

Differentiation:

• Escherichia coli → common bacterial cause, but less frequent than rotavirus in children
• Shigella → causes dysentery (bloody diarrhoea)
• Ascaris → helminth, not a typical cause of acute diarrhoea

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Multidrug-resistant (MDR) TB shows resistance to which of the following drugs?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Isoniazid and rifampicin

Multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB) is defined as resistance to at least both isoniazid (INH) and rifampicin, the two most potent first-line anti-TB drugs. These are the backbone of standard TB therapy → resistance makes treatment difficult

·     Related terms:

o    XDR-TB (Extensively drug-resistant TB): MDR-TB + resistance to any fluoroquinolone + at least one second-line injectable drug (e.g., amikacin, kanamycin, capreomycin)

·     Causes of resistance:

o    Incomplete/irregular treatment

o    Poor compliance

o    Inadequate drug regimens

Why not others:

·      Fluoroquinolone resistance alone ≠ MDR

·     Resistance to INH + rifampicin + others → goes beyond MDR (e.g., XDR)

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Mycobacterium tuberculosis is typically cultured in which medium?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Lowenstein-jensen medium

Mycobacterium tuberculosis is cultured on Lowenstein–Jensen (LJ) medium, a specialized medium designed for mycobacterial growth.

• LJ medium is an egg-based medium containing malachite green, which inhibits contaminating bacteria
• MTB grows slowly, producing rough, buff-colored colonies in 2–8 weeks
• Culture is the gold standard for diagnosis and drug susceptibility testing

Why not others:

• MacConkey agar → for Gram-negative enteric bacteria
• Sabouraud dextrose agar → for fungi
• Mueller-Hinton agar → for antibiotic sensitivity testing

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder, a lymphoma that follows organ transplantation, is associated with infection with which one of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Epstein-Barr virus

Post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder (PTLD) is a potentially serious complication of solid-organ and hematopoietic stem-cell transplantation, caused by uncontrolled lymphoid proliferation in the setting of immunosuppression.

• A. Epstein–Barr virus: Correct

• Most early PTLD cases are associated with EBV, which infects B lymphocytes.
• Immunosuppression reduces T-cell surveillance, allowing EBV-infected B cells to proliferate.

• B. Mycobacterium tuberculosis: Incorrect

• Causes opportunistic tuberculosis in transplant recipients but is not the classic cause of PTLD.

• C. Capnocytophaga canimorsus: Incorrect

• Associated with severe infections, particularly after dog exposure, in immunocompromised or asplenic individuals.

• D. Histoplasma capsulatum: Incorrect

• Causes disseminated histoplasmosis in immunocompromised patients but is not the classic association with PTLD.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Primaquine destroys hypnozoites of Plasmodium vivax for radical cure in which one of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Liver

Primaquine is the only routinely used antimalarial that eradicates dormant liver forms (hypnozoites) of Plasmodium vivax and Plasmodium ovale, thereby achieving radical cure and preventing relapse.

Why not the other options?

• B. Peripheral blood: Blood schizonts are treated by chloroquine (where sensitive) or ACTs, not primaquine.
• C. Brain: No hypnozoite stage occurs in the brain.
• D. Bone marrow: Hypnozoites do not reside in the bone marrow.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Raju, a 6-year-old boy, was returning home from school. At the gate, he was scratched by a dog and there was some bleeding from the wound. Which option should be followed for the post-exposure prophylaxis?
options: Wash the wound and administer a shot of tetanus toxoid
Wash the wound, vaccinate with ARV and administer immunoglobulin
Wash the wound and vaccinate with ARV only
Wash and apply antiseptic to the wound
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Wash the wound, vaccinate with ARV and administer immunoglobulin

Rabies post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) depends on the WHO category of animal exposure. A scratch with bleeding is classified as Category III exposure, which requires immediate wound washing, anti-rabies vaccine (ARV), and rabies immunoglobulin (RIG).

A scratch with bleeding = Category III exposure, which requires:

• Immediate wound washing
• Anti-rabies vaccine (ARV)
• Rabies Immunoglobulin (RIG)

| Category | Exposure | PEP

| -------- | -------- | ---

| Category I | Touching/feeding animals, licking on intact skin | No PEP

| Category II | Minor scratches or abrasions without bleeding, nibbling of uncovered skin | Wound washing + ARV

| Category III | Single/multiple transdermal bites or scratches with bleeding, licks on broken skin, mucosal exposure | Wound washing + ARV + RIG

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Rickettsia typhi is the causative agent of which of the following diseases?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Endemic typhus

Rickettsia typhi causes endemic (murine) typhus, a flea-borne rickettsial infection associated with rodents.

·         Vector: rat flea (Xenopsylla cheopis)

·         Reservoir: rodents (especially rats)

·         Transmission: inoculation of infected flea feces into skin via scratching

·  Clinical features:

o    Fever, headache, myalgia

o    Rash (less prominent, starts on trunk)

o    Milder disease compared to epidemic typhus

Differentiate from others:

·         Epidemic typhus: caused by Rickettsia prowazekii (louse-borne, severe)

·         Scrub typhus: caused by Orientia tsutsugamushi (mite/chigger-borne, eschar present)

·         Indian tick typhus: caused by Rickettsia conorii (tick-borne)

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: The Duffy antigen system serves as receptor for which one of the following protozoal parasites?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Plasmodium vivax

The Duffy antigen (Duffy antigen receptor for chemokines, DARC/Fy antigen) on red blood cells acts as the receptor for Plasmodium vivax, allowing the parasite to invade erythrocytes. Individuals who are Duffy antigen-negative [Fy(a−b−)] are naturally resistant to P. vivax infection.

Why not the other options?

• A. Giardia lamblia: Infects the small intestine; does not use the Duffy antigen.
• C. Entamoeba histolytica: Invades the colon and liver; no relation to the Duffy antigen.
• D. Balantidium coli: A ciliated protozoan causing colitis; does not invade RBCs.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: The National Framework for Malaria Elimination in India (2016–2030) has defined certain milestones and targets. Among the following, which is the specific target that has to be met by the year 2027?
options: All states and UTs must reduce API to less than 1 case per 1000 population at risk.
All states and UTs must establish fully functional malaria surveillance to track, investigate and respond to each case.
Entire country is to have no indigenous cases and no deaths due to malaria.
Entire country has to initiate the process for certification of malaria elimination.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Entire country is to have no indigenous cases and no deaths due to malaria.

The National Framework for Malaria Elimination (NFME) in India 2016–2030 provides a phased roadmap to eliminate malaria from India in line with the WHO Global Technical Strategy for Malaria. It defines specific milestones and targets to achieve malaria elimination by 2030.

The 2027 target is Entire country to have no indigenous malaria cases and no deaths due to malaria.  This represents the achievement of malaria elimination, after which the country enters the phase of preventing re-establishment of transmission.

Why not the other options?

• A. All states and UTs must reduce API to <1 per 1000 population at risk: This was an earlier milestone, not the 2027 target.
• B. All states and UTs must establish fully functional malaria surveillance to track, investigate and respond to each case: Strengthening surveillance is an ongoing strategy initiated much earlier.
• D. Entire country has to initiate the process for certification of malaria elimination: WHO certification is sought after maintaining zero indigenous cases for at least 3 consecutive years, following elimination.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: To be effective, the size of the openings in the mosquito net should not exceed:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 0.0475 inch in diameter

For a mosquito net to effectively prevent mosquito entry, the mesh openings should not exceed approximately 0.0475 inch (≈1.2 mm) in diameter.

• (a) 0.0475 inch — Correct
• (b) 0.00475 inch — Too small
• (c) 0.0475 cm — Incorrect: This equals 0.475 mm, which is smaller than the standard value.
• (d) 0.00475 cm — Incorrect: This equals 0.0475 mm, which is far too small.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which among the following is a ssRNA virus?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Respiratory syncytial virus

Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is a single-stranded RNA (ssRNA) virus belonging to the Paramyxoviridae family.

• Genome: Negative-sense ssRNA
• Family: Paramyxoviridae
• Transmission: respiratory droplets
•

Common diseases:

o    Bronchiolitis (most common cause in infants)

o    Pneumonia in young children and elderly

•

Characteristic feature: Formation of syncytia (multinucleated giant cells) in respiratory epithelium

Why not others:

• Human papillomavirus (HPV): double-stranded DNA virus
• Adenovirus: double-stranded DNA virus
• Parvovirus: single-stranded DNA virus (only ssDNA virus)

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which among the following is the most common cause of diarrhea in adults?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Norovirus

Norovirus:

• Leading cause of outbreak-related diarrhea in adults
• Spread via fecal–oral route (contaminated food/water, person-to-person)
• Common in closed settings (cruise ships, hostels, hospitals)
• Causes acute onset vomiting + watery diarrhea

Why not others:

• Rotavirus → most common in infants and young children
• Adenovirus 40/41 → pediatric diarrhea
• Astrovirus → mild diarrhea, mainly in children and elderly

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following antimalarial drugs are commonly used for the clinical cure of malaria? a. Artemisinin b. Sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine c. Chloroquine d. Primaquine
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. a, b, c

Clinical cure of malaria refers to clearance of asexual erythrocytic forms responsible for symptoms.

Drugs used for clinical cure:

• Artemisinin (and ACTs) → rapidly clears parasitemia
• Sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine → inhibits folate synthesis in parasites
• Chloroquine → effective against sensitive strains

Not used for clinical cure:

• Primaquine → acts on hepatic hypnozoites and gametocytes (used for radical cure and transmission blocking, not for treating acute blood-stage infection)

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following are true about measles? 1. It is highly infectious in the phase following the appearance of rash. 2. Infection usually confers lifelong immunity. 3. It has a low secondary attack rate. Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 2 only

Measles is a highly contagious viral disease caused by the measles virus (Morbillivirus, Paramyxoviridae). It spreads by respiratory droplets and airborne transmission and has one of the highest secondary attack rates among infectious diseases.

• Statement 1. It is highly infectious in the phase following the appearance of rash❌: Incorrect. Measles is most infectious from about 4 days before to 4 days after the onset of rash, with maximum infectivity during the prodromal (catarrhal) phase, before the rash appears.
• Statement 2. Infection usually confers lifelong immunity✅: Correct. Natural measles infection generally produces lifelong immunity.
• Statement 3. It has a low secondary attack rate❌: Incorrect. Measles has a very high secondary attack rate (>90%) among susceptible household contacts.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following drugs are used for clinical cure of malaria? 1. Artemether 2. Sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine 3. Chloroquine 4. Primaquine
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 2 and 3

| Term | Meaning | Target stage

| ---- | ------- | ------------

| Clinical cure | Relief of symptoms (fever ↓) | Blood schizonts

| Radical cure | Prevent relapse | Liver hypnozoites

| Suppressive cure | Prevent symptoms | Blood stage

| Gametocidal | Prevent transmission | Gametocytes

Clinical cure requires drugs that clear erythrocytic schizonts, which produce symptoms. Artemether, chloroquine, and sulfadoxine–pyrimethamine act on blood stages and achieve symptomatic cure. Primaquine mainly eradicates hepatic hypnozoites and gametocytes for radical cure. Hence only 1, 2, and 3 are used for clinical cure.

Students think: “antimalarial = include primaquine”

BUT: It is for radical cure, NOT clinical cure

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following drugs have been used as part of mass drug administration (MDA) for elimination of lymphatic filariasis in some or more districts of India? 1. Albendazole 2. Diethylcarbamazine 3. Ivermectin 4. Metronidazole Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 2 and 3

The drugs used in mass drug administration (MDA) for lymphatic filariasis elimination in India include:

1. Albendazole — Correct

• Given along with DEC during MDA.
• Typical regimen: Albendazole 400 mg + DEC 6 mg/kg as a single annual dose.

2. Diethylcarbamazine (DEC) — Correct

• The key antifilarial drug used in India’s LF elimination programme.

3. Ivermectin — Correct

• Used in some endemic areas as part of the triple-drug regimen (IDA): Ivermectin + DEC + Albendazole.

4. Metronidazole — Incorrect

• It is not used for MDA of lymphatic filariasis.

Therefore, the correct answer is C. 1, 2 and 3.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following investigations may be used for the diagnosis of pulmonary tuberculosis? 1. Nucleic acid amplification 2. Culture in Middlebrook medium 3. Light emitting diode fluorescent microscopy with auramine staining 4. Peripheral blood smear Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2 and 3

The diagnosis of pulmonary tuberculosis (TB) is based on the demonstration of Mycobacterium tuberculosis using microbiological, molecular, and culture-based methods.

Explanation of the statements:

• Statement 1. Nucleic acid amplification: Correct. Nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs) (e.g., CBNAAT/Xpert MTB-RIF, Truenat) rapidly detect M. tuberculosis DNA and can identify rifampicin resistance.
• Statement 2. Culture in Middlebrook medium: Correct. Culture on Middlebrook medium (agar-based medium) is a sensitive method for isolating M. tuberculosis and allows drug susceptibility testing. (Lowenstein–Jensen medium is another commonly used culture medium.)
• Statement 3. Light emitting diode fluorescent microscopy with auramine staining: Correct. LED fluorescent microscopy using auramine staining is recommended for detecting acid-fast bacilli (AFB) and is more sensitive and faster than conventional Ziehl–Neelsen staining.
• Statement 4. Peripheral blood smear: Incorrect. Peripheral blood smear has no role in diagnosing pulmonary tuberculosis.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following is best for the malaria species identification?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Thin smear with Giemsa

Peripheral smear examination remains the gold standard for malaria diagnosis and species identification.

• Thin smear with Giemsa stain is best for species identification

• Preserves morphology of RBCs and parasites
• Helps differentiate Plasmodium species (falciparum, vivax, ovale, malariae)

• Thick smear with Giemsa is more sensitive for detection of parasites

• Used for screening when parasitemia is low

• QBC and acridine orange are rapid methods but less reliable for species differentiation

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following is not caused by parvovirus B19?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Petechial rash

Parvovirus B19 primarily infects erythroid precursor cells, leading to hematological manifestations.

Caused by Parvovirus B19:

• Pure red cell aplasia (especially in immunocompromised patients)
• Aplastic crisis (in patients with hemolytic anemias)
• Hydrops fetalis (due to severe fetal anemia in pregnancy)

Not caused: Petechial rash → more typical of platelet disorders or other viral infections (e.g., dengue)

Key points:

• Causes erythema infectiosum (“slapped cheek” rash) in children
• Targets erythroid precursors via P antigen

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following is not considered in the clinical criteria for the diagnosis of Kawasaki disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Purulent conjunctival discharge

Kawasaki disease is an acute medium-vessel vasculitis of childhood diagnosed clinically by fever for ≥5 days plus ≥4 of the 5 principal clinical features. The conjunctivitis of Kawasaki disease is bilateral, non-purulent bulbar conjunctival injection. Therefore, purulent conjunctival discharge suggests an alternative diagnosis, such as bacterial conjunctivitis.

• Purulent conjunctival discharge is not a diagnostic criterion for Kawasaki disease.
• Kawasaki disease causes bilateral non-exudative (non-purulent) conjunctivitis.

Why not the other options?

• A. Polymorphous rash ✓: One of the principal diagnostic criteria.
• C. Cervical lymphadenopathy ✓: Usually unilateral and ≥1.5 cm, included in the diagnostic criteria.
• D. Periungual peeling ✓: A characteristic feature seen in the subacute phase of Kawasaki disease.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following methods are appropriate for identifying different strains of the same species of Mycobacterium tuberculosis? a. RFLP (Restriction Fragment Length Polymorphism) b. Chromosomal mutation detection c. Spoligotyping d. Multiple interspaced repetitive unit typing (MIRU-VNTR)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. a, b, c & d

Strain typing methods are used to differentiate strains of Mycobacterium tuberculosis for epidemiological tracking and outbreak analysis.

Correct methods:

• RFLP (Restriction Fragment Length Polymorphism) → analyzes DNA fragment patterns
• Spoligotyping → detects spacer sequences in the DR (direct repeat) region
• MIRU-VNTR → evaluates variable number tandem repeats at multiple loci
• Chromosome mutation detection : Detection of chromosomal mutations (e.g., mutations in rpoB, katG, inhA) can distinguish genetic variants and identify drug-resistant mutants. With modern sequencing approaches, chromosomal mutation analysis is indeed used to differentiate MTB strains and lineages

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following pharmacological agents can be used for the treatment of visceral leishmaniasis? 1. Pentavalent antimonials 2. Amphotericin B 3. Spiramycin 4. Paromomycin Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 2 and 4

Visceral leishmaniasis (Kala-azar) is caused by Leishmania donovani, transmitted by the female sandfly (Phlebotomus). Treatment depends on the geographic region and drug resistance pattern. Liposomal Amphotericin B is the drug of choice, while pentavalent antimonials and paromomycin are effective alternatives in selected settings.

Why is B correct?

• 1. Pentavalent antimonials✅: Sodium stibogluconate and meglumine antimoniate are effective in susceptible regions.
• 2. Amphotericin B✅: Liposomal Amphotericin B is the drug of choice for visceral leishmaniasis.
• 4. Paromomycin✅: An aminoglycoside effective against visceral leishmaniasis, often used in combination regimens.

Incorrect option:

• 3. Spiramycin❌: A macrolide antibiotic used mainly for toxoplasmosis in pregnancy; it has no role in leishmaniasis.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following statements are correct regarding Kyasanur Forest Disease? 1. It is commonly seen in North-Eastern States of India. 2. Monkeys act as reservoir of the disease. 3. Transmission happens through tick bite. 4. Inactivated vaccine is available for its prevention. Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 2, 3 and 4

Kyasanur Forest Disease (KFD) is a tick-borne viral hemorrhagic fever caused by a Flavivirus. It is endemic to the forested regions of Karnataka and has spread to parts of Kerala, Goa, Maharashtra, Tamil Nadu, and other adjoining states. Monkeys are important amplifying hosts/sentinel animals, transmission occurs through the bite of infected Haemaphysalis ticks, and an inactivated (killed) vaccine is available for prevention in endemic areas.

Why not statement 1?

• KFD is not commonly seen in North-Eastern India; it is primarily confined to the Western Ghats region.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following statements is true regarding pretomanid?
options: Its use is contraindicated along with CYP2C9 inducers
It can be used for resistant malaria
It is approved for treatment of XDR tuberculosis in combination with Bedaquiline and Linezolid
It acts by formation of reactive oxygen species
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. It is approved for treatment of XDR tuberculosis in combination with Bedaquiline and Linezolid

Pretomanid is a newer antitubercular drug used in drug-resistant tuberculosis.

• Approved for use in XDR-TB and MDR-TB as part of the BPaL regimen (Bedaquiline + Pretomanid + Linezolid)
• It is a nitroimidazole prodrug that acts against Mycobacterium tuberculosis under both aerobic and anaerobic conditions
• Mechanism: Releases reactive nitrogen species (not primarily reactive oxygen species), leading to inhibition of mycolic acid synthesis and bacterial killing

Why not others:

• A. Its use is contraindicated along with CYP2C9 inducers: Drug interactions are mainly with CYP3A4 inducers (not specifically CYP2C9)
• B. It can be used for resistant malaria: Not used for malaria
• D. It acts by formation of reactive oxygen species: Mechanism is via reactive nitrogen species, so ROS statement is incorrect

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following statements regarding Rifampicin are true? 1. It should be taken with fatty meals 2. Resistance is associated with the rpoB gene mutation 3. It undergoes enterohepatic circulation 4. It is pumped out of the CNS mainly by P-glycoprotein pumps
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 2 and 3

Rifampicin pharmacology and resistance patterns are important for exam-based elimination.

Correct concepts:

• Resistance is due to mutation in the rpoB gene encoding DNA-dependent RNA polymerase
• Rifampicin undergoes enterohepatic circulation, prolonging its half-life

Incorrect concepts:

• It should not be taken with fatty meals; food decreases its absorption, so it is taken on an empty stomach
• CNS penetration is good in inflamed meninges, and it is not primarily limited by P-glycoprotein pumps

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following virus–genome pairs is correctly matched?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Rotavirus – dsRNA

| Virus | Genome Type | Key Feature

| ----- | ----------- | -----------

| Rotavirus | dsRNA | Reoviridae family

| SARS-CoV-2 | ssRNA | Coronavirus, positive-sense RNA

| Parvovirus | ssDNA | Smallest DNA virus

| HPV | dsDNA | Papillomavirus causing warts & cancer

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which one is not a criterion for Kawasaki disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Purulent conjunctivitis

Kawasaki disease is a pediatric vasculitis diagnosed clinically using specific criteria.

Diagnostic criteria (fever ≥5 days + ≥4 of the following):

• Bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis
• Polymorphous rash
• Cervical lymphadenopathy
• Oral mucosal changes (strawberry tongue, cracked lips)
• Changes in extremities (edema, erythema, desquamation)

Incorrect option: Purulent conjunctivitis is not a feature; conjunctivitis in Kawasaki is non-purulent

Key points:

• Risk of coronary artery aneurysms if untreated
• Treated with IVIG and aspirin

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which one of the following is the vector for Leishmania donovani, the causative organism of Visceral Leishmaniasis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Sandfly

Leishmania donovani, the causative organism of visceral leishmaniasis (Kala-azar), is transmitted by the bite of the female Phlebotomus sandfly.

Why not other options?

• A. Tsetse fly: Vector for Trypanosoma brucei → African sleeping sickness
• B. Sandfly: Correct. Leishmania donovani → Visceral leishmaniasis
• C. Anopheles mosquito: Vector for Plasmodium → Malaria
• D. Reduviid bug: Vector for Trypanosoma cruzi → Chagas disease

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which virus requires reverse transcriptase PCR for detection?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. RSV

Reverse transcriptase PCR (RT-PCR) is used for detection of RNA viruses.

RNA viruses require conversion of RNA to complementary DNA (cDNA) using reverse transcriptase before amplification

Correct answer: RSV (Respiratory syncytial virus) → RNA virus → requires RT-PCR

Why not others:

• Herpes virus → DNA virus
• EBV → DNA virus
• CMV → DNA virus

Key points:

• RT-PCR is the diagnostic method of choice for many RNA viruses (e.g., RSV, influenza, SARS-CoV-2)
• DNA viruses can be detected directly by PCR without reverse transcription
